News.title: Nottingham killer left disturbing notes about bomb-making & large concert venues in twisted writings HIDDEN by cops
News.content:
NOTTINGHAM killer Valdo Calocane made sinister notes about explosives and researched large event venues – but police failed to tell prosecutors or psychiatric experts, a public inquiry has heard.

Cops discovered disturbing scribblings inside a recycling bin behind the paranoid schizophrenic’s house after he was arrested for stabbing university students Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley-Kumar, both 19, and school caretaker Ian Coates, 65, to death in June 2023.



One handwritten note, titled “Thoughts”, included a list of apparent bomb components.

But the material was never made available to the Crown Prosecution Service, the judge, or psychiatric experts during Calocane’s trial or sentencing.



It was disclosed for the first time to the public inquiry team in July of this year after oral evidence had concluded.

In his closing submissions yesterday, Tim Moloney KC, who represents the bereaved families, said the list included “primary explosives” and “recipes for creating secondary explosives at home, or the basic ingredients for it”.

He said the note also mentioned a “booster tube” used to connect homemade bombs.

He told the Inquiry how one “highly unstable primary explosive” referenced by Calocane “can be made at home and was used in the 7/7 Tube and Manchester Arena bombings to name a few.”



Mr Moloney said the note also included the words, “Manchester Arena”, “Rwanda”, “Watergate” and “Iraq”.

He told the hearing how computer analysis showed the triple killer, 34, had researched large concert venues in Nottingham.

The lawyer added: “In light of the other information, those bookmarks might just have been worth asking about.”

The Inquiry heard Nottinghamshire Police also failed to disclosea hold-all belonging to Calocane, which contained several notepads, to the Inquiry until June due to an “oversight”.

The bag was discovered at the killer’s house three days after the attacks, but officers did not search it for three months and it was later deemed not of “evidential value” to the criminal investigation.



Rachel Langdale KC, Counsel to the Inquiry, said that in one Pukka pad the killer wrote the Latin phrase “mea culpa” – meaning “my fault” – and the words “illegal actions”.

He also wrote that he was “a tree guarding the key between heaven and hell”, described himself as “a god”, and claimed he had the “power to resurrect people”.

Ms Langdale KC said it was “regrettable” that Inquiry witnesses could not be questioned about the material.



The hearing was told that further violent assaults by Calocane on colleagues at warehouses were also not disclosed to the Inquiry team until after the oral evidence concluded.

Inquiry Chair Her Honour Deborah Taylor said it is “highly disappointing” that new evidence has emerged now.

She is due to report back her findings by May 2027. Closing submissions continue today.

The Inquiry also heard that Barnaby Webber’s death was “potentially preventable” had he received better medical treatment at the scene.

The 19-year-old went into cardiac arrest on more than one occasion and could not be resuscitated in the ambulance.



But a panel of medical experts found that if volume resuscitation – the replacement of fluids including blood transfusions – had been more aggressive then he might have made it to hospital where surgeons could immediately operate.

Ms Langdale said there was a “small chance” he may have survived his injuries.

Valdo Calocane was sentenced to an indefinite hospital order in a high security facility in January last year after being convicted of manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility.

News.title: Moment I was ambushed by people-smuggling cartel in New Jungle migrant camp – gangsters’ had no regard for human life
News.content:
WE were driving slowly along the public road that bisects the infamous New Jungle migrant camp when the first rock smashed into the Volkswagen’s bodywork.

The dull thud was followed by another then another before our rear window shattered to the evident glee of our tormentors.



Photographer Ian Whittaker and I had just passed the collection of rickety stalls where goons connected to the cross-Channel people smuggling cartels like to hang out.

A gaggle of young men had earlier seen Ian’s cameras and mob rule erupted in this lawless patch of scrubland not far from the French port of Dunkirk.



A shower of at least five stones were hurled at the VW as Ian struggled to find first gear to make a quick escape.

As expletives rang out inside our vehicle, I frantically implored him:



“Keep going mate.”

Shattered glass was strewn across the car’s back seat but mercifully neither of us had sustained any injuries in the incident in June.



It was a hairy moment nonetheless.

For this anarchic shanty town is run from the barrel of a gun by gangsters with little regard for human life.

The rampant criminality here was underlined last week when it emerged a BBC cameraman had been left with stitches after being attacked in the camp.

Angry at being filmed, a people smuggler tried to grab his camera before launching rocks at him.

The BBC published a photograph showing the film maker with a tissue over his eye and blood running down his right cheek.



Last year Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp was pelted with bottles and had a machete pulled on him while speaking to migrants at the camp.

Philp said he found it “pretty shocking” and fled the camp quickly.

So what’s every day life like inside this people smuggling haven?



Like any city on Earth, The Jungle has its good and bad souls.

And, after reporting on dozens of occasions on the migration chaos on the French coast since my first visit in 2003, I have met plenty of both.

A few minutes before our car was targeted, we had been in a patch of woodland at the sprawling camp when we chanced upon Ethiopian David Sitotan raking up discarded debris and foliage on the forest floor.

Despite his dismal lodgings being a cramped and leaky tent, he wanted to make the best of his surroundings.

Fleeing war and political repression in his beleaguered homeland, this chatty and amiable character far away from home liked to fill his days productively.



Happy to pose for a picture, David, 22, told me: “I don’t just want to hang around reading social media so I decided to tidy up the camp.”

With a crucifix dangling from his neck, he added: “I’m desperate to work when I get to Britain. I have experience servicing mobile phones, as a forklift driver and in a clothes shop.“

Back in the early 2000s when I first visited the camps here, those seeking a new beginning in Britain – whether fleeing war, political repression, or just looking for a better life – would stow away on lorries, vans, cars or trains.

To prove how lax security was at the Channel Tunnel, I even sneaked into the UK that year hidden behind some old crates in the back of a white van.

The van was stopped by French border officers.



One even climbed into the back of the vehicle but failed to discover me.

We were simply waved through by British officials at the UK border without any checks.

Then, in the spring of 2014, I witnessed mayhem unfurling as dozens of migrants attempted to clamber onto lorries queuing on the N216 dual carriageway to enter the Calais ferry port.



In broad daylight and in full view of British holidaymakers, one young Afghan in his 20s emerged from a shallow ditch beside the busy road and crawled under a Polish HGV as it edged along.

Then he carefully hoisted himself on to the lorry’s spare tyre and clung on as the UK-bound truck picked up speed – his leg dangling perilously close to the road below.

We last saw the truck heading towards the French border crossing at the busy terminal.

When we returned to our car, the vehicle was again pelted with stones by a migrant.

On another visit to the area, myself and a photographer had our motor surrounded, with one migrant splaying themselves on the bonnet.



Others then attempted to smash the vehicle’s windows with stones held in their palms.

It was unclear on either occasion whether our assailants were connected to the smuggling gangs.

Yet the criminality entwined in the people smuggling industry breeds violence.

The huge numbers of migrants arriving on France’s northern shoreline means many wait weeks or even months before securing passage to the UK.

In 1999 the sheer mass of humanity led the French government to help open a Red Cross centre in Sangatte, a village about a mile from the Eurotunnel entrance .



The idea was to provide humanitarian assistance.

As thousands arrived at the centre it was soon being nicknamed the Departure Lounge and the UK government claimed it had become a springboard for people trying to enter Britain.

It was shuttered in 2002.

After Sangatte’s closure, many of the migrants simply moved into dense woodland surrounding Calais.

Christened The Jungle by its inhabitants, it was a squalid and unsanitary sprawl of discarded rubbish, rotting food and open air latrines.



The authorities battled to break up the shanty town but by 2015 it morphed into a vast, 5,000-strong encampment built on a 44-acre former landfill site east of Calais port.

The makeshift camp seemed to be becoming permanent.

It had a theatre, a library, places of worship, hairdressers and a selection of eateries.

Critic AA Gill even visited to pen a restaurant review.

The French initially tolerated the slum settlement but it proved a magnet for migrants using Calais as a jumping off point for the UK.



Amid rioting and arson, the camp was finally bulldozed in October 2016.

Increased security at ferry ports meant criminal syndicates began sending inflatable dinghies across the Channel from 2014.

Migrants then moved up the coast to form camps around the port of Dunkirk.

A tented settlement began forming in scrub between a railway and a dual carriageway not far from the village of Loon-Plage.

It became known as The New Jungle.



A waystation for migrants travelling to the UK, it’s also a bazaar for venal people smugglers seeking to amass human cargo.

Regularly raided by cops, the tents and stalls are dismantled but simply pop up again further east.

Smuggling cartels here often resort to firearms to settle their differences.

Migrants have often told me of their fears as gunshots ring out after dark.

There have been a string of murders and knee cappings as gangs fight turf wars over the smuggling business which is estimated to have grossed a billion pounds in a decade.



These roughnecks think nothing of sending families on flimsy vessels into the world’s busiest shipping lanes.

Back in November 2021, I met Iraqi Kurdish mum Khazal Hussein and children Hadiya, 22, Mubin, 16, and seven-year-old Hasty in a freezing field close to the New Jungle.

Wrapped in scarves and wearing woolly hats, they seemed full of hope despite the awful conditions.

They were happy to chat and pose for pictures.

Big sister Hadiya, 22, an art student, told me she wanted to be an actress, adding: “In Iraq, we have no money. We just want a good life.”



Little Hasty, wearing a pink kitten hat and winter overalls, giggled as she played as if on a camping trip.

I took a snap on my phone as she swung on the ropes of the family’s tent.

Three days later I received the devastating news that Hasty, her siblings and her mum were all dead.

The young family were among 31 lost in the deadliest small-boat crossing disaster recorded in the Channel.

Yesterday 14 people went on trial in Paris facing charges including manslaughter and criminal conspiracy over the tragedy.



The investigating judge accused the majority of the defendants of taking part in “the launching of a low-quality small boat, not certified, unfit for navigation on the high seas, overloaded and lacking suitable life jackets.”

Most deny any wrongdoing.

Some insist they were migrants rather than people smugglers.

More than 17,000 migrants have crossed the Channel so far this year.

Numbers are dramatically down on 2025 yet overcrowding on the deathtrap small boats is increasing.



Last month a grim new record was established when 230 people were crammed onto a so-called mega-dinghy by gangsters.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Despite tough pledges by a succession of British governments to Stop the Boats and Smash the Gangs – and over a billion pounds funneled to the French to police the Channel coast – the New Jungle still stands.

A shanty town of misery and menace where the desperate are preyed upon by the villainous.

News.title: Tanker hit by ‘Iranian drone strike’ off coast of Dubai as war lands on doorstep of Brit holiday hotspot AGAIN
News.content:
A TANKER has been hit by a suspected Iranian drone strike off the coast of Dubai, bringing war to the doorstop of the glam Brit holiday hotspot.

It comes amid an escalation of attacks between the US and Iran, with back-and-forth vessel attacks in the embattled Strait of Hormuz.



The stricken vessel was seen listing in the water mere miles off the coast of Port Rashid, near Dubai’s strip of luxury hotels.

The glitzy Emirati city has been the target of numerous Iranian attacks over the course of the protracted conflict.



Hours after Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu launched Operation Epic Fury against Iran’s tyrannical leadership, the Islamic Guard Corps fired a barrage of missiles and drones at the city.

Dubai’s iconic Burj Al Arab was struck and footage showed a raging fire and thick plumes of smoke pouring from its base.

An Iranian suicide drone then ploughed in Dubai airport, forcing flight cancellations and sparking travel panic for hundreds of fleeing Brits.

The city’s financial centre also came under attack, with jaw-dropping footage showing the aftermath of a powerful drone strike.

Repressive rules in the UAE forbade residents and influencers travelling to the city from reporting on the terrifying drone attacks – with some even jailed.



In an eerily similar incident to today, a fully-loaded crude oil liner was struck while it was anchored in Dubai port.

News.title: Shocking moment bungling lawyer attempts to shoot ex-wife dead in restaurant before being tackled by waiter
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a bungling lawyer tries to shoot his ex-wife in a restaurant but forgets to take the safety off.

Dramatic CCTV footage shows Matthew Exton storm into the Ohio eatery and aim a gun at his ex before a heroic waiter tackles him from behind.



The restaurant suddenly erupts as patrons and staff dive on the would-be killer.

Exton, 43, was found convicted of attempted murder, two counts of felonious assault and multiple firearm charges and will be sentenced on September 21.





A jury found him not guilty on one remaining count of felonious assault.

The former lawyer had been drinking at a bar in Toledo, Ohio, on April 11, 2025, before spotting his ex-wife and her family eating at a nearby restaurant, according to prosecutor Julia R. Bates.



Exton entered the eatery, ordered a drink at the bar to be sent to their table and spat towards them as he walked out.

He later stormed in with a gun, charged at their table and attempted to shoot his ex-wife.

Fortunately, the firearm did not go off as the bungling assassin left the safety on.

A brave waiter tackled Exton to the floor before he could try again.



The gun had one round in the chamber and seven more in the magazine, according to prosecutors.

Bates said: “Nothing in their training and soft openings at the restaurant could have prepared the staff for what walked through that door.

“The defendant did not come with the intention of having a meal.

“He came with anger in him and with the intention to commit a public execution of his ex-wife at the restaurant that day.”



She praised the employees and patrons who stepped in to stop Exton, calling them heroes.

Exton, who had law offices in Sylvania and Traverse City, had his licence suspended in May 2025 following the attempted killing.

He claimed that he did not intend to pull the trigger, and instead pointed the gun at his ex-wife in an attempt to pressure her into speeding up the sale of their former home.

News.title: Boy and girl, 11 & 7, killed in horror crash on way home from school as five other children rushed to hospital
News.content:
TWO children from the same family have been killed and five others injured in a horror rollover crash as they all headed home from school.

Sarah El Hawli, seven, died at the scene as Ossama El Hawli, 11, was rushed to hospital alongside the other children before his death was confirmed overnight.



A 34-year-old female driver and the seven children were inside the car when it flipped and “inexplicably rolled” near Bacchus Marsh, Victoria.

Emergency services were called to the Nerowie and Parwan-Exford road intersection just before 4.30pm on Tuesday.



Medics managed to pull everyone from the wreckage but confirmed Sarah had died.

Ossama was airlifted to the Royal Children’s Hospital in critical condition, before he passed away hours later.

It is unclear what the relationship of the victims is, with some reports saying they were siblings and others saying cousins.

Five of the other children were hospitalised with non-life-threatening upper-body injuries, including a toddler, three primary-aged children and a teenager.

All remain in a stable condition.

The driver was taken to Royal Melbourne Hospital for observation but was discharged on Wednesday afternoon.



Australia’s Islamic community has been hit hard by the tragic passing of the two children in the horrific crash.

The Australian Islamic Centre (AIC) extended their support to the devastated families for funeral and burial arrangements, calling the two children “beloved members of our community.”

They said in a statement: “It is with profound sadness that the Australian Islamic Centre mourns the passing of Ossama El Hawli and Sarah El Hawli.



“Their loss has deeply affected our entire AIC community. Our hearts are with their parents, family, and loved ones as they face an unimaginable loss.”



Detective Sergeant Tony Gentile said: “From my understanding, the scene was quite hectic with family coming as well and there were people everywhere.

“Witnesses who witnessed it, they stopped and rendered assistance.

“Obviously with seven children they were distressed and they were cared for by paramedics, members of the public and police.”

A fleet of ambulance crews attended the scene, including two helicopter crews, two intensive care paramedic crews and seven Advanced Life Support (ALS) paramedic crews.

Major Collision Investigation Unit detectives are investigating the circumstances behind the fatal crash.

News.title: Body found in search for teenage boy, 15, swept out to sea two weeks ago while on family holiday
News.content:
SEA TRAGEDY Body found in search for teenage boy, 15, swept out to sea two weeks ago while on family holiday

A BODY has been found in the search for a 15-year-old boy who was swept out to sea nearly two weeks ago while on a family holiday.

The teenager went missing after entering the sea with his dad on August 30, as rescue services launched a massive search.



It followed reports of a family-of-three from Yorkshire – understood to be a dad and two sons – getting into difficulty at Marloes Sands in Pembrokeshire, Wales.

Local Councillor Claire George said it is understood the boy was in the water when he hit his head on rocks and was knocked unconscious.



The other members of the group were able to get themselves to safety.

Emergency services including the RNLI, HM Coastguard and police called off the search at Marloes Sands after nearly 24 hours.



Cops today confirmed a body has been found.

A spokesperson said: “Sadly, we can confirm that a body has been found during the search for a 15-year-old boy who was reported to have gotten into difficulty at Marloes Sands, Milford Haven on Sunday 30 August.



“Next of kin have been informed, and our thoughts are with them at this time.”

Marloes Sands is a popular “hidden gem” beach in the tourist hotspot of Pembrokeshire but it can experience strong currents and challenging sea conditions.

Cllr George, who represents the St Ishmael’s ward on Pembrokeshire Council, said her heart went out to the boy’s family and described it as a “dreadfully upsetting” incident.

“It’s my understanding that there were a lot of people on the beach who stood up to assist as much as they could (when the group got into difficulties).

“I think you cannot warn people enough about the danger of the sea. It looks sunny and bright and does not take much to change.



“It is my understranding he hit his head on a rock and had gone unconscious and the water took him. You can’t have a lifeguard on every beach. Marloes Sands is a remote beach.

“This is a tragedy. It is really heartbreaking. It is very painful for the family.”

Dyfed-Powys Police said at the time: “Dyfed-Powys Police received a request for assistance from HM Coastguard, following a report of three people getting into difficulty at Marloes Sands, Milford Haven on Sunday 30 August.

“Two of the three individuals self-rescued, returning themselves safely to shore.

“A 15 year-old boy, visiting on holiday from the Yorkshire area, remains unaccounted for, and a multi-agency search was launched.”



It comes after a summer of tragedy with a number of people dying in lakes, rivers and the sea.

News.title: Brit dad charged after son, two, plunged to his death at Cyprus hotel window begs for case to be dropped
News.content:
‘DEEPLY TRAUMATIC’ Brit dad charged after son, two, plunged to his death at Cyprus hotel window begs for case to be dropped

A BRITISH dad whose toddler plunged to his death from a fourth-floor hotel window in Cyprus has begged for his charges to be dropped.

The two-year-old boy died at a luxury Cyprus hotel after allegedly slipping from his dad’s arms and falling 33ft to the veranda below.



The 37-year-old city executive has filed an official request for dismissal with the Attorney General of Cyprus as he faces accusations of causing the death of his son by a reckless act.

A decision concerning the potential dismissal is expected to be handed down today.



The Essex-born man is believed to have placed the toddler on the windowsill on July 12 while waiting for the lift at the King Evelthon Hotel near Paphos, thinking the window was closed.

He was arrested at the resort and jailed for eight days, during which time he was forced to Facetime his young daughter to explain the tragedy.



He was later charged, released on bail and allowed to return to the UK to attend his son’s funeral.

The father, who works at a big four consultancy firm, was ordered to pay an additional £8,500 deposit to ensure he returned to Cyprus for the beginning of the trial on September 17.

If convicted, he faces a prison sentence of up to four years.

Alexandros Alexandrou, the father’s lawyer, stressed there was no public interest in prosecuting the grieving father and that a prolonged prosecution would further traumatise the family.



He said: “We have asked the attorney-general to discontinue this prosecution on public interest and humanitarian grounds.

“In these exceptional circumstances we do not believe a continued criminal process serves the public interest.

“The family has already suffered an unimaginable loss, and the focus now should be on their welfare and recovery.”



The man is due back in Cyprus next week to enter his plea, but he hopes the trip won’t be necessary after his legal team put the formal request to Attorney General George Savvides.

If he does not drop the case, the father will be forced to return to Cyprus and surrender his passport.

The case provoked outrage in Cyprus with local press describing his detention as the “cruellest act”.

The horror fall happened just hours after the family arrived on the sunny island for their summer holiday.

The circumstances of the boy’s fatal fall remain disputed.



While the father claims he merely sat his son on a hotel window ledge while waiting for dinner, prosecutors argue he was swinging the boy from side to side before the fall – an allegation the father denies.

Investigators have said they think the Brit could have been unaware that the window was open.

A friend of the family said the young boy was a “truly special easy-going little boy who brought joy to everyone around him.”

A source close to the family told The Times: “This continues to be deeply traumatic for the family.

“They have lost their child in the most horrific circumstances, and nothing can undo that.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“This was a tragic accident and prolonging the criminal process adds nothing but more suffering to the parents, who need to be together to support each other and their surviving child.”

The resort’s safety record has since come under scrutiny after it emerged that the toddler is the third British tourist to die there since 2022.

News.title: Shane Richie faces trial after pleading not guilty to drink-driving after petrol station arrest
News.content:
Shane Richie faces trial after pleading not guilty to drink-driving after petrol station arrest

EastEnders star Shane Richie, 62, today appeared at Colchester magistrates court accused of drink-driving at the end of July

View Image Richie appeared at Colchester magistrates court via video-link (Image: BBC/Jack Barnes/Kieron McCarron)

Shane Richie will go on trial next year after pleading not guilty to drink-driving.

‌



The EastEnders star appeared via video-link at Colchester magistrates court on Wednesday morning, where a a judge heard how he was allegedly over the limit, with a recorded 65mg of alcohol in 100mg of breath, when police stopped him at a petrol station in Harlow, Essex, shortly before midnight on July 29. The court heard the reading was nearly double the legal limit.

‌



Richie, who has played Alfie Moon on and off on the hit BBC TV show since 2002, was arrested after officers responded to reports the 62-year-old had driven his white Hyundai onto the station's forecourt after apparently suffering a flat tyre, before arguing with staff about claims he was vaping near the pumps.

‌



Richie today appeared in court under his real name Shane Roche. He spoke to give his plea and also confirmed his name, address and date of birth. His internet connection went down twice during the hearing. After returning the first time, Richie told the judge: "Sorry about that. I'm in a hotel up north and I quickly switched it from my ipad to my phone."

When he returned the second time, Richie said: "Hi everybody, I totally apologise". Asked by the judge if he could hear him, he replied: "Yes Sir, I can."

Article continues below

Deputy district judge Christopher Maynard said the one-day trial will be heard by a full-time district judge on November 17, next year at Colchester Magistartes Court. He told Richie: "You will be expected to appear in person. Hopefully that date is far enough ahead to reserve your diary to enable your attendance. Until that point you are going to be released on unconditional bail."

Since his arrest, it has been reported dad-of-five Richie split with his wife Christie just six days before being arrested and charged for the drink-driving offence. It has also since been reported that the couple have now sold their home in Surrey, subject to contract.

Shane, who has three children with Christie, 47, was previously married to Loose Women star. Coleen Nolan, 61. They split in 1997 amid accusations Richie had cheated.

News.title: Heathrow and Gatwick live: Hundreds more flights cancelled today as cyber attack ruled out
News.content:
EasyJet, BA, Ryanair, KLM and Eurowings flights have all been cancelled at major airports including Heathrow and Gatwick today following the air traffic control issues on Tuesday

Hundreds of flights have been cancelled in the UK today, with experts warning the "knock-on" effect of yesterday's air traffic control outage will take a long time to clear.

According to FlightRadar, 246 flights had been cancelled at Heathrow Airport by 6am today, while Gatwick passengers have faced 33 cancellations. British Airways said it has been "left with no choice but to cancel more than 190 flights" from its original schedule today.

It comes after more than 1,000 flights to and from at least 16 UK airports were impacted on Tuesday due to a major technical problem that hit National Air Traffic Services (NATS), the UK's air traffic control provider. Tens of thousands of holidaymakers were left stranded for hours, with distressed passengers reporting being left waiting on runways.

Airports hit by the disruption included Heathrow, Gatwick, Stansted, London City, London Southend, Manchester, Birmingham, Bristol, East Midlands, Edinburgh, Liverpool John Lennon, Aberdeen, Belfast, EMA, Southampton, Leeds and Jersey.

NATS CEO Martin Rolfe apologised, telling the BBC there would be a full investigation into what had gone wrong, after NATS said resolving the issue had taken "longer than hoped". On the cause of the problem, Mr Rolfe said a “thorough” investigation would take place, but ruled out a cyber attack.

News.title: Dad-of-five dies weeks after being found 'face down' in cruise ship swimming pool
News.content:
Dad-of-five dies weeks after being found 'face down' in cruise ship swimming pool

Minnesota dad and pastor Stephen Junker, 58, died after being found 'face down and unresponsive' in a swimming pool aboard the Sun Princess cruise ship, his family said

View 3 Images Stephen Junker, 58, suffered a spinal cord injury on August 16 (Image: GoFundMe)

A dad-of-five from Minnesota has died after suffering a devastating spinal cord injury while on board a cruise ship celebrating his son's wedding in Italy.

‌



Stephen Junker, 58, fell into a swimming pool aboard the Sun Princess ship, operated by Princess Cruises, on August 16. He was found "face down and unresponsive", according to a fundraiser set up on GoFundMe by his family.

‌



Mr Junker, a pastor at Chippewa Lutheran Church in Brandon, Minnesota, died from his injuries on September 5.

‌



He was taken by an Italian Coast Guard boat to a hospital in Naples, where doctors discovered severe compression of his spinal cord at the C3-C4 level of his neck, the family said.

View 3 Images Stephen Junker underwent emergency spinal surgery on August 17 (Image: GoFundMe)

Junker underwent emergency spinal surgery on August 17 and was subsequently diagnosed as quadriplegic. He was unable to breathe without mechanical ventilation.

‌



"Our biggest challenge right now is navigating the Italian healthcare system," the family said at the time. "While they’re doing their best, they are not well equipped for this type of situation, nor will they cooperate with us regarding his care, independent of the language barrier."

On August 23, he was transferred from the Italian hospital to Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, on a transatlantic medevac flight, according to an update on the GoFundMe page.

His family later said further diagnostic testing at Mayo Clinic had revealed injuries that were not treatable.

‌



View 3 Images A fundraiser to support Stephen Junker and his family had raised more than $34,900 (Image: GoFundMe)

The family expressed their gratitude to people who donated to the fundraiser, which had raised more than $34,900 (around £25,750) at the time of reporting.

They also thanked medical staff at Mayo Clinic, saying: "We’re glad we were able to give him the opportunity to receive world-class care and reassured that everything that could possibly be done to help him was done."

‌



Mr Junker had served the congregation and community at Chippewa Lutheran Church for nearly a decade, according to his obituary, which described being a minister as "among the greatest joys and honors of his life".

"He was known for his animated sermons, his love of a good conversation on nearly any subject, and his readiness to help anyone in need, whether that meant offering counsel or simply producing the right tool for the job from his ever-prepared pockets," the obituary reads.

"Above all, Steve loved his family. He was a devoted husband to Jeanine and a loving father to his five children. His grandson, Jonah, held a special and cherished place in his heart."

Article continues below

A visitation will be held at 10am on Friday, September 11, at Chippewa Lutheran Church, followed by a funeral service at 11am.

The Mirror has contacted Princess Cruises for comment.

News.title: US strikes five Iranian 'shadow' tankers as fears of all-out war in Middle East rise
News.content:
US strikes five Iranian 'shadow' tankers as fears of all-out war in Middle East rise

American forces have hit five Iranian tankers, sinking one, as pressure mounts on the US to end the war on Iran, and Tehran launches a chilling campaign to deploy proxy forces

View 5 Images US Central Command -issued image of Iranian tanker destroyed (Image: US Central Command Public Affairs/AFP via Getty Images)

American forces have struck five “shadow network” oil tankers, after Tehran’s troops targeted a US warship in the region, US Central Command has confirmed.

‌



American intelligence believed that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) is using the secretive tanker trade to continue to fund their military operations. At least four IRGC-linked vessels were hit in the Gulf of Oman, and another close to Kharg Island was also attacked near a major oil terminal.

‌



Tehran claimed revenge attacks were launched at a US base in Jordan, forcing the American military to shoot down missiles and the IRGC also opened fire on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. Close-up satellite imagery issued by Central Command showed one Gulf of Oman Iranian ship being hit by US missiles as the conflict plunged into a long-term war, seemingly without end. It is believed the ship sank.

‌



View 5 Images US strike on Gulf of Oman Iranian tanker (Image: US Central Command Public Affairs/AFP via Getty Images)

Images revealed today by CentCom were aimed at displaying US military might, amid fears Washington cannot find a route to peace and Tehran refuses to back down. The latest Washington strategy for the worsening conflict is to choke Iran’s ports and economy as the population suffers a plunging economy and poverty.

Tit-for-tat exchanges of missiles have escalated in the past week, more than six months after the US and Israel launched their first assault on Iran on February 28. Jordan shot down 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, while two of them fell in unpopulated areas, according to the Jordanian Armed Forces said.

‌



View 5 Images US forces hunt down Iranian "shadow" tanker (Image: CENTCOM / SWNS)

Iran warning as tensions with US soar over Israel-Lebanon attacks READ MORE :

The latest worrying escalation happened after Iran targeted a US warship with ballistic missiles, which Centcom claimed it "successfully evaded”.

US military chiefs said in a statement: “The US warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed.”

‌



Tehran’s shadowy IRGC networks were actively gathering supporters among their proxy systems in Lebanon, the Houthis in Yemen and Iraq to boost the threat towards the US.

Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran’s parliament speaker, wrote in June: “Iran has a hybrid strategy in the current war. We are not fighting on one front and we are not using one tool.”

Ahmed Nagi, senior Yemen analyst at the think tank Crisis Group, said: “The Houthis’ growing prominence during the Gaza war opened up a new horizon in Iraq. Many groups there became eager to support the Houthis, and in return, the Houthis started sharing their military expertise with Iraqi militias.”

‌



This week, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacked energy depots and housing in several cities in Saudi Arabia, injuring 73 people and further de-stabilising the region.

View 5 Images Entrenched in war: US President Donald Trump (Image: Getty Images)

The drone and missile attack caused fires at oil facilities and installations that led to a temporary halt in operations, Saudi Arabia's military and energy ministry said.

‌



In Tehran the IRGC claimed it captured a secretive US “submarine drone” after American forces admitted an unmanned maritime vessel had malfunctioned. American military chiefs say the drone was an older model and was not being used for sensitive operations.

View 5 Images Clashes between Saudi-backed trops and Houthi rebels (Image: AFPTV/AFP via Getty Images)

Earlier, Iran celebrated its capture of a £2m American unmanned underwater vessel near the Strait of Hormuz. And the IRGC said it had “trapped one of the most modern, intelligent and unmanned submarines of the terrorist American army at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz”.

Article continues below

The US military is investing heavily in unmanned naval systems, including underwater and surface vessels, as it seeks cheaper ways to monitor vast areas ‌of ocean and gather intelligence.

It is believed the captured vessel was a Dive -LD model which can operate for up to 10 days without returning to base and is designed ‌to dive to depths of as much as 19,700 ‌feet.

News.title: New 76 plate warning as drivers risk £300 fine and six points over insurance mistake
News.content:
New 76 plate warning as drivers risk £300 fine and six points over insurance mistake

The arrival of the new '76' registration plate is expected to drive a significant surge in dealership visits

View 2 Images Expert shares warning about insurance ‘blind spot’ as thousands of drivers prepare to collect new '76' plate cars (Image: Getty )

The launch of the new '76' registration plate is set to spark a major surge in car dealership footfall, test drives and new vehicle collections throughout September. Industry analysts at The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders Ltd (SMMT) forecast that 75,000 new vehicles will roll out of UK dealerships this week alone, with the figure potentially surpassing 300,000 by the close of September.

‌



However, drivers looking to take advantage of the new plate launch are being warned to carry out one crucial check. Motorists are being advised to confirm they have the correct insurance cover in place before getting behind the wheel of their brand-new car.

‌



Specialists at temporary car insurance provider Covertime.com have stepped in to offer vital guidance, warning that many drivers wrongly assume they are automatically fully covered when test-driving or collecting a newly purchased vehicle, reports Wales Online.

‌



Tom Warsop, motor insurance specialist at Covertime, said: "The arrival of a new registration plate is one of the busiest times of year for new car sales, so it's understandable that buyers are focused on choosing the right vehicle and securing the best deal. However, insurance is just as important.

"Many drivers assume they are automatically covered when test-driving a vehicle or collecting their new car, but that's not always the case. It is actually a worryingly common insurance blind spot. Before getting behind the wheel for a test drive, motorists should check exactly what cover is in place and ensure they are fully insured for the journey ahead."

View 2 Images Dealerships also aren’t legally required to ensure cover is place when they hand over the keys of a new vehicle (Image: Getty)

‌



"While most franchised and independent dealerships will have some form of motor trade insurance that allows prospective buyers to test drive vehicles. But the level of protection can vary, and drivers shouldn't assume all dealerships offer comprehensive cover.

"In some circumstances, cover will be third-party only, meaning damage to other people or property may be covered, but damage to the vehicle itself may not be. Additional conditions, such as age restrictions, licence requirements, accompanied test drives or excess payments may also apply".

Covertime is urging motorists planning to purchase a new vehicle this September to verify several details. These include:

‌



Make sure to check what insurance is set up before you go for a test drive.

Look into any rules or conditions that might come with the insurance from the dealership.

Confirm that you have a valid insurance policy in place before you drive your new car home.

Getting behind the wheel without valid insurance is against the law and can lead to penalty points, fines and vehicle seizure. If you're caught on the road without valid cover, you could face a £300 fine and six penalty points on your licence, while more serious cases can result in an unlimited fine, a driving ban, or even your vehicle being seized.

Article continues below

Tom also shared some considerations for drivers on collection day. He said: "Collecting a new car is exciting, but it's also one of the easiest times for drivers to make assumptions about their insurance cover. While some dealerships may ask buyers to confirm insurance arrangements before collection, they aren't legally required to check cover is in place before they hand over the keys.

"Ultimately, it's the driver's responsibility to ensure they are properly insured before driving away. For situations where drivers only need short-term cover, temporary car insurance can often provide a practical solution. The most important thing is making sure appropriate cover is arranged before the vehicle moves."

News.title: Kent Police 'knew about Dover protest day before far-right thugs in balaclavas blocked port'
News.content:
Kent Police 'knew about Dover protest day before far-right thugs in balaclavas blocked port'

Despite the police originally claiming they were unaware about the protest, the force has recently confirmed receiving 'non-emergency' information on the day before the protest took place

View 3 Images The force said they received "non-emergency information"

Kent Police has confirmed it received information about a possible protest a day before around 300 masked demonstrators blocked access to the Port of Dover.

‌



Hundreds of men dressed head-to-toe in black, wearing masks and balaclavas, descended on the UK’s busiest ferry port on Saturday morning, chanting ‘England till I die, whose streets? Our Streets’ and ‘Stop the boats’. Days later, Kent Police said it had been unaware of the protest in advance and described it as “spontaneous”, prompting accusations of an intelligence failure.

‌



But the force has now confirmed a review found it received "non-emergency information" late on Friday which, if properly assessed, may have allowed officers to “consider its resourcing”.

‌



View 3 Images Dover and Deal MP Mike Tapp said he is fed up of "idiots" going to Dover

A force spokesperson said: “The protest organisers adopted a different approach to previous protests, and as part of our commitment to public safety we have examined our decision-making to identify any lessons, to ensure we are well prepared for future events organised in a similar way.

“During that initial review, we found the force had received non-emergency information late on Friday evening that a protest could take place in the town the following day. This information was not fully assessed. If it was, it may have allowed the force to consider its resourcing.”

‌



Danny Thomas, an associate of Tommy Robinson, has claimed to have masterminded the protest as part of his ‘Patriot Platform’ movement and previously said it had groups across the country. After the demonstration, he posted on Facebook: “This is only the beginning.”

Sharing a video of demonstrators on Instagram, he wrote: “It’s time! Protect our country! And more importantly our women and children! This is our warning!” He later added on Facebook: “Well done, lads and lasses You stuck to the plan and maintained complete discipline. I’m so proud of all of you! You all understood how important this was. And this is only the beginning.”

Dover District Council deputy leader Edward Biggs called Kent Police’s admission “very worrying” and “really poor”. He added: “It’s very disappointing. We rely on the police providing us information so that we can inform the community and take whatever steps we need to take.”

‌



However, Kent Police said the information it received “would not have prevented the lawful protest from taking place, nor the disruption experienced by the town, port and wider community”.

Kent’s police and crime commissioner Matthew Scott said he welcomed an independent learning review by the College of Policing and had asked it to examine both how information was triaged and the force’s communications response. He said he would ensure the chief constable was held to account over any recommendations.

View 3 Images Dover District Council Leader said the Police appeared quite slow to resolve the disruption (Image: SKY News)

‌



He added: “It is essential that we understand how this happened, and that lessons are learnt. This is separate to the response of officers, staff and specials on the ground, who did the best they could, in the circumstances they were presented with, to bring the disruption to an end as soon as they did.”

The force has faced criticism for describing the protest as ‘spontaneous’ and for its response as roads around Dover, the UK’s busiest ferry and pedestrian port, were blocked for hours.

Dover District Council leader Kevin Mills told the BBC the “exceptionally well organised” protest had “caught several agencies on the hoof”.

Article continues below

He also said the force “appeared to be quite slow to keep the roads and the networks open, which is disappointing. The protesters knew what they were doing, I’m not sure the police did know what was going to happen. But then I accept that the police resource is stretched.”

Dover and Deal MP Mike Tapp wrote for The Mirror that small-boat arrivals were down 46% this summer compared with last year. He added: “People have every right to protest about immigration. They have every right to demand stronger borders. But intimidating a town in balaclavas and blocking one of Britain’s most important ports? That isn’t the way to do it.”

In a social media post, the MP wrote: “Park run cancelled and port access disrupted. I am fed up with idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption. I bet if you asked any one of those ‘protesters’ they wouldn’t know small boat crossing are down by 40% and we are working hard to fix the mess. Go home, enjoy your weekend/get a job.”

News.title: Barcelona El Prat airport flights cancelled today after severe weather warnings
News.content:
Barcelona El Prat airport flights cancelled today after severe weather warnings

More than 50 flights at Barcelona have been cancelled, while hundreds are delayed, as northeastern Spain battles severe thunderstorms following weather warnings

View 3 Images Dozens of flights have been cancelled (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Dozens of flights have been cancelled at Barcelona Airport as northeastern Spain battles severe thunderstorms, bringing torrential rain, heavy gusts and hail to the city's coastline.

‌



More than 50 flights from the holiday hotspot have been grounded, while more than 220 are delayed, FlightRadar data shows.

‌



It comes as the Catalan meteorological agency issued a severe thunderstorm and rain alert this morning, with those in Barcelona warned to expect "hail and very strong wind gusts".

‌



Travellers flying to and from the airport have been urged to check the status of their flights due to "adverse weather" in the region.

View 3 Images Weather warnings have been issued for storms in Barcelona (Image: AEMET)

Heathrow and Gatwick live: Hundreds more flights cancelled today as cyber attack ruled out READ MORE :

RAF Poseidon MRA1 plane declares mid-air emergency in skies over Scotland READ MORE :

Are you being impacted by the disruption at Barcelona Airport? Get in touch at livenews@reachplc.com.

‌



A warning message reads: "Adverse weather. If you are planning to fly to/from Josep Tarradellas Barcelona-El Prat Airport, please check with your airline for the status of your flight."

Enaire, Spain's national air navigation service provider, said a "very severe storm over Barcelona is greatly complicating approach manoeuvres for pilots".

Safety regulations are being activated for arrivals at Barcelona-El Prat Airport, it added. "If you're planning to fly, check with your airline about the status of your flight."

‌



View 3 Images Flights have been left stranded at Barcelona El-Prat airport (Image: Flight Radar)

Vueling Airlines told passengers in a post on X that some of its flights may be affected "due to adverse weather conditions in Barcelona and the Balearic Islands."

"Please check the status of your flight before heading to the airport," the airline added. "We will notify you by email of any changes. If you made your booking through a travel agency, please contact them directly."

‌



Enaire said the full recovery of services will depend on the movement of the storms throughout the day, with passengers warned further disruptions to scheduled flights could occur.

Severe weather has also forced the Catalan government to restrict movement and suspend outdoor sporting activities.

"Be prepared [...] severe damages to people and properties may occur, especially to those vulnerable or in exposed areas," the state meteorological agency warned.

Article continues below

It said those in the peninsular Mediterranean area and Balearic Islands could expect to see "very heavy and persistent showers and storms, with possible flooding" as well as damage to infrastructure from wind and hail.

News.title: Ed Miliband rejects chief rabbi's criticism over Israeli settler sanctions - 'right thing to do'
News.content:
Ed Miliband rejects chief rabbi's criticism over Israeli settler sanctions - 'right thing to do'

Ed Miliband said he does not agree with chief rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis, who branded the government's imposition of sanctions on Israeli settlements a 'dark day for British Jews'

Ed Miliband rejects notion that Israel sanctions put British Jews at risk

Ed Miliband has rejected criticism from Britain's chief rabbi after the government announced sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements.

‌



The UK was among 12 countries backing the move, which has sparked fury in Israel. Mr Miliband said announcing the measures in response to settler violence in the West Bank was "the right thing to do".

‌



And he said he disagrees with chief rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis, who branded it a "truly dark day for British Jews" and said the measure would embolden those who stir up hatred.

‌



In a dramatic hardening of the UK's stance toward Israel, Mr Miliband yesterday accused the Israeli government of turning a blind eye to "ethnic cleansing of Palestinians" in the West Bank. Mr Miliband said imports of produce from Israeli settlements would be banned, which includes products like dates, mangoes, avocados, grapes and herbs, as well as olive oil and kosher wine.

Top Reform supporter quits party with explosive civil war claim and jab at Nigel Farage READ MORE :

View 3 Images Ed Miliband said the sanctions - carried out in conjunction with 11 other countires - are the right thing to do

The Foreign Secretary told Sky News: "I'm a proud British Jew and I don't agree with the chief rabbi. I have great respect for the chief rabbi, but I don't agree with him.

‌



"And I believe that it must be possible to do what we did yesterday, which is to stand up for British values of the rule of law, of dignity for people, of the prevention of injustice, and do so in a way, as I did yesterday, to say to anyone in our country who holds British Jews responsible for the actions of the Israeli government: that is anti-Semitism, pure and simple.

"And we all need to do more to tackle antisemitism. But I believe we can do that and stand up for British values."

View 3 Images Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis criticised the measures announced on Monday (Image: PA Wire/PA Images)

‌



He also said he regrets Israel's furious response to the sanctions, which saw it close the British consulate in East Jerusalem. Mr Miliband said: "I regret what the Israeli government has announced, but I'm proud of what we did yesterday and it was the right thing to do."

He said: "It will be damaging, that's true, but we weighed up the costs and the benefits in advance of this. And we did something very important. We talked to the representatives of the Palestinian people, the Palestinian prime minister, the representative here, and they both said to us with a very clear voice, you need to act from our point of view."

He added: "I would prefer that Israel hadn't announced what it did, but overall, I strongly believe that what we did, along with other international allies, was absolutely the right thing to do."

‌



View 3 Images Palestinian children look at the damage after a house was demolished in the West Bank (Image: Getty)

Following the government's announcement of sanctions on Monday, Sir Ephraim Mirvis said: "The measures announced amount to little more than political flag bearing for mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric and those who harbour a dangerous obsession with the Jewish State.

"These measures will succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to target."

‌



The measure had been expected to spark fury from Donald Trump - but the unpredictable US President has yet to respond. Mr Miliband said: "I'll let our American friends speak for themselves.

"We obviously talked to them in advance of our announcement. You know, I think the whole international community has been quite frustrated, to put it mildly, with some of the actions of the Israeli government.

"I will let them say what what they feel, but I think there is real concern about what is happening. And it's this point that underlying so many of the conflicts in the Middle East, is this failure to really grasp the situation between Israel and Palestine, and this is why it's in our interest to act."

‌



Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the sanctions are "the right thing to do". He said they are aimed "not at the Israeli people", but at bringing peace in the region.

He stated: "The Israeli people are not responsible for the actions of their government. And nor is the Jewish community in the UK. Blaming British Jews for the actions of Benjamin Netanyahu's government is wrong, plain and simple. And it is antisemitism, plain and simple.

"I met the representatives of the Jewish community just last week. I know the fear they live with day by day. My Government will stop at nothing to ensure they are safe and to stamp out antisemitism in every part of our society."

Article continues below

Israeli foreign minister Gideon Saar announced that the UK's consulate in Jerusalem would be closed as part of a package of retaliatory measures. He also said Israel would ban 11 MPs and a campaigner involved in what he claimed was "antisemitic and anti-Israel activity" from entry to the country.

They include former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and veteran Labour MP Diane Abbott, as well as all five Green Party MPs. Mr Saar said he had spoken to Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch on Tuesday night and thanked her for her opposition to the "hostile Labour Government's announcement".

News.title: Chris Mason: Burnham looks to show he will go further than Starmer with West Bank sanctions
News.content:
There is little doubt that the UK's decision to ban imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank is another significant shift in Britain's posture in the Middle East.

The announcement from the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, with the Prime Minister Andy Burnham alongside him in the House of Commons, comes almost exactly a year after the UK formally recognised a Palestinian state. And it comes garnished with blunt language about Israel's conduct.

This latest announcement is both a logical extension of that decision of 12 months ago, senior figures argue, but also, in words and actions, an expression of Burnham's desire to go further than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer was willing to.

It is, Miliband believes, a re-assertion of the logic of eventually arriving at a two-state solution â a viable Palestinian state alongside Israel.

The foreign secretary passionately argued that the UK did have agency and could act â and to do nothing would amount to failure. "A strategy of passivity in the face of what is happening is not a strategy," is how Miliband put it in an interview with Jewish News, external.

There is a pride among his team that after a diplomatic effort over the summer, there is a breadth to the coordinated international action on this, with 11 other countries, including France and Canada, sharing the same approach.

"We provided a convening and coordinating role in pulling this together," one source told me, "but we didn't have to convince others to do this. They were coming to the same view themselves, so we agreed we should all go out and say this at the same time."

The hope is that coordinated action increases the likelihood that the measures will have an impact and minimises the blowback to any one country from Israel or America.

UK officials had anticipated one likely reaction from Israel would be the enforced closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem, which has indeed happened.

And while there is a weary acknowledgement that no one can be certain what President Donald Trump might say next about anything ever, it is noted in Whitehall that the initial reaction of the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was pretty understated.

News.title: Drug gangs exploited and raped us as teens, then police failed us, women tell BBC
News.content:
Warning: Contains details of sexual exploitation

"It was the thrill of being with a bad boy."

Christine was 13 when she began exchanging messages online with someone she believed was a teenage boy.

On their first meeting, she discovered he was a grown man 10 years older than herself. He also told her he was involved with gangs and drugs.

"I always knew, OK, he's probably hurt someone, but in terms of hurting me, I didn't think it would get to that point," she says.

Over the next few years, he would use Christine to courier drugs, subject her to extreme sexual exploitation, and assault her so violently she feared she might die.

Christine is one of four women who have chosen to waive their anonymity and speak publicly to the BBC documentary, Britain's Forgotten Girls, about how they were targeted by criminals when they were children.

Their stories, covering 2002 to last year, differ in detail - but reveal strikingly similar patterns of abuse. All four describe being targeted by boys and older men connected to drug gangs, manipulated into abusive relationships, then repeatedly sexually exploited.

All believe the authorities failed to protect them and did not take their allegations seriously.

The sexual and criminal exploitation of girls by drug gangs has long been overshadowed in public discussion by the focus on sexual grooming gangs, according to front-line social workers and experts in the field.

"For grooming gangs, the primary purpose is often the sexual exploitation of those girls, but the primary purpose of a drug gang is to make money off selling drugs and other criminal activity," says Connie Muttock from the children's charity, Centre for Young Lives.

Girls are brought in to generate money, says Muttock, but many are also sexually abused by gang members.

News.title: More than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans', says Anthropic researcher
News.content:
A top safety researcher at Anthropic has warned AI is advancing so quickly there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

Evan Hubinger said in a post on X, external that the risk from the models which currently exist was "low" but he was "worried" the technology might become able to improve itself soon to the point where it posed an existential risk to humanity.

It comes after the Financial Times reported, external Anthropic withheld its latest model from the UK's AI Safety Institute (AISI), one of the leading bodies in the world for assessing AI risk.

The BBC has approached Anthropic for comment.

A Cabinet Office spokesperson did not comment on whether the latest model had been withheld from the AISI - instead saying it "continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic, to make models safer".

Neil Lawrence, Professor of Machine Learning at University of Cambridge, told the Today Programme on BBC Radio 4 that the report was credible.

"I suppose it's unsurprising against a background where there's a perception where the United States very much sees AI as a race between themselves and China and is moving more towards isolationist positions, that it might be that the administration is saying that they should reduce cooperation with some of their allies," he said.

News.title: Shelton beats Alcaraz in late-night epic to reach US Open semis
News.content:
Carlos Alcaraz's US Open title defence came to an end in a dramatic five-set quarter-final loss to Ben Shelton that ended at 03:34 local time - the latest finish in the tournament's history.

A large crowd remained captivated deep into the night as a modern classic unfolded over an unpredictable four hours and 28 minutes on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

The match did not begin until about 11pm in New York, after the start of the night session was delayed by Tuesday's earlier matches.

At its conclusion, eighth seed Shelton basked in a standing ovation from a delirious audience after completing a 6-7 (5-7) 6-1 6-3 1-6 7-6 (10-7) victory that will live long in the memory of all those present.

"That was a war, an epic match, so physical," Shelton said.

"Carlos is one of the greatest champions in our sport already at 23 years old.

"It's ridiculous some of the stuff he comes up with sometimes - the most enjoyable match that I've had in my career, for sure."

This was the biggest - and certainly most significant - win of Shelton's career.

He had not beaten a top-three player in 17 attempts, and had lost each of his three previous matches against Spain's Alcaraz.

It also boosted home hopes of a first American men's singles champion in New York for 23 years.

Shelton was less than a year old when Andy Roddick won the US Open in 2003 - but an American finalist is guaranteed when he and Frances Tiafoe meet in Friday's semi-finals.

World number three Alcaraz was competing at his first tournament since a lengthy injury lay-off, but that is to take nothing away from Shelton, who produced a phenomenal performance.

Seven-time major winner Alcaraz had exceeded expectations on his return after more than four months out with a wrist injury, including sweeping past 20th seed Tommy Paul to reach the last eight.

But the 23-year-old's lack of match fitness appeared to finally catch up with him in a high-octane encounter filled with breathless exchanges and astounding displays of athleticism.

Even when it appeared Alcaraz had emptied the tank, the two-time winner not only forced a deciding set but would go the distance as the players engaged in a tense 10-point match tie-break that provided a fitting conclusion to the contest.

"It was close. So I'm just not going to be disappointed about not getting the win at the end," said Alcaraz.

"I'm just proud about myself, about how I fought. I leave the court with a smile, healthy, and this is what I needed."

News.title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk
News.content:
The work by Oxford University, which is published in the International Journal of Cancer, defines any drink at 65 degrees Celsuis or above as "very hot" and posing a potential risk.

Consuming six or more hot drinks per day also raises the risk, according to data from 977,282 middle-aged men and women.

Although adding milk can cool drinks down slightly, a milky tea or coffee may still be far too hot, researchers say.

Tea made immediately after a kettle is fully boiled is touching boiling point, which is 100 degrees C (212 degrees F). Once poured into a cup, that lowers to around 90 or 95 degrees C.

The advice is to wait a few minutes before drinking so the beverage cools to a safer temperature.

Cancer Research UK says it's difficult to put an exact time on how long a hot drink should be left to cool.

"But if you're worried, we'd suggest just waiting until it's comfortable to drink rather than drinking it while it's still very hot," the charity said.

Lead researcher Dr Keren Papier said research in South America - where many people drink a very hot herbal beverage called mate - had already shown a similar link between hot drinks and oesophageal cancer.

But she said: "More research is now needed to identify the exact drink temperatures linked to this increased risk."

A separate study, external of 118 young adults who did multiple tastings of different black coffees found most only deemed the drinks to be too hot if the temperature was 70 degrees C or above.

According to one takeaway coffee cup manufacturer, the ideal temperature for hot coffee on the go is between 49 and 60 degrees C.

Should a barista want the coffee to stay hotter for longer - if a customer requests extra hot - it can be served at over 82 degrees C, says MTPak Coffee.

News.title: Police officer's funeral to take place after A66 crash that killed seven
News.content:
The funeral of one of the two police officers killed in a wrong-way crash is to take place later.

PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died when a Volkswagen Passat collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, on 22 August. Five young men were also killed.

Road closures will be in place in Hartlepool for PC Blades' funeral from 07:30 BST to allow for a full police ceremonial funeral.

Speaking on behalf of his family, Cleveland Police Federation chair Lauren Somerville said "life feels unbearably quiet" without the father-of-two's "silly jokes" and laughter.

Somerville said flowers had been delivered to the force's stations and people from Australia, France and America had been in touch.

"The support has been overwhelming, and it's been comforting," she said.

Somerville added even small acknowledgements of respect from the public, such as a nod or a thank you when they see police out and about, had brought officers "so much strength".

Officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned onto the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.

PC Blades and PC Clough were in a vehicle looking for the Passat after its cloned registration plates triggered an automated number plate recognition camera, although they were not involved in the pursuit, according to the IOPC.

Cole Worthy and Theo Rae, both 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Michael Cahill and Jakub Matusiak also died in the crash.

News.title: Alan Carr holds back tears on special night at National Television Awards
News.content:
You can see a full list of winners at the bottom of this article

Alan Carr had an emotional night at the 31st National Television Awards on Tuesday as he received the Special Recognition prize following a whirlwind year for the comedian.

The London audience had just been treated to a Traitors-themed musical performance in his honour, which included fellow cast member Paloma Faith emerging from a coffin, when he was given the surprise award.

Speaking to BBC News on the red carpet before the ceremony, Carr had played down his chances of winning for his semi-autobiographical comedy Changing Ends.

He joked: "Comedy is so subjective... Mrs Brown's Boys wins every year, why am I even here?"

News.title: Learner drivers still waiting 20 weeks to book tests
News.content:
Learner drivers have to wait an average 20 weeks before booking a practical test, according to new figures, despite attempts to reduce delays.

The data from the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) for August is only a marginal improvement from an 20.2 weeks in July.

The average wait time between booking and sitting a test is unchanged at 11.1 weeks.

The DVSA initially had a target of reducing the average waiting time to seven weeks by the end of last year. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander pushed the target back to summer 2026, but subsequently admitted even that would not be possible.

The DVSA made a number of changes to its practical driving test booking system earlier this year.

Only the learner driver themself is now able to book their driving test, blocking an instructor or third parties from booking using the learner's details.

There is also a geographical restriction which means a learner can only book a test at their three local test centres, rather than one at the other side of the country if they found a test available.

The number of times a would-be driver can swap a test date has also been restricted.

News.title: Divorcing abusive husband cost woman £105k
News.content:
A woman who endured years of abusive controlling behaviour by her ex-husband says it has cost her more than Â£105,000 to divorce him.

Annabelle Boucher, 48, from Somerset, wants the law changed after she paid Â£75,000 to David Rogers, 61, despite him admitting to coercive and controlling behaviour. She also had to pay her legal costs.

"I thought being stuck in this relationship I couldn't get out of would be highlighted within the divorce procedure," Boucher said. "But the divorce law doesn't take into account the fact that he was a criminal."

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said it had begun a consultation to reform the law so "family courts meet the needs of domestic abuse victims".

Boucher, a mother from Chiselborough, said Rogers had come into her life in "a whirlwind" in 2017 and the pair got married two years later.

It was once they were married that things started to "take a turn", she said, and "some very extreme behaviour started to happen".

"It creeps up on you and you're in it, and so you don't kind of notice what is happening."

Boucher said she had ended up "shutting down emotionally" and "cutting off from everyone" because she feared what would happen.

"You find that you're trapped within a situation that you can't get out of."

News.title: Man charged over fatal crash with cyclists
News.content:
A man has been charged with causing death by dangerous driving after a car hit three cyclists, killing two and injuring another.

Kent Police said it had charged Aaron Turner, 22, from Hermitage Road in Higham, after the fatal crash near Gravesend on Sunday.

A man in his 60s and a woman in her 50s died in the crash while the third cyclist was treated in hospital for minor injuries, a police spokesperson said.

A white Ford Focus was travelling south-west near the village of Sole Street at about 07:45 BST when it was involved in the crash, according to police.

In addition to two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, Turner has been charged with failing to stop at the scene of a crash and possession of a class C drug.

He is due to appear at Medway Magistrates' Court later.

A 21-year-old man who was arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving and a 19-year-old woman who was detained on suspicion of assisting an offender have been released on bail.

Investigators are asking anyone who saw the car or cyclists before the incident, or who witnessed the crash near the junction of Sole Street and Round Street, to contact them.

They also appealed for members of the public with CCTV or dashcam footage to get in touch.

News.title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns
News.content:
There could be tens of thousands more teenagers who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) than official statistics suggest, the children's commissioner for England has warned.

A report by Dame Rachel de Souza said around 42,000 16- and 17-year-olds in England were officially classed as studying at college, but were not showing up at least half of the time.

She said they had gone "under the radar" and were "not getting the support that they need".

The Department for Education (DfE) said it planned to help colleges track attendance and ultimately to gather that data centrally.

Unlike schools, further education and sixth form colleges in England are not required to collect or report attendance data.

Dame Rachel's report is based on attendance data obtained from 262 college groups in England and says rates are "substantially lower" than in schools.

It suggests that more than half (52.2%) of 16- and 17-year-olds are estimated to be persistently absent by the standards used in schools, meaning they are missing 10% or more of college sessions.

And around 42,000 (5.9%) are severely absent, meaning they are missing at least half of college sessions.

The DfE estimates that 57,000 16- and 17-year-olds in England are Neet, and Dame Rachel's report argues that these persistently absent teenagers should be considered as "hidden" Neets alongside them.

Dame Rachel told the BBC a range of factors led to teenagers missing college, including part-time work and travel costs, and that some had been largely absent from education since the Covid pandemic.

She said while those juggling part-time employment were likely to miss college every so often, it was those who are "far more vulnerable" who were likely to be severely absent.

She added that it was "shocking" that the DfE did not collect the data as it meant the issue was "ignored".

"It's under the radar and these kids are not getting the support that they need," she said.

News.title: Cowboy builder tore my home apart and disappeared off the face of the Earth with £14k
News.content:
A rogue builder tore Sheri Ingram's home apart and "disappeared off the face of the Earth" with Â£14,000.

In February, Lee Slocombe, from Swansea, was jailed for six years after defrauding nine victims of Â£400,000 - with this his latest conviction in a decade of offending.

The UK government announced in August plans to give people greater protections against "cowboy builders" through a database of trusted traders.

Ingram, from Cardiff, welcomed it, but questioned where the incentive would be for tradespeople to sign up to the voluntary scheme.

Another couple who were "scarred for life" by a rogue trader who left them Â£30,000 out of pocket said it would give more confidence to homeowners.

"He (Slocombe) was recommended to us by a serving police officer who my ex knew," Ingram said.

"So why on earth would we have not trusted him?"

Slocombe's offending covered a period of 11 years, and he even targeted nine people to carry out work on their homes when on bail using a false name.

It began in 2015 after Ingram and her now ex-partner bought a house in Aberbeeg, Blaenau Gwent, which they planned to renovate and move into.

The then 21-year-old appointed Slocombe to build an extension and make the ground floor of the home open plan.

She admitted they were not experts in building work, and while it looked like lots was going on, Slocombe kept finding problems and asking for more cash to solve them.

For the first six weeks, he was "very responsive", Ingram said he then "disappeared off the face of the earth" with Â£14,000.

News.title: When is the rain going to stop?
News.content:
Fortunes are set to change by midweek with drier conditions forecast following a deluge for many parts of the UK on Tuesday.

However, the pattern of wet weather followed by drier conditions is set to continue as more low pressure systems line up in the Atlantic.

It comes as last week was was the wettest for England since early February, according to the Environment Agency.

While there is no prolonged dry spell of weather in the immediate forecast, some models suggest conditions could become more settled by the end of next week.

News.title: Glastonbury confirms ticket sale dates - and highest ever price
News.content:
After taking a fallow year in 2026, the Glastonbury Festival has confirmed that tickets for next year's event will go on sale in October.

Tickets for the weekend will cost Â£408 including a Â£5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of Â£29.50 from 2025.

Headliners for the festival, which takes place from 23 to 27 June, have yet to be announced, but rumours are already swirling, with everyone from Harry Styles and Fontaines DC to Taylor Swift and Stevie Wonder said to be in the mix.

Tickets for the festival typically sell out in less than an hour, with thousands of fans joining online queues to fight for their place.

In a post on the official Glastonbury Instagram page, external, organisers said tickets with coach travel would go on sale at 18:00 BST on Thursday, 1 October.

General admission tickets go on sale a couple of days later, at 09:00 BST on Sunday 4 October.

As part of an ongoing campaign to stop touts, anyone wanting to attend Glastonbury had to be registered in advance. You can check your registration on its website. , external

In recent years, the festival has also introduced an automatic queuing system on the day of sale, with fans needing to be online before the start of the sale with a valid registration number.

News.title: RNLI volunteers facing 'unacceptable' abuse, chief says
News.content:
RNLI staff have faced "unacceptable" online and physical abuse since anti-migrant protests at the weekend, the charity's chief executive has said.

On Sunday, police faced off with demonstrators who blocked roads in Portsmouth in an effort to stop 140 people who arrived at the Eastney Landing ferry port area with the RNLI's assistance.

Chief executive Peter Sparkes said the abuse of volunteers was "wholly unacceptable in a civilised society".

He said there had been "deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding" about the charity, and condemned threats by "those who would hide behind a balaclava or a keyboard".

The protest in Portsmouth followed a separate demonstration the previous day, in which hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters brought the Port of Dover to a standstill.

Footage was subsequently posted on social media showing volunteers of the Poole-based charity labelled as "traitors".

News.title: Prince George attends first day at Eton College
News.content:
Prince George has officially started his first term at Eton College.

The 13-year-old, who is second in line for the British throne, was dropped off at the all-boys boarding school by his parents, the Prince of Wales and Catherine, Princess of Wales.

The future king follows in the footsteps of his father in attending the elite private school, which has taught 20 British prime ministers and where fees are around Â£65,000 a year.

The BBC's royal correspondent Daniela Relph explains what the prince is likely to expect at his new school.

News.title: Volkswagen ID. Polo review: VW gets back to its best with a stunning supermini you’ll love
News.content:
