The Volkswagen Polo has been around for more than 50 years, sold more than 20 million cars and built its reputation by not trying too hard. It has always been the sensible little Volkswagen: smart without being showy, grown-up without being boring and, above all, straightforward. Now, seven generations in, the biggest change in the Polo’s history has arrived. It’s electric.

The new ID. Polo isn’t replacing the petrol-powered Polo straight away, but it does take a familiar name into Volkswagen’s electric ID range for the first time. It’s also the first Volkswagen electric car to put its motor at the front and drive the front wheels, rather than use the rear-wheel-drive or four-wheel-drive layout of the bigger ID models. Underneath is Volkswagen’s latest MEB+ electric platform, specifically developed to make smaller EVs roomy, efficient and relatively affordable.

And affordable is an important word here. UK prices start at £23,945 for the ID. Polo Life when it goes on sale on 10 September, while the big-battery versions qualify for the Government’s £1,500 Electric Car Grant. That puts the ID. Polo straight into one of the busiest new parts of the electric-car market, where buyers will also be looking at cars such as the Renault 5, Kia EV2 and Hyundai Ioniq 3.

At 4,053mm long, 1,816mm wide and 1,530mm tall, the ID. Polo is still very much a supermini, but the 2,592mm wheelbase and clever packaging mean there’s much more going on inside than those outside dimensions might suggest. There’s room for five (just), while the 441-litre boot is actually bigger than the space in the current Volkswagen Golf and ID.3.

Volkswagen design boss Andreas Mindt calls the company’s latest design philosophy Pure Positive. Strip away the designer-speak and what you get is a car that looks recognisably like a Volkswagen, but wearing a smile. It doesn’t shout about being electric and it isn’t trying to frighten small children with an enormous blanked-off grille. There’s a friendly look to the front, a strong C-pillar that deliberately nods back towards earlier Golfs and, depending on trim, illuminated Volkswagen badges and a light bar.

But the biggest change compared with some of Volkswagen’s earlier ID cars becomes obvious once you climb in. Volkswagen has listened and righted the wrongs of some of its most recent cars, especially early ID models. There are real buttons on the steering wheel, proper controls for the heating and ventilation, normal mirror controls and even – praise be – a physical knob for volume and for changing tracks or radio stations.

And that’s before you get to the quality. My top-spec, big-battery car felt genuinely premium inside, not just impressive for a small car. The mix of fabrics, colours and materials gives the cabin real warmth and a posh feel, the switchgear feels expensive and the whole thing has the solid, reassuring character you’d hope to find in a Volkswagen. My immediate reaction after spending a lot of time with it in Austria was pretty simple: this is exactly how a Volkswagen Polo should feel.

How I tested

I drove the ID. Polo extensively on its international launch in Austria, covering motorways, towns, villages and country roads, while assessing its comfort, quality, practicality, technology and everyday usability too.

Volkswagen ID. Polo: from £23,945, Volkswagen.co.uk

open image in gallery The new ID. Polo feels very Volkswagen on the road: comfortable and easy to drive ( Volkswagen )

Independent rating: 9/10

Pros: Premium-feeling cabin, beautifully weighted controls, easy-to-use technology, huge boot, impressive refinement, strong efficiency

Premium-feeling cabin, beautifully weighted controls, easy-to-use technology, huge boot, impressive refinement, strong efficiency Cons: A bit of wind noise at motorway speeds, rear space is only okay

A bit of wind noise at motorway speeds, rear space is only okay Price from: £23,945

£23,945 Battery size: 37kWh or 52kWh

37kWh or 52kWh Maximum claimed range: 281 miles

281 miles Maximum charging rate: Up to 105kW DC, 10 to 80 per cent from 24 minutes

Battery, range, charging, performance and drive

There are two battery sizes and three power outputs in the ID. Polo range for the UK. The smaller 37kWh battery is an LFP, or lithium iron phosphate, unit and comes with either 114bhp or 133bhp. The larger 52kWh battery uses NMC chemistry and is paired with the most powerful 208bhp motor, which is the version I drove.

open image in gallery The new Volkswagen ID. Polo will go for up to 281 miles on a full charge ( Steve Fowler )

The 133bhp cars have an official range of between 203 and 206 miles depending on trim. Move up to the 52kWh battery and the figure rises to as much as 281 miles.

Charging speeds aren’t headline-grabbing, but the relatively small batteries mean you shouldn’t be sitting around for too long. The 37kWh battery can rapid-charge at up to 90kW and go from 10 to 80 per cent in about 23 minutes, while the 52kWh version tops out at 105kW and takes around 24 minutes for the same charge. All versions can charge at up to 11kW on AC power.

There’s an optional heat pump to help reduce the amount of battery power used to warm the cabin in cold weather, while you can also get vehicle-to-load capability. Volkswagen’s PowerSocket system can provide up to 3.6kW for external electrical equipment, so you could use the Polo to charge an e-bike or run camping equipment, for example.

The 208bhp version gets 290Nm of torque and goes from 0-62mph in 7.1 seconds, while the 133bhp car takes 9.5 seconds. All are limited to around 99mph.

That 208bhp car certainly doesn’t feel short of performance. There’s plenty of instant response when you need it and it feels pleasingly brisk without turning what is still, fundamentally, a Polo into something silly – there is a GTI model still to come, though, which VW folk all spoke about with big smiles on their faces!

There is one little reminder that Volkswagen has opted for front-wheel-drive layout, though. Be very quick with the accelerator when pulling out of a junction and the front tyres can momentarily lose grip, with the steering going light for a second in a way that feels like proper old-fashioned torque steer. It doesn’t last long, but you notice it.

For the rest of the time it has the easy, natural character I’d expect from a Polo. Volkswagen has developed the suspension specifically for this front-wheel-drive electric layout, with MacPherson struts at the front and a compact torsion beam at the rear, while the battery sits low between the axles. The ride quality is really nice – comfortably firm and connected without ever jolting you over broken surfaces. Again, it feels very Volkswagen, as does the steering with just about enough weight to give you confidence through corners, while being easy enough around town.

Visibility is good, too, making the car easy to drive and park, without any nasty blind spots either forwards when approaching roundabouts or over your shoulder when overtaking.

There’s also a new braking system with discs front and rear that blends regenerative and conventional braking, plus proper one-pedal driving. Select B rather than D using the drive selector and lifting off the accelerator can slow the Polo all the way to a standstill, which is especially useful around town and all feels very natural.

open image in gallery ID. Polo styling is smart, yet conservative with some neat treatments for the front and rear lights, plus illuminated badges ( Steve Fowler )

Refinement is mostly strong. The electric motor is little more than a distant hum and the rest of the car is impressively quiet around towns and villages. The exception came on the motorway, where I could hear more wind noise than I expected. At one stage I found myself checking whether all the windows were properly shut – it stands out all the more because everything else is so quiet.

If you want to tow with your ID. Polo, you can. The 114bhp and 133bhp versions can tow up to 500kg, while the 208bhp car increases that to 1,200kg, enough for a small caravan.

Interior, practicality and boot space

The ID. Polo’s interior might just be its strongest feature. Volkswagen has talked a lot about getting back to the things people liked about its cars in the first place, and this is where you see – and feel – the results.

open image in gallery The inside of the ID. Polo is a highlight, with high quality materials and a smart design ( Steve Fowler )

There’s fabric in all the right places to give the cabin some warmth, including across the dash and doors, with material that matches the seats. It looks great and I particularly like the darker material across the top of the dash with its slightly more rugged finish, while the tasteful combination of textures and colours lifts what could easily have become another rather gloomy small-car interior.

It all feels very premium. And plenty of credit should go to the people who worked on the switchgear, because almost everything you touch has clearly had some thought put into it. The window controls, mirror adjustment and even the indicator stalk – which also has to deal with the lights and wipers – have a nicely weighted, expensive action. This is one area where the ID. Polo feels a cut above plenty of the newer Chinese rivals I’ve driven, which is exactly where Volkswagen needs to be.

There are harder plastics where you’d expect them, including the tops and lower sections of the doors, but I’ve no problem with that. There’s little point covering parts you rarely touch with expensive soft-touch material just for the sake of it. What’s more telling is something as simple as the glovebox: open it and it drops in a nicely damped way rather than crashing down.

There’s plenty of recycled material, too. Volkswagen says the textiles used in the seats and doors, as well as the upper headlining and carpets, are made from recycled PET material, while the Style seats use fabric produced from recycled ocean plastic.

open image in gallery Rear seat legroom in the ID. Polo is just about good enough for adults ( Steve Fowler )

Space is pretty good rather than miraculous. Volkswagen says the all-electric platform has created 19mm more usable interior length compared with the petrol Polo, as well as more width and a higher seating position without sacrificing headroom. I’m close to six feet tall and could sit behind a driver’s seat set for me with a little room to spare, so adults can use the back without feeling like they’ve been folded up. It’s okay rather than enormous, but for a car only just over 4,000mm long it does its job well.

Visibility is as straightforward as you’d expect from a Polo. The driving position is easy to get comfortable in and the view around you is good. I wouldn’t object to the windscreen being a little deeper, but it never became an issue.

The real surprise is behind the rear seats. At 441 litres, the boot is huge for a car this size – more than 25 per cent larger than the petrol Polo’s and, remarkably, more than Volkswagen offers in the larger Golf or ID.3. Fold the back seats and you get 1,240 litres.

There is a small caveat though, since most of that extra usefulness comes from depth rather than the boot being exceptionally long or wide. The load space on the car I tried also had a clever three-stage floor arrangement, letting you trade outright depth for a flatter or more convenient loading area depending on what you’re carrying. The official figures give 658mm of load length with the rear seats up and 1,393mm with them folded, with 984mm between the wheelarches.

open image in gallery The ID. Polo boot is deep with even more space beneath the floor ( Steve Fowler )

There are ISOFIX points on the outer rear seats and front passenger seat, while the roof is rated for up to 75kg. Add together the optional tow bar, big boot and decent passenger space, and the ID. Polo proves it’s a proper everyday car, not an electric supermini only suited to short urban trips.

Technology, stereo and infotainment

There’s lots of technology in the ID. Polo, but the best bit is how little effort it takes to use most of it. Volkswagen appears to have taken a long look at some of the criticism aimed at its earlier ID interiors and decided that perhaps making people swipe and prod at a screen for everything wasn’t such a brilliant idea after all.

open image in gallery The new tech in the Volkswagen ID. Polo is impressive for its usability and features ( Steve Fowler )

So, there are buttons – real ones. There are proper buttons on the new steering wheel, a separate bank of physical controls for the heating and ventilation, and normal mirror adjustment where you expect it. Then, between the phone tray and cupholders, there’s a proper rotary volume control that can also be nudged left or right tp change tracks or radio stations. Such a simple idea shouldn’t feel quite so exciting in 2026, but here we are.

The touchscreen itself is good, too. UK cars get a 12.9-inch central display and the menu structure is clean and intuitive. Frequently used functions can be kept where they’re easy to reach, while shortcuts for the main menu and vehicle controls reduce the amount of hunting around. Wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are available, plus wireless phone charging.

In front of the driver is a lovely 10-inch digital display, sitting behind a slightly squared-off steering wheel that gives an unobstructed view of the instruments. The wheel itself feels good in your hands, too.

Then there are those retro displays, which are pure theatre. Press the View button and the modern driver’s display turns itself into something inspired by a first-generation Golf, complete with an old analogue speedometer and something resembling a rev counter, although on an EV it shows power use and energy recovery instead. You can give the touchscreen a retro makeover as well, with old-fashioned graphics including a cassette-style media player and a radio frequency display.

It’s great fun and exactly the sort of little detail that gives a car some personality. Would I keep it switched on permanently? Probably not. The modern displays are clearer and more useful day to day, but I’m glad it’s there.

My fully loaded launch car also had ID.Light, an LED strip that runs across the top of the dashboard and into the doors. It can work with the navigation using light to point you in the direction you need to go, as well as giving warnings. Again, it’s technology that manages to be useful without demanding much attention.

The optional Harman Kardon sound system is another impressive extra. It has 425 watts of output and I found it punchy, with good clarity and far better sound than you’d normally expect from a small car. Electrically adjustable 12-way front seats with three massage programmes are also available on higher-spec cars, bringing another feature you’d normally associate with something much bigger and more expensive.

The driver-assistance technology follows the same theme. All ID. Polos get a useful spread of systems including autonomous emergency braking with pedestrian and cyclist detection, lane-keeping assistance, Side Assist, Rear Traffic Alert, an exit warning system, traffic-sign recognition and a driver attention and drowsiness monitor. Life and Style cars add adaptive cruise control, front cross-traffic assistance, parking sensors front and rear and a reversing camera.

Connected Travel Assist goes further. On the motorway, it combines adaptive cruise control with lane assistance and can help with lane changes, and I found it worked well. Away from motorways it can also use information about the road ahead and even recognise traffic lights, bringing the car to a stop at a red light within the system’s limits. I’m still not entirely convinced by using that level of assistance around town, though. It’s clever, but it’s still assisted driving and a long way from anything you’d describe as full self-driving.

open image in gallery Retro dials in the Volkswagen ID. Polo are a fun choice, and mirrored by a retro look for the infotainment screen, too ( Steve Fowler )

Other optional systems include Area View with a 360-degree camera and Park Assist Pro, which can remember parking manoeuvres and even allow the car to be moved into or out of a space remotely using a compatible smartphone. There’s an Emergency Assist function that can bring the car to a halt if the driver becomes unresponsive.

Prices and running costs

Volkswagen has kept the ID. Polo range relatively simple, although there are some launch editions to complicate things slightly at the beginning. The important number is £23,945: that’s the starting price of the regular series-production ID. Polo Life with the 37kWh battery and 114bhp motor.

open image in gallery The new Volkswagen ID. Polo starts at a very competitive £23,945 ( Steve Fowler )

The 133bhp Life with the same battery costs £25,055, while moving up to the 52kWh battery and 208bhp motor takes the Life to £28,330. The Style starts at £28,470 with the 37kWh battery and 133bhp motor, while the 52kWh, 208bhp Style I drove is £31,745. All of the 52kWh, 208bhp versions qualify for the Government’s £1,500 Electric Car Grant.

Before those regular cars arrive, Volkswagen is offering a small number of Launch Edition models. The 37kWh, 133bhp Life Launch Edition is £25,555 and available from stock only, while the 52kWh, 208bhp Life Launch Edition costs £28,830. The 52kWh Style Launch Edition is £32,995.

The launch cars provide extra kit for your money. Life versions add two-zone climate control, heated front seats and a heated steering wheel, while the Style Launch Edition piles on a lovely panoramic glass roof, massage front seats, Area View cameras, Travel Assist, Park Assist Pro and rear privacy glass.

The regular Life is hardly bare. Standard UK equipment includes parking sensors, selectable driving modes, a reversing camera, the 12.9-inch touchscreen, wireless phone charging with AppConnect and a height-adjustable boot floor. Style adds IQ.Light matrix LED headlights, illuminated Volkswagen logos and a front light bar, ambient lighting with ID.Light, 18-inch alloy wheels, front sports comfort seats and fun little play and pause symbols on the accelerator and brake pedals.

There are more options if you want to push the Polo further upmarket, including the panoramic roof, massage seats, Harman Kardon stereo, extra driver assistance and a heat pump. That makes the £31,745 Style quite a different proposition from the £23,945 entry car, so choosing how much luxury and technology you actually want will make a considerable difference to the bill.

As an EV, though, the ID. Polo’s efficiency figures look strong on paper. The most efficient 52kWh version is rated at the equivalent of around 4.7 miles/kWh, while even the smaller-battery cars sit around the 4.5 miles/kWh mark on official figures – I was impressed by the efficiency shown over a mixed route on my test.

open image in gallery The Volkswagen ID. Polo was efficient on my test drive ( Steve Fowler )

The smaller battery will make most sense for drivers whose regular journeys are relatively short and who can charge easily, while the 281-mile maximum range of the 52kWh version gives the Polo much greater flexibility for longer trips. The 24-minute 10-to-80 per cent rapid-charge time also means the modest 105kW peak figure isn’t as limiting as it might first sound, since it’s a relatively small battery.

The verdict: Volkswagen ID. Polo

The ID. Polo feels exactly how a modern electric Polo should: comfortable, practical, beautifully finished and refreshingly easy to use, with clever tech, sensible controls and no major flaws.

FAQs

How long does it take to charge?

The Volkswagen ID. Polo with the 37kWh battery can charge from 10 to 80 per cent in around 23 minutes using a suitable rapid charger, with a maximum DC rate of 90kW. The 52kWh car can manage the same 10-to-80 per cent charge in around 24 minutes at up to 105kW. All versions support AC charging at up to 11kW.

How much does it cost – is it worth it?

The regular ID. Polo range starts at £23,945 for the 37kWh, 114bhp Life and rises to £31,745 for the 52kWh, 208bhp Style, while limited Launch Editions run from £25,555 to £32,995. On the evidence of my drive, the Polo’s strongest cards are its premium-feeling interior, huge boot, straightforward controls, impressive technology and the way it still manages to feel exactly like a Volkswagen Polo. The 52kWh versions also qualify for the Government’s £1,500 Electric Car Grant.

Does Volkswagen replace batteries for free?

There’s a standard eight-year battery on all electric Volkswagens, as with other cars. There is small print around the retained capacity over time, which are worth checking on.

Why trust us

Our team of motoring experts have decades of experience driving, reviewing and reporting on the latest EV cars, and our verdicts are reached with every kind of driver in mind. We thoroughly test drive every car we recommend, so you can be sure our verdicts are honest, unbiased and authentic.

With more than 30 years of experience, Steve Fowler is one of the UK’s best-known automative journalists. Steve has interviewed key industry figures, from Tesla’s Elon Musk to Ford’s Jim Farley, and is a judge for both Germany’s and India’s Car of the Year Awards, as well as being a director of World Car of the Year. When it comes to electric vehicles, Steve reviews all the latest models for The Independent as they launch, from Abarth to Zeekr, and he uses his expert knowledge of car buyers' needs to provide a comprehensive verdict.

After a year off, Glastonbury will be back in 2027 – and while there’s still quite some time to go until Worthy Farm opens its gates, the time to try purchasing tickets is almost upon us.

Organisers have announced plans for this year’s main sale, which will take place over two days: Thursday 1 October for coach and ticket packages, and Sunday 4 October for general admission.

There’s another date for your diary too: the deadline to register is Friday 25 September at 5pm. Anyone who wants to a buy ticket needs to submit their details and a passport photo before this date. You’ll then be given a registration number that you’ll need to input if you’re lucky enough to succeed in the online sale.

Tickets will only be available from this link and can be purchased with a UK debit card or Visa or Mastercard credit cards.

International tickets can only be bought using a Visa Credit Card or Mastercard Credit Card. Depending on your device settings, you might be offered other payment methods such as Google Pay and Apple Pay, just make sure you’re set up with the relevant service before the resale begins. American Express is not accepted.

In order to secure tickets, you’ll need to put down a £100 deposit for every member of your group – so if there are six of you, make sure £600 is avaliable in someone’s bank account. And for the coach sale, you’ll also have to pay up front for your travel too.

Ahead of the inevitable frenzy when the ticket sale opens, Glastonbury’s organisers have offered a number of tips on how best to maximise your chances.

( Getty )

Top tips for getting tickets to Glastonbury Festival 2027

1. A good internet connection. The last thing you need is your broadband failing at the precise moment the transaction is going through.

2. The time. You need to be on the tickets page on the Glastonbury website at precisely 6pm on Thursday 1 October, or 9am on Sunday 4 October for the general admission sale. So set your alarms!

3. Money at the ready. Make sure your correct bank details, including the right billing address, and know the answers to any additional security questions you might be asked by your card issuer (this is likely if you’re buying multiple tickets). If you plan on using a payment device such as Apple Pay or Google Pay, make sure it’s set up on your device before the sale begins.

Accept the terms and conditions and make sure you complete the check out within the allocated time slot. Once you reach the payment page you will have five minutes to submit your payment information, so make sure you enter all the information accurately. The time remaining will be shown on the right hand side of your screen.

4. It’s not over until the SOLD OUT sign appears on the Glastonbury website. So don’t freak out if you see a message notifying fans that “all available tickets have now been allocated”. That means the orders are being processed, but at least a few people end up running out of time... meaning the tickets are up for grabs again.

A word of caution: your registration numbers will be locked for up to five minutes if your details are entered incorrectly, an attempt to book is already held against your registration number, or your five minutes on the booking page ends. If the transaction fails and tickets are still available, your registration number will be released to give you the chance to try again.

5. Avoid multiple tabs. As stated on the Glastonbury website, trying to buy tickets on multiple tabs could actually put you at risk of confusing the ticket sales process and result in a failed transaction. “We strongly advise that you use just one browser tab when trying to book tickets, in order to avoid possible problems with your transaction,” Glastonbury says.

6. Avoid multiple devices too. While it might seem like a good idea to try on your laptop, phone and a tablet at the same time, doing so could harm your chances as the ticketing system may think you’re a bot – especially if the devices are all hooked up to the same WiFi network. Go for two devices maximum: One on your WiFi, and a phone on 5G.

And remember, if you’re not successful, there will be another chance to try when the resale takes place in April 2027.

You can find more information about the Glastonbury ticket sale here.

News.title: Moving abroad? How to prepare for healthcare overseas
News.content:
However exciting the prospect of moving abroad may be, it also means becoming a beginner again. The routines you’ve long since stopped thinking about, whether it’s the school run or a quick trip to the post office, suddenly require a little more thought. The same goes for looking after your health. At home, if you’re feeling unwell, you already know where to turn, but in a new country, even working out who you're supposed to call can send you down an internet rabbit hole.

Few people put medical care at the top of their relocation checklist, yet it’s one of the first things you’ll want to understand if the unexpected happens. Every destination has its own rules, whether that’s registering with a doctor or refilling a prescription, so spending a little time planning before you move can save a great deal of uncertainty later on.

For those living, working or studying overseas, understanding how you’ll access healthcare should be an important part of that preparation. For some, that may mean arranging local healthcare registration. For others, it could mean getting the right health insurance in place so you have access to care, plus support that’s relevant to your circumstances.

With more than 60 years of history, Cigna Healthcare supports internationally mobile individuals through services available across more than 200 countries and jurisdictions. Its international health insurance plans are designed for people living abroad, with different geographical areas of cover available depending on the plan selected.

Here are some of the key considerations to keep in mind before you relocate.

( iStock )

Healthcare looks different everywhere you go

One of the first things to understand before relocating is that no two healthcare systems are exactly alike. Depending on where you’re moving to, the balance between public and private care can differ, along with how people typically access treatment. Spending some time familiarising yourself with the system before you relocate can help you feel more prepared should you ever need medical attention.

It’s also worth thinking beyond emergencies. If you live with a pre-existing condition or receive ongoing treatment, understanding how your care will continue after you move can make the transition much smoother. For people building a life abroad, having access to healthcare when they need it matters. Cigna Healthcare supports customers living overseas through an international network of more than 2.2 million hospitals and healthcare professionals.

Considering these questions before you leave gives you one less thing to think about once you’re settling into your new home.

Preparation goes beyond the packing list

Building your healthcare plan into your preparations doesn’t have to be complicated. Simply taking the time to understand how you’ll access care, what support may be available and what arrangements you might need to make before you travel can help provide peace of mind.

For people relocating abroad, health insurance can help provide reassurance beyond simply finding a local doctor or understanding the workings of a foreign healthcare system. Cigna Healthcare offers different plan options depending on your circumstances, from globally mobile professionals and families who need international flexibility, to those looking for cover in their country of residence and home country.

Support for people living abroad

With more than 60 years of experience supporting globally mobile individuals, Cigna Healthcare’s Global Individual Health business helps people access healthcare while living and working abroad. Its international health insurance plans are designed for a wide range of needs and budgets, with options for individuals, families, professionals, retirees and students.

Customers can also tailor their cover with optional benefits, including International Outpatient, Vision & Dental, International Health & Wellbeing and International Medical Evacuation. Customers can access multilingual service centres 24 hours a day, seven days a week for support with policy and healthcare-related queries. Eligible customers may also have access to Global Telehealth, allowing them to speak with a doctor remotely.

( Getty Images )

A confident start after relocating

Relocating overseas always comes with a learning curve but understanding how you’ll access medical care doesn’t have to be part of the trial and error. For many people, the biggest questions are practical ones: how will they continue managing an existing condition, and what healthcare options may be available as their circumstances change?

Cigna Healthcare’s plans can offer cover for pre-existing conditions where eligible, subject to medical underwriting, and its international health plans have no upper age limit, meaning customers can apply or renew at any age.

A little preparation before you leave can make settling into a new country far less daunting.

Ready to start your next adventure abroad? Learn more about Cigna Healthcare’s international health insurance plans, optional benefits and global support services, and see how you can prepare for life overseas with a clearer understanding of your healthcare options.

The Premier League’s Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel has supported the decision to award a Manchester United goal against Ipswich, despite a contentious handball involving Harry Maguire, although one panellist believed the use of the arm was deliberate.

During United's 5-2 victory on 30 August, the ball appeared to strike Maguire’s hand as he brought it under control outside the 18-yard box. His subsequent shot was heading off-target before diverting into the net via Ipswich defender Jacob Greaves.

Match official Craig Pawson and VAR Jarred Gillett determined the handball to be accidental. Under current regulations, because Maguire did not score directly from his shot, the goal was permitted to stand.

Composed of three former players or coaches, a Premier League official, and a representative from Pro Ref, the independent panel is publishing its assessments of key match-week decisions for the first time this season.

open image in gallery The decision to allow Man United's second goal to stand following an apparent handball by Harry Maguire has been backed by an expert panel ( Getty )

In notes released on Wednesday morning, the panel stated: "Maguire’s arms are within his bodyline, meaning that the contact with his right arm was accidental and not a punishable handball offence given that Maguire was not the goal scorer.

"The shot was clearly off-target and then deflected in via the defender for a clear own goal. The panel supported the referee’s call to award the goal, 4:1, with one panellist considering the handball to be deliberate."

Following the fixture, the Premier League’s Match Centre account on X explained: "The referee’s call of goal for Manchester United was checked and confirmed by VAR – with it deemed that Maguire was not the immediate goalscorer after an accidental handball."

It added a statement from the VAR: "It’s an own goal and the accidental handball is not punishable, so we recommend you award the goal."

Elsewhere, the panel concluded that VAR should have stepped in to grant Arsenal a penalty during their match at Aston Villa on 31 August for Ian Maatsen’s challenge on Bruno Guimaraes. Although no foul was given during play, the panel unanimously agreed a penalty should have been awarded, either on the pitch or following a review.

"Clear contact was made on the attacker’s standing leg and Maatsen made no contact with the ball," the panel notes read.

"They also felt that VAR should have intervened as the non-penalty award was a clear and obvious error."

open image in gallery The panel felt Bruno Guimaraes should have been awarded a penalty following a tackle by Ian Maatsen ( Getty )

The panel also viewed Maatsen’s "reckless" challenge as worthy of a second caution.

Regarding Nottingham Forest’s penalty at Liverpool on 29 August for Alisson Becker’s challenge on Neco Williams, the panel disagreed 3-2 with the on-field award. However, members felt VAR was right not to intervene as it did not reach the clear and obvious error threshold.

A 4-1 majority also disagreed with the decision not to award Brentford a penalty at Leeds on the same date following Jayden Bogle’s challenge on Kevin Schade. Again, the panel felt it lacked the threshold required for VAR to overturn the call.

In total, 21 Key Match Incidents were evaluated from the second match round. Initial on-field decision accuracy stood at 76 per cent, rising to 90 per cent following VAR interventions.

Female reproductive organ development in infants may be influenced by prenatal exposure to Tylenol, according to new research, though investigators stress that the study does not prove the painkiller is the cause or demonstrate any impact on future fertility.

Margit Bistrup Fischer, lead author at Rigshospitalet in Copenhagen, said determining whether these physical variations in infants affect adult fertility or the timing of menopause will require extended, long-term evaluation.

Fischer noted that women who took Tylenol—also sold as acetaminophen, or paracetamol outside the U.S.—during pregnancy should not be alarmed by the findings.

open image in gallery Tylenol for infants, for sale at a Target store in Valley Stream, New York ( Reuters )

Her research team evaluated 302 three-month-old female infants whose mothers' Tylenol consumption was recorded throughout pregnancy.

Of the total group, 92 infants were first exposed to Tylenol in utero prior to 17 weeks of gestation, 67 were first exposed after 17 weeks, and 143 were born to mothers who did not take the drug.

Researchers determined Tylenol levels using periodic urine samples provided by the women. The mothers took relatively small amounts, with none exceeding the maximum recommended daily limit of 4,000 milligrams, mostly using the medication for headaches or musculoskeletal discomfort.

On average, infants exposed in utero exhibited smaller ovaries, fewer ovarian follicles—the cellular structures containing immature eggs—smaller uteruses, and reduced levels of reproductive hormones, the team reported Wednesday in Human Reproduction Open.

Researchers explained that a woman's lifelong reproductive capacity is established while still in the womb, as females are born with all the eggs they will ever possess.

While animal studies previously suggested that prenatal exposure to Tylenol—the most widely used medication during pregnancy—might alter egg reserves and later reproductive health, no similar human findings had been recorded until now.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has linked Tylenol use in pregnancy to autism, a claim widely rejected by the medical community and leading health authorities as lacking scientific proof ( Reuters )

President Donald Trump has linked Tylenol use in pregnancy to autism, a claim widely rejected by the medical community and leading health authorities as lacking scientific proof.

Infants at three months old who were exposed to Tylenol in utero showed, on average, a 40% reduction in ovarian volume, a 13% smaller uterine volume, and 23% fewer ovarian follicles, researchers discovered.

Infants exposed earlier in pregnancy—before 17 weeks—also demonstrated lower concentrations of Anti-Müllerian hormone, a marker measuring egg quantity and quality.

The investigators additionally evaluated a distinct group of 1,210 girls followed from infancy into adolescence whose mothers reported using Tylenol while pregnant. In that cohort, prenatal exposure was linked to smaller uteruses at puberty and smaller ovaries during adolescence.

Fischer highlighted that the study cannot forecast outcomes for individual mothers or children, pointing out that many women who took Tylenol had daughters with ovarian dimensions similar to those born to unexposed mothers.

open image in gallery Tylenol is manfactured by Kenvue, a company that spun off from Johnson & Johnson in 2023 ( Getty )

Medical guidelines currently continue to recommend Tylenol as a safe option for treating pain and fever during pregnancy. Leaving severe pain or high fever untreated presents its own health risks to both mother and fetus, Fischer noted.

In an accompanying commentary, Dr. Christian De Geyter, a reproductive medicine specialist at University Hospital of Basel in Switzerland, said the findings align well with existing animal data.

He noted that long-term tracking of girls exposed to Tylenol in utero should continue through menopause, adding that current recommendations regarding its use during pregnancy ought to be reconsidered.

News.title: Man City survive tunnel clash and Porto fury thanks to Haaland double
News.content:
Enzo Maresca takes charge of his first Champions League game in charge of Manchester City as they have travelled to Portugal to take on Porto at the Estadio do Dragao. These sides last met during the Champions League group stages during the 2020/21 season. Manchester City won 3-1 at home before the two sides drew 0-0 in this stadium.

Manchester City were busy late on in the transfer window, bringing in both Iliman Ndiaye and Enzo Fernandez as they spent nearly £200m on deadline day alone. They come into tonight’s game off the back of three straight Premier League victories to kick off the Maresca era. Maresca has limited Champions League experience as a manager, which came with Chelsea last season. Manchester City have won their opening game of a Champions League campaign in six of the last seven seasons but this will be the first time since 2015/16 that Manchester City embark on a Champions League campaign without Pep Guardiola at the helm.

“It is a hard place to come [Porto],” said Maresca. “They have started really well. In the last 14/15 games in Europe they lost just one, that shows a difficult place to come, but we will try our best and try to win the game. It is a very, very good team. They have different players, but in terms of the team it is very clear in the way they play. They are aggressive without the ball and on the ball, they have a clear style. But we will try our best and try to win the game. The ambition is the same; try to be ourselves and to win games and then we will see.”

Porto, managed by Francesco Farioli, have won every league game so far this season and already sit four points clear at the summit of Liga Portugal. Farioli takes charge of his first game as a manger in the Champions League and the club make their return to the elite European competition after two seasons away.

“We are going to face one of the big favourites to win the competition,” Farioli said. “It will be a game that will demand that we be at our best, and we know that whenever we step onto the Dragão pitch, something special can happen. I am happy to be in the Champions League for the first time at 37 years old. This will be my first game, but we approach every game with the same attention to detail and the same focus. It is easy for the players to be motivated tomorrow [tonight]. But the key will be our strategy and our ability to execute it, individually and collectively.”

Porto were in the Europa League last season, making it to the quarter-finals, where they were knocked out by Nottingham Forest 2-1 on aggregate. The omens would not appear to be on Porto’s side tonight; they have only won two of their last 16 games against English opposition in major European competition.

Team news from Portugal to follow shortly.

News.title: Newcastle scrape past Millwall to extend Jaissle’s unbeaten start
News.content:
Joe Willock’s deft finish ensured Newcastle United survived a tough test against Millwall to keep their excellent run in the Carabao Cup intact.

This competition had been fruitful for Newcastle under former manager Eddie Howe and although this match was hard work – as well as hard to watch at times – his successor Matthias Jaissle guided them through a difficult trip to south-east London.

He called it “job done,” and that was pretty much all it was. “We needed patience on one hand, but also to be passionate and tough. We had the chance [to score] and took it,” he said.

Newcastle have reached the semi-finals of this competition three times in the last four years, but struggled to get any sort of tempo going against their Championship opponents.

You could argue the winning goal came against the run of play late in the second half, moments after Millwall substitute Taïryk Arconte had smashed a low shot against the post.

News.title: Villa end goal drought to finally give Emery’s new era lift-off
News.content:
Unai Emery is building Aston Villa 2.0 and this was a night when his new kids on the block produced clear signs of lift-off for the next chapter.

Emery always springs into life on European nights and his reconstructed team secured their first win and goals of the season to leave Villa’s 1,700 fans singing in the rain.

Ten summer signings have arrived during a summer of upheaval, which included plenty of high-profile departures after the club’s Europa League triumph in May.

Yet this was an evening that will have further energised Emery on his return to the Champions League.

Nicolas Jackson, Zion Suzuki and João Gomes embody this new Villa team and all stood out here in Bruges.

Record £65m signing Jackson’s fine individual goal proved to be the winner to settle a chaotic, absorbing contest with the Belgian Pro League champions.

News.title: Bird flu threatens French foie gras amid new duck cull
News.content:
The latest cull - like previous ones - was undertaken to protect both animal and human health.

Ducks are killed to stop the spread of the disease between farms, as well as to protect the health of farmers and minimise the risk of the virus mutating.

It is thought foie gras itself does not pose a risk to human health, even if it came from a bird-flu-infected duck, because it is almost always heat-treated before it is sold, which effectively destroys the virus, according to Public Health France.

“The consumption of meat, foie gras and eggs – and more generally of any food product based on poultry – presents no risk to humans,” said a spokesman for the Maine-et-Loire prefecture.

Veterinary experts say ducks are especially problematic regarding H5N1 because they can carry the virus without showing symptoms and have been described as the Chevaux de Troie or “Trojan horses” of bird flu.

It is unclear how the birds in the latest outbreak, located on a farm in Longué-Jumelles, contracted the virus, although it is typically spread by wild birds which shed the virus through their droppings.

It is for this reason that British poultry were forced into lockdown or “flockdown” from late October to April of this year.

This included so-called “free-range” birds, which, as the Telegraph reported in November continued to be described as free-range despite never seeing the light of day under a dispensation given by the Department for Environment, Food, and Rural Affairs (DEFRA).

Ducks reared for foie gras typically spend the first 90 days of their lives being reared in their tens of thousands in barns with very little access to natural light.

Animal rights campaigners say most never see water.

They then are put through a rigorous 12-16 day “fattening up” period where they are force-fed through a tube to significantly enlarge their livers, before being slaughtered.

While France introduced a vaccination programme to protect its duck population from bird flu in 2023, the jabs do not entirely stop the virus from getting into a flock.

Data collected by the French Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health & Safety suggested that between 50 and 55 per cent of the country’s ducks are unvaccinated at any given time, due to a 20-day gap between the first and second dose of the vaccine and waning immunity over time.

The ducks subject to the latest bird-flu cull in Western France had received their first dose of the H5N1 vaccine, but not the second, meaning they were not fully protected, according to the disease monitoring firm Airfinity.

The threat to France’s £2 billion foie gras industry comes amid increasing global competition.

Once the dominant producer, it is now being challenged by China, which has rapidly scaled up its output of the delicacy and now accounts for 45 per cent of global production.

A tin of Chinese foie gras costs roughly £3.70, while a typical tin of French foie gras made from duck liver costs between £10 and £15. French foie gras produced from Geese costs anywhere between £70 and £150.

China is also said to operate a more rigorous poultry vaccination programme, according to an analysis by DEFRA.

It applies to all farmed birds in the country, which has managed to keep outbreaks of bird flu on farms relatively low compared with European levels.

The H5N1 avian flu pandemic has now been running for six years and has decimated flocks of farmed chickens and turkeys across the globe.

In the UK alone, more than five million farmed birds have been culled since 2021, costing an estimated £48 million in farmers’ compensation alone.

Last week, the virus was detected on a mink farm in the US state of Utah.

Minks in captivity have previously been described as pandemic “time bombs”. The size and density of fur farms – where thousands of the animals are crammed together in tight proximity – give invading viruses a perfect environment in which to mutate.

The virus has also done huge damage to wild birds and other animals. In South America alone, more than 600,000 wild seabirds have died since 2022.

Dozens of other mammals have been infected and died across the globe, including foxes, otters, sea lions, bears, and seals.

In June, the virus was found in Australia for the first time – the last continent on earth to record a case – and the government has since launched a vaccination programme to protect the country’s rare species, including birds like orange-bellied parrots and black cockatoos.

Scientists have long warned that if H5N1 gains the mutations necessary to spread between people, it could trigger a human-pandemic, something that would be of “enormous concern”, according to the World Health Organization (WHO), given the virus’s 50 per cent case fatality rate.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: The Chancellor’s speech, as it happened
News.content:
John Healey failed to rule out tax rises at next month’s Budget in his first major speech as Chancellor.

Mr Healey also sought to blame Liz Truss and her mini-Budget in 2022 for the high borrowing costs being paid by the Treasury.

During a speech in Coventry, the Chancellor said he would be “honest” about the need to control public spending during his time in Number 11.

He was speaking days after the cost of government borrowing hit its highest level since 2007.

It was also overshadowed by Jaguar Land Rover announcing plans to cut 4,000 jobs in the face of “intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”.

Read our report on the Chancellor’s speech.

News.title: Maitland-Niles’ last-gasp debut goal salvages Everton’s miserable week
News.content:
At the final whistle, the first song the stadium DJ played was Spirit of the Blues and how those relieved Evertonians lapped it up after a week of angst.

Their team had been on the precipice of a defeat that would have exacerbated all the frustrations that bubbled away following the chaotic conclusion to the transfer window. Indeed, it was 10 seconds over the allotted five minutes of added time when the ball fell to Ainsley Maitland-Niles.

It had been three years since the former Arsenal full-back had played in the Premier League – his last goal in England was on October 30, 2019, in an EFL Cup tie with Liverpool at Anfield that ended 5-5 – and he would not have joined Everton if their attempt to sign Kenny Tete from Fulham had not failed.

But here he was 30 yards from goal, with no need to break his stride as Manchester United’s backtracking defenders presented him with an invitation to shoot. So that’s what he did. With one perfectly timed swish of his right foot, an unlikely hero transformed the mood of a club.

Sports.title: Former Liverpool wonderkid looking for new club on LinkedIn as he makes transfer plea following latest exit
Sports.content:
EX-LIVERPOOL wonderkid Ovie Ejaria is searching for a new club on LinkedIn following his latest transfer exit.

Ejaria, 28, played for the Premier League outfit between 2016 and 2020.



The midfielder played just eight times for the Reds’ senior team before his departure.

After his Anfield exit, Ejaria starred for Reading in the EFL.



His time there ended in 2024, before he wound up at Real Oviedo.

However, his contract with the La Liga side expired in the summer, having played eight games for the Spanish club.



And he has now taken to LinkedIn in an effort to find his next team.

Taking to the social media website, he said: “Free agent. Central midfielder. London.

“I’m currently a free agent and looking for the right opportunity.

“Was playing for Real Oviedo last season.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“Primary position – Central midfield (6, 8, 10) – Secondary position – Left winger.

“28 years old, London-based.

“Played for Liverpool, Sunderland, Rangers, Reading and Real Oviedo.

“I’m keeping details brief for now, but if there’s an opportunity or you know of a club looking for a midfielder – (6, 8, 10) or someone who can play as a left winger, please feel free to DM me.”

Sports.title: Mixed night for Mbappe brothers as Kylian scores but Ethan is SENT OFF for shocking elbow in Champions League clash
Sports.content:
TUESDAY evening was one of celebration for Kylian Mbappe – while younger brother Ethan probably suffered a sleepless night.

Kylian, 27, piled in his 71st Champions League goal in a 2-1 win over Inter Milan, drawing him level with Real Madrid icon Raul on the all-time list.



Only Karim Benzema (90), Robert Lewandowski (109), Lionel Messi (129) and Cristiano Ronaldo (140) have scored more than the pair in joint-fifth.

And Kylian hit his mark in just 99 games – almost a half-century fewer than Raul’s 142.



France‘s record goal-scorer put Real ahead from just inside the box at the Bernabeu.

Fede Valverde then doubled the advantage, with Carlos Augusto’s 77th-minute strike coming too late for Inter to complete a comeback.

An impressive win for Los Blancos came on the same night 19-year-old Ethan Mbappe was sent off in disgrace.

The teenage midfielder started Lille’s home clash with Real Betis and assisted Ayase Ueda’s opening goal.

But by the 56th minute it had all gone pear-shaped for the hosts.

With Lille 3-2 behind, VAR picked up on Ethan swinging a reckless elbow at Natan off the ball.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Replays were not kind to the youngster, with one fan writing on X: “That is about as clear-cut as you’ll ever see.”

And Betis held on to their lead in the final half-hour, with Irishman Troy Parrott on the scoresheet for the second time in four games following his summer move from AZ.

Sports.title: ‘I could watch this the rest of the day’ – Fans in hysterics as Vinicius Jr gets brutally bodied trying cheeky trick
Sports.content:
FANS were left in stitches after Yan Bisseck brutally bodied Vinicius Junior after his rainbow flick fail.

The Brazil superstar appeared in Real Madrid‘s blockbuster 2-1 Champions League victory over Inter Milan on Tuesday night.



Amidst the box office action, Vini, 26, attempted to roll the ball up the back of his leg, before flicking it over his own head and Bisseck’s.

Unfortunately for the winger, the 6ft5in Inter centre-back was waiting for it – and left Vinicius in a heap on the floor.



Eager fans rushed online to comment on the tough block.

One X user wrote: “Why does he think he’s Neymar, he’s tried rainbow flick so many times and he’s failed.”

Another said: “The way he got bodied.”

Someone else added: “New nonchalant gimmick video everyday.”

A fourth quipped: “Bro thought he had aura.”

Unfortunately for Vinicius, who signed a huge new six-year contract with Real in August, it is not the first time he’s been flattened mid-trick.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

At the Club World Cup last summer, fans brutally mocked him after his failed rainbow flick against Mexican side Pachuca.

Reports also claim Vinicius attempted the flick previously against Barcelona defender Jules Kounde in El Clasico in 2024.

Not to mention, his same blunder against AC Milan again that year.

Vinicius made headlines this summer following a dramatic series of shuddering talks between him and Real.



Arsenal were tipped to secure the star in a record-breaking move, before the ace opted to stay at the Bernabeu.

Real overcame the Serie A giants in a 2-1 win following first-half goals from Kylian Mbappe and Federico Valverde.

And while Carlos Augusto clawed one back for the visitors in the second-half, it was not enough to secure points in the European league phase.

The fifteen-time European champions will turn their attention back to LaLiga this weekend, before their next Champions League game away at Roma on October 14.

In another universe, Vinicius would have been starting for the Gunners tonight, who are bidding to become finalists once again as they face Napoli.

Sports.title: Shelton beats Alcaraz at 3.33am in New York epic
Sports.content:
Ben Shelton clinched the biggest win of his career as he defeated defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in a five-set epic stretching deep into the New York night to reach the semi-finals of the US Open.

The American prevailed 6-7 (5-7) 6-1 6-3 1-6 7-6 (10-7) over four hours and 28 minutes to reward a raucous Arthur Ashe Stadium crowd gripped until 3.33am in what was the latest-ever finish to a US Open match.

It marked Shelton's first career win over a top-three player, against which he had been 0-17 coming into the match.

Shelton will now play Frances Tiafoe in the final four after his fellow countryman's thrilling five-set victory over Alex Michelsen earlier in the evening.

"For me it's always about the people in the crowd, whether it's my coaches, team or friends and family, or the city of New York that showed up tonight until 3am with the USA chants, that's what kept me going and what got me this win," Shelton said on-court.

"It's incredible. This is the greatest sports city and greatest stadium in the world. I'm hoping my best friend and sister don't have to be at work at 6am.

"I'm so grateful, so blessed to be in front of you guys and share the court with Carlos is an absolute honour."

Image: Shelton celebrates his US Open victory over Alcaraz

Shelton's victory means the United States is guaranteed representation in Sunday's men's final, with Andy Roddick the last American man to win a major title back in 2003.

It also spelled the end of Alcaraz's courageous return to the court having been out for more than four months with a wrist injury and initially been a doubt to compete in New York.

The seven-time major champion, playing his first tournament since April, was seen vomiting before the beginning of the final set, which culminated in a 10-point match-deciding tie-break.

Shelton heads into his third Grand Slam semi-final having previously reached the final four of the 2023 US Open and the 2025 Australian Open.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch this insane point from the match between Shelton and Alcaraz

Having lost the opening tie-break, the 23-year-old stormed to nine straight games on his way to dominant second and third sets. Back came Alcaraz to send it to a decider, where he would win four successive points to lead 5-3 in the tie-break before inviting Shelton to turn things around.

In true Shelton fashion, he iced the game with a serve of 146mph that Alcaraz failed to tame, bringing the New York crowd to their feet.

Tiafoe reaches US Open semis in thrilling fightback

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the US Open quarter-final match between Frances Tiafoe and Alex Michelsen

Frances Tiafoe recovered from two sets and ‌erased a 0-3 deficit in the fifth set to beat American compatriot Alex Michelsen 5-7 3-6 7-5 6-3 7-6 (10-6), reaching the semi-finals for a third time.

The 11th seed ​appeared to have lost all the magic of his early campaign before claiming the momentum in the third set and clinching ​it with a forehand winner to the deafening cheers of ‌the fans on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Michelsen had flown under the radar in his deepest major run but ​earned respect on the biggest stage of American tennis with 21 aces, and Tiafoe cut his own celebration short to comfort the 22-year-old in an emotional ​embrace.

"I hope he gets tight," Tiafoe said of his mindset at 4-5 down in the third set. "He gave me some gifts, a couple of double faults there.

"But then I slowly started to get my rhythm there, snuck out the third set and slowly started playing better and better.

"He is a hell of a player. He should've easily won today, so shout out Alex Michelsen."

Sports.title: F1's toughest street track ever? Why new Madring could cause Spanish GP chaos
Sports.content:
Formula 1 has a brand-new track to look forward to this weekend and the expectation is there will be carnage and the drivers will be seriously tested at the Madring.

The Spanish Grand Prix has moved from its traditional circuit in Barcelona to a high-speed street track in Madrid and has been described as "Jeddah on steroids" by Formula 3 drivers who tested there last month - the Jeddah track itself is one of the most challenging circuits in F1.

So why is the Madring so difficult and how will it impact the racing we see this weekend, live on Sky Sports F1?

A lap around the Madring

There are 22 official corners on the 3.365-mile Madring circuit, although unusually the track layout has Turns 5A and 20A - so maybe there are 24.

Whatever the number, after the start/finish straight the driver will almost always be turning the steering wheel at some point as there are few straights.

The left-right chicane of Turns 1 and 2 is one of just a few overtaking spots thanks to its heavy braking zone before a long blast through Turns 3 and 4 towards arguably the most awkward chicane in F1 since the old 'Singapore Sling' chicane which was used at the Singapore Grand Prix between 2008 and 2012.

Just how much speed and how much kerb the drivers can use at Turn 5 will be a critical point of the circuit. If cars go side by side approaching Turn 5, hold your breath, because you cannot fit two cars through there alongside each other. However, the long flat-out zone before the chicane means drivers will be keen to make an overtake here...

Image: The Madring F1 track layout (Credit: F1)

After that, the track goes up and down into a really tricky uphill braking zone of Turn 7 where we may see drivers glancing the barriers on the outside.

The track then veers left, right and left, which may be flat out come qualifying when the track is clean after plenty of rubber has gone down from the practice sessions.

Then comes, what could become iconic, Turn 12, known as La Monumental. A huge banked corner that turns 180 degrees at 24 per cent gradient (13.5 degrees) where the drivers will try to stay hard on the throttle as much as possible while experiencing massive G-forces.

Image: The banked Turn 12 known as La Monumental will be a big test for the drivers to stay on the throttle (Photo by Aaron Heredia/NurPhoto)

After a left-hand flick at Turn 13, the next few corners should be flat out until you arrive at a 90-degree right hander of Turn 17 before the drivers dance through Turns 18 and 19 at high speed, then hit the brakes into a sharp left hander at Turn 20.

The last corner of Turn 22 is a 90-degree right hander where the inside barriers jut out, so the drivers will need to be careful not to cut the apex too much as they arrive on the main straight to complete a rollercoaster lap which should be around 90 seconds in qualifying.

New F1 tracks from last 10 years 2026: Madring

2023: Las Vegas Strip Circuit

2022: Miami International Autodrome

2021: Lusail International Circuit

2021: Jeddah Corniche Circuit

2020: Portimao

2020: Mugello

2016: Baku City Circuit

What have the drivers said?

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, plus Williams' Carlos Sainz are the only drivers to have any experience of driving the circuit.

Sainz is a Madring ambassador and gave input on the Turn 12 La Monumental banking so track designers could ensure it is safe, while still being unique.

Leclerc said: "It's a very, very special corner. It's a corner where I feel in qualifying, we'll have to, I will say it in a polite way, but we'll have to be very brave because it's going to be on the limit.

"And so that's going to be really cool, I think. It's going to be a really cool corner. I do believe it can become one of the most iconic corners of the season, especially once the grandstand will be built. I think that will add also to the experience of that corner."

Image: Madrid has a contract to host F1 races until at least 2035

Leclerc and Hamilton conducted a filming day in July when the track had only just finished its completion, so it was extremely hot and dusty.

"As you would expect, there was no grip. So your tyres were basically just covered in dust, and that's the whole time," said Hamilton.

"It looks like it will be a qualifying lap sort of circuit, and there's not really any straights. So it looks like a difficult place to overtake."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player A first look at F1's newest circuit - the Madring

For much of the track, if the drivers are slightly off the racing line by turning at the wrong time or carrying a little too much speed, they could easily find themselves in the barriers at high speed.

The risk-versus-reward stakes will be very high and the bravest drivers, who get it right, will come out on top.

"I think definitely with the way they've put the barriers and the design of the track it's going to be one of the biggest challenges in Formula 1 recently," said Sainz.

"The track reminds me a lot of Jeddah, it reminds me a lot of Baku, even reminds me a bit of Macau in some ways. So having that in an F1 [car] with 1,000 horsepower is going to be quite an interesting challenge, so let's see how it goes."

Image: F1 Drivers' Championship ahead of the Spanish Grand Prix

So we are going to get safety cars and red flags?

In short, almost certainly. Such is the difficulty of the track, it is a question of how many red flags will we see across practice, qualifying and the race. As we saw at the Italian Grand Prix, if any barriers need to be repaired for crashes, that will definitely require a red flag.

In the two-day F3 test, there were 19 red flags - albeit not all of them were for crashes.

"Looking at the track and hearing of what happened in the F3 test, I think we are all expecting safety cars, red flags and yellow flags in qualy and things like this," said Sainz.

"It has been a fashion or a tendency of Formula 1 to go to these kind of tracks like Jeddah, Baku recently that are closer to the city - and Miami - but they have more walls and we haven't had any issues with it. The races actually seem to be going quite well to every place we've gone, so it's that similar trend we're going towards."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch F3 drivers complete in-season testing at the Madring for the first time

Predicting the pecking order is anyone's guess but the track layout will suit cars that are strong in the corners - akin to what we saw at the Hungaroring and Zandvoort when McLaren's Lando Norris won.

McLaren and Ferrari will hope to wrestle some momentum back off Mercedes and Kimi Antonelli following the Italian's stunning victory at Monza.

Avoiding a qualifying or race-ending crash for the title contenders this weekend will be pivotal. But we all know F1 drivers will push the limits, but they must all be careful when attacking the new Madring because this track will bite you, and bite hard.

Sports.title: Carra: Haaland will be greatest goalscorer of all time
Sports.content:
Jamie Carragher believes Erling Haaland will be the "best goalscorer of all time" after his double earned Manchester City a 2-0 win at Porto in the Champions League.

Haaland's brace in Portugal saw him become Man City's third highest goalscorer of all time, taking his tally to 167 in just 203 appearances and is now 93 goals behind record-holder Sergio Aguero.

The 26-year-old has now hit 364 goals for top-flight clubs and country in his 424-game career - and Carragher has backed the Norway international to become a record-breaker.

He told CBS Sports: "I just can't see Haaland not scoring 1,000 goals or being the best goalscorer of all time.

"I've never seen anything like it in terms of goals and numbers, and it is every game - but because he does it so often, it does not feel that big.

"He has just scored two goals away from home in the Champions League - any other striker does that; it is an amazing night. It just feels like a normal night.



"I just can't see how he does not end up being the greatest goalscorer or getting the most goals we have ever seen anybody get."

Haaland has scored 42 goals in 39 appearances in the group stage/league phase of the Champions League, the most of any player since his first season in the competition in 2019-20.

Porto boss Francesco Farioli described Haaland as a "monster" at his post-match press conference.

Haaland needs one goal to become Man City's all-time top Champions League scorer after equalling Aguero's record of 36 goals.

Haaland has scored 59 goals in 59 Champions League appearances but will now turn his attention to the Premier League, where City go to rivals Manchester United on Sunday, live on Sky Sports.

Manchester United

Manchester City Sunday 13th September 4:00pm Kick off 4:30pm

Haaland: I could've scored more in Porto win

Haaland has hit five goals in five appearances across all competitions under new boss Enzo Maresca - but the ex-Borussia Dortmund forward felt he could have scored more against Porto.

He told Amazon Prime: "Amazing game against the champions of Portugal. We knew it was going to be a difficult fight, man against man. They're a top team, impressive, all of them. They play amazing football.

"Well done to them. But with all the pressure, we have to deliver on the biggest stage. That's what we did tonight.

"Honestly, we controlled the whole first half. Of course, it's a bit uncomfortable when they come high. But we created a lot of chances. I could have easily had a few more goals.

"But second half, we scored and they managed to push us for a good 25 minutes. We managed to hold through and finish the game.

"These are the games we have to win. We had a great start to the season, and in the Champions League, you have to win games. If not, you get all the pressure."

Sports.title: From honeymoon vision to the Super Bowl - can Seahawks win it all again?
Sports.content:
Honeymoons are for newlyweds celebrating true love and for future NFL head coaches plotting Super Bowl glory. At least in the case of Mike Macdonald, who has now turned to the Chicago Bulls as his recipe reference for a repeat.

Mystic Macdonald went viral earlier this year when the Seattle Seahawks released footage of his first-ever team meeting upon being appointed in 2024. Within it, he had strayed from his script to forecast a place at the NFC Championship Game and an 'inevitable' feel to a 'won't die, won't quit' machine.

"It probably came to me about 30 minutes before the meeting," Macdonald tells Sky Sports of his viral speech.

Between some fine fortune-telling and a relentless winning formula, that vision became a reality 21 months later as Seattle beat the Los Angeles Rams to reach Super Bowl LX.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from Super Bowl 60 as the Seattle Seahawks took on the New England Patriots in California

It would eventually culminate in Macdonald's skyward gaze towards the cloud of confetti and fireworks honouring his Seahawks as NFL champions following their victory over the New England Patriots at Levi's Stadium in February.

"The message wasn't winning the NFC Championship, it was the feeling of our team that we were trying to create, of the trust, the bond, the connection and toughness, and trying to get them to feel compelled of where we wanted to go, and understand the daily inputs and things we can do to create that way of life and habits to make that vision be allowed to come to life.

"Everybody is worried about their first team meeting. I overthought it tremendously. It's like your wedding speech, you write out something like crazy and toss the paper in the garbage and end up speaking from the heart."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Divisional Round matchup between the Los Angeles Rams and the Seattle Seahawks

The message relayed this year was similar as Macdonald retained the same united principles in Seattle's bid to reach successive Super Bowls. It came with the reminder that the Chicago Bulls were more than simply their prized No 23.

"The 91 Bulls, you think it's the first year of the three-peat," Macdonald explained. "It was from the first time Phil Jackson took over the Bulls and the vision he had for their basketball team, like the spirit and energy behind their offense and how they wanted to play team basketball and the flow state they were trying to create.

"It's from a book called Sacred Hoops. I read that back on my Honeymoon in 2021 and it was the first time I had the vision of what it would look like if I was in charge of a team and what we would be like.

"That was kind of the grassroots or origin story of 12 is One, the synergy behind the team. It's explaining how that vision came to life with Phil Jackson and how everybody had to buy in to become the team they wanted to become.

"They had the best player in the world, but to become the best team in the world they all had to buy in rather than just defer to Michael (Jordan) every play."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Seattle's defensive coordinator Aden Durde was in a buoyant mood after he became the first British coach to win a Super Bowl

JSN: Darnold shut up the doubters

Among those central to Seattle's success last season was Jaxon Smith-Njigba as he led the NFL with 1,793 receiving yards on the way to winning Offensive Player of the Year.

His connection with Sam Darnold buried any doubts that may have still existed over the quarterback's ability to steer Seattle towards a championship.

Darnold signed with the Seahawks during the 2025 offseason after resurrecting his career with the Minnesota Vikings the previous campaign.

"It was awesome to be a part of his journey," Smith-Njigba told Sky Sports. "His journey is definitely crazy, a lot of ups and downs; that's how life is.

"With the quarterback position you get a lot of publicity and a lot of media attention, if we lose it's on you, if we win it's the team, so for me to just be out there with him, being there when I can for him, staying open, catching the ball and doing my job for him, it felt great.

"I was happy we could shut a lot of doubters and naysayers up; they can't say too much now. The proof is in the pudding."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The best plays from the impressive connection between quarterback Sam Darnold and wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba

Smith-Njigba was rewarded for his emergence as one of the NFL's premier receivers with a four-year, $168m contract extension, making him the highest-paid player in his position in league history.

"It's a blessing. I want to be here. I love putting on the Seahawks helmet and being in this facility around great people; for me to add a few years to this extension is a dream come true for me," he said.

"I wouldn't want to be anywhere else. For us to get it done early I really appreciate it so I can lock in and focus on the next step.

"I think this offseason was a great time for me to figure myself out and grow as a player and person. I think growing as a person evolves me into a better player.

"I think you'll see a different level from me coming into the season."

The only notable changes to the Seahawks this offseason came on offense. Super Bowl running back Kenneth Walker III signed with the Kansas City Chiefs in free agency, while offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak was hired as the new head coach of the Las Vegas Raiders.

The latter's departure has paved the way for a new voice on offense in the form of Brian Fleury, who previously served as San Francisco 49ers run game coordinator and tight ends coach.

"I've been lucky enough to deal with great football minds; he's definitely one, and it's exciting to be around that," said Smith-Njigba.

While Macdonald continues to preach the same values and mindset that inspired Seattle's Super Bowl run, he too has welcomed the addition of a fresh outlook and encouraged Fleury to stamp his mark.

"Brian has done a great job," said Macdonald. "The challenge he has is he's coming into a team with a lot of continuity within the staff, and a lot with the personnel.

"The easy thing to do is fall in line, but that's not how we want to operate; we want him to add his vision and empower him to add what he sees and his talents to the whole engine, and see where it takes us."

Smith-Njigba recalls the moment the clocks hit zero at Super Bowl 60, and the ensuing rush to find a teammate to embrace. The person he came across was cornerback and draft classmate Devon Witherspoon, prompting screaming and I love yous amid Seattle euphoria.

He had always envisioned it ending this way.

"I was very very confident going into the Super Bowl," he reflected. "The Patriots are a great team and in football anything can happen but I was just really confident.

"I knew we were going to win the game. I knew our gameplan was good, we just had to go out there and prove it.

It was an unbelievable experience."

But this is a new story, a new Seahawks team, and a new opportunity. As far as Macdonald, Smith-Njigba and the champions are concerned, the celebrations are over.

"We really just want to be in the moment," he said. "We'll take it one step at a time and let the story tell itself."
