Sports.title: Why Wolff compared Antonelli to an “AI agent" after Italian GP win
Sports.content:
Mercedes boss Toto Wolff admits that even he has been surprised by the rapid growth shown by Kimi Antonelli over the course of the 2026 Formula 1 season, likening him to an "AI agent" that is always improving.

The 20-year-old Italian is in just his second F1 season after being fast-tracked to the top tier as a replacement for Lewis Hamilton when he left the Silver Arrows ahead of the 2025 season.

In his first year, Antonelli faced an up and down campaign, and struggled over the European rounds in particular. This led to some onlookers to question Wolff’s decision to promote the youngster, but he always stood by the move.

“Last year was according to plan,” the Austrian said. “I've said there are going to be moments of brilliance, difficult moments.

“I think he started the season at a time when he found himself like a deer in the headlights. In his zone, in the car, extraordinary performances already, but not continuous.

“Then he had this negative spell where he made over nine races without scoring points. I remember Spa was terrible for him and he was feeling down. Monza was the point where I for the first time said to him, 'listen, you've got to wake up here'. But never doubting. That's why we gave him the opportunity.”

Kimi Antonelli had a rough debut season with Mercedes in 2025 Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

The topsy-turvy results were gone after the winter break, however, when F1 entered its new era and Mercedes made the jump from scrapping to make the podium to being a title-contending team once again.

Along with the improvement made to the team’s performance came a leap in Antonelli’s own results, and the Italian now leads the F1 standings over team-mate George Russell who lags 66 points behind. This, Wolff admits, came as a shock to even him.

"He came out after the winter, out of the blocks in a way that no one saw coming,” Wolff said.

“The ability, how he processed last year. He's been at all the races. He's seen the pressure of the media, the attention that he gets. It's in a way that the system has been processed and saved. And that's why [he's had] the results that we've seen afterwards.

“But it is still surprising and amazing to see how quickly he develops. For me, it's like an AI agent that continuously self-improves and learns. That's the speed.

“Also his age is for sure beneficial. The ability cognitively, intellectually to constantly become better.”

Toto Wolff stands by his decision to promote Kimi Antonelli to partner George Russell Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Despite the impressive turnaround in his results, which was exemplified in Monza where he charged to victory from 19th after taking an engine penalty, Antonelli isn’t getting ahead of himself.

He has remained calm after each victory and taken stock on the odd occasion that he has made mistakes in 2026. Now, with a substantial lead over his more experienced team-mate, Antonelli said he is just taking the season as it comes.

“I just take race by race because you never know what can happen,” Antonelli told Sky Sports after the Italian GP. “Today went well, we had a massive opportunity and we took it, but of course next week we have Madrid and it's going to be a new challenge.

“We will have to be on top of the game because it's a new track for everyone and it's going to be important to be on point in order to maximise the track time and everything.

“I'm going to enjoy this moment and then focus on the next one and then focus on the next one again until the end of the season.”

F1 will return to action this weekend with the Spanish Grand Prix, which moves from its traditional home in Barcelona to the new Madring circuit.

Sports.title: Hadjar to miss third F1 race due to injury
Sports.content:
Isack Hadjar requires more time to recover from his wrist injury, which will see the Frenchman sit out his third consecutive grand prix at this weekend's Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid.

Liam Lawson will return to the RB22 to partner Max Verstappen, while Yuki Tsunoda gets another race with Racing Bulls.

"The decision has been taken as Isack's recovery continues to progress positively," Red Bull communicated on Monday evening. "While he is not yet ready to return to the cockpit, he will be in Madrid supporting the team."

Hadjar sustained a wrist fracture at the end of the summer break while boxing, which is a regular part of his workout routine. It forced the sophomore driver out of August's Dutch Grand Prix, with Red Bull moving regular Racing Bulls driver Lawson to the parent team's car alongside Verstappen while reserve driver Tsunoda was handed an F1 comeback with the junior team.

With Red Bull not keen to take any risk with Hadjar's injury, Lawson and Tsunoda remained on station for last weekend's Italian Grand Prix in Monza.

Isack Hadjar, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

Given the short turnaround to this weekend's Madrid race as part of a double-header, Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies had already indicated a return to competition at the brand-new Madring circuit would be "tricky" for Hadjar. Now it has been confirmed that Hadjar will miss his third grand prix in a row.

In Hadjar's absence, Lawson enjoyed his return to Red Bull in much less turbulent circumstances than his curtailed two-race stint at the start of 2025. The New Zealander took seventh in Zandvoort, while he was unable to recover from an engine penalty to score points in Monza.

Tsunoda took his first point of the campaign at the Italian round in 10th place, though Audi is still considering an appeal against the stewards' decision not to penalise the Japanese driver for causing an extra formation lap.

Sports.title: How Monza introduced oval-like slipstream racing to F1
Sports.content:
There have been several examples of Formula 1 2026's regulations radically changing the style of racing at some of the 24 circuits on the calendar, but Monza's slipstream festival was the most dramatic example yet.

A brand-new term coined to describe this year's spectacle is the so-called yo-yo racing, where cars are easily able to complete overtakes using the extra grunt from the battery but then are unable to break away or keep that position as they run out of energy.

Monza's 53-lapper was perhaps to most extreme version of yo-yo racing yet, with cars hounding each other in packs without being able to break away, because the huge tow on Monza's long straights further boosted the effectiveness of the electric overtake mode, allowing intrinsically slower cars to keep up with the car in front.

That was most obvious with Red Bull's Max Verstappen, who did not have the power unit performance to genuinely challenge the Mercedes cars for the win. But the huge slipstream effect combined with 2026's energy deployment needs meant he was still able to stick with George Russell for a long time as the Briton was unable to break away, only to be a sitting duck whenever the Dutchman found a way past.

"To be honest, [I didn’t enjoy it] a lot when people just drive by you like you’re a turtle," Verstappen said. "With the overtake mode, it looked quite promising, but as soon as I got in the lead, it was very hard to defend. Even when we had the VSC, we boxed, had better tyres, I’m overtaking cars, but as soon as they can hang in that overtake mode, it’s just too powerful for us to actually defend against that."

Oscar Piastri and Lewis Hamilton, who had lost touch with the lead pair before the mid-race virtual safety car, also formed an initial pocket of cars, as did Lando Norris and Pierre Gasly.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

This is where veteran oval drivers would perhaps try and work together and trade the lead on purpose as efficiently as possible. But on an F1 road course that's much harder to do, and Russell and Verstappen cost each other enough time for Kimi Antonelli to make a spectacular comeback through the field.

"Somehow with these Formula 1 [regulations], it's not easy to get an overtake completed and move on," McLaren team boss Andrea Stella explained. "If you see how much it took for Lando to pass Gasly and then start to close the gap to the cars ahead.

"We see that there's certainly been quite a lot of entertainment, but to some extent there were also some issues for a quicker car to be able to compete if you don't start at the front of the grid."

Ferrari team boss Fred Vasseur added: "The race pace was probably okay-ish. The main issue was top speed and overtaking. It was quite impossible for us to attack or to defend. When we were attacking someone, we were draining the battery, and next straight line we were losing the position."

Stella called the Italian GP weekend one of the busiest weekends of the year for his crew as it tried to optimise the strategy and set-up for this new style of racing, which has dominated the conversation around energy-hungry circuits.

"Very, very busy for everyone, drivers and engineers, with managing the power unit and the battery on a circuit like Monza," he added. "This becomes the dominating element of racing. We see that jointly with the slipstream a faster car actually can struggle then to pull away from a slower car.

Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

"This could make a [difference per lap] of as much as half a second, the combination of the slipstream and the fact that you have a car behind that you start to use the boost to defend [against] and then you lose a lot of pace.

"Monza 2026, I think, will be remembered as the most relevant race with the new regulations. It required a high quality from an execution point of view. I think we did, but overall we were not in contention for the victory because Mercedes had a step advantage on everyone else."

Indeed, eventual winner Antonelli was the only driver to buck that pack racing trend, as he marched up the order form 19th on the grid. Antonelli did a lot of the hard work early on by running has high as sixth after the lap 6 restart, which gave him chance of an unlikely comeback win.

But while some of Antonelli's astonishing progress can be ascribed to Mercedes' superior energy deployment, the fact that he was the only driver to move up from group to group while team-mate Russell couldn't break away from Verstappen at the front also shows the driver deserves plenty of credit, with the 20-year-old Italian showcasing aggressive but meticulous overtaking skills and car placement.

"The differentiator today was the ability going through the traffic," said Antonelli's team boss Toto Wolff. "And we've seen it with other great ones in the past. Lewis, who did it at some of the races, and that's what Kimi has shown today. There's just no stopping [him]. When a driver and a car are one, then there's nothing that can stop them."

Sports.title: What doesn't make sense about Hamilton and Leclerc's Italian GP clash
Sports.content:
There is nothing particularly new in the way Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton conducted themselves on and off the track on Sunday, either in the history of Formula 1 or motorsport more generally.

Clashes between team-mates have, in some cases, reached levels of tension that make what happened between the two Ferrari drivers at Monza look relatively minor. But in this particular case, something does not quite add up. Perhaps there is something we are missing - because otherwise it remains difficult to understand.

The major clashes of the past between team-mates regarded as "top drivers" have always had a clear objective.

Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost, Nigel Mansell and Nelson Piquet, Mark Webber and Sebastian Vettel, Nico Rosberg and Hamilton: all of these pairings became fierce rivals when they had a car capable of fighting for the world championship - when, in other words, success depended almost entirely on their ability to beat the driver on the other side of the garage.

Take the most recent example. In 2013, Hamilton's first year at Mercedes, the car allowed him to win one race, while Rosberg ended the season with two victories. The W04 was not a championship-winning car, and the relationship between the two Mercedes drivers remained excellent. The following season, with the arrival of Mercedes' formidable first hybrid power unit, things changed dramatically. Suddenly, the biggest prize was at stake, and the pair went from eating pizza together in Monaco to an intense sporting rivalry that extended well beyond the track.

With Leclerc and Hamilton, the motive is a mystery.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

It is worth stressing that what has happened between the Ferrari drivers is not comparable to the examples above. Whatever Ferrari may say publicly about its ambitions - not least to keep motivation high both at the track and at the factory - it is difficult to seriously believe that its drivers are currently fighting for the world title. The numbers say so, as does the story of this season.

Nor is there a future to secure or contractual status to fight for. Both have the same opportunities, and both have their 2027 plans long since settled. And both, after all, are paid handsomely enough to make a joke heard in the Monza paddock yesterday rather inappropriate: no, this is definitely not a case of two people fighting over crumbs.

And that last point is important: ultimately, both are paid by Ferrari to deliver for Ferrari. They are established drivers, from whom you would expect an approach that always takes the team's interests into account - particularly when they don't have a car capable of making a world championship fight a realistic prospect.

Hamilton spent the whole of 2025 swallowing his frustration, unable to produce the level of performance that his team-mate consistently delivered. Having rediscovered his pace, he is probably enjoying the chance to prove a few points to everyone, Leclerc included.

Leclerc, meanwhile, saw his status grow considerably last year after consistently outperforming the seven-time world champion. Just 12 months later, the situation has changed, with Hamilton now comfortably ahead of him in the championship standings.

But the need to prove yourself against your team-mate is usually more pressing in the midfield, where one podium can define a whole season and a driver's future is rarely guaranteed. Beating your team-mate at any cost may be a priority for someone fighting to keep their seat - not for two established stars whose futures are already secure.

Frédéric Vasseur, Ferrari Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

Now the ball is in Fred Vasseur's court. Ferrari's team principal met both drivers in his office at Monza before the race, but it appears a second meeting may be required.

The principle is simple: the interests of the team must come before individual ambitions. Especially when the prize they are fighting for is not a world championship.

A rivalry can be an asset when it pushes a team towards success. But when there is no world championship at stake and it starts working against the interests of the team, it becomes nothing more than another problem - and Ferrari already has enough of those.

Sports.title: Hamilton says Ferrari has left it "too late" to back him in F1 title fight
Sports.content:
The Italian Grand Prix is probably the worst venue for a spat to brew up between team-mates but that is what happened at Monza as Lewis Hamilton finished a distant sixth after Charles Leclerc barged him into the gravel on the opening lap.

Leclerc then spun off into the Parabolica barrier at high speed at the end of the second lap, inducing a red flag. The outcome of the weekend was that Hamilton lost more ground to Mercedes team-mates Kimi Antonelli and George Russell in the title race, while Ferrari slipped 122 points behind Mercedes in the constructors' standings.

Antonelli is now 66 points ahead of Russell and 76 clear of Hamilton, while Leclerc lies fifth, 112 points adrift of Antonelli.

Hamilton has been critical of Ferrari's execution on several occasions this year, especially when dealing with team orders in scenarios where the drivers are on different strategies. In the Dutch GP, he felt a podium finish was left on the table when the team appeared to dither over how to get Leclerc out of his way at a point where Hamilton was running faster on fresher tyres.

Hamilton clearly feels that he should have been prioritised, given he is closer to the Mercedes drivers than Leclerc in the drivers' championship, but the opportunity has slipped away.

Hamilton spoke frankly about his championship prospects after finishing sixth in Monza Photo by: Getty Images

"I think from today, we've just lost so much ground to them [Mercedes] on points," he told media including Motorsport.com at Monza.

"It's far too late for those decisions to come. It's many, many weeks too late.

"All I can do is just try and turn up. I'll get up tomorrow morning and I'll give it my best. Ultimately today, I feel massively gutted for the tifosi, who showed up for us today.

"The guys back at the factory, who really, really are giving it everything. You know yesterday we didn't really execute that well. I think the same today.

"It's tough. I'm giving it everything I can, but sometimes it's just not enough. You need all the other stuff to come together.

Ferrari might not have had a car quick enough to challenge for outright victory at Monza, but it made the job of maximising it potential needlessly difficult. Throughout qualifying it struggled to orchestrate its drivers to provide a slipstream for one another – essential at this circuit, given the number of straights – to the point where Hamilton was almost eliminated in Q2.

In his first Q3 run, Hamilton was sent out of the pits late, so he struggled to pick up a slipstream from the cars ahead. He did obtain a tow from Leclerc on his second run and lined up just behind his team-mate on the grid as they were promoted to third and fourth by Oscar Piastri's impeding penalty.

Hamilton appeared to get his nose ahead on the inside line into Turn 1, then was still ahead at Turn 2 only for Leclerc to push him wide, onto the gravel. Leclerc held on to third while Hamilton dropped to 10th.

After the race, Leclerc framed the incident in terms of mutual responsibility, saying, "we went too far". But Hamilton saw otherwise – although taking the inside line into the first part of this chicane tends to put the driver on the outside line into the left-hander that follows, inviting collisions such as this.

Diversion via the gravel dropped Hamilton to P10 Photo by: Getty Images

"I was ahead in Turn 2. By the apex, I was ahead. There was no 'we' in it.

"Look, I don't race dirty. I've always raced clean and fairly and always left space.

"I've come into the team and tried to be respectful of space and definitely not put the team in jeopardy. I stand by that and all I can talk about is on my side. You have to speak to Fred [Vasseur, team principal] about the other side and decisions that are taken there.

"Ultimately it comes from the top. It trickles down, decisions. It starts with Fred.

"There's only so much you can say, so much you can push and shout from the mountain top. Yesterday, I said we've got to look at how we communicate. If we continue to travel the same path, we get the same result.

"We keep getting the same result. We've got to change things because it's not helping us move forward. I think they're receptive to it and we'll take it offline over the next, probably not next week, but particularly after the next race, to try and look at how we can procedurally make things different so that the same thing can't happen.

"I think the guys in the factory are doing a really great job. We're not executing as cleanly as well as we can. Easily not as well as now the other teams are. But we were at some points in the season."

Executing team orders is a challenging proposition for Ferrari, given Leclerc's status within the organisation. It's understood that his management was instrumental in Vasseur's appointment, having convinced senior management that regime change was required when Mattia Binotto was team principal.

But if team-mates take points off one another, the damage can extend beyond the race to the drivers' title. The constructors' trophy may be less important to fans, but the order of that championship determines the team's share of the commercial revenues. Indiscipline can therefore have a direct effect on the balance sheet.

"I think it comes down to rules of engagement," said Hamilton.

"When I was at Mercedes, we had a written rule of engagement. We never really had it too bad. Maybe moments with me and Nico [Rosberg] a couple of times. But more often than not it was good.

"Here, there are no rules."

Sports.title: Audi signals appeal over Tsunoda’s Italian GP non-penalty
Sports.content:
The Audi Formula 1 team has notified the FIA of its intention to appeal against Yuki Tsunoda's non-penalty in the Italian Grand Prix.

Amid confusion over where he was supposed to line up on a lap 6 restart, Tsunoda parked in his correct 14th grid slot, but at an angle towards the inside wall. Race director Rui Marques was "not comfortable" with Tsunoda's position, so imposed an extra formation lap.

According to Article B5.9.4 of the F1 2026 sporting regulations, "any driver who caused an extra formation lap, and is then able to start the, or any subsequent, extra formation lap must enter the Pit Lane at the end of the lap and must start ... from the end of the Pit Lane."

But according to the FIA race stewards, Tsunoda didn't technically cause the extra formation lap because the race director acted out of an abundance of caution, Tsunoda wasn't out of his grid slot and didn't impact other competitors. The crux of the issue is that race control hadn't informed Racing Bulls that its driver had caused the extra formation lap either, so therefore the team had no reason to tell Tsunoda to start from the pitlane.

Tsunoda escaped a stop-and-go penalty and went on to score the final point in 10th. The decision not to punish the Japanese driver impacted Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto, who crossed the line in 11th.

As a result, Audi has notified the FIA of its intention to appeal against the non-penalty for Tsunoda.

"Following the Italian Grand Prix, we raised a concern regarding the application of Article B5.9.4, which requires a driver who causes an extra formation lap to enter the pit lane and resume the race from there," Audi said in a statement. "The Stewards issued a decision of No Further Action, and we have notified our intention to appeal. As the matter is now subject to the FIA appeal process, we will not comment further at this stage."

Gabriel Bortoleto would have gained a point in Monza if Yuki Tsunoda had been handed a penalty. Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Per article 15.4 of the FIA's International Sporting Code, competitors have one hour after the stewards' decision to notify their intention to appeal. That does not mean Audi is actually appealing against the verdict just yet. But it gives the team an additional 96-hour time window to further study the case to see if there is an element to appeal against before following through on it.

In their verdict, the stewards wrote: "The extra formation lap resulted from the Race Director’s assessment of the situation, rather than being directly caused by the driver of Car 22.

"Further, Article B5.9.4 goes on to specify that if a driver who causes the extra formation lap and is then able to start the extra formation lap, he must enter the Pit Lane at the end of the lap and start from the Pit Lane. It is only then, if the driver fails to do this, that the mandatory penalty of a Stop and Go penalty is imposed.

"In other words, the penalty is for failing to come into the Pit Lane and start from there. The penalty is not for causing the extra formation lap, if indeed, he caused the extra formation lap in the first place.

"A critical issue emerges here, in that in order to comply with the requirement to enter and start from the Pit Lane, a driver would need to know that he was the cause of the extra formation lap."

The stewards added: "The team, based on the fact that the car was positioned within its starting grid box in compliance with the regulations, had, in our determination, no reason to instruct its driver to enter and start from the Pit Lane.

"Accordingly, irrespective of whether or not the driver directly caused the extra formation lap, the team and driver were unaware that they were being considered as the cause, therefore we determine that we are unable to impose a Stop and Go penalty in this case, and decide to take no further action."

Sports.title: Why Mercedes didn't pit Russell under virtual safety car in Italian GP
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli's sensational win from the back of the grid in the Italian Grand Prix was thanks to a great drive, but perhaps also a little help from strategy and a timely virtual safety car.

The Italian was the only Mercedes driver to make a pitstop during the race - and ultimately defeated his team-mate and championship rival George Russell.

Mercedes split the strategies between its drivers, putting Antonelli on mediums after the early red flag. That was the only option for the Italian to go to the end without stopping, having started the race on hards. Russell, on the other hand, started on mediums and switched to hards after the race was stopped following Charles Leclerc's crash - and stayed on that tyre for the rest of the distance.

For Antonelli, Mercedes used the opportunity to put him on a new set of mediums when Lance Stroll's stoppage caused a virtual safety car on lap 27.

By that point, Antonelli had already made his way through the field and was battling Russell for the lead - although Mercedes asked him not to attack his team-mate after the initial phase of the fight, allowing them to try to build a gap to Max Verstappen.

Then came the call for Antonelli to pit. And although the Italian was able to come back and overtake his team-mate on fresher tyres, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff said the team itself didn't know which strategy would ultimately prove better.

“We didn't know what was the better strategy," he told the media, including Autosport, after the race. "At that stage, the system said that the one-stop [for Russell] comes out ahead. That two-stop was coming close to the end, but wouldn't catch. So that's what the software said.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

“It was also the right thing to split the strategies because it was unknown what the better one would be. In the morning meeting we said the hard tyre is going to go forever. You can start on it and finish on it and you can see with George it was a forever tyre but it didn't have the performance that of the medium.”

The decision to stop Antonelli was made despite him reporting that his tyres were in good shape.

“We didn't talk to Kimi about the stop," Wolff confirmed. "We asked for the state of the tyre and he said, 'Well it's actually good' but it was clear that we saw abrasion and I think it was on Lewis' car. We saw some abrasion on a McLaren. So it was the right thing to do. And that's why it didn't need any big discussion.

“But then having said that, Kimi was able to extract 35 laps or 40 laps from that tyre in a consistent way and that's certainly his skill.”

Russell himself believes he had enough pace to win the race had Antonelli stayed on the same strategy.

"I would have loved to have continued on the same strategy," he said during the post-race press conference. "Because I felt in a good position in that battle. I knew exactly what I needed to do with the energy management to defend but also when to attack and make those moves and I put a lot of preparation into this race in that regard.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

"Then of course when the VSC came out, it came out at that perfect point for the drivers to pull the trigger and take the pitstop."

Asked whether he had considered stopping for fresh rubber at that point, Russell said: "I didn't. I actually thought the guys behind me were going to stay out as well but I'm sure the team were quite nervous on the pitwall watching our battle and were probably quite happy to send us on different strategies.

"When we had Max in the mix as well from a team perspective, you're covering off both scenarios. So, today Kimi did a great job.

"I was on the hard tyre and Kimi was on the medium tyre. So if either of us were to pit, it was going to be Kimi. And that's why I was just a little bit annoyed with the timing of that VSC, because I think it would have been tough for those guys on the medium to have competed with anybody on the hard tyre.

"But, it takes nothing away from Kimi's drive altogether. It would have been very interesting to see how the race would have panned out if there was no VSC."

After the race at Monza, Russell trails Antonelli by 66 points in the championship.

Sports.title: Lawson and Tsunoda are proof of how “unnatural” 2026 F1 rules are – Verstappen | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen says the ease with which drivers can adapt to new cars show how unchallenging Formula 1 has become.

The Red Bull driver says F1’s 2026 regulations have removed much of the challenge of driving cars at the limit.

“In the history of the sport, normally the driver that is the most committed, the latest on the brakes, earlier on throttle, committing in the high speed, they get rewarded, because you just gain that time in the corner,” Verstappen told the BBC.

“But now you’re constantly thinking about, ‘In this corner I might have to hold in a bit. Go later on throttle. Or brake earlier. Or lift off. And then I have more top speed.’ Stuff like that. It’s so unnatural. It’s so not how it should be.”

Liam Lawson rejoined Verstappen at Red Bull two rounds ago as a substitute for the injured Isack Hadjar. Yuki Tsunoda, another of Verstappen’s former team mates, took Lawson’s place at Racing Bulls. Both adapted to their new cars quickly.

Indicating his comments were not intended as a criticism of his rivals, Verstappen said the fact both drivers were able to adapt so quickly shows F1’s 2026 cars give poor rewards to the drivers who wring the most out of them.

“No disrespect,” he said. “And I hope no-one picks up on this. But look at Yuki. He jumps in the car [at the Dutch Grand Prix]. Never driven the car before. Immediately competitive.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“Liam jumps from the Racing Bulls to the Red Bull – immediately competitive. It’s because these cars are numb to your driver inputs.

“Of course, yes, you still have to do a good lap. And you still have to commit. The fastest drivers will always come out on top. But it’s really, really limited, like a choke hold or something. You’re held back.”

Despite his repeated criticisms of F1’s 2026 regulations, Verstappen recently signed a new deal to continue racing for Red Bull in the series. However he wants to see F1 go further with the changes to the rules it has announced for the coming seasons.

“[I’m] hoping that it will be better in the future. Accepting where we are at the moment. Still the love for the sport. Not at the moment the driving. But the love for the sport.

“I love competition, naturally. I just hope that in the coming years, towards 2030, it can only get better. And to start to make the best of it, because these are the rules for the next four or five years.”

Sports.title: Stats: Antonelli scores first home win for an Italian Formula 1 driver in 36 years | 2026 Italian Grand Prix stats and facts
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli scored the 50th grand prix victory for an Italian driver last weekend in his home event.

However there have been more recent home victories for Italians. Riccardo Patrese won at Imola in 1990 when the race carried the title ‘San Marino’ Grand Prix. Another Italian, Elio de Angelis, won the same race five years earlier, though this was a conspicuously obscure triumph as he never led a lap, inheriting victory when Alain Prost was disqualified.

Antonelli’s seventh career win means his tally of wins now matches that of team mate George Russell. For the first time in five rounds Russell led a grand prix, but despite heading the field for 40 out of 53 laps he had to settle for second place.

The most outstanding aspect of Antonelli’s win was that he started 19th on the grid. Only one of the previous 1,161 world championship rounds was won from a lower starting position: John Watson’s victory in the 1983 United States Grand Prix West at Long Beach, from 22nd on the grid. One other driver also won from 19th: Bill Vukovich in the 1954 Indianapolis 500.

Antonelli also set the fastest lap, for the 10th time in his career. He now has as many as Graham Hill, John Surtees and Mario Andretti.

Pierre Gasly led a race for the first time this year and the second time in his career. The only other F1 race he led was also at Monza, when he scored his shock victory in 2020 for AlphaTauri.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Making up for the disappointment of losing his Monaco Grand Prix podium finish on Friday, Gasly scored his and Alpine’s first pole position the following day. Only one driver in F1 history has started more races before taking a pole position: Sergio Perez took 216 starts, Gasly 191.

Gasly is the 108th different driver in F1 history to take pole position. That made France the fourth country to have 10 different pole-winners, the others being Britain, the USA and Italy. Gasly joins Alain Prost, Rene Arnoux, Jacques Laffite, Jean-Pierre Jabouille, Patrick Tambay, Didier Pironi, Jean-Pierre Jarier, Jean Alesi and Patrick Depailler.

With the changes made to the cars this year, the pole position time for this year’s Italian Grand Prix was the slowest in dry weather conditions for more than a decade. Gasly’s 1’21.786 was almost two-and-a-half seconds off Max Verstappen’s record-breaking pace 12 months ago.

In his second race back in an F1 car, Yuki Tsunoda finished 10th and scored the 125th point of his career. That ties him with Kamui Kobayashi for the most points scored by a Japanese driver. However Audi is appealing a decision made by the stewards regarding Tsunoda, so that could change.

It was a weekend to forget for Ferrari as Charles Leclerc crashed out at Parabolica, in another parallel with the 2020 race. He had already forced Lewis Hamilton off at the start, though he recovered to finish sixth. However Mercedes’ latest victory means their engines have now powered 250 grand prix victories. Ferrari remain ahead on 251, but they look likely to lose their status as F1’s most successful engine builder before the year is over – thanks in no small part to the efforts of Italy’s new star.

Sports.title: Featured Comment: Is F1’s racing in 2026 better or worse than the DRS era? | Brief
Sports.content:
Has Formula 1 racing become better or worse – or more or less authentic – after swapping last year’s Drag Reduction System for its new regulations? Here’s part of N2000’s detailed assessment:

I kept watching out of a hope that F1 would get better over the years: hoping DRS was temporary, to 2022 fixing the issues of the previous era of regulations, to 2026 getting away from the failure of the ground effect era, but now I’m done.

[DRS] is the start of the current era F1 finds itself in. Ever since then, F1’s leadership has given up on organically improving the racing, choosing to spice up the racing with artificial elements like DRS, the early Pirelli tires, and now the 2026 batteries. After 2009’s aerodynamic regulations and 2010’s refuelling ban organically improving the racing, F1’s leadership decided to introduce DRS for the 2011. I was surprised to learn that this decision was made in June or July in 2010, because the common narrative around DRS’s introduction was that it was in response to Abu Dhabi 2010. By the way, not even DRS could improve racing at that awful track.

Back then, DRS was extremely powerful, and many fans criticised it for being overpowered, offering suggestions to reduce its effect like limiting its uses over the race. To give you an idea of what it was like in the post-2008 era, overtaking at Monaco was extremely difficult, but not near impossible like it is now. I can concede that DRS was actually good for Monaco, even if I am against its existence in principle.

As I mentioned above, I was one of those that naively believed that DRS was a temporary solution. But then we got 2017, undoing everything 2009 set out to accomplish, now using DRS as a crutch. I am sorry, but I am not going to cheer for “DRS wide open!” because I can tell something is wrong about pressing the button in the designated zone to pass. As an aside, I would not be surprised if F1’s leadership thought they could combat the increased dirty air from the 2017 aerodynamic regulations with DRS.

Not surprisingly, 2022 set out to fix 2017, but the ground effects brought their own issues.

This takes us to 2026, and we have more artificial racing thanks to the batteries and clipping. I thought we would replace DRS with using battery boost (like a significantly more powerful KERS), but it has led to yo-yo racing, and it is awfully predictable. And then there is a clipping, which makes the cars look pathetic. The 2014-2025 cars suffered from clipping, true, but always at the end of a straight when drag was at its highest, so it made sense to clip there. But now, cars are obviously clipping when they have not braked for too long. Fast corners, where drivers have had to demonstrate their commitment, are now cruised through because the car loses sufficient speed prior to the corner.

Somehow 2026 has managed to make DRS look good. At least with DRS we can tell who has the advantage. Battery charge is mostly kept hidden from us.

I write all of this because over the years – and recently thanks to Domenicali’s comments – F1 has made it clear that it cares more for the show than the integrity of the sport. The show is always a consideration for sports, but we can watch F1 in its current era and notice something is wrong, especially in 2026.

Sports.title: FIA won’t “jump the gun” over cancelling F1’s Middle East races – Ben Sulayem | Formula 1
Sports.content:
FIA president Mohamed Ben Sulayem says the governing body will not rush to relocate this year’s final two Formula 1 races unless it has to.

The status of the season-closing races in Qatar and the United Arab Emirates has been in doubt since the USA and Israel began bombing Iran earlier this year, leading to a wave of retaliatory strikes in the region.

A ceasefire agreement was reached in June. Both sides have launched further strikes since then, though not as extensively as they did when fighting first broke out.

Formula 1 CEO Stefano Domenicali previously said the series could relocate its final two rounds to Europe. However Ben Sulayem told the Associated Press it is “business as usual” for the governing body at present and “we are not changing anything unless we have to.”

“Being from that part of the world, we can’t jump the gun and just say, that’s it, we are canceling and then cancel,” he said.

“Are we going to allow our people, our staff, the drivers or the teams to go at risk? No, of course not. We will not. But we’ll have also to listen to the governments and to the local promoter there.”

The FIA’s World Endurance Championship has already abandoned its attempts to race in Qatar this year. It postponed its March season-opener at the Losail International Circuit until October, then called it off altogether two months ago. WEC has also shelved its plans to race in Bahrain in November.

F1 cancelled its races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia which were due to take place in April. It will instead hold an event titled the ‘Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia’ at the Sepang International Circuit next month.

Domenicali has indicated F1 will make its plans for the final races of the season clear in the middle of September.

Sports.title: Dana White Leaves Fury Joshua Accusation Unfinished
Sports.content:
“Tyson, thank you for all the kind words. You don’t have to be rocket scientists to see what’s going on here. I’ve been saying the same thing since Bournemouth. Since we had the fight in Bournemouth, I’ve been saying the same thing.”

White stopped there, but the target was not difficult to identify. Fury recently thanked him for arranging the Netflix agreement and helping get the proposed Joshua fight “over the line.” He has also accused Joshua and Eddie Hearn of blocking the event by insisting upon Wembley Stadium rather than Madison Square Garden.

That confidence dates to June. Following Zuffa Boxing’s Chris Billam-Smith card in Bournemouth, he told the media to “watch what happens over the next 30 days.” He later claimed TKO had completed the television and venue deals.

Three months later, no location has been confirmed, Fury is shopping for another opponent, and White has replaced his promised specifics with a cryptic response. By attaching a 30-day clock to his prediction, he created his own test of authority, and the continued delay has weakened his credibility.

Netflix and TKO have commercial reasons for favoring New York. A Friday night event at Madison Square Garden gives Netflix a valuable American prime time attraction without running directly against the NFL’s Sunday schedule. Wembley offers the historic British occasion, but accommodating American viewers may require an overnight main event that leaves local supporters with a 2 a.m. ring walk.

The intended conclusion is that Joshua and Hearn are refusing to cooperate. Hearn maintains that Joshua signed for a British venue and that TKO’s attempt to take the fight to New York requires different terms. Fury accepted the American proposal because his contract apparently did not restrict the event to Britain.

His Usyk callout also looks more like public pressure than a serious replacement plan. Usyk has already beaten Fury twice, and his manager Sergey Lapin dismissed the idea of becoming Fury’s backup option. Calling out Usyk gives Fury another way to portray Joshua as the obstacle while pressing him to accept the American venue.

The dispute has also exposed the limits of White’s control in boxing. Within the UFC, he controls the promotion, broadcaster, and matchmaking system. Fury versus Joshua involves separate contracts, rival promoters, Saudi financing, Netflix, TKO, and two fighters with conflicting venue provisions.

White can blame boxing’s fractured structure, but he has not found a way through it.

Sports.title: Conor Benn Questions Ryan Garcia’s Faceoff Absence
Sports.content:
Skipping the event fits Ryan’s refusal to follow the standard promotional script. Still, disappearing this late raises unnecessary concerns about his preparation. Everyone else is left to fill the empty space.

His unpredictability may irritate Benn more than another exchange of insults. Benn fights with emotion and clearly wanted the confrontation. Ryan denied him that opportunity while forcing the challenger to handle the promotional work alone.

The greater concern was Benn’s appearance. He looked painfully thin while standing on a balcony overlooking the Las Vegas Strip, with dark circles underneath both eyes. That does not prove he is struggling with the 147-pound limit, but his drawn face will receive plenty of attention when he steps on the scale Friday.

The champion’s history adds interest to that moment. He came in 3.2 pounds above the contracted limit for his 2024 fight with Devin Haney, paid a financial penalty and fought anyway. There is no indication that he will repeat that against Benn, but his previous disregard for the limit gives the challenger another reason to study the numbers closely.

Much of Benn’s recent career has been spent above welterweight. Returning to 147 demands a stricter cut, and the real concern is how effectively he rehydrates afterward. He depends on explosive hooks, constant pressure, and enough stamina to chase opponents for twelve rounds.

Kell Brook offers a cautionary comparison. Brook jumped from welterweight to middleweight for Gennadiy Golovkin, then returned to 147 to defend his title against Errol Spence Jr. He struggled late and was stopped in the eleventh round, although another orbital injury also contributed to the ending.

After two physical middleweight fights with Chris Eubank Jr., Benn is cutting back to welterweight. His recovery following Friday’s official weight check matters more than the number itself.

He cannot afford to drain himself while Ryan arrives comfortably at the limit. Benn’s tactical case depends on closing distance and forcing exchanges. If he lacks the strength or energy to pressure Ryan, he is unlikely to win a controlled fight behind the jab.

The weight issue connects directly to Ryan’s counter left hook. Benn often leaps inside with hooks and overhand rights, leaving openings as he attacks. Once Ryan begins timing those forward bursts, Benn will need something beyond aggression.

A high output is not required to punish those mistakes. One clean counter left hook may be enough to alter the fight, especially if returning to welterweight has reduced Benn’s punch resistance.

Saturday will also be Ryan’s first defense of the WBC title he won from Mario Barrios. He is no longer the unpredictable challenger with nothing to protect. Missing a scheduled faceoff during the week of that defense renews familiar doubts about his discipline, even if it reveals little about his physical preparation.

Benn won Wednesday’s argument without throwing a punch. The real evidence comes Friday, when his condition afterward provides the first clue about what returning to 147 has cost him.

Sports.title: Katie Taylor The GWOAT?
Sports.content:
Five years later, at the age of 15, Katie Taylor and Alanna Audley fought in Ireland’s first-ever sanctioned female amateur boxing match. Taylor would go on to compete and win the gold medal in the 2012 London Olympics.

Taylor made her pro boxing debut in November 2016 when she stopped Karina Kopinska in the third round. A year later, Taylor would win her first world title when she defeated Anahi Sanchez and won the WBA lightweight belt.

After becoming a unified world champion, Taylor defeated Cindy Serrano by way of unanimous decision. Four years later, as the undisputed lightweight world champion, Taylor would make history with Cindy’s younger sister.

On April 30, 2022, Katie Taylor and Amanda Serrano made history when they became the first women boxers to headline an event at Madison Square Garden. In the icon vs icon battle, Katie Taylor won via split decision.

Taylor would experience adversity for the first time in her homecoming bout when Chantelle Cameron outpointed her and retained the undisputed super-lightweight world title. In the immediate rematch, Taylor won via majority decision.

With the victory, Katie Taylor became a two-weight undisputed world champion. Next on Taylor’s agenda was a rematch with Amanda Serrano. Taylor would defeat Serrano in back-to-back bouts to tally a trilogy record of 3-0.

She concluded her career in Dublin, Ireland, at Croke Park, where she beat the previously undefeated Flora Pili and won the undisputed super-lightweight crown. Now, as she calls it a career, Katie Taylor (26-1, 6 KOs) is locked in with another iconic star regarding the GWOAT status.

For a significant amount of time, Claressa Shields has labeled herself as the GWOAT. Along with Taylor, Claressa Shields, Amanda Serrano, and Alycia Baumgardner are the pioneers of this new era of women’s boxing.

Right now, if you had to choose one GWOAT, who would it be? Katie Taylor and Claressa Shields are the leading candidates, as Shields has the accolades, but Taylor has accolades and impact.

Back in April 2019, Claressa Shields became the first female boxer to become an undisputed world champion in the four-belt era. Two months later, Katie Taylor became the second women’s boxer to win the undisputed crown.

Shields has won a total of 21 world titles while Taylor has won a total of 19. Both Taylor and Shields are three-time undisputed champions, as Shields did it in three divisions and Taylor won undisputed once at 135 and twice at 140.

In her last career bout, Katie Taylor fought in front of 84,000 fans at Croke Park in Dublin, Ireland. When she defeated Flora Pili, the 40-year-old Katie Taylor became the oldest boxer to win the undisputed crown.

Currently in the NBA, an ongoing viral debate has fans divided as they contemplate whether the NBA GOAT is Jordan or LeBron. Now, women’s boxing will have a similar debate when fans ask who the GWOAT is: Katie or Claressa?

Sports.title: How Canelo Alvarez Took Golovkin’s Rivalry Away
Sports.content:
Many viewers believed Golovkin had done enough to win. Instead, the judges returned a split draw. Dave Moretti scored it 115 to 113 for Golovkin, Don Trella had it 114 to 114, and Adelaide Byrd produced the infamous 118 to 110 card for Canelo.

Byrd’s score was impossible to defend. Awarding Canelo ten rounds turned a competitive fight into something that barely resembled what happened in the ring. The result denied Golovkin the biggest victory of his career and allowed Canelo to leave Las Vegas without an official defeat.

Golovkin’s attack also contained a weakness that became more important in the rematch. He landed only eight body punches in the first fight. His pursuit was aimed almost entirely at Canelo’s head, which made it easier for Canelo to anticipate where the punches were coming from.

The rematch was originally scheduled for May 5, 2018, but Canelo tested positive for clenbuterol in two samples collected that February. He blamed contaminated meat, withdrew from the May date, and received a six-month suspension from the Nevada State Athletic Commission.

Golovkin still fought Vanes Martirosyan on May 5, stopping him in the second round. The Canelo rematch was eventually held on September 15, almost exactly one year after their first meeting.

That four-month postponement favored the younger fighter. Canelo was 28 by the time of the rematch, while Golovkin was 36. A few additional months meant little to Canelo but represented more lost time for an aging middleweight champion.

After being criticized for giving ground in the opening fight, Canelo held the center and forced Golovkin to box while moving backward. Golovkin relied heavily on his jab and landed plenty of clean punches, particularly during the later rounds. Canelo attacked the body and landed the harder individual shots.

The body punching difference was enormous. Canelo landed 46 shots downstairs, while Golovkin connected with only six. That work helped Canelo control the middle portion of the fight, although Golovkin was still strong enough to rally late.

Moretti and Steve Weisfeld scored it 115 to 113 for Canelo, while Glenn Feldman had it 114 to 114. I agreed with the two cards for Canelo. Golovkin boxed well, but he surrendered too much ground and allowed Canelo to determine the type of fight being fought.

All three meetings were staged at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas, where Canelo was unquestionably the commercial attraction. Golovkin repeatedly accepted the challenger’s preferred location because that was where the money was. The outrageous Byrd card showed the danger of entering an opponent’s territory without making the result undeniable.

Golovkin separated from longtime trainer Abel Sanchez in April 2019, seven months after the second fight, and hired Johnathon Banks.

Banks tried to make Golovkin less dependent on pressure by adding more movement and combination punching. There were flashes of success, but Golovkin was already 37 when they began working together.

Changing trainers at that age was unlikely to produce an entirely different fighter. Golovkin’s jab remained excellent, but the aggressive pressure and right hand that had defined his best years gradually became less dependable.

The trilogy was completed on September 17, 2022, four years after the rematch. Golovkin was 40 and moving to super middleweight for the first time.

He spent most of the opening eight rounds pawing with his jab while rarely committing to the right hand. Golovkin looked reluctant to plant his feet and give Canelo countering opportunities. Age, inactivity and physical wear offered more convincing explanations than the trainer standing in his corner.

Golovkin had also fought only once in the previous 21 months, stopping Ryota Murata five months before the trilogy. Against Canelo, his punches lacked their old speed and menace.

Canelo controlled most of the contest and won by scores of 116 to 112 and 115 to 113 twice. The two closer cards were generous to Golovkin. His late effort made the fight more respectable, but he never resembled the relentless middleweight who had driven Canelo to the ropes five years earlier.

The third bout became Golovkin’s final professional appearance. He later became president of Kazakhstan’s National Olympic Committee and was elected president of World Boxing in November 2025. World Boxing confirmed his election and current position.

Canelo continued fighting at super middleweight, collecting large purses against carefully selected opposition before Terence Crawford defeated him in September 2025.

That is what makes the trilogy memorable beyond the disputed judging. Golovkin arguably deserved the first fight, Canelo earned the second, and time decided the third before either man entered the ring.

Sports.title: Will Matchroom Keep Alan Chaves After Garcia Loss?
Sports.content:
“I have one more fight left with Matchroom, so it will possibly be in December,” Chaves said to La Casaca Boxing Club.

Winning that fight alone might not be enough. He may need to look exceptional against a credible opponent to persuade Matchroom that he remains worth another contract.

Hearn visited Chaves in the dressing room before the Garcia fight but did not see him afterward or join him in the ring. Chaves said his promoter, Georgina Rivero, was unhappy about Hearn’s absence.

Initially, Chaves claimed it did not bother him, but his later comments revealed that he noticed.

“There are many people who disappear when these things happen, as in this case with the promoter,” Chaves said.

The timing is difficult to ignore. He received promotional attention when he was knocking out opponents and being presented as one of Argentina’s brightest prospects. Once Garcia beat him, Hearn was no longer there.

None of this proves Matchroom has already decided to let Chaves leave after December. It does show how quickly a young import’s position can change after the zero disappears. Promotional enthusiasm is easy when a prospect is producing knockouts. The real test comes when the company must determine if it wants to spend money rebuilding him.

Matchroom has already learned that Chaves is not ready for a top lightweight. Now it must determine if his weaknesses can be repaired or if it merely bought an inflated record.

Chaves deserves credit for accepting responsibility, but his explanation also raises serious questions about his corner.

“They studied me 100 percent, and we as a team made the mistake of watching very little of Eridson,” Chaves said. “From the little we watched, we imagined he would come out and do the same thing.”

Preparing for a significant fight in Newark without properly studying the opponent is inexcusable. Chaves and his team assumed Garcia would come forward and trade because that was how he had fought in the footage they watched. They did not prepare for movement, counters, or changes in rhythm.

“I trained to go forward because that was what had worked for me in all these fights,” Chaves said. “We didn’t have a Plan B, Plan C or Plan D other than going forward and exchanging.”

Once Garcia refused to cooperate, Chaves had nothing else. He followed him around the ring, struggled to cut off his exits, and walked into counters throughout the fight. Even after four knockdowns, neither the fighter nor his corner found a different approach.

What happened was more than a bad performance. It was tactical negligence built on overconfidence.

His 19 knockouts in Argentina encouraged the team to believe that aggression and power would travel without the supporting skills. Garcia showed what happens when a puncher accustomed to compliant opposition meets a crafty boxer who controls distance and refuses to remain in front of him.

The knockout percentage concealed Chaves’ mechanical weaknesses. His feet did not position him to trap Garcia, his attacks became predictable, and he lacked the defensive awareness to enter safely. Those deficiencies were always there. Garcia was simply the first opponent skilled enough to reveal all of them.

Hearn now has two bad matchmaking options. One route is to give Chaves a ham and egger, allow him to score another knockout, and advertise the performance as a successful return. Fans will recognize that rehabilitation job immediately. Stopping someone selected to lose would not show that he learned anything from Newark.

Instead, Matchroom can match him against a capable lightweight who can move and counter. Such an opponent would give Chaves a genuine chance to redeem himself, but it also risks another one-sided defeat that ends any discussion about a new agreement.

A top opponent is not necessary. Chaves does need someone good enough to test the areas Garcia punished. Matchroom must find a fighter who forces him to cut off the ring, control his aggression, and change tactics during the fight.

A decisive win under those conditions would give Hearn a reason to consider another deal. Knocking out a soft target would leave the questions unanswered. Another boxer taking him apart would likely finish his Matchroom run when the contract expires.

An immediate rematch with Eridson is not something Chaves believes he deserves. That is another honest admission. He knows he must earn it by beating someone else first.

December is not merely a comeback date. It may determine if Chaves remains a Matchroom fighter or becomes another heavily promoted puncher whose value disappeared once his record met a real test.

Sports.title: Usyk Camp Rejects Tyson Fury’s Backup Plan
Sports.content:
Usyk’s manager, Sergey Lapin, was unimpressed by the public offer.

“Usyk is not Tyson’s backup plan,” Lapin told Sky Sports. “If Fury needs an opponent, he should visit the Ready to Fight platform. They can help him find a worthy opponent there. Oleksandr is always open to big challenges. But serious intentions are backed by a concrete offer, not statements in the press.”

The Joshua negotiations have not stalled because neither boxer has formally refused to fight. Both men signed individual contracts, but their teams remain divided over the venue.

Joshua and Matchroom want Wembley Stadium, which they believe was included in the agreement. The organizers and broadcast partners favor Madison Square Garden in New York, where the event can be staged at a more convenient hour for Netflix’s American audience.

A Wembley event designed around United States viewing hours may require an early morning ring walk in London. That creates transportation, licensing, and logistical issues while asking British ticket buyers to attend a fight at an unreasonable hour.

Declaring the fight dead and naming Usyk gives Fury a way to pressure Joshua into accepting New York without admitting that the original contest remains under negotiation.

It is unclear how serious Fury is about pursuing the trilogy. Calling out Usyk gives him another famous name to mention while the Joshua event remains tied up over its venue.

Actually fighting Usyk would be a far greater risk. Fury lost both previous meetings on points and came close to being stopped in the ninth round of their first contest. A third defeat would make the Joshua event an even harder sell. The contest is already based largely on nostalgia. Both men are former champions in the later stages of their careers, and each has suffered damaging defeats.

If Fury lost to Usyk again, he and Joshua would hold a combined record of zero wins and five losses against the Ukrainian. Promoters would then be selling a meeting between two aging British heavyweights who repeatedly failed against the same opponent.

Having vacated his remaining heavyweight belts, Usyk can now select the final fights of his career without mandatory obligations controlling his schedule. He has no sporting reason to rescue Fury’s November date through a hastily arranged trilogy.

A pair of victories already settled matters in Usyk’s mind. Stepping in again calls for massive purses, extensive camp preparations, plus contract clauses honoring the undisputed winner of their first two bouts. Lapin’s reaction guards those advantages. The champion keeps possibilities open without letting Fury treat him like an easy backup while Joshua talks stall.

Ultimatums, false retirement vows, and substitute names constantly pop up whenever Fury sits at the bargaining table. This callout fits the usual routine: fabricate panic, point fingers, then pretend another blockbuster remains ready to sign. A trilogy could still materialize eventually. Yet a social media challenge hardly counts as an actual contract talk.

The real threat facing Fury and Joshua is letting this matchup disappear altogether. Without championship belts between them, another setback for either man would instantly erode their commercial draw. Every prolonged holdout simply turns the contest into a nostalgic showcase of past glories rather than a fight that matters in the present.

Until Fury’s team sends Usyk a concrete proposal, the trilogy callout is best understood as leverage in the Joshua venue dispute.

Sports.title: Andy Cruz Gets Second IBF Title Chance
Sports.content:
Raymond Muratalla surrendered the belt after struggling to make 135 pounds for his recent defense against Robson Conceição. He plans to continue his career at light welterweight, creating an opening for the IBF’s two highest-ranked available contenders.

Cruz (7-1, 4 KOs) lost a majority decision to Muratalla in January after challenging for the championship in only his seventh professional appearance. Muratalla’s pressure and activity became increasingly effective during the later rounds, showing that Cruz’s extensive amateur background had not fully prepared him for the physical demands of a hard professional fight.

The 31-year-old Cuban returned in July and stopped late replacement Abraham Montoya in three rounds. His brief comeback gave no clear indication that he had corrected the weaknesses exposed by Muratalla.

An exceptional counterpuncher with world-class reflexes, Cruz often depends on distance, quick reactions, and single clean shots. Those tools can control shorter amateur bouts. Over 12 rounds, repeatedly changing direction and escaping exchanges can drain a fighter who is not comfortable holding his ground or working inside.

Subkhankulov (12-0, 6 KOs) will try to force that type of contest. The 34-year-old Russian southpaw earned his position by stopping Bakhodur Usmonov in the 12th round of their April eliminator. Usmonov went down four times across the final three rounds before the referee ended the action.

His southpaw position will also test Cruz’s lead foot placement and ability to land the right hand without remaining in range for counters. Subkhankulov is unlikely to be discouraged by feints or a difficult opening six rounds. His best chance is to attack the body, keep Cruz working, and turn the final third into another test of stamina.

There is history between them. Cruz defeated Subkhankulov by split decision when they met in the semifinals of the Ústí nad Labem Grand Prix in May 2019. The three-round amateur result offers Cruz some familiarity, but it says little about how their styles will interact over a professional championship distance.

The October 7 deadline may determine more than the fighters’ pay. Cruz has spent his professional career fighting in the United States, while Subkhankulov has done much of his work in Russia and on IBA-promoted cards. If negotiations fail and Subkhankulov’s side wins the purse bid, Cruz may have to pursue the championship far from his usual surroundings.

This is still a favorable route back for Cruz. He avoids another meeting with Muratalla and faces someone he has already beaten. However, two championship appearances within his first nine professional outings show how aggressively his career is being pushed.

At 31, Cruz does not have years to spend developing against mid-level opposition. Winning the vacant belt against Subkhankulov may be the calculated shortcut his team needs. Losing would show that the rush from decorated amateur to professional champion asked too much of him too quickly.

Sports.title: Jack Dempsey Escapes Without A Verdict Against Miske
Sports.content:
At 22 years of age, Dempsey was tearing through the heavyweight division with his aggressive style and crushing left hook. Miske, 24, had the benefit of fighting before his hometown supporters, but he was far more than a protected local attraction.

Dempsey weighed 187½ pounds, while Miske came in at 182.

Known as the “St. Paul Thunderbolt,” Miske was a fast, clever boxer who understood how to block punches, smother attacks, and work at close range. Those skills gave Dempsey one of his hardest tests during his climb toward Jess Willard’s heavyweight championship.

The local favorite supplied a tactical lesson for smaller fighters facing dangerous punchers. Instead of continually backing away, he stepped into Dempsey’s punching range and crowded him. Retreating would have given Dempsey space to drive forward, build speed, and launch his leaping left hook. Miske took away that leverage by getting close, controlling Dempsey’s arms and preventing him from completing his punches.

The rolling movement associated with Dempsey’s attacks depended upon momentum. He bobbed his upper body from side to side, shifted his weight, and sprang forward with hooks from changing angles. An opponent who backed away gave that attack time to gather force.

Meeting Dempsey chest to chest changed the exchanges into an arm wrestle. His long swings lost much of their force as Miske blocked the hook, jammed the punching arm, and answered with short shots before tying him up.

Quick punches inside prevented the younger man from finding a steady rhythm. Dempsey had productive stretches in the second and third rounds, but Miske answered with a hard right cross in the third.

Years later, Dempsey admitted that Miske was landing more punches and building what looked like a lead. He also recalled being hurt during one exchange and struggling to remain upright until the bell.

“Miske had landed more telling blows than I had,” Dempsey recalled. “He suddenly came at me with a volley that nearly put me out.”

It was a revealing admission from a fighter remembered for overwhelming opponents. Raw aggression had run into a boxer who understood distance, timing and leverage. The visiting fighter finally produced his strongest attack in the seventh. A heavy left to the body followed by a right to the jaw troubled Miske and helped Dempsey recover ground. Neither man scored a knockdown, leaving the newspapers to decide which work they valued more.

Miske’s approach was almost the opposite of the one Jess Willard used against Dempsey in Toledo the following year. The 6’6″ champion tried to control the challenger from long range but remained too upright and stationary.

That distance allowed Dempsey to leap forward with hooks and overhand punches. Willard became an easy target once the challenger closed the distance, leading to seven knockdowns during the savage opening round.

Such a runway was never available against Miske. He moved toward the danger, shortened the punches, and forced Dempsey to work without full leverage. Willard waited at the end of Dempsey’s forward rush, while Miske intercepted it before the punches reached full speed.

The St. Paul fight showed that smothering Dempsey was safer than surrendering the ring and waiting for him to attack. Gene Tunney receives credit for solving Dempsey in 1926 and repeating the result one year later. Miske had exposed several of the same weaknesses eight years earlier. Their tactics were not identical. Tunney relied more heavily on footwork, his jab, and movement at long range. Miske was more willing to hold his position, work inside, and smother Dempsey physically.

Both remained composed when Dempsey attacked. They refused to become stationary targets at his preferred distance and punished him when his forward movement became predictable.

Before their first fight, Tunney studied films of Dempsey and brought former opponents and sparring partners into camp. There is no firm evidence that Miske personally supplied Tunney’s plan, but the St. Paul contest had established the central principle: Dempsey became less effective when an opponent denied him momentum and forced him to restart his attacks.

Miske supplied the early evidence that denying Dempsey momentum made him less effective, and Tunney later produced the polished championship version.

The St. Paul Pioneer Press surveyed eight writers at ringside. Four favored Dempsey, one selected Miske and three scored the fight even. The newspaper published the bout as a draw, although other reports awarded Dempsey a narrow newspaper decision based on his aggression and heavier punches.

A later collection drawing upon additional newspaper sources produced seven verdicts for Dempsey, four draws and one for Miske. That broader tally included reports beyond the eight writers questioned in St. Paul.

Such disagreement exposed the weakness of the no decision era. A boxer’s official record remained untouched after a distance fight, even when most observers believed he had lost. Local sports editors became unofficial judges without a uniform scoring system or any requirement to agree.

Reports from St. Paul do not support the claim that hometown writers simply protected Miske. Four of the eight surveyed writers favored the visiting Dempsey, while only one selected Miske. Regional loyalty may have influenced individual accounts, but the split also reflected a genuinely close fight.

Miske landed more often and controlled long portions of the contest, while Dempsey delivered the harder individual blows. Some writers valued activity and craft; others favored aggression and damage.

Promoters benefited from the uncertainty. Dempsey survived a difficult night without receiving an official loss, allowing his handlers to continue selling him as the next threat to Willard. Miske also avoided a formal defeat and remained a leading heavyweight attraction in Minnesota. Jack Kearns wanted knockouts that would sell Dempsey to a national audience. Taking him into Miske’s hometown against a fast, experienced boxer was a serious gamble.

The no decision format reduced the danger because only a knockout placed an official loss on the record. It did not remove the promotional risk. A decisive beating reported across the country still would have damaged Dempsey’s growing reputation.

Kearns learned that clever defensive fighters presented a different challenge from the large, slower heavyweights Dempsey destroyed. His fighter continued facing dangerous opposition, including Fred Fulton, Battling Levinsky, Bill Brennan and Miske himself, but the first fight supplied a warning. Dempsey’s power did not automatically solve every style.

The pair met again in Philadelphia on November 28, 1918, with most newspapers favoring Dempsey after six rounds. By then, the future champion had gained more experience against Miske’s troublesome methods.

Their third fight came on September 6, 1920, after Dempsey had taken the heavyweight championship from Willard. Miske was suffering from Bright’s disease and was knocked out in the third round of Dempsey’s first title defense.

His illness was not common public knowledge, so there is no basis for claiming Kearns selected Miske because he knew the challenger was dying. In hindsight, the physical decline made the title fight far less dangerous than their first meeting had been.

That knockout became the lasting image of their rivalry. Miske is now remembered primarily as the sick challenger who needed money, while Dempsey remains one of boxing’s most recognizable champions.

The familiar family story belongs mainly to the end of Miske’s life, not the 1920 title fight. A gravely ill Miske returned against Bill Brennan in November 1923, scored a fourth-round knockout, and used the money to give his family a memorable Christmas. He died on January 1, 1924.

Remembering only the tragedy reduces Miske to a sympathetic opponent in Dempsey’s championship story. Reports from 1918 present the fuller picture.

At that time, the St. Paul Thunderbolt was one of the sharpest technical boxers in the heavyweight division, possessing the timing, defense, and composure to frustrate Dempsey near his physical peak. He survived 10 rounds and forced the future champion to abandon many of his preferred attacks. The press left St. Paul unable to agree on a winner.

Ghana News.title: Oil hits $100 a barrel for first time since July after US and Houthi strikes
Ghana News.content:
Oil prices rose past $100 (£74) a barrel on Wednesday after further strikes in the US and Iran conflict and continuing Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia.

In back and forth attacks, the US hit five Iranian tankers in reprisal strikes after Tehran targeted one of its warships.

Brent crude - which is the global benchmark for prices - has not been as expensive since the end of July, when a ceasefire between Iran and the US collapsed.

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement also attacked oil facilities in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday and have been targeting tankers in the Red Sea.

Brent crude did dip back down to $99.90 a barrel, but any fresh flare-ups in the Middle East could see it pushed higher again.

The US strikes on the five Iranian tankers saw four in the Gulf of Oman linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) hit as well as another near Kharg Island.

Tehran responded by launching missiles at a US base in Jordan - most of which were shot down - and said it attacked two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Houthis and Saudi Arabia have also been exchanging strikes since July after their own informal ceasefire unravelled.

Houthi missile attacks started on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

They said it was retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports and an air strike on Sanaa airport they accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out.

On Monday they accused Saudi Arabia of bombing a prison in al-Hazm and killing 11 people.

Then on Tuesday the Saudi authorities said Houthis had struck civilian and economic sites in the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran.

Oil prices have fluctuated wildly during the Iran US war, which started on 28 February this year.

Before the conflict Brent crude had been priced at about $70 (£52) a barrel.

But the war saw the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which carries 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG).

The rising costs have sparked huge price leaps in petrol around the world for motorists at the pumps.

Tit-for-tat strikes between Iran and the US have escalated in the past week, more than six months after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on 28 February..

Jordan said it had shot down 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, while two of them fell in unpopulated areas, an official spokesperson for the Jordanian Armed Forces said.

After warning of further retaliatory strikes, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday they had attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers and 10 "non-compliant vessels" trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

The latest round of escalation comes after Iran targeted a US warship with ballistic missiles, which Centcom said were "successfully evaded". It added that no American troops were harmed during the attacks.

In response, the US said that the five Iranian oil tankers it targeted were "part of a multi-billion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies".

One of the ships it had struck, the M/T Riesco, sunk in the Gulf of Oman, Centcom later said, posting a video on X of the damaged vessel.

Kharg Island - where one Iranian tanker was attacked in the latest round of US strikes - hosts Iran's main terminal for exporting oil.

Some 90% of the country's crude oil passes through the island in the Gulf, transported through pipes from the mainland.

Pressure on oil prices has been exacerbated by wider regional instability.

Also on Tuesday, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement attacked energy facilities and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, injuring 73 people, according to Saudi authorities.

The drone and missile attack caused fires at oil facilities and installations that led to a temporary halt in operations, Saudi Arabia's military and energy ministry said.



When asked by reporters about the latest tit-for-tat strikes between the US and Iran, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the situation was "pretty straightforward".

"Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships. And, for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today," Rubio told reporters during a trip in Colombia.

The US strikes on Tuesday came hours after Iran's Navy claimed it had seized an uncrewed US submarine in the Strait of Hormuz.

US Navy Capt Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Centcom, said that the "underwater drone operated by US forces malfunctioned more than a day ago" and was used to survey regional waters "in support of ongoing operations".

The defective drone was "an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment", he said, adding that US operations in regional waters were ongoing.
