With the preliminary examination withdrawn, attention could now shift toward the grand jury process and whether prosecutors will secure an indictment that moves the matter further toward trial.

For Howard-Taylor’s supporters, that stage will be another opportunity to insist that the former vice president be judged on evidence rather than public accusations.

For prosecutors, it will be a test of whether the allegations against one of Liberia’s most prominent political figures can withstand formal judicial scrutiny.

The case has therefore evolved beyond a conventional criminal prosecution. It is increasingly a battle over evidence, due process, public perception and confidence in Liberia’s justice system.

For now, the message from Howard-Taylor’s camp is clear: she may be accused, but she has not been convicted.

And with the “Justice for Jewel” campaign now taking the fight directly to the public, the courtroom is no longer the only arena in which the battle over her fate is being fought.

World.title: Liberia: Civil Society Coalition Presses Boakai on War Crimes, Anti-Corruption Courts Ahead of UN Security Council Presidency
World.content:
Monrovia — A coalition of Liberian civil society organizations has accused the Joseph Nyuma Boakai administration of dragging its feet on the establishment of Liberia’s proposed War and Economic Crimes Court and Specialized National Anti-Corruption Court, warning that continued delays could undermine the country’s credibility as it prepares to assume the presidency of the United Nations Security Council in December 2026.

By Francis Boayue

In a strongly worded statement issued Tuesday, the National Civil Society Consortium for Transitional Justice said nearly three years into the Boakai administration, the government has yet to secure enactment of the legislation required to establish and operationalize the two courts.

The consortium said Liberia’s international leadership must be matched by concrete action at home, arguing that the country cannot credibly champion justice, human rights, accountability, peacebuilding and the rule of law internationally while leaving major justice reforms unfinished domestically.

“Accountability Delayed — Liberia Must Match Global Leadership with Domestic Accountability and Justice,” the group said in the statement.

Liberia was elected to a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for the 2026–2027 term, a development the consortium said reflected international confidence in the country’s transition from conflict to peace and its emerging role in international peace and security.

With Liberia scheduled to hold the Council’s rotating presidency in December, civil society leaders said the government faces a critical test of whether its international commitments are reflected in its domestic governance.

‘Justice Cannot Wait’

The consortium acknowledged steps already taken by the government, including the 55th Legislature’s passage of a joint resolution in April 2024 supporting the establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court.

It also credited President Boakai with creating the Office for the Establishment of War and Economic Crimes Court for Liberia (OWECC) and submitting draft legislation aimed at establishing the proposed courts.

But the coalition said those measures are insufficient without final legislative action, adequate funding and full operationalization.

“Government must decisively act to complete the process,” the consortium said, calling for the enactment of the enabling statutes needed to establish and fund both institutions.

The civil society organizations said victims and survivors of Liberia’s civil wars, particularly women and children, have waited for decades for justice.

They argued that the absence of a specialized war crimes court continues to perpetuate impunity, deny victims closure and undermine national reconciliation more than two decades after Liberia’s civil conflicts.

The group specifically highlighted conflict-related sexual and gender-based violence, displacement, loss of livelihoods and other serious human rights violations suffered during the wars.

Women’s Rights at Stake

According to the consortium, establishing the War and Economic Crimes Court is also critical to Liberia’s implementation of the Women, Peace and Security agenda under United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325 and subsequent resolutions.

The coalition said a credible, victim-centered and gender-responsive court would help transform Liberia’s international commitments on women, peace and security into tangible justice for survivors.

It said women, children and other victims must be treated not merely as symbols of Liberia’s peace narrative, but as rights-holders entitled to truth, justice, remedies and guarantees that abuses will not recur.

Corruption Court Also Critical

The coalition also linked the proposed National Anti-Corruption Court to Liberia’s broader governance and development challenges.

It warned that entrenched corruption and the abuse of public resources continue to undermine democratic governance, erode public trust and contribute to poverty and inequality.

According to the group, corruption also has a direct impact on citizens’ access to essential services, including healthcare, education and electricity.

A specialized anti-corruption court, once established and adequately resourced, would therefore help strengthen accountability, protect public resources and support inclusive and sustainable economic development, the consortium argued.

‘Non-Negotiable’

The civil society coalition described the establishment of both courts as “non-negotiable,” saying they are consistent with Liberia’s obligations under international human rights law, international humanitarian law and broader UN rule-of-law principles.

It called for the courts to operate according to international standards, including judicial independence, equality before the law, due process, fair-trial guarantees, protection of victims and witnesses and meaningful participation by victims.

The consortium argued that the two institutions could collectively strengthen the rule of law, increase public confidence in government, advance economic and social justice, deter future abuses, reinforce reconciliation and demonstrate that no individual is above the law.

Warning to Legislature

The group also directed its criticism toward the National Legislature, urging lawmakers to act without further delay on the proposed legislation.

It cautioned against using constituency consultations as a justification for prolonged legislative inaction, recalling what it described as previous delays surrounding implementation of the recommendations of Liberia’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

While acknowledging the importance of lawmakers engaging their constituents, the coalition said such engagement should not become an excuse for delaying action on the court legislation.

Seven-Point Demand

The consortium outlined seven recommendations, calling on President Boakai to urgently engage the Senate and House of Representatives to ensure timely passage of the two bills.

It further urged the President to ensure that the 2027 National Budget includes dedicated funding for both courts while mobilizing international support for their establishment and sustainability.

The Legislature, the group said, must prioritize passage of the bills, while the Executive and lawmakers must ensure that both courts are adequately resourced and operationally independent, impartial, transparent, victim-centered and gender-responsive.

The coalition also called for Liberia’s domestic justice and anti-corruption agenda to be aligned with its international commitments on human rights, peace and security, transitional justice and Women, Peace and Security.

It urged the government to use its December 2026 UN Security Council presidency as an opportunity to demonstrate leadership by example—promoting accountability internationally while institutionalizing justice at home.

The group also called on the United Nations, European Union, United States and other international partners to continue supporting Liberians’ demands for accountability and to press for the establishment and financing of both courts.

Finally, it urged the Office for the Establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court to deepen collaboration with the Executive, Legislature, Judiciary and other stakeholders to move the process forward.

‘The Boakai Administration Must Act Now’

The National Civil Society Consortium said it remains prepared to work with national institutions and international partners to ensure the timely establishment and sustainability of the two courts.

But it issued a blunt closing warning to the government:

“Justice delayed is justice denied. And justice denied is a recipe for human rights violations, impunity, violence, poverty and underdevelopment.”

The coalition concluded: “The Boakai administration must act now!”

The statement was signed by representatives of the Press Union of Liberia (PUL), Center for Transparency and Accountability (CENTAL), Women’s NGO Secretariat of Liberia (WONGOSOL), Association of Female Lawyers of Liberia (AFELL), National Muslim Council of Liberia (NMCL), and Liberia Council of Churches (LCC).

World.title: Liberia- Former Police Crime Commissioner Johnny Dean Freed on US$15K Property Bond After Bribery, Criminal Conspiracy Charges
World.content:
Monrovia— Former Liberia National Police Commissioner for Crime Services Johnny Bolar Dean has been released from custody on a US$15,000 property valuation bond after being arrested and forwarded to court on allegations that he accepted US$10,000 while police were investigating a major drug-trafficking case.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Dean, a former Unit 106 commander and senior figure within Liberia’s criminal investigation structure, faces charges of criminal conspiracy, bribery, tampering with a criminal investigation, and obstruction of government functions by a public servant.

Despite the seriousness of the allegations, the offenses charged are bailable, allowing Dean to remain out of custody pending further proceedings, subject to the conditions imposed by the court.

His release does not amount to an acquittal or a judicial finding that the allegations are without merit. The property bond is intended to secure his appearance before the court as the case proceeds.

Why US$15,000 for an Alleged US$10,000 Bribe?

The value of the bond has prompted questions because the property presented to secure Dean’s release was valued at US$15,000, while the alleged bribe at the center of the case is US$10,000. The two amounts, however, serve different purposes.

The US$10,000 is the subject of the prosecution’s allegations. Police contend that the money was connected to an effort to influence or compromise an ongoing criminal investigation.

The US$15,000 property valuation, on the other hand, is a bail-security mechanism. It is not a determination of the value of the alleged bribe and does not constitute a fine or punishment.

A property bond generally requires the accused or a surety to demonstrate sufficient interest in real property to secure the defendant’s appearance in court.

At the bail stage, the court’s primary concern is whether the accused will comply with the judicial process—not whether he is guilty.

The US$10,000 That Triggered the Case

According to a police charge sheet dated September 1, Dean is accused of accepting US$10,000 from Stephanie Fefe Mensah while authorities were investigating individuals identified in the case as Edison Brown and Alpha Bah.

The investigation is linked to Liberia’s broader cocaine-trafficking case involving a shipment authority have valued at approximately US$317 million.

Police allege that Dean used his position within the security apparatus to interfere with the investigation, disclose confidential information and frustrate efforts to investigate individuals connected to the alleged drug operation.

Dean, however, has reportedly provided investigators with a different explanation for the money.

According to the charge sheet, he admitted receiving the US$10,000 but told investigators that Mensah gave him the money for safekeeping. He also reportedly described Mensah as his lover.

Police rejected that explanation and alleged that the payment was connected to the criminal investigation and intended to influence the handling of the case. Investigators subsequently recovered the money.

The circumstances surrounding the payment are therefore expected to become a central factual dispute at trial: whether the money was simply entrusted to Dean, as he reportedly claims, or whether it constituted an illicit payment intended to influence a police investigation.

From Police Commander to Criminal Defendant

The allegations carry particular significance because of Dean’s former position. As Commissioner of Crime Services, he occupied a senior role within the Liberia National Police, with responsibilities connected to the investigation of serious criminal offenses.

His previous service as a Unit 106 commander also places the case against him within the context of a career spent in Liberia’s security and criminal-investigation apparatus. Prosecutors are essentially alleging that a senior police official abused the authority of his office while a major criminal investigation was underway.

If proven, such allegations could raise broader questions about professional ethics, internal controls and the ability of law-enforcement agencies to protect sensitive investigations from interference.

An Investigation Inside the Police

The case reportedly emerged from an administrative inquiry conducted by the Professional Standards Division of the Liberia National Police.

Dean and Mensah were reportedly turned over to the Crime Services Department on August 18 following that administrative process.

A Special Investigative Team headed by Assistant Commissioner of Police Harold T. Jones subsequently conducted the criminal investigation.

That inquiry ultimately resulted in Dean being charged and forwarded to court.

The sequence places the allegations within an internal police process that escalated into a criminal case.

The court will now have to determine whether the evidence gathered by investigators is sufficient to sustain the charges.

Dean: “I Am Not Connected to Any Drug Cartel”

Dean has rejected allegations linking him to any drug-trafficking organization.

The former police commissioner has maintained that he is not connected to a drug cartel and has challenged claims portraying him as a participant in criminal activity.

His explanation concerning the US$10,000 is also central to his defense.

Rather than acknowledging the payment as a bribe, Dean reportedly told investigators that the money was given to him for safekeeping.

That distinction could prove critical.

For the prosecution, the challenge will be to establish not simply that Dean received the money, but that it was connected to a criminal purpose and intended to influence or interfere with an ongoing investigation.

The defense, meanwhile, is expected to challenge the prosecution’s interpretation of the transaction and the evidence supporting the charges.

What the Court Will Have to Determine

As the case progresses, several issues are likely to come under judicial scrutiny.

The court may examine the circumstances under which the US$10,000 was delivered, communications between Dean and Mensah, the relationship between the two parties, and the nature of the investigation involving Brown and Bah.

Prosecutors may also seek to establish whether Dean disclosed confidential information, improperly used his official position or took actions intended to frustrate police efforts.

The defense is expected to challenge those allegations and the evidentiary basis for the charges.

The US$15,000 property bond does not resolve any of these questions. It simply permits Dean to remain outside custody while the judicial process continues.

A Larger Test for Liberia’s Drug Fight

The Dean case comes at a sensitive moment for Liberia’s law-enforcement institutions. The country’s investigation into a massive cocaine-trafficking operation has already brought suspected traffickers, security personnel and other actors under scrutiny.

The allegation that a former senior police commander may have accepted money and interfered with an investigation adds an institutional dimension to the case.

It raises a difficult question for Liberia’s fight against organized crime: If criminal networks can allegedly reach into institutions responsible for investigating them, how secure are those investigations?

At the same time, the case raises an equally important legal question: whether criminal liability can be established from a disputed financial transaction without prosecutors proving its criminal purpose beyond a reasonable doubt. Those questions cannot be settled by allegations alone. They must ultimately be determined through evidence presented before a court.

Road Ahead

Dean’s release on a US$15,000 property valuation bond means he will face the case from outside detention unless the court later orders otherwise. His release should not be interpreted as a declaration of innocence, just as his arrest and charging should not be treated as proof of guilt.

The prosecution retains the burden of proving the allegations.

At trial, the court will ultimately be asked to determine whether the US$10,000 was an innocent transaction or an illicit payment; whether Dean used his official authority to interfere with an investigation; whether confidential information was disclosed; and whether his conduct amounted to the offenses contained in the charge sheet.

For a former commander entrusted with fighting serious crime, the stakes are considerable.

For Liberia, the case could become an important test of accountability within the security sector—and of whether institutions tasked with combating organized crime can withstand the criminal influences they are expected to confront.

For now, Johnny Bolar Dean remains a defendant, not a convicted criminal. The allegations against him remain unproven, and he is presumed innocent unless and until a court of competent jurisdiction determines otherwise.

World.title: Liberia: In Monrovia’s Slums, Boys Are Learning to Talk About Periods Too
World.content:
Monrovia, – Maxine Lussine didn’t expect two men to run her group session that day. Her usual facilitator, Ms. Juwa, was gone. In her place stood Jerome Naa Wlalee and a colleague.

By Patience M. Jones, [email protected]

“They started talking about how boys also have a part to play in menstruation,” said the 17-year-old from Old Road, a member of a peer support group under Healing Bridge Liberia. “For our setting, where I grew up, I’ve never seen my dad really taking part in menstruation and all that. So it was really confusing to me, because those are things I’ve seen in movies.”

That confusion is the wall Healing Bridge is trying to knock down. In Liberia, periods, sex, and reproductive health have long been treated as women’s business; fathers, brothers, and boyfriends stay out of. Healing Bridge’s leadership believes that silence helps explain why teenage pregnancy has stayed stubbornly high for decades. Liberia’s 2029/2020 demographic and health survey found 32 percent of girls aged 15 to 19 are already pregnant or mothers, and adolescent girls make up 60 percent of the country’s obstetric fistula cases.

The day it happened, Maxine Lussine remembers being caught off guard. Their usual facilitator, a woman the girls called Ms. Juwa, wasn’t there. In her place stood two men, Jerome Naa Wlalee and a colleague, ready to lead the session anyway. What came next stayed with her.

“They started talking about how boys also have a part to play in menstruation,” said the 17-year-old from Old Road community, who is part of a peer support group under Healing Bridge Liberia. “For our setting, where I grew up, I’ve never seen my dad really taking part in menstruation and all that. So it was really confusing to me, because those are things I’ve seen in movies.”

That confusion is exactly the barrier Healing Bridge is trying to break down. In Liberia, conversations about periods, sex, and reproductive health have long been treated as women’s business, something fathers, brothers, and boyfriends stay out of. Healing Bridge’s leadership argues that silence is part of why teenage pregnancy has stayed stubbornly high for decades. According toLiberia’s 2029/2020 demographic and health survey , 32 percent of girls between 15 and 19 are already pregnant, or mothers, and adolescent girls account for 60 percent of the country’s obstetric fistula cases.

The program is part of the Nurture, Empower, and Protect (NEP) project, a five-year, €7 million initiative funded by the Embassy of Ireland and jointly run by UNICEF and UNFPA, targeting more than 107,000 adolescent girls across Montserrado, Grand Gedeh, and Rivercess counties by 2030. Healing Bridge is one of the community organizations selected by the Clinton Health Access Initiative to carry that work into five communities: Old Road, Clara Town, Slipway, PHP Community, and West Point.

But unlike many reproductive health programs that focus only on girls, Healing Bridge built men and boys into the design from the start. Niagulali, the organization’s executive director, said trained male volunteers don’t wait for people to come to them. They go out looking for conversation. “They met people at the attire shop, at the market, the seaside, the fishermen, all of those different places,” he said, describing informal dialogue sessions the volunteers hold in daily gathering spots around the five communities. “They did everything. It was very, very good.”

The goal, Wlalee said, is to shift what he calls a generational habit of silence, one where fathers avoid the subject entirely and mothers are left to explain everything alone, often too late or too vaguely to matter. “We also engage men and boys because they too need to get involved with this entire empowerment stuff as well,” he said.

Members of Healing Bridge Liberia’s peer support groups gather for a group photo at a graduation event under the Nurture, Empower, and Protect (NEP) project, which brings boys and men into conversations once treated as women-only.

For Maxine, the lesson went further than menstruation. It reshaped how she understood her own authority over her body. “They told me that I have the final say concerning my body,” she said, describing a separate session on consent. “My yes, me yes. My no, me no.” She said she now feels she can turn to her own mother with questions she once would have kept to herself, something she credits partly to watching men in the program speak openly about a subject she’d always been taught was off-limits to them.

Wlalee is candid that shifting an entire community’s habits doesn’t happen in one workshop, or even one graduating class of 25 girls. Healing Bridge is now restructuring its model into shorter, rolling cohorts so it can reach more communities faster, aware that the wider NEP project’s targets are enormous compared to what one organization can do alone. But he points to the male volunteers’ reports and the testimonies coming back from caregivers as early proof that something is moving. “Some participants gave testimonies that they now can talk to their parents about certain things,” he said. “It’s not more like a taboo anymore.”

He said for a program built on the idea that girls should not be treated only as beneficiaries but as agents of change in their own communities, getting boys and men into that same conversation may be one of the quieter, but more lasting, shifts underway in Monrovia’s slums.

World.title: Gbowee Challenges Defeated Politicians Seeking Political Comebacks
World.content:
MONROVIA — Former Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Leymah Gbowee has questioned the growing push by politicians who have been voted out of office to return to public service, urging them to explore opportunities outside politics.

By J.H. Webster [email protected]

Gbowee, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2011, made the comments amid renewed political discussions about the 2029 Presidential and Legislative Elections and efforts by opposition politicians to regroup following their defeat in the 2023 Presidential and Legislative Elections.

Her remarks came just days after former President George Manneh Weah, who served as Liberia’s president from 2018 to 2024, held a two-day opposition parties roundtable meeting aimed at uniting the opposition ahead of the 2029 Elections and unseating the ruling Unity Party..

In a social media post on Tuesday, Gbowee offered what she described as a “free consultation” to politicians seeking to return to public office, encouraging them to consider life and careers beyond politics.

“Welcome to Troublesome Tuesday. I have a burning question for Liberian politicians. After being voted out of office, are there no other options?” Gbowee asked.

She further stated: “Why is everyone fighting to make a comeback? I want to offer free consultation on how to make it outside of politics. Jobs plenty oh. You just need to be creative.” Her comments quickly triggered mixed reactions on social media, with some Liberians supporting her position while others accused her of being politically biased.

‘Political Defeat Is Not Political Retirement’

Sekou Kalasco Damaro, a former aide to ex-President George Manneh Weah, pushed back against Gbowee’s argument, saying electoral defeat does not mean the end of a political movement.

Damaro pointed to the United States, Ghana and other countries where politicians who lost elections later returned to power.

He cautioned Gbowee against equating political defeat with permanent retirement from public life. “In a democracy, being voted out does not mean you lose your voice, your relevance, or your right to seek another mandate,” Damaro said.

He argued that politicians can lose elections at one point and return to the ballot box at another, describing democracy as a system that allows voters to change their minds.

In his words, the ballot box can remove you today and bring you back tomorrow, adding that it is democracy, not a permanent political death sentence.

“Look at the man who currently occupies the presidency of the United States, Donald Trump. He lost the 2020 presidential election, stepped away from office, rebuilt his political movement, returned to the ballot, and won again,” he stressed.

Damaro asked: “So, does America have no jobs? Or is the difference simply that Americans understand that political office is a temporary mandate, not a permanent entitlement?”

Critics Question Gbowee’s Timing

Rudolf Ban Daniel Tamba also challenged Gbowee’s position, questioning why she did not make a similar statement during the 2023 elections.

“You should have posted this or similar in 2023 also. Posting this now makes me believe you are biased,” Tamba said.

Gbowee previously served as National Orator during Liberia’s 173rd Independence Day celebration in 2020.

Morris Saryon similarly argued that Gbowee should have made such comments during her tenure as National Orator.

“You should have reasonably shared this in 2020 when you had the opportunity to speak to your no position, in position and opposition. Many of you so called advocates are bunch of hypocrites in Liberia,” Saryon said.

Saye Nehwon also referenced the Unity Party’s return to power after its defeat in 2017.

“After Unity Party 12 years in power and they were defeated in 2017, we saw them fighting to come back to power. I’m here wondering if the current president had any professional ideas on how to make it outside politics,” Nehwon said.

Anthony N. Wleh also challenged Gbowee’s assertion, pointing to other countries where politicians have returned to power after losing elections. “Go ask Ghana, Sierra Leone, The United States of America about what led them to bring back people they previously voted out,” Wleh said.

Others Agree with Gbowee

Despite the criticism, some Liberians supported Gbowee’s argument that political office should not be viewed as the only pathway to a meaningful career.

Thomas Lukaku Walters said he agreed with the Nobel laureate, arguing that losing political office should not signal the end of an individual’s relevance or career.

“Absolutely, I agree with you. There is life and opportunity outside politics. Losing political office should not mean the end of one’s career or relevance. With creativity, skills, and the willingness to work, there are many opportunities available. Sometimes, it’s about looking beyond government positions and creating your own path,” Walters said.

Joe P. B. Kai, a civil servant, said he is not among those seeking a return to politics, although he acknowledged that civil service jobs do not always provide the income he desires.

Kai, however, asked Gbowee to provide practical guidance on how people can explore legitimate opportunities outside government employment.

“So, I would like take your advice: while thinking beyond government, what are those best creative avenues, that can be explored as a mean of opportunities outside the civil service. What are those legitimate ways to build a successful career and create additional income without depending on political office,” Kai asked.

‘Their Only Career Is Politics’

Kromah Alhaji, a former student leader at the University of Liberia now based in the United States, argued that for some Liberians, leaving politics is difficult because political engagement has become their primary career path.

“But seriously, how are some of these politicians supposed to make it outside politics when politics is the only career they’ve mastered?” Alhaji asked.

According to him, many politicians have relied for years on patronage, connections, government positions and allegations of corruption.

“Take away the title, government vehicle, influence, and access to public resources-what’s left? That’s the real challenge,” he said.

Alhaji added: “Maybe instead of planning another political comeback, it’s time to learn entrepreneurship, technology, business management, agriculture, consulting, and other productive skills.

Liberia has opportunities beyond politics. The question is: can you survive without a government position? Now that is the real test.”

World.title: ‘We Must Strengthen Teachers Professionalization’ -Education Minister Jallah Says Ahead of 2027 AFTRA Conference
World.content:
Congo Town– Liberia is stepping onto the continental stage of education reform as it prepares to host the 14th Africa Federation of Teaching Regulatory Authorities (AFTRA) Conference and 16th Roundtable in 2027, bringing together education leaders, regulators, researchers and policymakers from across Africa to discuss the future of teaching and learning.

By Jaheim T. [email protected]

AFTRA is a continental organization established in 2010 through an initiative led by education ministers from South Africa and Nigeria.

The body brings together teaching councils, ministries of education, teacher service commissions, teacher unions, and development partners to promote professional standards, best practices and collaboration in education across Africa.

It serves as a platform where countries share experiences and lessons on teaching and learning.

Delivering her remarks, Education Minister, Jarso Maley Jallah, called for stronger efforts to professionalize the country’s teaching workforce as the nation prepares to host the 2027 Conference of the Africa Federation of Teaching Regulatory Authorities (AFTRA).

Minister Jallah said the gathering should be viewed not only as an honor for the country but also as a responsibility that must lead to tangible improvements in the education sector.

“We must strengthen the professionalization of our teaching workforce,” Minister Jallah said, noting that Liberia continues to face challenges including “qualification gaps, teacher shortages, inequitable deployment, retention, continuous professional development and the need for stronger systems of professional accountability.”

She emphasized that improving the teaching profession is a concern shared by countries across Africa.

She said no country has found all the answers to the challenges facing teachers, making collaboration among African nations essential.

“None of our countries has answered every question about the teaching profession. But none of us should have to confront those questions alone,” she stated.

The Education Minister noted that the ultimate measure of any education system should be the confidence parents have in the people teaching their children.

She argued that teacher preparation, professional standards, accountability and continuous learning must work together to build public trust.

“A parent should be able to trust that the person has been properly prepared,” she said. “There are professional standards governing the work that person does, that professional learning did not end with qualification that brought the teacher into the classroom.”

She also highlighted Liberia’s ongoing work to introduce stronger systems for teacher licensing and professional regulation. Minister Jallah said the country has benefited from lessons learned in other African nations while recognizing that reforms must be adapted to local realities.

“We must build a professional framework that responds to the realities of Liberia,” Minister Jallah intimated.

“But we can ask one another better questions. We can examine what has worked. We can be candid about what has not.”

Looking ahead to the 2027 AFTRA conference, Minister Jallah averred that Liberia hopes to demonstrate meaningful progress rather than simply hosting another international event.

She said the period between the current executive meeting and next year’s conference should be used to advance reforms in teacher development and accountability.

“When ACTRA returns to Liberia next year, I do not want the only difference to be that there are more delegates in the room, a larger program, and a conference banner outside,” she said. “I want you to find that something has moved.”

The Education Minister said Liberia should be able to present clear evidence of progress in strengthening teacher standards, improving professional development opportunities and enhancing accountability mechanisms.

“We should be able to sit together and speak more concretely about the progress Liberia has made in strengthening its teacher professionalization,” she said.

The Education Minister stressed that professionalization efforts must support both future teachers and those already working in classrooms. She said raising standards must go hand in hand with providing teachers opportunities to improve their skills and advance their careers.

“If a teacher needs further preparation, the system must have a pathway for that development,” she said. “If teachers are expected to meet higher professional standards, they must know those standards and have meaningful opportunities to develop them and also be compensated for them.”

She further argued that teacher development and accountability should not be treated as separate issues. “Accountability and professional development have to speak to each other,” Minister Jallah said.

The minister described Liberia’s hosting of the AFTRA conference as an opportunity to hold itself accountable for progress in education reform. She said the return of delegates in 2027 will provide a chance to evaluate both achievements and remaining challenges.

“Hosting should create accountability for us,” she said. “When we welcome you next year, we should be prepared to discuss what we attempted, what worked, what did not work, and what we learned.”

Minister Jallah reminded participants that the success of educational reforms would ultimately be measured not in conference halls but in classrooms across the country.

“The greater responsibility is to use this opportunity to strengthen the profession that stands at the center of every education reform we hope to achieve,” she said.

“After the conference next year, the delegates will return to their respective countries. Our teachers will return to their classrooms. Our children will be waiting for them. That is where the value of everything we discuss here must eventually be seen.”

Delivering his special remarks, AFTRA President Dr. Ebby Mubanga described Liberia’s selection as host country as an important opportunity not only for education but also for national visibility and international engagement.

He said the annual conference creates a platform for African countries to exchange ideas and showcase successful approaches to teaching and learning.

“What we do every year in the month of May, we organize a conference on teaching and learning in Africa,” Mubanga said. “This is an opportunity or a platform for the exchange of best practices in teaching and learning in Africa.”

Mubanga said discussions about Liberia hosting the conference began several years ago following Minister Jallah’s participation in the AFTRA conference held in Angola.

He praised Liberia’s willingness to accept the responsibility and expressed confidence that the country is capable of hosting a successful event. “It is an opportunity for Liberia to host this conference because, first of all, you’ll be marketing your country,” he said. “Apart from just marketing your country in education, you’ll also be marketing it in terms of tourism, business and opportunities.”

The AFTRA president also highlighted the organization’s broad continental reach and the participation of international institutions, including the African Union and several education-focused partners.

He stated that the gathering provides a space for researchers, policymakers, and educators to share innovations and solutions that can strengthen educational systems across Africa.

“Knowledge not shared is not knowledge at all,” Mubanga said. “As educators, I think we should always share what we come across.”

Also speaking, Deputy Minister for Fiscal Affairs at the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, Anthony G. Myers, underscored the importance of teachers in shaping society.

He said every successful individual is a product of educators whose contributions often leave a lasting impact. “We have to be here because we learn to read and write,” Deputy Myers said.

“To learn to read and write means there was a teacher in your life.”

Deputy Myers praised Minister Jallah for pursuing what he described as deep-rooted reforms aimed at addressing long-standing challenges in Liberia’s education system.

He said her efforts have focused not just on examination results but on fundamental classroom issues affecting teaching quality.

“She has been getting to the roots and branches, where she has been bold enough to state the problem as is,” Deputy Minister Myers said.

“For example, a teacher not being able to do lesson planning.”

The Deputy Minister said hosting AFTRA’s continental gathering will also help Liberia reconnect with developments taking place elsewhere in education after years of conflict and recovery slowed progress in the sector. “This forum offers opportunity for knowledge exchange,” Deputy Myers asserted.

“So that our teacher and teaching regulators can see new developments happening out there.,’’ he added.

World.title: Liberia: ANC’s Ex-Secretary General Aloysius Toe Resigns After Leadership Chatroom Removal
World.content:
Cllr. J. Aloysius Toe

The former Secretary General of the Alternative National Congress (ANC), Cllr. J. Aloysius Toe, has resigned from the party, days after he said Political Leader Alexander Cummings removed him from the ANC’s core leadership chatroom.

By Augustus D.R [email protected]

In his letter of resignation dated Sunday, September 6 and addressed to the National Chairman of the ANC, Cllr. Lafayette E.O. Gould , Cllr. Toe said, ‘’please accept this letter as formal notice of my resignation from the Alternative National Congress(ANC) effective immediately, following my arbitrary removal by the Political Leader from the ANC New core Leaders chartroom on September 5, 2026-a platform comprising current and former party leaders and eminent partisans-without any cause or triggering event known to me-without explanation, and without the courtesy of prior conversation.’’

‘‘ Under these circumstances, I can no longer continue my membership in the party, and I respectfully request that the ANC update its records accordingly,’’ he added.

Cllr. Toe said he was removed despite having committed no wrongdoing.

According to sources, relations between Cllr. Toe and the ANC have been strained following his appointment by President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to the Board of Directors of the Liberia Petroleum Refining Company (LPRC).

Meanwhile, the ANC and Cllr. Cummings have yet to publicly response to Cllr. Toe’s resignation or his account of the chatroom removal.

World.title: Liberia: Disability Rights Activist Urges Boakai to Appoint Senior Disability Adviser
World.content:
Monrovia — Disability Rights Activist Dakpannah U-Thant Nicholas Smith has called on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai Sr. to appoint a Senior Special Assistant to the President on Special Needs and Equal Opportunities to ensure that issues affecting persons with disabilities receive greater attention at the highest level of government.

By Patience M. Jones,[email protected]

Smith made the appeal Monday through an open letter addressed to President Boakai and posted on his official Facebook page, arguing that disability inclusion must become a central part of Liberia’s national development agenda.

In the letter, Smith urged the President to establish the proposed position within the Ministry of State for Presidential Affairs, saying the appointment would provide direct and expert advice to the Presidency on policies, programs and decisions affecting persons with disabilities and other vulnerable groups.

According to Smith, persons with disabilities continue to face significant barriers in Liberia, including poverty, limited access to education, inadequate economic opportunities and exclusion from political and social participation.

He also pointed to persistent cultural stigma surrounding disability, noting that some people continue to associate disabilities with curses, witchcraft or punishment rather than viewing them through a human rights and development lens.

Smith acknowledged Liberia’s progress in establishing legal and institutional mechanisms for disability inclusion, including the country’s ratification of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), the establishment of the National Commission on Disabilities, and the adoption of a National Action Plan on Disability.

However, he maintained that implementation remains uneven and fragmented across government institutions.

Smith said the absence of a senior disability adviser at the presidential level risks leaving disability-related initiatives disconnected from broader government policies and programs.

“A Senior Special Assistant on Special Needs and Equal Opportunities would, at minimum, be mandated to provide direct, expert counsel to the President on laws, policies, and programs affecting persons with disabilities,” Smith said in his appeal.

He proposed that the adviser coordinate disability-related initiatives across key government institutions, including the Ministries of Education, Health, Gender, Children and Social Protection, Labour, Public Works, Transport and Justice.

The proposed office, he argued, should also help promote inclusive budgeting, particularly for special education, assistive devices, accessible infrastructure and social protection programs.

Smith further called for stronger disability data collection and evidence-based planning through collaboration among the Liberia Institute of Statistics and Geo-Information Services (LISGIS), the National Commission on Disabilities and disability-focused civil society organizations.

‘Nothing About Us Without Us’

Another major responsibility proposed for the position is to serve as a formal link between the Presidency and organizations representing persons with disabilities.

Smith specifically referenced disability organizations and networks, including the National Union of Organizations of the Disabled (NUOD) and the Liberian National Association of the Deaf, stressing that persons with disabilities should be directly consulted on policies that affect their lives.

He argued that the proposed appointment would not duplicate the work of existing institutions but would instead elevate disability concerns to the highest level of national decision-making.

Smith also noted that advocacy groups have previously called for the appointment of a dedicated disability adviser, particularly as the President’s advisory structure includes experts covering several areas but lacks a dedicated adviser focused specifically on disability inclusion.

Appeal to President Boakai

Smith commended President Boakai for what he described as commitments toward inclusion and social justice, including the President’s engagement with deaf students and educators and his support for inclusive education.

However, he said stronger institutional action is needed to translate such commitments into sustainable policies and programs.

He urged the President to initiate consultations with the Minister of State for Presidential Affairs, the National Commission on Disabilities and disability organizations to determine the appropriate steps for establishing and filling the proposed position.

Smith said the appointment would send a strong message that persons with disabilities are not merely recipients of charity but rights-holders and equal citizens whose voices should influence national policy and development.

He further argued that placing disability inclusion at the heart of the Presidency would strengthen Liberia’s compliance with its international human rights commitments and demonstrate the government’s commitment to building a more inclusive society.

“Persons with disabilities and special needs will see their rights, voices, and aspirations more fully reflected at the heart of governance,” Smith said, expressing hope that President Boakai would give serious consideration to the appeal.

The activist concluded by assuring the President that disability advocates, organizations and families remain willing to work with the government to build stronger bridges between the Presidency, ministries and communities across Liberia.

World.title: HoDs sensitised on access to Information law
World.content:
The Ministry of Information and Media (MIM) has successfully sensitised Heads of Government Departments (HoDs) in Chipata on the Access to Information law, which was enacted in December 2023.

The sensitisation exercise was aimed at equipping officers who serve as information officers in different departments with adequate knowledge on public expectations, as well as the dos and don’ts required to effectively carry out their information‑sharing mandate.

Eastern Province Permanent Secretary (PS) Paul Thole, who was represented by Deputy Permanent Secretary Lewis Mwape at the meeting, highlighted that access to information is a human right, and that administrative penalties will apply on individuals failing in their duties of providing information.

“Government has mandated the Human Rights Commission as the statutory body that puts administrative penalties on you HODs who may deliberately fail to comply,” he said.

Mr Thole further warned that no government officer will be allowed to use public resources to pay penalties, but their own funds, to serve as a warning to would-be offenders.

He reiterated that the government enacted the law to promote transparency in the running of public affairs.

“President Hakainde Hichilema signed this law to ensure the public service works according to the expectations of the people it serves by ensuring transparency in the system,” he indicated.

And in his presentation, MIM Director in Charge of Press and Media Development, Modern Mayembe disclosed that the law allows for institutions to appoint information officers responsible to give out information to the public.

He called on Departments to quicken this process that is key to the implementation of the Access to Information Act, adding that the law enhances service delivery and reduces corrupt practices in public offices.

“In an event where you fail to appoint an Information Officer, Heads of Departments will act as Information Officers until someone is put in place, ” the Director guided.

The meeting availed the HoDs with a number of guidelines on information sharing as provided for by the law, while indicating exceptions where information can be withheld, including matters bordering on state security and personal information in instances that compromise the safety and well-being of concerned individuals.

It was also disclosed during the meeting that requests and responses on information sharing need to be in written form, for records keeping.

World.title: Crocodile meat lands Nchelenge man 60 months imprisonment
World.content:
The Nchelenge Magistrate’s Court has sentenced a 50-year-old man to 60 months imprisonment with hard labour for unlawful possession of a crocodile carcass.

‎John Mukuka of Kapema Village in Nchelenge District pleaded guilty to unlawful possession of a protected trophy, contrary to Section 130 of the Wildlife Act No. 14 of 2015 of the Laws of Zambia, as read with Statutory Instrument No. 42 of 2016.

‎

‎The particulars of the offence are that on August 28, 2026, in Chienge District, Mukuka was found in possession of a full carcass of a crocodile without lawful authority.

‎

‎The court heard from State prosecutor Sinyinda Mbangweta that on the same day, around 13:00 hours, officers from the Department of National Parks and Wildlife were patrolling in Lusenga National Park when they found Mukuka with the crocodile carcass.

‎

‎Mbangweta said that the officers asked him to produce documents authorizing him to possess the protected trophy, but he failed to produce any.

‎

‎”He was subsequently apprehended and taken to Nchelenge Police Station, where he was detained for safe custody, while the crocodile carcass was seized,” said Mbangweta.

‎

‎He added that the carcass was later examined and confirmed to be that of a crocodile, which is a protected animal.

‎

‎When asked if the facts presented by the state were true and correct, Mukuka responded in affirmative.

‎

‎Upon his own admission of the facts, Resident Magistrate Luckson Mbewe, convicted Mukuka accordingly.

‎In mitigation, Mukula pleaded with the court for leniency.

‎Magistrate Mbewe said he took into consideration that Mukuka was a first offender who readily admitted the charge without wasting the court’s time, noting that being found in possession of a government trophy is a very serious offence.

‎”I am sending you to prison for 60 months with hard labour so that others can learn from you,” Magistrate Mbewe ruled.

World.title: RDA set for restructuring to improve service delivery
World.content:
The Road Development Agency (RDA) has announced that the institution will soon implement an organizational restructuring process to improve service delivery and operational efficiency.

RDA Director and Chief Executive Officer, Nelson Chuma says the organizational changes will strengthen the agency’s contribution to the Grow Zambia Mission, an ambitious national economic expansion strategy recently pronounced by President Hakainde Hichilema.

Speaking at a media briefing in Lusaka , Eng. Chuma explained that to remain effective and responsive, the institution needs to embark on faster decision making and execution, which he said will better position RDA to deliver sustainable results.

He said restructuring the institution will enhance accountability and performance management while encouraging greater collaboration across departments.

He emphasized that the restructuring initiative will focus on Strategic Realignment, Operational Efficiency, Strengthening Accountability, Investment in Talent and Capacity Building as well Technology and Innovation.

“This restructuring is a strategic step designed to improve efficiency, accountability, and impact. It aligns our organization with the goals of the Grow Zambia Mission and ensures we are better equipped to deliver sustainable growth and value for all stakeholders,” Eng. Chuma stressed.

Eng. Chuma acknowledged that the process can create uncertainty among employees but assured that the process will be managed responsibly, transparently and with respect to all employees.

“Throughout the transition, we will Maintain open communication with staff and stakeholders, provide guidance and support to affected employees, and ensure compliance with all relevant labour laws and regulations,” he said.

He stated that the institution will ensure that there is business continuity and uninterrupted service delivery to stakeholders and clients.

During President Hichilema’s inauguration last week, he pledged to more than double Zambia’s economy, a move anchored on the Grow Zambia Agenda, an economic strategy aimed at accelerating growth and investment.

World.title: Former Constitutional Court judge Ann-Mwewa Sitali freed on bail
World.content:
Former Constitutional Court judge Anne Mwewa Sitali was picked up on a Wednesday night and detained at the Richard Kachingwe Police Post, accused of intending to commit a felony over legal advice she gave on the election petition filed by Brian Mundubile against President Hakainde Hichilema. She has since been released on bail. She had also applied for a writ of habeas corpus while in custody.

The charge reaches back into Justice Sitali’s own history with the bench she once sat on. On October 20, 2024, President Hichilema removed her from the Constitutional Court, together with fellow judges Mungeni Mulenga and Palan Mulonda. Critics at the time called the removals political manoeuvring ahead of this year’s elections. Less than two years later, the same court she was ousted from has become the battleground over her freedom.

Supporters of the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance, which Mr Mundubile leads, maintain that he secured a surprise win in the 2026 presidential election, pointing to parallel vote tabulations they say support that outcome. Government and the Electoral Commission of Zambia dispute this, and Mr Hichilema was declared winner for a second term with 60 per cent of the vote against Mr Mundubile’s 38 per cent.

It was in the middle of that dispute that Justice Sitali became entangled. Opposition lawyers say the case against her stems from professional legal advice she gave to attorneys preparing Mr Mundubile’s petition challenging the election outcome — work that put a former constitutional judge on the same side of a legal fight as the man now facing treason charges over the same disputed result.

Her case sits within a much larger sweep. Opposition sources and human rights monitors describe her as one of more than 300 people arrested since the August 13 election, a figure government has not confirmed. Others still held include Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance secretary general Celestine Mambula Mukandila, arrested August 20, and youths Yona Longwe and Mwape. Detainees are being held across multiple facilities in Lusaka, including Chelstone, Kabwata, Lusaka Central and Richard Kachingwe police stations and posts.

The Human Rights Commission (HRC) has confirmed a lower but still substantial figure: at least 84 individuals remain under its active monitoring in connection with the election. HRC chairperson Dr Pamela Towela Sambo said many have been held past legal limits without formal charges or timely court appearances, in violation of Articles 13 and 18 of the Constitution, which guarantee the right to liberty and a fair hearing.

“The commission is monitoring several cases,” Dr Sambo said, citing specific instances of detainees held for 19 days or more without being formally charged. She called on police and prosecutors to “immediately charge, grant bond to, or release” all those whose detention lacks legal justification.

Acting Attorney-General Marshall Muchende rejects the political-detention framing. “Zambia has no prisoners of conscience or political prisoners,” he said this week, maintaining that those in custody face serious criminal charges. Authorities have accused opposition figures of plotting an armed insurgency, allegations the accused have denied.

Civil society groups and opposition leaders argue the arrests are designed to prevent any legal challenge to an election they contend was flawed. They say courts were sealed off on the final day for filing petitions, blocking a broader court challenge to the results. Mr Mundubile, who came second with 38 per cent of the vote, was himself arrested on treason charges after taking refuge at a United Nations facility.

The HRC says it will keep monitoring detention facilities and engaging with prosecutors to ensure constitutional protections are observed. “Release all those whose continued detention exposes the risk of ill-treatment, restricts access to legal representation and undermines public confidence,” Dr Sambo said.

Justice Sitali’s release resolves her own case. What remains unresolved is the wider dispute now running through it: a disputed election result, a petition still contested, and a sacked judge whose legal advice on that petition became, briefly, a criminal matter of its own.

World.title: Kafwaya’s death reaches The Hague for a second time
World.content:
Second ICC complaint over Kafwaya killing names Zyeele, Shapwaya, seeks probe into Hichilema’s role

A second formal complaint has been lodged with the International Criminal Court in The Hague over the August killing of Mutotwe Kafwaya, a former Zambian cabinet minister shot dead during a security operation at the home of a presidential candidate.

The submission, dated September 7, names Lieutenant General Geoffrey Choongo Zyeele, commander of the Zambian Army, and Brigadier General Moses Shapwaya, reported to be associated with a special forces command unit, as the leaders of the operation that resulted in Mr Kafwaya’s death. It also asks the court to investigate whether President Hakainde Hichilema authorised or directed the security forces’ actions — an allegation the complaint makes, not a finding the court has reached.

Mr Kafwaya was killed on August 14 during a joint security forces raid on a private residence in the Kabulonga neighbourhood of Lusaka. The property belonged to Brian Mundubile, a presidential candidate for the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Progress (NRPUP). Mr Mundubile has said he personally witnessed Mr Kafwaya being shot twice during the assault.

For five days, government did not confirm Mr Kafwaya’s identity or whereabouts, despite pleas from his family and political allies. His wife, Dinis Ng’andu Kafwaya, initiated habeas corpus proceedings in the High Court to compel authorities to produce him. Government acknowledged his death on August 19, with Inspector General of Police Graphel Musamba confirming that Mr Kafwaya was the unidentified man fatally wounded in an exchange of gunfire.

The new complaint goes further than the initial outcry from opposition figures and human rights groups. It explicitly requests an independent investigation into the origins, manner and chain of command behind the use of lethal force. It alleges that Lt Gen Zyeele and Brig Gen Shapwaya acted on instructions originating from the President or other senior government authorities, and calls on the court to establish, through documentary evidence, communications and witness testimony, whether President Hichilema authorised the operation.

Lt Gen Zyeele has been a prominent figure throughout the election period. In June, he drew criticism for stating that the army would police the country before, during and after the polls, a remark civil society groups described as unconstitutional at the time.

The killing occurred against a backdrop of wider post-election turmoil. Opposition parties have alleged that the vote was rigged in favour of President Hichilema, who was declared the winner for a second term. In the days following the election, security forces arrested at least 11 people, including several opposition figures, on treason charges.

Amnesty International has called on Zambian authorities to conduct an independent investigation into Mr Kafwaya’s death, noting that it followed a series of arbitrary arrests and detentions of opposition members. The rights group has urged government to provide full information to the family and ensure that those responsible are brought to justice.

The filing of a second ICC complaint suggests that domestic avenues for accountability are viewed as insufficient by a section of Zambians. Citizens First party president Harry Kalaba has been among the most vocal proponents of ICC intervention, saying international institutions should provide support to the family in its pursuit of justice.

Zambia is a state party to the Rome Statute, which gives the ICC jurisdiction over war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide committed on its territory. Whether the complaint meets that threshold, and whether the court takes it up, remains to be determined by the ICC itself.

For now, the unanswered questions around Mr Kafwaya’s death sit alongside the broader detention of opposition figures as one of the defining disputes of the post-election period, with the family’s pursuit of accountability now extending from Zambia’s own courts to an international one.

World.title: Let courts decide, historian says of Mukandila dispute
World.content:
Historian Dr Eustone Chiputa says the dispute over detained lawyer Celestine Mukandila’s nationality should be settled by a court of law, not by ministers or permanent secretaries, as the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance separately demands his immediate and unconditional release along with the restoration of his National Registration Card and passport.

Mr Mukandila, secretary general of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) and of the wider Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance, was arrested on August 20 after the Department of Immigration detained him on the allegation that he is not Zambian. Government has since revoked his identity card and passport.

Dr Chiputa said questions of this nature belong squarely with the judiciary. “They should not be settled by ministers or permanent secretaries; those are not experts at law. That is why we have the Judiciary, anything that is contested let it be settled by the court of law,” he said.

He argued that a court ruling would settle the matter cleanly, removing the personal element that has defined the dispute so far. “If the government took the gentleman to court and the court proved that it was true, it will be the case settled by the court of law and he will not be looking at individuals. For now, he is looking at individuals as people who are victimising him.”

Dr Chiputa said leaders handling contested legal questions should remain impartial rather than emotional. “Let that case go to court and let him prove he is Zambian,” he said, adding that a fair hearing would protect both sides: government, if its allegation held up, and Mr Mukandila, if it did not.

“If, for example, for argument’s sake they bundle him out of Zambia, he will go to the international system and say he was victimised because he was never allowed to go to court,” Dr Chiputa said.

He drew a comparison with ordinary criminal process, noting that law enforcement agencies routinely take suspects to court rather than deciding guilt themselves, even when evidence appears clear-cut. “The case is tested in court. The conviction is secured and the person is locked up. It takes a judicial face rather than the faces of individuals who are handling the case,” he said.

Mr Mukandila’s own account is that he is Zambian by descent. He says his mother was Zambian, from Chief Matanda’s chiefdom in Luapula Province, while his father was Congolese. He has taken the matter to court himself, and the Lusaka High Court has since granted him leave to apply for a writ of habeas corpus, ordering the state to justify his continued detention.

Tonse-Pamodzi has now built a constitutional argument around that claim. In a statement issued by media director Brian Matambo, the alliance cited Article 36 of the Constitution, which recognises as a citizen by descent any person born outside Zambia where at least one parent was a Zambian citizen by birth or descent.

The alliance drew a pointed comparison to footballer Frankie Musonda, born in England to a Zambian father and an English mother, who represents Zambia’s Chipolopolo. “If a son of a Zambian can wear our national colours on the football pitch, why should a son of a Zambian suddenly become a foreigner when he enters the political arena and uses his legal brilliance to challenge government?” the statement asked. “If Frankie Musonda can play for Zambia, Celestine Mukandila can participate in Zambian politics. The Constitution cannot change depending on whether the citizen is scoring goals for Zambia or challenging the President in court.”

The statement also placed Mr Mukandila’s case in a wider legal history. It noted that he was among the lawyers who successfully challenged the constitutional amendment process behind Bill 7, with the Constitutional Court ruling that the process required wider public consultation. Parliament’s own records list him as one of the petitioners in that case. The Bill was later revived and assented to as Act No. 13 of 2025.

Tonse-Pamodzi linked Mr Mukandila’s case to the continued detention of Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and Bishop Trevor Mwamba on treason charges, arguing that the state should place credible evidence before an independent court “without delay” or release all those held. “Stop governing Zambia through fear. Stop manufacturing enemies. Let the Constitution, evidence and the courts speak,” the statement said.

For now, the matter sits where Dr Chiputa says it belongs: before the courts. With the High Court having granted leave for a habeas corpus application, the next step is a hearing that will test, on the record, whether the state can justify Mr Mukandila’s continued detention.

World.title: Recognise HH first, Zimba tells Mundubile, as dialogue push gathers pace
World.content:
Recognise HH first, Zimba tells mundubile, as dialogue push gathers pace

Tonse Alliance founder Zumani Zimba has urged National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) presidential candidate Brian mundubile to publicly recognise President Hakainde Hichilema as Head of State, arguing that recognition, not confrontation, is the fastest route to dialogue between the two camps. The Tonse Alliance founder, who also holds the NRPUP secretary-general and chief presidential adviser portfolios, made the call in a statement as pressure builds from multiple directions for Zambia’s two leading political camps to sit down.

“The fastest way to get HH’s attention to dialogue is for Mr mundubile to publicly recognise that Mr Hichilema won the election and is the President,” he said. “How can HH be motivated to dialogue or reconcile with people who don’t recognise him as President?”

Mr Mundubile came second in the polls with 38 per cent of the vote against Mr Hichilema’s 60 per cent. He, his running mate Makebi Zulu, and 16 others remain in detention, charged with treason.

The Tonse Alliance founder was direct about what the detained pair stand to gain from a change in posture. “Accepting HH as sitting President and respectfully appealing — not demanding — for dialogue with his government is the best way out for the freedom of BM and the team,” he said, cautioning against the alternative path some supporters have taken.

“For BM and MZ supporters, the idea of attacking, insulting and denouncing HH will not and will never help to resolve the problem of BM and MZ, either today or tomorrow.”

His appeal rested on a wider point about how Zambian presidents have historically been treated once accepted in office: “Whenever a Republican President was recognised, regardless of how he won, by his competitors, he or she feels comfortable, free and confident to be engaged in any national political discourse.” He called on the Church, traditional leaders, and regional and global bodies to keep pushing for dialogue and reconciliation between the President and Mr Mundubile.

The appeal is not coming from one quarter alone. Former Nkana member of Parliament Binwell Mpundu has shifted his own public tone in recent days, moving from confrontation towards an olive branch aimed squarely at State House. “I’m taking that first step, I’m reaching out to President HH for peace,” he posted on Facebook.

The recognition push lands at a moment when NRPUP is working to project unity from within Parliament, even with its presidential and vice-presidential candidates behind bars. Party leader Ezra Tembo told journalists at the National Assembly that all 59 NRPUP law-makers sworn in this week remain loyal to the current leadership structure. “When it comes to allegiance to the party leadership by MPs, we are a team,” he said. “We do not have any problem in terms of loyalty because there is nothing that has changed in terms of leadership. The party is intact, and MPs and other elected officials are loyal to the party leadership.”

Secretary-general Nonde Mubanga was said to be meeting NRPUP MPs individually to align them on the party’s position going forward. The party is also expecting 16 additional seats through the proportional representation system, on top of its 59 constituency wins. Feira MP Emmanuel Tembo and his Chama Central counterpart Yotam Mtayachalo both said they had no issue with the party leadership, while Lupososhi law-maker Shadreck Katuta said his own focus in the new Parliament would be women’s and youth empowerment through the Constituency Development Fund.

That show of parliamentary cohesion gives the recognition argument added weight: a party functioning normally in the House, even as its top two leaders sit in custody, strengthens the case that dialogue rather than deadlock is the more useful posture for all sides.

Not every voice in the aftermath of the election has been calming. The Commonwealth Lawyers Association (CLA) has separately raised concerns about the post-election period, citing worries over access to justice and judicial independence. Its president, Steven Thiru, said the organisation was not taking a position on the merits of the election outcome, describing its intervention as focused strictly on the rule of law and the safety of lawyers.

The recognition message, however, stays fixed on the practical next step rather than on the events of the campaign itself. The ball now sits with Mr Mundubile. Whether he takes up the suggestion, or waits on the courts to rule on the matters still before them, will determine whether the coming weeks bring the two camps to a table or leave both sides exactly where they started.

World.title: Dialogue Cannot Be a Substitute for Justice and Accountability
World.content:
By Farai Ruvanyathi

Signals from the Tonse Alliance calling for forgiveness, unity, reconciliation and national healing initially emerged as distant murmurs, reverberating through news outlets and across social media. At first, they appeared to be little more than rumours promoted by self-styled political experts such as ‘Dr’ Zumani Zimba. Those calls have since grown louder. Yesterday, from his European hideout, Binwell Mpundu, the very man who first raised the spectre of a possible armed insurrection through his now-infamous declaration, “to kill or be killed”, called upon President Hakainde Hichilema to facilitate healing, forgiveness and dialogue.

Dialogue is a constructive exchange of views between two or more parties, intended to promote understanding, resolve differences or establish common ground. Ordinarily, parties entering dialogue bring legitimate interests, grievances or proposals to the table. In the present circumstances, however, the call for dialogue is profoundly misplaced. Several Tonse Alliance leaders are in custody facing grave allegations of treason and involvement in a possible armed insurrection. What, precisely, are they proposing to bring to the table? More importantly, what would such dialogue mean for the laws governing treason and the constitutional duty of the State to investigate threats to national security?

It is bizarre to demand dialogue before the truth has been established. Such a demand risks becoming an attempt to evade accountability, obscure the alleged crimes and substitute a political arrangement for a judicial determination. These are the same individuals whose prevailing narrative has been that the treason charges were concocted and that the election was stolen. That is precisely why a full and transparent trial is necessary: the evidence must be tested in open court so that their claims may either be proved or disproved.

Only after the judicial process has established the truth can meaningful dialogue, reconciliation or the question of clemency properly arise. Until then, calls for reconciliation misrepresent the circumstances and risk interfering with the administration of justice. If the accused are vindicated, they should regain their freedom and reputations. If they are convicted, they must face the consequences prescribed by law. Due process, not political bargaining, must determine the outcome.

The President’s constitutional duty is to protect the Republic and its people from anyone alleged to have attempted to circumvent democratic processes and usurp power. Any presidential prerogative relating to clemency should be considered only after the courts have completed their work. Dialogue at this stage would establish a dangerous precedent by suggesting that serious allegations against the State may be negotiated away before the evidence is heard. Why are they in a hurry and what are they hiding? This is no laughing matter.

When President Hakainde Hichilema consistently preached, promoted and preserved peace, certain opposition figures responded with inflammatory rhetoric and threats of confrontation. Now that their reckless political project has failed, they seek forgiveness, dialogue and reconciliation without first accepting responsibility or submitting their claims to judicial scrutiny. Reconciliation cannot be credible when it is invoked merely as an escape route from accountability.

Forgiveness does not erase the law, and reconciliation cannot replace justice. Those accused must be treated firmly but fairly, with their constitutional rights fully protected. Should the courts find them guilty, they must serve the sentences imposed upon them. If they genuinely wish to serve the State, they must first demonstrate respect for its Constitution, democratic institutions and laws.

The State must neither persecute nor indulge them. It must proceed resolutely, lawfully and without political interference. Individuals convicted of attempting to subvert constitutional government cannot be entrusted with public power merely because they describe themselves as politicians or aspirants to public office. Criminal conduct does not become legitimate political activity simply because it is committed in pursuit of power.

They must therefore not be handled with undue leniency. The allegations are exceptionally serious, and the law must be allowed to take its full and impartial course. Justice must be firm, transparent and consistent, booth to establish the truth and to safeguard Zambia’s peace, unity, security and constitutional order.

Farai Ruvanyathi is a Zambian international political and governance analyst based in Kimberley, Northern Cape, South Africa
