Last month, Mexico and the United States signed a defense agreement on new technologies that allows Defensa to acquire drones and counter-unmanned aerial systems in the U.S. Army’s online marketplace. However, the Defense Ministry said at the time that it hadn’t made any purchase commitment.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Cosan Leaves the New York Stock Exchange on September 18
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts — What happened. Cosan filed to withdraw its American depositary shares from the New York Stock Exchange.

Cosan filed to withdraw its American depositary shares from the New York Stock Exchange. — The date. The last day of trading on the exchange is Friday 18 September 2026.

The last day of trading on the exchange is Friday 18 September 2026. — The catch. The receipts do not disappear. They keep trading over the counter under a lower-tier programme.

The receipts do not disappear. They keep trading over the counter under a lower-tier programme. — What holders must do. Nothing. No surrender or conversion is required, and none has been announced.

Nothing. No surrender or conversion is required, and none has been announced. — Why the company says it did it. To simplify its capital structure, cut costs and focus on its core businesses.

To simplify its capital structure, cut costs and focus on its core businesses. — Where the shares still trade. On Brazil’s B3 exchange, where the company says its trading is concentrated.

Cosan is taking its shares off the New York Stock Exchange after years of a dual listing. What happens to the receipts themselves is the part worth reading twice.

The New York Stock Exchange. Cosan’s American depositary shares stop trading there on September 18 (Photo: Yiyuanju, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

A delisting sounds final. In this case the American receipts survive it, and an earlier filing said the opposite.

The Dates

Cosan’s board approved the withdrawal on 14 August 2026. It formally notified the New York Stock Exchange on 18 August.

The company filed the delisting form with the securities regulator on 8 September.

The last day the receipts trade on the exchange is 18 September 2026.

Under the rules, a withdrawal takes effect ten days after that filing. Deregistration from the exchange follows about ninety days later.

Cosan has not published its own date for that final step. Those timings are what the rules provide, not company guidance.

What Cosan does. Cosan S.A. engages in the fuel distribution business. It operates through Raízen, Compass, Moove, Rumo, and Radar segments. The company's Raízen segment engages in the production, marketing, origination, and trading of sugar, as well as ethanol; production and marketing of bioenergy, and solar energy and biogas; trading and resale of electricity; and…

The Detail Two Filings Disagree On

The August notice said the company had not arranged for the receipts to be listed or quoted anywhere else.

The September notice says the opposite. Cosan will keep its programme at the first level, letting the receipts trade over the counter in the United States.

The later filing governs. Anyone working from the August language has stale information.

A first-level programme is the simplest kind. It trades off-exchange, with lighter reporting and thinner liquidity.

Cosan also remains a registered filer with the American regulator. It has not filed to deregister entirely.

What Holders Have to Do

Nothing is required. No filing sets out a surrender or cancellation procedure, because the programme survives.

Holders can keep the receipts and trade them over the counter. They can also instruct the depositary to cancel them for ordinary shares in Brazil.

Each receipt represents four ordinary shares. That ratio is unchanged.

Nobody should report a forced conversion. That is not what is happening here.

The Reason Cosan Gives

The company describes the move as part of an objective to simplify and optimise its capital structure.

It cites cost reductions and greater focus on its most strategically relevant business areas.

It also notes that trading in its shares is predominantly concentrated on the Brazilian exchange.

That last point is the honest core of it. A second listing costs money and, in this case, was carrying little volume.

The Balance Sheet Behind the Decision

Cosan is a Brazilian holding company with interests in fuel distribution, sugar and ethanol, logistics, gas and land.

It reported a second-quarter net loss of R$320 million, about US$62.9 million, down 66% from R$946 million a year earlier.

Conversions use 5.0856 reais to the US dollar, the Banco Central closing rate for 8 September 2026.

Net debt at the holding level fell 47% year on year to R$9.2 billion, about US$1.81 billion.

The company prepaid R$8.8 billion of debt principal in the first half, roughly US$1.73 billion.

It also signed a letter of intent to sell a port terminal for about R$300 million, or US$59 million, plus earn-outs.

The Raízen Problem in the Background

Cosan’s holding in Raízen, its fuel and sugar joint venture with Shell, was written down to zero at the end of 2025.

Raízen’s out-of-court restructuring plan was approved during the second quarter of 2026.

That is the single largest reason the group has spent this year cutting debt and selling assets.

Raízen separately completed the sale of its Argentine business earlier this month, for US$1.42 billion.

What a Delisting Does and Does Not Signal

Leaving a foreign exchange is not the same as leaving public markets. Cosan remains listed in São Paulo.

Companies do this when the second listing costs more than it delivers in liquidity or visibility.

For an American investor the practical change is real. Over-the-counter trading means wider spreads and less coverage.

For a Brazilian investor almost nothing changes. The shares trade where they always did.

Foreign readers holding the receipts should check with their broker before 18 September. Some brokers restrict over-the-counter trading.

What Cosan Actually Owns

The group runs Raízen with Shell, in sugar, ethanol and fuel distribution. That is its largest and most troubled holding.

Compass distributes natural gas and went to market in its own listing, raising about R$2.3 billion net for Cosan.

That is roughly US$452 million, and it was one of the year’s main sources of cash for cutting debt.

Rumo runs the country’s largest rail freight network, moving grain from the interior to the ports.

Radar holds farmland, and the group also has a stake in the mining company Vale. Together they make Cosan a holding company rather than an operator.

For a foreign reader that structure is the point. A loss at one arm does not describe the group, and a delisting does not describe the business.

Frequently Asked Questions

When do Cosan’s American receipts stop trading in New York? The last day of trading on the New York Stock Exchange is 18 September 2026. The withdrawal filing was made on 8 September. Do holders lose their receipts? No. Cosan is keeping a first-level programme, so the receipts continue to trade over the counter in the United States. Does anything need to be done before the delisting? No action is required. Holders may keep the receipts or instruct the depositary to cancel them for ordinary Brazilian shares. Why is Cosan doing this? It says the move simplifies its capital structure, cuts costs and reflects that trading in its shares is concentrated on Brazil’s exchange.

Sources: US Securities and Exchange Commission, the delisting form, Cosan, notice to the market of 8 September 2026, Cosan, material fact of 18 August 2026, InfoMoney, the second-quarter results, Banco Central do Brasil, the dollar reference rate

World.title: Brazil’s First Presidential Debate Is Off, and Nobody Said Why
World.content:
Brazil · Elections

Key Facts — What happened. Eleven media outlets cancelled their joint presidential debate, which was set for 14 September.

Eleven media outlets cancelled their joint presidential debate, which was set for 14 September. — Why it fell apart. Neither Lula nor Flávio Bolsonaro confirmed by the deadline of 7 September.

Neither Lula nor Flávio Bolsonaro confirmed by the deadline of 7 September. — The catch. Neither campaign refused. They simply did not answer, and neither has explained.

Neither campaign refused. They simply did not answer, and neither has explained. — Who did confirm. Four candidates said yes, including the governors of Goiás and Minas Gerais.

Four candidates said yes, including the governors of Goiás and Minas Gerais. — Where the race is. Quaest puts Lula on 36% and Flávio Bolsonaro on 29% in the first round.

Quaest puts Lula on 36% and Flávio Bolsonaro on 29% in the first round. — What comes next. Brazil votes on 4 October, with a runoff on 25 October if nobody wins outright.

Two front-runners let a deadline pass in silence, and a debate involving eleven broadcasters collapsed. Brazil votes in under four weeks.

Inside Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court in Brasília, where both leading campaigns have filed actions against each other (Photo: Tribunal Superior Eleitoral, public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

The interesting part is not that they declined. It is that neither of them said anything at all.

What Was Cancelled

Eleven outlets had joined to stage a presidential debate under the banner The Moment of Decision.

They include CNN Brasil, SBT, RedeTV!, Exame, Metrópoles, Terra, VEJA and Rádio Itatiaia.

The debate was set for 14 September. The deadline for candidates to confirm was 7 September.

The cancellation was announced on 8 September, after the deadline passed.

A São Paulo governor’s debate scheduled for 18 September was cancelled too, after the incumbent also failed to confirm.

Nobody Actually Said No

President Lula did not confirm. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro did not confirm either.

Neither campaign issued a statement. Neither declined in terms, and neither gave a reason.

That distinction matters for how this is reported. Silence is not a refusal, though the effect is the same.

Four candidates did confirm. They are Ronaldo Caiado, Romeu Zema, Augusto Cury and Renan Santos.

Caiado, the governor of Goiás, called the cancellation a blow to Brazilian democracy.

Where the Race Actually Stands

Quaest surveyed 2,004 people between 3 and 6 September for a Globo company, with a margin of error of two points.

In the first round it puts Lula on 36% and Flávio Bolsonaro on 29%.

Augusto Cury follows on 8%, then Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos on 3% each, and Romeu Zema on 2%.

In a runoff the same poll has them level at 41% each. Other polls this week point the same way or slightly the other.

One has Flávio ahead 46 to 45. Another has them tied at 44.

So the first round has a leader and the second round does not. That is the state of the race in one line.

Who the Candidates Are

Lula is seeking a fourth term for the Workers’ Party, with Geraldo Alckmin as his running mate.

Flávio Bolsonaro is a senator for Rio de Janeiro and the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

He announced his candidacy in December 2025, after visiting his father in custody. His running mate is a federal deputy from Alagoas.

Jair Bolsonaro is not a candidate. He was convicted of attempting a coup and sentenced to 27 years and three months.

He is serving that sentence under house arrest in Brasília, with visits restricted to doctors and lawyers.

Flávio is barred from visiting him. That restriction was imposed by the same court now fighting with itself in public.

The State Races Under It

Quaest also polled five governor’s races, with fieldwork from 4 to 7 September.

In São Paulo, Tarcísio de Freitas leads Fernando Haddad by 42% to 27%.

In Rio de Janeiro, Eduardo Paes leads on 39%, with Douglas Ruas on 18%.

Celina Leão leads the Federal District on 35%. Cleitinho leads Minas Gerais on 32%.

Pernambuco is the close one. Raquel Lyra has 43% to João Campos’s 37%, and the pollster calls that a tie at the edge of the margin.

Anyone describing Pernambuco as a clear lead is overreading a six-point gap at three points of error.

Two Legal Actions Running in Parallel

On 8 September, Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign asked the electoral court to cancel the registration of the Lula ticket.

The ground is alleged abuse of political and economic power over a February Carnival parade at Rio’s sambadrome that honoured Lula.

The filing alleges public money was used and seeks eight years of ineligibility. There has been no ruling.

The same day, the court accepted a case filed by Lula’s coalition against Flávio Bolsonaro and his running mate.

It concerns campaigning from the main stage of a rodeo festival in Barretos in late August, before around 60,000 people.

The allegation is indirect corporate campaign funding, because the stage was paid for by private companies. Flávio has five days to answer.

Both actions seek the same remedy against the other side. Neither has produced a decision.

Why Any of This Matters to a Foreign Reader

Brazil is the largest economy in Latin America and its most consequential election this year.

The first round is on Sunday 4 October, with a runoff on 25 October if nobody clears 50%.

A cancelled debate removes the only scheduled moment where the two front-runners would face each other before voting starts.

Whether more debates happen is now an open question. Broadcasters have shown they will cancel rather than stage a half-empty stage.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why was Brazil’s presidential debate cancelled? Neither Lula nor Flávio Bolsonaro confirmed attendance by the 7 September deadline, so the eleven broadcasters cancelled the 14 September event. Did the candidates refuse to attend? Not in terms. Neither campaign issued a statement or gave a reason, and the debate fell through on non-response rather than refusal. Who is leading the race? Quaest has Lula on 36% and Flávio Bolsonaro on 29% in the first round. The two are level at 41% each in a runoff. When does Brazil vote? The first round is on 4 October 2026. A runoff follows on 25 October if nobody wins more than half the valid votes.

World.title: Brazil’s Supreme Court Crisis Deepens Before the October Election
World.content:
BRAZIL · ANALYSIS

Key Facts — The moment: Two Supreme Court justices are formally trying to investigate each other, weeks before Brazil votes.

— The number: The Senate held 109 impeachment requests against the Court’s ten sitting justices as of 1 September.

— The walkout: Eleven of the Federal Police’s fifteen directors offered to quit after Mendonça removed its chief.

— The elders: Thirteen retired justices, including three former chief justices, want the Court investigated in public.

— The timing: Brazil votes on 4 October, with Jair Bolsonaro’s son Flávio now tied with President Lula.

— The catch: Almost everything above is an allegation, a filing or a letter — not a verdict.

Brazil’s Supreme Court is investigating itself, its own police force is in open revolt, and its most senior alumni say the crisis is the worst in the Court’s modern history. It is happening five weeks before an election too close to call.

Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court in Brasília. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

Two justices of Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court are each trying to get the other investigated. Alexandre de Moraes wants colleague André Mendonça, a Bolsonaro appointee, investigated, and Mendonça wants Moraes removed.

Mendonça made his move first. He removed the Federal Police’s top two officials, saying they had spied on him.

Eleven of the force’s fifteen directors then offered to resign in solidarity. They back the officials Mendonça removed.

Thirteen retired justices, including three former chief justices, have taken the unusual step of writing to the sitting Court. They want its response held in public, not behind closed doors.

None of this proves wrongdoing by anyone named in it. But the sheer volume of it, five weeks before Brazilians vote for a president, is itself the story.

How the Court Got Here

Start with Justice Alexandre de Moraes, the figure at the center of most of this. His authority expanded sharply after 2019, when he began overseeing a standing inquiry into threats against the Court itself.

He used that inquiry to order the removal of social media accounts. In 2024, he suspended Elon Musk’s platform X across all of Brazil.

Musk called it censorship. Moraes called it a defense of democracy against coordinated disinformation.

The stakes rose after 8 January 2023, when Bolsonaro supporters stormed government buildings in Brasília days after Lula’s inauguration. Moraes led the Court’s response, and dozens of defendants received long sentences.

In September 2025, the Court’s First Panel convicted Jair Bolsonaro of plotting a coup to overturn his 2022 election loss. He received 27 years, and the ruling was not unanimous.

Justice Luiz Fux dissented, arguing the Court lacked jurisdiction. He said the rule letting it try Bolsonaro was adopted only after the alleged offenses.

The following June, a separate panel convicted Eduardo Bolsonaro, one of the former president’s sons, of coercion. Judges found he pressured US officials to force Brazil’s courts to drop his father’s case.

A month later, Washington granted him a green card. It shields him from his Brazilian prison sentence while he stays in the US.

A third son, Rio city councilman Carlos Bolsonaro, faces a separate trial. Investigators allege an illegal spy network that surveilled justices, journalists and rivals during his father’s presidency.

Only Jair Bolsonaro himself was barred from voting and running this year. His sons remain free to do both.

The Case That Something Is Badly Wrong

Start with what critics call unchecked power. One justice suspended a foreign platform used by millions, fined it daily, and blocked accounts without a jury or a public trial.

The Trump administration treated this as serious enough to act on. It sanctioned Moraes personally in 2025 under the Global Magnitsky Act.

That law is usually reserved for authoritarian officials. Washington later extended sanctions to Moraes’s wife and her law firm.

Washington added 50% tariffs on many Brazilian exports the same year. No US administration had previously sanctioned a sitting justice of a major democratic ally.

Musk asked in 2025 whether Brazil was following Venezuela’s path, comparing Moraes’s tactics to those used against dissent under Nicolás Maduro. This newspaper reported at the time that a growing number of Brazilians and foreign observers were making the same comparison.

This week’s crisis adds a domestic dimension to that argument. Three of Brazil’s largest newspapers made the same demand this month.

Estadão, Folha de S.Paulo and O Globo all published editorials. Each said Justice Moraes should leave the Court.

A sitting presidential candidate said he sees no way Moraes can stay. The Senate president himself called 109 pending impeachment requests against the Court’s justices simply not normal.

The police revolt belongs in this tally too. Mendonça removed the Federal Police’s two most senior officers himself, without any request from prosecutors.

Eleven of fifteen directors backed the ousted chief by offering to quit. It is the clearest sign yet that this crisis cuts in both directions, not only against Moraes.

A colleague, Justice Gilmar Mendes, has separately proposed banning police staff from justices’ chambers entirely.

Federal Police headquarters in Brasília, where most of the force’s directors offered to resign this week. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

The Case That This Is Accountability, Not Persecution

The counter-case starts with 8 January 2023. Investigators found extensive evidence of a plan to keep Bolsonaro in power after he lost.

Courts in other countries have punished coup attempts far more lightly, defenders of the ruling note.

The Bolsonaro verdict was not a one-man decision. A panel of justices heard it, and Fux’s dissent was published alongside the majority ruling.

Defenders argue that alone shows the Court tolerates internal disagreement, rather than enforcing a single line.

Foreign sanctions on a country’s own judges are themselves an extraordinary act. Many Brazilian officials, across the political spectrum, call it interference in a sovereign court’s decisions rather than proof those decisions were wrong.

Chief Justice Fachin has already intervened once. He took the request to investigate Mendonça away from the inquiry Moraes personally runs.

That is not a verdict. Defenders say it shows the Court can still correct itself from within, rather than only under outside pressure.

The pattern of weaponized leaks is not one-sided, either. In September, a free-market anti-corruption candidate put a different justice’s confidential family data into a public election filing.

Justice Cristiano Zanin, appointed by Lula, sought criminal accountability for the candidate responsible. No court has found the candidate broke any law.

Public distrust of the Court predates this month’s crisis by years. An AtlasIntel poll found half of Brazilians already distrusted the STF in 2024.

By April 2026, 75% told Datafolha the Court holds too much power. That unease existed before anyone alleged wrongdoing by Moraes or Mendonça specifically.

The anti-Court campaign has its own tangles, too. An April 2026 Senate report accused three justices of financial ties to the same Banco Master collapse.

It sought their impeachment, but the government reshuffled the committee hours before the vote. The report died 6 to 4, and whether that protected the Court or protected allies depends on who is asked.

Mass impeachment filing itself has become a tool both sides use freely. Almost none of the 109 requests will reach a Senate vote.

Removal needs 54 of the 81 senators, and the Senate president screens each request first. No sitting justice has ever been removed this way.

That gatekeeping is why impeachment threats function more as pressure than as a real removal mechanism.

An Election Sitting on Top of All of It

Jair Bolsonaro cannot run again until 2030, so his movement passed to his eldest son. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro has made attacking Moraes central to his campaign, calling him a “rotten orange” inside the Court.

A Nexus poll published on 8 September put Flávio one point ahead of Lula in a runoff. It was the first time in that series he had led.

The gap sits inside the margin of error. But the direction has moved steadily his way for six weeks.

Brazil votes on 4 October, with a runoff on 25 October if nobody wins a majority. Every presidential election since 2002 has gone to a second round.

Days before this month’s crisis broke, Lula’s coalition made its own move. It asked the electoral court to disqualify Flávio Bolsonaro over a rally at a rodeo festival.

The case has not been decided.

Whoever is right about the Court, both sides now have a stake in how it is seen. A discredited Court is a weaker referee for an election this close, no matter which side ends up needing it to rule.

What Is Proven, and What Is Not

It is proven that Bolsonaro and his son Eduardo were both convicted. It is proven that Moraes suspended X across Brazil.

It is proven that the US sanctioned a sitting Brazilian justice for the first time in the Court’s history.

It is proven that 109 impeachment requests exist and that eleven police directors offered to resign this week. Those are matters of record, confirmed by the Senate president and the Court’s own filings.

It is not proven that Moraes acted improperly toward Daniel Vorcaro, the jailed banker at the center of the Banco Master case. Federal Police material alleges contact and a request for “protection,” but no court has ruled on it.

It is not proven that evidence was manipulated in the Bolsonaro trial, despite a former adviser’s testimony alleging a backdated report. Moraes disputes the account, and the Court rejected a motion to pause the trial over it.

It is not proven that any justice is acting from political motive rather than legal judgment. That question sits at the heart of every filing, editorial and resignation letter described here, and none of them settles it.

The Question Brazil Cannot Yet Answer

A common argument on the Brazilian right holds that the country will not find peace until the Court is brought under control.

A common argument on the left holds that this is exactly what a coup movement would want people to believe.

Both arguments can be sincerely held. Neither one is proven by the events of the past two weeks.

Those events show a Court in genuine crisis. They do not show who caused it, or why.

What is clear is the timing. Brazil’s institutions are tearing at each other in public, five weeks before they are asked to certify who runs the country next.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Sources: The Rio Times archives, September 2025 – September 2026; Associated Press; Senate President Davi Alcolumbre; Federal Police statements; Estadão, Folha de S.Paulo and O Globo editorials; Poder360; CNN Brasil; Metrópoles; AS/COA Brazil 2026 election tracker.

World.title: Brazil’s Bar Opens an Ethics Case Over a Justice’s Family Law Firm
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts — What happened. The Brasília bar association opened ethics proceedings against partners of a law firm on 8 September.

The Brasília bar association opened ethics proceedings against partners of a law firm on 8 September. — Who the partners are. They include Viviane Barci de Moraes, wife of Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes.

They include Viviane Barci de Moraes, wife of Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes. — What it concerns. Reported contracts between the family’s legal practice and Daniel Vorcaro’s Banco Master.

Reported contracts between the family’s legal practice and Daniel Vorcaro’s Banco Master. — The catch. An opening is not a finding. The bar itself says no judgment of guilt has been made.

An opening is not a finding. The bar itself says no judgment of guilt has been made. — Who started it. Nobody complained. The bar’s president opened it himself, citing facts recently made public.

Nobody complained. The bar’s president opened it himself, citing facts recently made public. — What the firm says. It says the facts were examined and shelved by prosecutors, and objects to their use now.

The Brasília bar has opened two ethics proceedings tied to the Banco Master affair. One of them reaches into a Supreme Court justice’s family.

The Esplanada dos Ministerios in Brasília. The city’s bar association opened two ethics proceedings tied to the Banco Master affair (Photo: Joehawkins, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

This is a procedural step at the start of a process, not a verdict. It is worth reporting precisely, because the temptation to overstate it is obvious.

What Was Opened

The Brasília section of Brazil’s bar association opened an ethics and disciplinary proceeding on 8 September.

It is directed at the partners of a law firm registered with that section, not at the firm as an entity.

A second, separate proceeding was opened the same day against another lawyer described as a link between figures in the affair.

Both were opened by the section’s president on his own initiative. No outside party filed a complaint.

His stated basis was facts recently made public in a Federal Police report.

Who Is Named

The named partners reported by Brazilian outlets include Viviane Barci de Moraes, wife of Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes.

Her two children and a sister-in-law are also reported among the respondents, along with a fifth lawyer.

Those names appear in press accounts rather than in the bar’s own note. The note itself does not list them.

There is a naming trap here that most coverage falls into. The firm registered in Brasília is not the same entity as the São Paulo practice named in the Banco Master contract reporting.

The two have similar names and overlapping people. Treating them as one firm is the most common error in this story.

The Alleged Conduct

The subject is contracts between the family’s legal practice and Banco Master, controlled by Daniel Vorcaro.

Brazilian outlets report a contract signed in January 2024 worth R$3 million a month over 36 months.

That would be about R$131.3 million in total, roughly US$25.8 million at the Banco Central rate of R$5.0856 for 8 September 2026.

A further contract with a company linked to Vorcaro is reported at R$50 million, about US$9.8 million.

The context is a Federal Police report on messages between Vorcaro and people around the court.

We are reporting what has been alleged and opened. No finding has been made about any of it.

What the Bar Actually Said

The bar’s note confirms only that two proceedings were opened. That is the whole of its public statement.

It says explicitly that opening them does not imply any prior judgment of guilt.

It also says the cases will observe due process and confidentiality.

Those are the standard protections in Brazilian disciplinary proceedings, and they mean the file will not be public.

So the next visible step may be a long way off.

The Response

The firm said the facts had already been examined and shelved by the prosecutor general’s office.

It objected to their use in what it called an electoral context. Brazil votes on 4 October.

It asked the bar section’s president to reconsider his public statements.

No response from Justice Alexandre de Moraes has been reported. None from Viviane Barci de Moraes personally has either.

We are not attributing a comment to either of them, because there is none on the record.

Where This Sits in a Bigger Fight

The Banco Master affair has been running since 2025 and has reached almost every institution in Brasília.

The bank went into liquidation in November 2025. Daniel Vorcaro has been detained twice and remains in custody.

The securities regulator convicted him and fifteen others in a separate administrative case on 8 September.

The same week, a Supreme Court justice removed the Federal Police director-general over surveillance claims.

Eleven of the force’s fifteen directors then offered to give up their posts. Thirteen retired justices wrote to the court’s president.

All of it is happening four weeks before a presidential election. That timing is the argument every side is making about every other side.

How to Read Disciplinary Proceedings in Brazil

A disciplinary proceeding is run by the bar association, not by a court. It can suspend or strike off a lawyer.

It cannot impose a criminal penalty, and it does not decide whether a contract was lawful.

It begins with an opening, then investigation, then a defence, then a decision by a disciplinary tribunal. Appeals follow.

Cases routinely end without sanction. An opening tells you a body thought a question worth asking, and nothing more.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Brasília bar do? It opened two ethics and disciplinary proceedings on 8 September, one against partners of a law firm and one against another lawyer. Does this mean anyone has been found guilty? No. The bar’s own note says opening the proceedings implies no prior judgment of guilt, and the cases are confidential. Is Justice Alexandre de Moraes himself under investigation by the bar? No. The proceeding concerns partners of a law firm, among them his wife, and the bar has no jurisdiction over a sitting justice. What has the firm said? That the facts were already examined and shelved by the prosecutor general’s office. It also objects to their use in an election period.

Sources: OAB-DF, the section’s own note, Metrópoles, the named partners, Gazeta do Povo, the proceeding reported, CartaCapital, the opening and the firm’s response, Poder360, what is known about the contracts, Banco Central do Brasil, the dollar reference rate

World.title: Panama Is Not on Ratings Review, and Fitch Already Calls It Junk
World.content:
Panama · Economy

Key Facts — What happened. A Moody’s analyst said the agency is questioning whether Panama keeps its investment grade.

A Moody’s analyst said the agency is questioning whether Panama keeps its investment grade. — The catch. Panama is not on review. It has carried a negative outlook since late 2024.

Panama is not on review. It has carried a negative outlook since late 2024. — What the deficit is. US$2.642 billion through July, or 2.78% of GDP, against a legal ceiling of 3.5%.

US$2.642 billion through July, or 2.78% of GDP, against a legal ceiling of 3.5%. — What most reports miss. Fitch already rates Panama below investment grade, and has since March 2024.

Fitch already rates Panama below investment grade, and has since March 2024. — The single biggest factor. The Cobre Panama copper mine is still shut, with no reopening decision this year.

The Cobre Panama copper mine is still shut, with no reopening decision this year. — What comes next. Moody’s wants to resolve the outlook before the end of 2026, but says the timing is uncertain.

Panama’s public finances are improving and its credit rating is still in doubt. Both statements are true, and one widely reported detail is not.

Panama City’s financial district. The country’s deficit through July came to US.642 billion, inside its legal ceiling (Photo: Dronepicr, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

A ratings review and a negative outlook are different things. So is investment grade at two agencies and junk at the third.

Where the Ratings Actually Stand

Moody’s rates Panama Baa3, the lowest investment grade notch, with a negative outlook.

Standard and Poor’s rates it BBB minus, also the lowest investment grade notch, with a stable outlook.

Fitch rates it BB plus. That is below investment grade, and it has been since March 2024.

So describing Panama simply as investment grade is wrong. It holds that status at two agencies out of three.

Moody’s completed a periodic review on 30 May 2026. The agency itself says a periodic review is not a rating action.

Panama is not on review or watch. A negative outlook signals which way a future move would go, and nothing more.

What the Moody’s Analyst Said

Moody’s sovereign vice-president Jaime Reusche spoke to a news agency on 8 September.

He said the agency is questioning whether Panama should keep its investment grade.

He also said Moody’s intends to resolve the negative outlook before the end of 2026.

Then he qualified it. The timing is now uncertain, because the government says no mining decision will come before year end.

That is a real signal of concern. It is not a formal review, and it should not be reported as one.

The Deficit Figure, and Which One It Is

The finance ministry’s own report puts the non-financial public sector deficit at US$2.642 billion for January to July.

That equals 2.78% of gross domestic product. The same period last year was US$2.955 billion, or 3.27%.

So the deficit narrowed by US$313 million, an improvement of 10.6%.

There is a second and larger number. The central government deficit for the same period is US$3.371 billion, or 3.54%.

Anyone quoting a Panamanian deficit should say which measure they mean. The two differ by more than US$700 million.

Panama uses the balboa, pegged one to one with the US dollar, and the dollar circulates as legal tender. No conversion is needed.

The Legal Ceiling It Has to Meet

Panama’s fiscal responsibility law sets a declining path for the broad public sector deficit.

The ceiling is 4.0% of GDP for 2025 and 3.5% for 2026. It falls to 3.0% in 2027 and 2.5% in 2028.

By 2030 the limit is 1.5%. The reformed schedule was published in October 2024.

At 2.78% through July, the country is inside the 2026 ceiling. Full-year figures are what count, and 2025 closed at 3.68%.

That was down sharply from 6.23% in 2024. The direction of travel is the government’s strongest argument.

What Is Driving the Spending

Social security spending reached US$2.848 billion in the first seven months, up US$179 million on the year.

Interest payments came to US$1.732 billion. Those two lines are the bulk of the pressure.

A pension reform passed in March 2025 created a new capitalisation system with a solidarity guarantee.

Everyone hired from 18 March 2025 enters it. Existing members transition in 2036, so the savings are distant.

Debt is projected to settle at 66% to 67% of GDP by the end of 2026.

The Mine Everything Hangs On

Cobre Panama is a roughly US$10 billion copper mine operated by First Quantum. It was ordered shut in late 2023.

It is still closed. The government says no reopening decision will come before the end of this year.

Moody’s frames the outcome as binary. Reopening could add more than 0.4% of GDP in royalties.

An adverse arbitration outcome could cost up to nineteen percentage points of GDP. That is the range the rating sits inside.

The canal is the other side of the ledger. Fees and dividends run at roughly 3% of GDP a year.

Canal income now supplies about 28% of central government current income, up from 13% in 2016.

Two Smaller Items From This Week

The cabinet gave a favourable opinion on two new free trade zones on 8 September.

One is in La Chorrera in Panama Oeste, with investment of about US$1.95 million across two phases.

The other is in Cristobal in Colon province, at about US$18.78 million. The combined figure is roughly US$20.7 million.

More than 2,500 direct and indirect jobs are projected, a figure attached to the Colon zone.

These are modest sums, and the licences are issued by the free zones commission rather than by the cabinet itself.

A separate report said the International Monetary Fund would review Panama in mid-September. We could not confirm it.

Panama has no IMF programme, so there is nothing to review in that sense. The last consultation concluded in July 2025.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Moody’s put Panama on ratings review? No. Panama carries a negative outlook dating from late 2024, and a completed periodic review is not a rating action. Is Panama investment grade? At Moody’s and Standard and Poor’s, at the lowest notch of each. Fitch has rated Panama below investment grade since March 2024. How big is Panama’s deficit? US$2.642 billion for January to July, or 2.78% of GDP, on the broad public sector measure. The central government figure is US$3.371 billion. Why does the closed copper mine matter so much? Reopening could add more than 0.4% of GDP in royalties. An adverse arbitration ruling could cost up to nineteen percentage points of GDP.

World.title: Bolivia Lets Refineries Import Crude, but the Decree Is Not Yet Live
World.content:
Bolivia · Energy

Key Facts — What happened. A decree signed on 7 September lets refineries import crude and sell the fuel unsubsidised.

A decree signed on 7 September lets refineries import crude and sell the fuel unsubsidised. — The catch. It is not in force yet. It waits on a regulation from the hydrocarbons ministry.

It is not in force yet. It waits on a regulation from the hydrocarbons ministry. — What already works. Since July, private firms may import diesel and petrol and sell at market prices.

Since July, private firms may import diesel and petrol and sell at market prices. — What it does not do. The subsidy stays. This builds a second, unsubsidised tier beside the cheap state supply.

The subsidy stays. This builds a second, unsubsidised tier beside the cheap state supply. — The price gap. Subsidised diesel is 9.80 bolivianos a litre, about US$0.78. Imported diesel is 16.50.

Subsidised diesel is 9.80 bolivianos a litre, about US$0.78. Imported diesel is 16.50. — What changed underneath. Bolivia dropped its fixed exchange rate in June. The boliviano has gone from 6.96 to 12.60.

Bolivia has spent 2026 dismantling the fuel settlement it held for fifteen years. The newest decree is the biggest step so far, and it has not taken effect.

Camiri in southern Bolivia, long known as the country’s oil capital. Bolivia is opening fuel and crude imports to private firms (Photo: Ruditaly, CC BY 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Two decrees are being reported as one. One has been working since the summer, and the other is still waiting for its rulebook.

The New Decree

Supreme Decree 5701 was announced on 7 September by Economy Minister Christian Morales.

It authorises refineries to import crude oil, process it, and sell the products at market prices without subsidy.

It also sets the fuel tax at zero bolivianos a litre for that stream until 2030.

Here is the part most coverage misses. It enters into force only when the hydrocarbons ministry issues the implementing regulation.

That regulation is due within five working days of publication. It had not appeared when this was written.

So refineries cannot yet import crude under it. The decree exists, and the mechanism does not.

The Decree That Is Already Working

Supreme Decree 5644 came earlier, published in the official gazette on 1 July. It covers refined products rather than crude.

It allows individuals and companies, public and private, to import diesel and petrol.

The state oil company imports for sale at regulated prices. Private importers may import for their own use or for resale.

Where private firms resell, the article is explicit. Those sales are at market prices, with no subsidy.

Importers need authorisation from the hydrocarbons regulator. The rules require colour coding by fuel type and physically separate tanks.

Selling subsidised fuel at market prices costs the licence. Fines run from 2,000 to 10,000 units of the inflation-indexed accounting measure.

What This Does and Does Not Change

The subsidy has not been abolished. What exists now is a second, unsubsidised tier running alongside the cheap state supply.

Subsidised prices were set in January. Special petrol is 6.96 bolivianos a litre and diesel 9.80.

At 12.60 bolivianos to the US dollar, the central bank rate for 8 September 2026, that is about US$0.55 and US$0.78.

Large consumers pay more. Since August their diesel reference price has been 18 bolivianos, about US$1.43.

The regulator cut its reference price for imported diesel to 16.50 bolivianos on 3 September, about US$1.31.

One number is a trap for the unwary. Special petrol at 6.96 bolivianos is the same figure as the old exchange rate, and they are unrelated.

Whether Anyone Has Actually Imported Yet

Service stations projected selling privately imported fuel from 6 August. A farmers’ association had already run a diesel import desk.

The regulator now publishes a reference price for imported diesel, which suggests the channel is live.

The clearest case is not a private one. The Beni governorate arranged a diesel tanker from Rondônia in Brazil, due on 9 September.

That is a regional government buying fuel, not a company importing under the new rules.

We could not confirm that a private firm has completed an import. We are not asserting that one has.

The Exchange Rate Changed Too

Bolivia held its official rate at 6.96 bolivianos to the dollar from 2011. That peg is gone.

A flexible official rate took effect on 29 June 2026, opening at 9.73. The central bank now publishes it daily.

It was 12.58 on 7 September and 12.60 on 8 September. That is a slide of about 29% in ten weeks.

The parallel rate has essentially converged with the official one, and at times trades slightly below it.

That convergence is the strongest evidence the change worked. A gap between the two was the symptom the government was treating.

Beware stale pages saying the rate has been fixed since 2011 at 12.60. The 2011 peg was 6.96, and the figures are being mixed up.

Why Bolivia Is in This Position

Gas exports have fallen for a decade, with no major new discoveries. Bolivia went from energy exporter to net fuel importer.

It kept selling diesel and petrol below import cost, and paid the difference in dollars.

That drained reserves and produced a chronic hard-currency shortage, long queues and heavy smuggling to neighbouring countries.

Fuel sells for far more across the borders, which makes the arbitrage obvious and the enforcement hard.

President Rodrigo Paz took office on 8 November 2025. He has taken the old settlement apart in pieces.

A January decree raised regulated prices. Another declared an energy and social emergency.

The State of Exception, and Who Wants It Extended

A 90-day nationwide state of exception was declared on 20 June, after roughly seven weeks of road blockades.

It bans blockades and the use of weapons and explosives, and lets the military help police reopen strategic routes.

It expires on 18 September. Reports that Paz is seeking an extension do not match what he has said.

He ruled one out on 12 August, and his spokesman repeated in late August that it was not an immediate priority.

The six-month extension bill comes from a governing-party deputy, not from the presidency.

Two ministers have since opened the door to keeping it. Any extension needs approval from the legislature.

Coca, and the New Drug Policy

The United Nations drugs office reported on 8 September that coca cultivation reached 36,400 hectares in 2025.

That is up 7% from 34,000 hectares in 2024, and 14,400 hectares above the legal limit of 22,000.

Growth was concentrated in the Cochabamba tropics, up 22%. Eradication fell from about 10,000 hectares to 2,732.

The government presented a new anti-drug policy the same day, running from 2026 to 2030.

It has nine pillars and a budget of US$492 million over five years, with 56.3% expected from international cooperation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can Bolivian refineries import crude now? Not yet. The decree was announced on 7 September but takes effect only once the hydrocarbons ministry publishes the implementing regulation. Has Bolivia ended its fuel subsidy? No. Subsidised prices remain, and the new rules create a second unsubsidised tier alongside them for privately imported fuel. What do fuels cost in Bolivia? Subsidised diesel is 9.80 bolivianos a litre, about US$0.78, and special petrol 6.96, about US$0.55. Imported diesel has a reference price of 16.50. Is the boliviano still pegged to the dollar? No. It moved to a flexible rate on 29 June 2026, and has since gone from 9.73 to about 12.60 to the dollar.

Sources: Agencia Boliviana de Información, the new crude import decree, Agencia Boliviana de Información, the July fuel import decree, El Deber, the refinery decree, El Deber, the regulator’s rules for private importers, El Deber, the imported diesel reference price, Banco Central de Bolivia, the official exchange rate, Correo del Sur, the state of exception decree, La Razón, the coca cultivation figures

World.title: Chevron Says It Will More Than Double Its Drilling Rigs in Venezuela
World.content:
Venezuela · Energy

Key Facts — What happened. Chevron’s finance chief said the company will more than double its drilling rigs in Venezuela.

Chevron’s finance chief said the company will more than double its drilling rigs in Venezuela. — Where she said it. At an energy conference on 8 September, five days after Chevron announced its expansion.

At an energy conference on 8 September, five days after Chevron announced its expansion. — The catch. No starting or target rig count was given. Anyone printing a from and to figure is guessing.

No starting or target rig count was given. Anyone printing a from and to figure is guessing. — The money. Chevron has committed more than US$7 billion over five years, to 2031.

Chevron has committed more than US$7 billion over five years, to 2031. — The output goal. Production would rise from about 280,000 barrels a day to roughly 600,000.

Production would rise from about 280,000 barrels a day to roughly 600,000. — Who may operate. Only six named companies hold US authorisation to work in Venezuela today.

Chevron is the one Western oil company already producing in Venezuela at scale. Its finance chief has now put a number on how much harder it plans to drill.

An oil tanker on Lake Maracaibo, the heart of Venezuela’s oil industry. Chevron plans to more than double its drilling rigs in the country (Photo: Wilfredor, CC0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Two words in this story get mixed up constantly. Signing a contract and being licensed to operate are not the same thing.

What Was Actually Said

Chevron’s chief financial officer, Eimear Bonner, spoke at an energy and power conference on 8 September.

Her words were that the company intends to increase the number of rigs, so more than double the number of rigs.

Note the phrasing. It is more than double, not double, and it refers to drilling rigs rather than offshore platforms.

Those two words are not interchangeable, and several accounts have used the wrong one.

No base figure and no target figure were given. Nobody on the record has said how many rigs Chevron runs today.

So we are not printing a from and to number. It does not exist in any source we could reach.

The Money and the Production Target

Chevron announced its expanded position in Venezuela on 3 September. The commitment is more than US$7 billion over five years.

The period runs to 2031. Current production is described as about 280,000 to 290,000 barrels a day.

The target is roughly 600,000 barrels a day, with a plateau of 600,000 to 700,000 for five to ten years.

Total cost per barrel is put below US$20. That is what makes the arithmetic work at current prices.

Bonner said the rigs would be added under new contract terms signed with Venezuela the week before.

Chevron’s own release names stakes in three joint ventures and three new asset assignments. It contains no rig count at all.

Signing Is Not the Same as Operating

The United States controls this through general licences issued by its Treasury sanctions office.

One of those licences allows companies to negotiate and sign contingent contracts. It does not authorise them to perform.

That means no drilling, no production, no services and no payments under that licence alone.

A separate licence names the companies that may actually operate. There are six of them.

They are BP, Chevron, Eni, Repsol, Shell and Etablissements Maurel et Prom, plus their subsidiaries.

Everyone else holding a Venezuelan contract is holding a piece of paper they cannot yet act on.

Two Claims Circulating That Do Not Hold Up

One report says twenty-five companies have received market entry licences in Venezuela. That is not what happened.

A Colombian newspaper counted more than twenty-five companies weighing entry. That is an interest tally, not a register of licences.

An earlier count by another Colombian paper put the same number at seventeen. It is a moving press estimate.

A second claim concerns GeoPark and a figure of US$6.8 billion. We could not find that figure in any filing or release.

The actual deal is a share exchange. GeoPark issues 42.1 million shares to acquire a holding company from the Gilinski group.

The value cited is about US$160 million, and the result is that Gilinski takes majority control of GeoPark.

GeoPark’s own filing says closing depends on sanctions compliance. No US licence naming the company is on the public record.

What Happened to Petrodelta

Petrodelta is a joint venture between the state oil company and a private partner. The state holds 60% and operates it.

The private 40% was held by a Dutch vehicle belonging to the heirs of the late Venezuelan businessman Oswaldo Cisneros.

That stake and its rights were revoked by the oil ministry for alleged non-compliance. Proceedings opened in May and the revocation came in June.

The fields were transferred in July to Pacific Coast Energy Company, a firm based in Santa Barbara County, California.

The six fields are in Monagas Sur and Delta Amacuro, not the Orinoco Belt. Several reports place them wrongly.

The family says it invested more than US$2 billion plus a signing bonus above US$165 million, and is seeking about US$2 billion.

The revocation decision has never been published, and the government has neither confirmed nor denied the transfer.

The Argument Against All of This

Elliott Abrams, the special representative for Venezuela in the first Trump administration, published a critical column on 2 September.

His argument is that the arrangement gives the government a financial reason to stay. It also gives Washington a stake in that government’s stability.

His sharpest line is that the deal will fail if democracy returns, because most Venezuelans will oppose it.

This is an opinion column rather than testimony or a report. It should be read as one, and he is not the only critic writing that week.

The Poll You Will See Quoted

A Caracas pollster released a survey on 8 September saying 82% of Venezuelans back the oil alliance with the United States.

The sample was 700 people, interviewed in a single day, with a stated margin of error of 3.5 points.

The firm is long identified with pro-government positions, and the release was carried by state and government-aligned outlets.

Every item in the survey lands between 81% and 91%. No independent Venezuelan pollster has published anything comparable.

Treat it as a claim by an aligned pollster rather than a finding about Venezuelan opinion.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many rigs will Chevron run in Venezuela? Nobody has said. The finance chief said the company will more than double the number, but gave no starting or target count. How much is Chevron investing? More than US$7 billion over five years to 2031. Production is targeted to rise from about 280,000 barrels a day to roughly 600,000. Can any company now operate in Venezuela? No. Only six named companies hold operating authorisation: BP, Chevron, Eni, Repsol, Shell and Etablissements Maurel et Prom. Is the GeoPark deal worth US$6.8 billion? That figure appears in no filing we could find. The deal is a share exchange valued at about US$160 million that hands the Gilinski group control of GeoPark.

Sources: Chevron, its expanded position in Venezuela, Conference transcript, the chief financial officer’s remarks, Rigzone, the joint venture investment plan, US Treasury, Venezuela sanctions programme, GeoPark, the share exchange filing, Bloomberg Law, the Petrodelta claim, The Washington Post, Elliott Abrams on the deal

World.title: Peru Joins a US Security Coalition That Nobody Has Signed
World.content:
Peru · Politics

Key Facts — What happened. The United States announced Peru’s entry into a regional anti-cartel coalition on 8 September.

The United States announced Peru’s entry into a regional anti-cartel coalition on 8 September. — How it was announced. Marco Rubio said it in a column for the Lima daily El Comercio, before he arrived.

Marco Rubio said it in a column for the Lima daily El Comercio, before he arrived. — The catch. It is a political declaration, not a treaty. Peru signed no instrument.

It is a political declaration, not a treaty. Peru signed no instrument. — What Peru got earlier. Washington designated Peru a major non-NATO ally in January, by presidential determination.

Washington designated Peru a major non-NATO ally in January, by presidential determination. — Who is objecting. Members of Congress want the foreign minister to appear and explain the entry.

Members of Congress want the foreign minister to appear and explain the entry. — What comes next. Rubio was due to meet President Keiko Fujimori in Lima on 10 September.

Peru’s entry into a United States security coalition was announced in a newspaper column. There is no treaty behind it, and Congress noticed.

The Government Palace in Lima, where Marco Rubio was due to meet President Keiko Fujimori on September 10 (Photo: Ovruni, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)
