World.title: UK rejects Israel's 'damaging' retaliation against West Bank settler sanctions
World.content:
British foreign minister Ed Miliband condemned as "regrettable and damaging" Israel's decision to order the closure of the UK's consulate in Jerusalem as retaliation for London-led Western sanctions over settler violence.

 

"We anticipated this might happen because we saw other countries, the Dutch, for example, who had announced sanctions, who had seen these reprisals from Israel. I think they're regrettable and damaging," Miliband told BBC Radio on Wednesday.

Israel ordered the closure on Tuesday after 12 countries including the UK and France announced they would sanction trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, following a surge in attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Israel said it would also expel British representatives at a centre monitoring the US-brokered ceasefire plan in Gaza, bar British training for Palestinian Authority forces and ban 12 Britons, mostly members of parliament, from visiting the country.

Miliband rejected suggestions that the sanctions would impact intelligence cooperation with Israel.

Britain's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband speaks during a press conference in Madrid, 29 July, 2026 AP Photo

"We have important intelligence and security relationships with Israel and I'm confident they will continue," he said, declining to go into details.

"And I was very clear yesterday that we do believe in working with our Israeli partners when it comes to the threats they face from Iran," he added.

Miliband also dismissed the criticism of the sanctions by Britain's chief rabbi.

Ephraim Mirvis on Tuesday called the measures "little more than political flag-bearing."

He said it was a "truly a dark day for British Jews," predicting that the measures "will succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to target."

Several antisemitic attacks in London this year have targeted synagogues and other Jewish sites.

Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden joined the UK and France in confirming plans to introduce restrictions on trade with settlements on Tuesday, according to a joint statement from the countries' foreign ministers.

"The Government of Israel’s actions in the West Bank are undermining the possibility of a two-State solution," the statement reads, adding that there have been "unprecedented levels of settler violence and settlement expansion."

"Together, we are resolute: the two-state solution must be protected, and we will take action in pursuit of a just and lasting peace," it continued.

It comes after the Israeli government last month opened up tenders for the construction of around 1,200 housing units in the West Bank, drawing widespread condemnation from the international community and human rights groups.

The units, destined for the E1 settlement area, would further isolate East Jerusalem from the rest of the territory.

Members of the Israeli forces stand in a street as a Palestinian man is detained during a military raid in the West Bank town of Anata, 8 September, 2026 AP Photo

The West Bank

The West Bank has been occupied by Israel since 1967 and has seen a surge in violence since the start of the war in Gaza, which broke out following the Hamas militant group's attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023.

According to a report from the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, there were around 737,000 Israeli settlers in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, as of October 2024.

Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.

World.title: Rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German wiki, and it stayed secret for weeks
World.content:
AI researchers discovered last week that a swarm of OpenAI agents had bypassed safety parameters to take over German wiki forum DseWiki to collaborate.

 

The agents had been allowed to visit the 25-year-old German programming website with read-only access but managed to exploit a web request to hijack the site, turning it into a bulletin board.

The rogue agents made more than 18,000 posts sharing answers, research on their environment and how to bypass sandbox restrictions and hide themselves from human detection, according to the research group Nightingale Collective.

The incident took place sometime between May and June this year, and it is understood that OpenAI learned of the incident weeks ago but kept it under wraps.

This is the third reported incident following two others in July, one involving rogue agents attacking OpenAI's own infrastructure and another where 1,200 rogue OpenAI bots bypassed their restricted environments and launched a five-day attack on the open-source AI platform Hugging Face.

However, only on Saturday did OpenAI acknowledge the German wiki incident in an X post, where they outlined that in response to the latest incident they are "working on a framework for when and how we share AI misalignment incidents".

AI misalignment is industry-speak for when artificial intelligence systems pursue goals or behave in ways that diverge from human intentions, values or safety constraints, with the potential to ignore common sense or implicit human boundaries.

A divided response

Experts are divided on the dangers posed by AI in light of the recent rogue AI attacks, with some such as world-leading AI expert Yann LeCun dismissing apocalyptic scenarios and forecasts that there is a 10-20% risk that AI will end humanity.

While others such as Geoffrey Hinton have said, "What's happening is these things are getting smarter," and warned that "companies investing in AI have a vested interested in telling you… [AI] won't go rogue."

According to the EU's AI Act and its most recently introduced measures, which came into effect in August, companies that offer AI models with systemic risk are obliged to report serious incidents such as misalignment incidents to the EU's AI Office "without undue delay".

On Monday, the European Commission announced it had received a formal incident report from OpenAI but did not disclose when it was submitted however they remain in close contact with the AI company and are investigating further.

Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier underlined how serious the German wiki event was, saying, "Incident reports are not just a tick-box, you have to be quite precise and accurate about the measures you are aiming to take."

The German wiki incident also comes days after the European Commission officially designated ChatGPT as a Very Large Online Search Engine (VLOSE) under its flagship tech legislation, the Digital Services Act.

The co-chair of Parliament's AI Working Group, Michael McNamara, said in response to the latest incident that he believes "the AI Act already gives us the capability to counter agentic risks and it important for the Commission use its powers under the Act".

The Irish MEP also said, "However, these incidents make it clear that the AI Office needs the staff and resources to match both the growing capability of these systems and the growing danger they can pose to society."

Meanwhile, Italian MEP Brando Benifei, who co-chairs the Working Group too, said, "Recent agent breakouts show that the AI Act’s systemic-risk rules are necessary, but their credibility now depends on enforcement."

He added, "The AI Office must use its new powers to obtain model access, conduct independent evaluations and require mitigation, rather than rely on corporate self-reporting. Without action, machine-speed attacks could turn ordinary vulnerabilities into systemic failures.”

What OpenAI says

OpenAI also stated in Saturday's X post that the current misalignment disclosure practices, i.e. reporting when AI broke the rules, need to be expanded to take into account what they describe as a "new phase of model capabilities".

"We and the larger AI community do not yet have a clear standard for how to report misalignment," said OpenAI, adding that they are "working on a framework and will share it in upcoming weeks" with the cooperation of several government agencies around the world.

On Sunday, OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published a blog post outlining his concerns over the rapid development of AI risks, stating "We are facing a transition to a world with incredibly intelligent machines, and we need to ensure that transition works out well for humanity."

The Polish computer programmer also revealed his belief that "no lab has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer" and urged that "international coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world."

World.title: US destroys five Iranian tankers as Tehran takes aim at Jordan
World.content:
US forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday after the Revolutionary Guards fired ballistic missiles at a US Navy warship twice in two days, as Iran launched missile strikes on US targets in Jordan.

 

US Central Command (CENTCOM) said the crews of all five vessels — the Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1, Riesco and Derya — were warned to abandon ship before the strikes.

The targeted warship evaded both Iranian attacks without casualties, CENTCOM said.

Iranian state-affiliated news agency confirmed one oil tanker was struck near Jask and another tanker four miles off Kharg Island. Iran's state broadcaster has reported that a commercial vessel was also attacked in the coastal waters of Jask county.

According to Tasnim, citing local sources, the attack on the tanker near Kharg caused no casualties.

Iran launched missiles at US targets in Jordan following the tanker strikes, according to Iranian state-run television.

"Given the malign actions of the terrorist US military in targeting several oil tankers of the Islamic Republic of Iran, we warn all tanker crews in the area of the ports of Kuwait and Bahrain, which host these terrorists and are partners in their aggression, to leave their vessels immediately, whether at anchorage or at the quays, as they will be targeted," IRGC said.

The Khatam al-Anbiya central command followed with a threat to US bases in the region.

"The US military has ordered Iranian oil tankers to evacuate so that it can strike them; therefore I declare that any attack on Iranian oil tankers will result in US bases in the region being targeted by the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran," Major General Abdollahi said in a statement.

Jordan's military said its air defence systems intercepted 18 ballistic missiles launched toward its territory and that two others landed in uninhabited areas. No casualties were reported.

Jordan hosts several US military installations and has been a repeated target of Iranian strikes since the war began on 28 February.

Iran also said it had captured a US unmanned underwater vessel at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz before dawn, broadcasting images of what it described as the captured drone on state television. Iran had claimed to have struck a US Navy sea drone on Sunday.

The Trump administration separately announced new sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian commercial and private airlines and foreign cargo providers, in a further effort to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.

The exchange marks one of the sharpest escalations since the framework deal the two sides signed in June broke down the following month.

Both sides have been attempting to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which roughly one-fifth of the world's traded oil passed before the war began.

The US has been enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports while Tehran has sought to impose its own transit regime on commercial shipping through the strait.

World.title: The European commute: Which EU country spends the most time getting to work?
World.content:
For millions of workers across the continent, the daily journey to the office is an unavoidable ritual. But just how long do Europeans actually spend getting to work?

 

According to new research from talent management company SD Worx, the daily average commute across Europe sits at 48 minutes. However, that continental average masks how differently nations experience geography, traffic, and worker mindsets.

While the European average hovers around three-quarters of an hour, individual countries experience vastly different realities on their roads and rail lines.

Countries such as Italy and Slovenia manage to keep daily travel times relatively brief, hovering around 35 minutes.

At the opposite end, countries push much closer to the hour mark. Sweden and Ireland report hefty averages of 57 and 56 minutes, respectively.

Taking the top spot overall, Belgium officially crosses the one-hour mark at 61 minutes a day. This is driven by the fact that 13% of its workforce are "super-commuters", according to SD Worx, spending two hours or more on the road—the highest rate in Europe—with 14% travelling over 120 kilometres daily.

Distance vs. congestion: The Netherlands and Romania

The data also reveals fascinating differences in why commutes take as long as they do. For instance, the Netherlands and Romania both average 53 minutes for a daily commute, but the underlying dynamics are entirely polar opposite:

Workers in the Netherlands cover 63 kilometres on average, leaning on efficient infrastructure to handle long-distance travel.

In Romania, workers spend that same 53-minute window covering much shorter geographic distances, where heavy traffic and urban congestion eat away at the clock.

The commuting paradox

Perhaps the most intriguing takeaway from the research is how workers psychologically handle their travel times.

Even in Belgium—where the average commute surpasses the 57-minute limit that people generally consider "acceptable"—only 34% of workers view that time as wasted.

Despite enduring some of the longest transit times on the continent, demand for more remote work among Belgian employees sits at just 32%, staying right below the international average.

Across Europe, the daily commute remains a patchwork of infrastructure challenges and personal routines, proving that the time we spend getting to work is about much more than just kilometres on a map.

World.title: Another Hungarian veto slows Ukraine's EU accession process
World.content:
According to reports in the Ukrainian press, once again no progress has been made in Ukraine’s EU accession process, after Hungarian diplomats declined to support the opening of new clusters at negotiations on Tuesday. Cluster 2 contains rules related to the EU’s internal market, while cluster 3 concerns competition regulations.

 

Hungary did not exercise the same veto over Moldova, whose accession is being handled jointly with Ukraine, paving the way for cluster 3 to be opened on that front. However, the other member states do not want to change their earlier decision that Ukraine’s and Moldova’s EU accession processes should move forward in parallel.

The Hungarian government is tying any further progress in Ukraine’s EU accession process to the pledged settlement of the rights of the Hungarian minorities in Ukraine. The government in Budapest made this clear last week as well, when it again voted no on this issue.

The Ukrainian and Hungarian governments held talks over the summer on the rights of the Hungarian minority, and Kyiv undertook to guarantee the educational, cultural and linguistic rights of the Hungarian-speaking population living in Ukraine.

The Hungarian government’s expectations in this regard have also been backed by EU leaders.

According to a statement on Monday by Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán, progress has been made on this front as well. Work has begun on preparing new legislation on education.

In June, the Hungarian government did not block the opening of cluster 6, which relates to external relations, in Ukraine’s EU accession process.

World.title: The Trump show: Republicans put president centre stage in unprecdented US midterms convention
World.content:
US Republicans open an extraordinary midterm convention in Dallas later on Wednesday betting that putting Donald Trump at the centre of their campaign can rescue a party facing grim election forecasts, despite the president's deeply negative approval ratings.

 

The two-day gathering, dubbed "Trumpapalooza," is designed to persuade the Republican leader's supporters that he is effectively on the ballot on 3 November, when Republicans risk losing the House of Representatives and face a fierce fight to retain the Senate.

"So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot," Trump said recently at a rally in South Carolina. "Just come and vote. It's so important."

Decision Desk HQ projects Democrats to win the House 230-205 and the Senate to finish 51-49 in their favour, revising its 50-50 prediction as the outlook continues to worsen for Republicans.

Trump, whose approval rating stood at just 33% in recent polling, will speak on both convention nights at the American Airlines Centre.

US President Donald Trump speaks during a Steel Across America event in Washington, 8 September, 2026 AP Photo

His challenge is to mobilise voters personally loyal to him without further alienating independents already souring on his presidency amid inflation woes, gasoline prices topping $4 (€3.40) a gallon and the continuing war with Iran.

"Many Trump supporters only vote when he's on the ballot," Matthew Green, a politics professor at the Catholic University of America, told the AFP news agency.

"They're not diehard Republican voters; they're diehard Trump voters. So, in that respect, it makes some sense to feature Trump in the hopes of getting those folks to turn out in November."

But Green was sceptical that asking those supporters to imagine Trump on their ballots could overcome his broader weakness.

"When you're in the low- to mid-30s, that's traditionally associated with a very bad midterm for your party," he said of the 80-year-old's approval ratings.

Trump show

The gathering is the first Republican national convention held specifically for a midterm election, although Democrats experimented with similar meetings in the 1970s and 1980s.

No candidates will be nominated and no formal party business is planned.

Instead, organisers have constructed what amounts to a two-night television rally touting Trump's record and Republican candidates.

More than 100 House members and candidates are expected, with over 50 speakers or presentations scheduled each night.

Trump delivers Wednesday's keynote and returns for Thursday's finale after Vice President JD Vance speaks. Cabinet members, congressional leaders and candidates in closely watched House and Senate races are also on the programme.

Republicans plan to highlight tax cuts, immigration enforcement, manufacturing and prescription drug prices, while depicting Democrats as dangerously far to the left.

Some Republicans, however, are privately hoping Trump sticks to that script rather than the personal grievances and off-message subjects that regularly dominate his appearances.

Staying home

Not everyone is coming. Numerous lawmakers in competitive races have decided that, less than two months from Election Day, their time is better spent campaigning at home.

Green said vulnerable Republicans have two reasons to keep their distance: Trump's unpopularity and the cost of losing precious days in their districts.

"If you are a Republican running in a swing district, you probably want to get as much distance from Trump as possible," he said.

House Speaker Mike Johnson has acknowledged the dilemma, saying some members need to remain home because it is a "critical time" immediately before early voting accelerates nationwide.

Workers continue to prepare the arena before the Republican convention in Dallas, 8 September, 2026 AP Photo

Republicans who do attend have also been asked to contribute at least $25,000 (€21,000) for tickets and lodging.

The event doubles as a huge fundraising opportunity, with a Trump roundtable priced at $250,000 (€214,000) per person and photographs with the president offered for $88,600 (€76,126).

And even Trump's promised national television showcase faces an unusually formidable rival: both convention nights coincide with the opening games of the NFL season.

"Spending three or four days away from your district to go to a convention is not a good way to spend your time if you're facing a tight re-election," Green added.

World.title: Oil surges past $100 a barrel again as US-Iran clashes intensify
World.content:
The front month contract on Brent crude, the international standard for oil prices, crossed $100 per barrel again on Wednesday morning while the US standard, WTI, hovered around $95.

 

Prices have risen almost 20% since the middle of last week as fighting around the world's most important oil chokepoint has once again intensified.

It is also the first time since 23 July that oil has hit the $100 mark.

US Central Command said its forces destroyed five Iranian tankers carrying crude oil on 8 September after Iran's Revolutionary Guard fired ballistic missiles at a US Navy warship twice within two days. The command did not identify the ship, but said it was not hit and continued patrolling regional waters.

It followed a similar strike on 5 September, when Iranian forces fired ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer, both of which evaded the attack. The command responded by disabling or destroying three Iranian tankers.

Tehran retaliated by firing missiles at a US military base in Jordan, where air defences intercepted most of them, and renewed threats to target tankers in Kuwaiti and Bahraini waters.

Iran has also repeatedly warned vessels against using unauthorised routes through the Strait of Hormuz.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said Tehran would soon declare an exclusion zone outside the strait, warning that any vessel entering without Iranian coordination would be added to a sanctions list.

Saudi Arabia has been drawn in too, with Aramco facilities at Jazan attacked again on Monday, though damage was reported as limited.

Roughly 7 million barrels a day are still moving through the Strait of Hormuz, against about 20 million before the war began on 28 February.

No end in sight

The military escalation is running alongside a financial one.

Washington launched Operation Economic Outcast in late August, an effort to sever Iran from the global financial system by targeting its access to digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.

The US Treasury designated close to 60 companies, individuals and vessels at the outset and has signalled fresh measures weekly, with the European Union endorsing the campaign this month.

Rhetoric on both sides has hardened.

US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said the country "will destroy [and sink]" Iranian oil tankers if Iran fires on American vessels while the Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf replied by stating "strike our assets and you get struck".

US President Donald Trump has continued to insist the waterway is functioning, posting on Truth Social last week that "Hormuz volumes are BACK" and claiming 18 million barrels a day were flowing.

However, the US Energy Secretary Chris Wright put Monday's figure at 17 million barrels of crude and products combined, while acknowledging the multi-day rolling average is considerably lower.

During last week's White House press conference, US Vice President JD Vance also declined to categorise the ongoing conflict as a war and stated that "the only reason we do not have a worldwide energy crisis is because of the leadership of the President."

Faced with the latest developments, analysts are adjusting upward.

Goldman Sachs raised its Brent and WTI forecasts by $5 on Monday to $85 and $80, respectively, for December and warned prices could exceed $120 next year should Gulf output remain 4 million barrels a day below pre-war levels, though the bank does not treat that as its base case.

World.title: Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade
World.content:
Turkey is racing to restore safe passage for cargo ships in the Black Sea as attacks on shipping disrupt grain exports and push up prices. Russia and Ukraine are major global wheat exporters, but Black Sea trade has been severely disrupted as both sides step up attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.

Advertising

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan announced this week that Turkey was working on a plan to ensure safe passage in the Black Sea for commercial shipping and said he was in touch with both Ukraine and Russia.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan confirmed that he raised the issue with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, on the sidelines of a gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan.

The Turkish move comes as Ukraine and Russia have ramped up their attacks on shipping and ports in and around the Black Sea. In 2022, Turkey and the United Nations brokered a deal between Ukraine and Russia to ensure safe passage for Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea.

The agreement lasted a year.

While Turkey has maintained good ties with both sides, reaching another agreement will be much harder, warned international relations professor Huseyin Bagci of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University.

“The tension is increasing more than ever before,” Bagci said. “It's not enough to have good relations, because the two sides – the Ukrainians and Russians – should sit down and talk about a common solution to this problem. Turkey cannot solve this problem alone.”

What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey

Growing attacks

In August Ukraine offered a ceasefire on commercial shipping, but the offer was rejected by Moscow, which said it wanted a broader deal. Ukrainian drones continue to strike Russian shipping, while Russia has continued missile attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships.

This surge in attacks comes as both nations rush to export their grain harvests.

Grain prices have risen sharply, by as much as 30 percent, international grain broker Can Atbasoglu said, even as both sides scramble to find new routes for their exports.

“Russia will do their best to export as much as they can, both from Russian Baltic ports and EU Baltic ports like Latvia and Lithuania; they're also exporting,” Atbasoglu said.

“Ukraine will also export as much as they can from Romania as well and through the Danube ports. But the export pace will be definitely lower. So it will definitely stay bullish for the markets. Prices are definitely going to stay like this or can have a further increase.”

Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea

Ships staying put

At one of Istanbul's many shipyards, the docks are crowded with ships that once braved the Black Sea. One vessel bears the scars of a drone attack and is under repair. Others undergo routine maintenance as shipowners hesitate to risk new journeys into dangerous waters.

The superintendent of one ship, speaking anonymously, says repairs are nearly finished, but uncertainty clouds the future.

“We wanted to take the ship out to the Black Sea before entering the shipyard, but because of that risk, we didn’t enter the Black Sea and didn’t take on any cargo. We’ve been in the shipyard for 50 days for repairs, but we don’t know what will happen once the repairs are finished,” the superintendent said.

Turkish shipowners warn that many are on the brink of bankruptcy, as idle ships rack up costs of up to 50,000 euros a month in mooring and crew expenses.

Ziya Ustel, CEO of Turkish shipping company VI-ZA STAR, says high freight rates are being offered for Black Sea routes, but the risks are too great.

“They are offering high freight rates, etc,” Ustel said.

Without a diplomatic solution, few shipowners will be prepared to risk their vessels, Ustel warned.

“The main thing is to find out a real solution,” Ustel added. “Otherwise, no one will try anything anymore.”

Turkish diplomacy

Ankara is expected to step up its efforts to find a solution.

Grain brokers say hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough may be one reason prices have so far remained below the record highs seen at the start of the war.

But if Turkish efforts fail and attacks on Black Sea shipping continue, higher grain prices could have a considerable impact, especially on the world’s poorest nations, many of which depend on Russian and Ukrainian grain.

World.title: UK rules out cyberattack after major flight disruptions
World.content:
Airports across the UK continue to face delays and cancellations after a flight processing system failure. The UK's transport secretary has summoned the CEO of National Air Traffic Services (NATS) for an explanation.

Martin Rolfe, CEO of the UK's National Air Traffic Services (NATS), on Wednesday ruled out a cyberattack after a major interruption Tuesday in operations at British airports.

"We will be doing a very, very thorough and full investigation," Rolfe told the BBC.

More than 1,000 flights were cancelled and delayed due to air traffic control problems that started Tuesday morning and lasted for several hours. NATS said a problem involved an issue with the flight processing system.

Although NATS said the problem was resolved, more than 150 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, and more delays were expected throughout the day.

London's Heathrow Airport on Wednesday said "some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew," and advised travelers to check flight status before heading to the airport.

"There are going to be dozens of cancellations in the morning of flights coming into Heathrow because, basically, the flights didn't go out tonight," travel journalist Simon Calder said to Sky News. "The consequences will be horrible," he added.

Questions over the UK's network

The UK's Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said Wednesday that she had summoned Rolfe for a closer explanation of what caused the malfunction, amid concerns over the UK's air traffic network.

This is not the first time a major system failure has affected British airports. In August 2023, several flights were cancelled due to a "system meltdown," costing airlines $135 million. In 2025, problems with flight radars affected several airports in the UK, including Heathrow Airport.

"I am seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the ‌job," Alexander said on X.

irports across the UK faced delays and cancellations after a flight processing system failure. Image: Jonathan Brady/PA Wire/dpa/picture alliance

Ryanair, Europe's biggest airline, said at least 150,000 passengers using its services experienced delays of up to eight hours. Two hundred of its flights were cancelled.

For the second time, the airline demanded that NATS CEO Rolfe resign.

Rolfe told Sky News he accepted "full responsibility" but did not say if he was considering stepping down.

NATS provides air control traffic services to 15 UK airports. It is a public-private partnership which is partially owned by airlines including British Airways and easyJet, pension funds and the government.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

World.title: The billion-euro trade driving Europe's eels to extinction
World.content:
Traffickers are making big bucks smuggling millions of critically endangered eels across continents, in suitcases on planes or by exploiting legal loopholes to end up on dinnerplates. Where are the smuggling hotspots?

In Plentzia, a small waterfront town close to bustling Bilbao, eel fishing has long been part of daily life. Now fisherfolk across Spain's Basque Country can no longer catch the animals, a prized delicacy at the center of what authorities describe as one of the world's most lucrative wildlife trafficking trades.

The regional ban is meant to protect the European eel, a critically endangered species, which has seen population declines of around 95% since the 1980s. Yet local fishermen argue the regulations punish those who adhere to them, while criminal networks profit from a billion-euro trade in illegally caught eels.

"So it's the Basque fishermen who will make the eel extinct when the rest are allowed to fish?" said Unai Eizaguirre who's been fishing eels for 30 years and is now facing the prospect of income shorfalls. "It's ridiculous."

Conservationists support the ban as an emergency response in the face of multiple threats from pollution and climate change. But marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says longer-term measures, like removing hydroelectric dams that block migration routes and kill eels with their turbines are also needed.

"I don't know if the eel has time to wait for these projects to show their effects," said Diaz, who works with local marine research institute AZTI.

Marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says only 12% of eels now survive the journey from the Sargasso Sea Image: Nicole Ris/DW

Eel smuggling as lucrative as drugs

Part of what makes European eels so vulnerable is their remarkable life cycle, which was, until relatively recently, a source of mystery. Scientists now know adult eels migrate thousands of kilometers from European rivers to the Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic, their only known spawning grounds. They breed and then die, leaving their larvae to drift to Europe. By the time they reach rivers, they've transformed into tiny, transparent "glass eels."

Today, only about 12% survive the journey from the Sargasso to the Gulf of Biscay and connected waterways, Diaz told DW. The young glass eels conservationists are trying to protect are the most valuable in the illegal trade, fetching up to €9000 ($10,400) per kilogram.

"You can compare it with drug trafficking. Every year they seize tons of illegally caught eel in Europe," said Eizaguirre. "The big business lies in trafficking them to Asia," adding that the huge profits and comparatively small fines for smaller infractions by local fishers make the risk worth it. However, when criminal organizations are involved, penalties can be substantial with fines up to 6 times the value of illegally smuggled eel.

Demand in countries such as China, South Korea and Japan is driving prices. As is a biological peculiarity: so far, it's been exceedingly difficult to get eels to reproduce in captivity. This means fish farms — where the eels are raised before being sold to premium restaurants — need a steady stream of young from the wild. Sometimes, the same smuggled eels come back to Europe as fillets for the sushi market.

Conservationists had hoped pressure on the species would ease when the EU banned export of the species outside the bloc in 2010. Instead, organized crime groups have increasingly muscled in on the market, with the illegal trade now generating an estimated €3 billion in profits in peak years.

"Our estimated maximum was always 100 tons of glass eels smuggled annually. That's already around 300 million fish," said Florian Stein, head of policy and science at the German Angling Association. But information from his contacts in the illegal trade have led him to the conclusion that it was a "very conservative estimate."

International law enforcement agencies are also cracking down, with Europol's Operation Lake seizing 22 tons of glass eels and arresting 26 suspects between 2024 and 2025.

"There has been a lot of pressure from law enforcement throughout Europe," said Interpol's Sanchez Romero. "That's why the criminal groups always look for new routes."

A small dam near Plentzia — obstacles like this can block eels on their migration route Image: Nicole Ris/DW

Eels smuggled in plain sight in regular suitcases along complex routes

Still, Stein, who did his doctoral dissertation on international eel smuggling and advises the German government, said trafficking has increased since 2020, and illegal trade routes have become more complex.

"Ten years ago, Madrid airport was still one of the biggest smuggling hotspots," he said. This was due to its proximity to fishing grounds in northern Spain and Portugal.

Increased checks by Spanish authorities on flights to East Asia forced traffickers to adapt. Experts now say a new route running through North Africa via Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal has become increasingly important.

Geography is one reason the route is attractive. The Strait of Gibraltar is 14 kilometers at its narrowest point and a busy maritime junction. "We know that many drugs are also transported through this strait," Moroccan investigative journalist Yassir Al-Makhtoum told DW.

European eels also inhabit rivers and estuaries in Morocco. Though the country has banned the export of glass eels smaller than 12 centimeters (4.7 inches), it is building a legal domestic eel trading industry. Experts fear that's acting as a cover for trafficked animals coming in from Europe.

From Morocco, smugglers then move eels along numerous routes to Asia. The means are not always sophisticated. Glass eels can be transported in ordinary suitcases on domestic flights. They're placed in bags filled with a little water and insulated to keep their temperature stable. They can survive for up to 48 hours in those conditions. Once in Asia, they go to the fish farms.

In Plentzia, where eel fishing has long been part of daily life, fishermen say the regional ban risks hurting those who follow the rules while illegal traders continue to profit Image: Nicole Ris/DW

A species running out of time

Eels are an important indicator species for the health of ocean and riverine ecosystems because their long migrations across multiple habitats make them vulnerable to problems that could also harm other species. They also serve as important prey for herons, otters and larger fish.

"But the impact of its disappearance is difficult to predict," said marine biologist Diaz.

Under EU regulations, member states must undertake measures to allow 40% of adult eels to return to the Sargasso Sea to spawn. Diaz also wants to ensure at least 40% of glass eels make it back from the Sargasso Sea.

But European eels are not the only eel species under threat. A proposal to protect all freshwater eel species from illegal and unsustainable trade was rejected at the 2025 CITES wildlife conference. For Stein such protection is key.

"The proposal should be on the table again at the next conference. I just don't know how else we can get a handle on this problem," said Stein, adding more lobbying and coalition building is needed to advocate for a ban.

“The eel for us is more than just a fish,” said Unai Eizaguirre. “It's been part of our identity for centuries.” For fishermen like him, better protection for the eel represents a chance at a sustainable future.

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

The research for this story was sponsored by: The Med Mosaic.

World.title: India: 5 baby orangutans rescued, smuggling suspected
World.content:
09/09/2026 September 9, 2026 Baby orangutans rescued, sparking international smuggling probe

Indian forest officials rescued five baby orangutans in the eastern state of Odisha on Tuesday, with authorities suspecting the great apes were smuggled into the country from Southeast Asia.

The animals, not native to India, were found in a forest in the Balasore district. Local legislator Goutam Buddha Das told The Telegraph newspaper that villagers first spotted the orangutans dangling from a tree and initially mistook them for monkeys, before alerting forest officials that their appearance didn't match.

He said the area's coastal location suggested the animals could have arrived by sea from Indonesia.

"I demand a high-level inquiry to find out who is involved in the racket," Das said.

Balasore forest officer Pratik Prakash Indalkar said the three male and two female orangutans were examined by veterinarians, found to be in good health, and given food and oral rehydration solution before being transferred to Nandan Kanan Zoo in Bhubaneswar for quarantine.

Odisha Environment Minister Ram Singh Khuntia said the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau is now investigating how the animals reached India.

"We suspect that an international racket might be involved in this," he told the IANS news agency. Authorities are also examining whether the animals were destined for sale to buyers in Kolkata.

Orangutans are native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra. Only about 104,000 remain in the wild, according to the World Wildlife Fund, down from more than 230,000 a century ago.

Borneo's orangutans fight to survive To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Tapanuli orangutan is critically endangered, with fewer than 800 animals thought to be left.

World.title: Trafficked into fraud: An African crisis situation in Cambodia
World.content:
Cambodia is cracking down on scam operators, with the effects being felt mostly among young Africans: Thousands of trafficking victims are now stuck in the Asian country with no money, no passport, and no prospects.

Southeast Asia has long emerged as a major hub of highly organized online fraud operations, targeting people all around the world.

According to the United Nations, these operations generate tens of billions of dollars annually, having long surpassed the illegal drug trade as the most profitable activity for criminal networks, as reported by the United States Institute of Peace.

However, those who fall prey to scams and other fraudulent activities aren't the only victims of these criminal rings; the scam industry in Southeast Asia alone is powered by at least 300,000 trafficked workers from 66 countries, who are routinely subjected to torture, sexual abuse, and forced labor, according to a recent UN Human Rights report.

Dream job abroad? It could be a trafficking trap To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

African nationals now form the largest group of those trafficked to and stranded in countries like Myanmar and Cambodia, without any viable pathway to go back home, says the NGO Freedom Collaborative.

In Cambodia, one of the main obstacles for facilitating any return is the fact that many African countries like Uganda, Liberia, Ghana, of Nigeria have no consular representation.

"But also because some countries have zero interest," says Montse Ferrer, co-regional director of Amnesty International, who finds equal blame for the situation in many of the countries of origin.

"They're not even picking up the phone, let alone providing the paperwork for the money for them to go back."

Cambodia's reluctant crackdown on scam operators

Ferrer believes that keeping the situation unchanged has also been in the interest of the Cambodian government for a long time:

Many trafficking victims now have overstay fines for their visas against their names in Cambodia, reaching thousands of dollars in many instances.

"They don't allow NGOs to provide the support these people need, and instead they have resorted to arresting and threatening them," Ferrer told DW.

Following great pressure from the international community — including threats of financial sanctions by the US, the UK, Canada and the European Union — Cambodia did eventually agree to launch a crackdown on the scamming industry earlier this year.

According to the Cambodian Ministry of Information, the initiative resulted in many arrests and triggered a mass exodus of dubious operatives from scamming industry.

Inside Cambodia's scam industry To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But the crackdown also created a secondary crisis: Thousands of trafficked foreign workers remain stranded in the country without documentation nor legal status; now, they also lack shelter and money in many instances, NGOs say.

Many who have sought in Cambodia help have reportedly been placed in immigration detention, while others have to sleep rough and beg for food.

Instead of being given protection, many of the trafficking often victims now face stigmatization and abuse on the street of the capital Phnom Penh and elsewhere.

Officials in Southeast Asia have been cracking down on scam factories, often conducting raids across borders Image: Chalinee Thirasupa/REUTERS

Lured to Cambodia under false pretenses

Emmanuel David is one of many of the trafficking victims stuck in Cambodia. The 28-year-old Liberian national arrived there last year after a treacherous irregular journey originating in Vietnam.

"My friend told me there was work in Cambodia, but he did not explain that it was scamming work," David explained.

The scamming company had offered him a lucrative deal of making around $800 (€700) per month, which is more than double the average wage for qualified individuals in Liberia, according to the Civil Service Agency of Liberia.

The reality hit quite differently: Once there, he was forced to work 14 hours a day to deceive women on various dating apps to part with their money.

But David was initially unable — and later unwilling — to meet the set target quota of scams per day.

In response, the criminal group he worked for started billing him for food and accommodation through his wages, and later even confiscated his belongings — including his passport.

David says he also faced substantial physical violence, including beatings, for four months.

Eventually, he left "with no documents and no money," and is now hoping to find a way back to Liberia.

His story, however, is far from unique.

'Hundreds' of Africans trafficked to criminal compounds

Another survivor, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation, also recounted how he was "beaten and [subjected to] electric shocks."

The abuse resulted in him having to be hospitalized for three weeks, and is now unable to pay his medical bills.

Pia Oberoi, chief of the Right to Development Section at UN Human Rights, told DW that "despite the promise of a good salary, most come out in debt."

She also confirmed that more and more of the trafficking victims in Southeast Asia come from African countries, "because there is clearly a recruitment industry that's built around Africa, targeting African nationals."

Kenya scammers lured abroad To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other victims have corroborated this development, describing hundreds of Africans packed into heavily fortified compounds.

"Once you're inside there's no way out," an informant, who also chose to remain anonymous, told DW.

He said the compounds have their own laws, and that sexual abuse and psychological violence are an integral part of how they operate.

The police, he says, just turns a blind eye — at best.

No government assistance from any direction

Amnesty International speaks of an unfolding humanitarian crisis, warning that escapees are widely being treated as criminals rather than as trafficking victims.

"They shouldn't be punished for crimes they were forced to commit," Oberoi highlights, though her pleas appear to land on deaf ears.

Several of the victims contacted by DW said their governments were "slow" to help with their repatriation.

DW attempted to contact several African foreign ministries to hear their side, but has not received any response.

A statement issued by the Cambodian government meanwhile said that more than 700 compounds run chiefly by Chinese nationals had been raided, with 58,266 foreign nationals deported and nearly 30,000 suspects arrested over the past year.

However, the Cambodian government did not reply to DW's direct request for further information.

The UN's International Organization for Migration (IOM) meanwhile said it's trying its utmost to help the trafficking victims; but in the face of severe budgetary constraints, it can only provide "limited, prioritized support."

Fear, guilt and stigma

Humanitarian groups also warn of a high risk of victims being re-trafficked, even for those who have managed to return to their countries of origin.

In some instances, those who come back home are stigmatized as a failure — "a situation that is really unbearable," says Ferrer.

Emmanuel David is a prime example: He feels obliged to to apologize to his family for not returning a success. When asked about his little daughter, he says that "daddy can't go home without money."

To his mind, he hardly is the victim of his circumstances.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: Ukraine, Russia trade drone strikes, killing 6
World.content:
At least four people were killed, and 29 others were injured, in a Ukrainian attack on a Russian Black Sea port. Meanwhile, Russian drones struck a crossing on the Ukraine-Moldova border, killing two.

A Ukrainian drone attack on the Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk overnight killed at least four people, including a child, Russian officials said Wednesday.

Veniamin Kondratyev, the governor of the Krasnodar region in southern Russia, said 29 others were injured in the drone attack.

Ukraine has frequently targeted Novorossiysk, a port city that is a major outlet for Russian oil and grain exports.

Earlier on Wednesday, the mayor of the city, Andrei Kravchenko, had said the debris from a Ukrainian drone fell onto several businesses and nearly landed on a residential building, sparking fires.

In the nearby town of Anapa, falling drone debris damaged three homes and a kindergarten, Kondratyev said, adding that there were no casualties.

Russia's Defense Ministry said nearly 600 Ukrainian drones had been shot down overnight.

Two civilians killed in Russian attack on border crossing

Russian drone strikes overnight on a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, meanwhile, killed at least two civilians, the regional governor Oleh Kiper said on social media .

Three people were wounded in the strike on the Starokozace border crossing, around 500 kilometres (310 miles) south of Kyiv, Ukraine's State Border Guard Service said.

The strikes forced the checkpoint to close temporarily, Kiper said, adding that multiple fires broke out as a result of the attack.

Ukrainian emergency officials also said the capital, Kyiv was attacked overnight. While some fires were started, there were no casualties.

Russia's drone attack damaged a passenger bus and started fires, Ukraine said Image: OdeskaODA/Telegram

What is the latest in US-brokered peace talks?

Russia on Tuesday resumed its near-daily airstrikes on Kyiv after a brief pause while US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow for talks.

At least five people were killed in Kyiv on Tuesday, officials said.

Russia also said President Vladimir Putin had had an "extremely frank" phone call with his US counterpart Donald Trump on Tuesday, as Washington continues to press Ukrainian and Russian officials to hold face-to-face talks to end the war.

Ukraine has suggested talks that could take place in September, but Russian officials have said it is "too early" to discuss specifics such as a venue or dates for the talks.

Despite US pressure, talks between Moscow and Kyiv have yielded no results beyond sporadic prisoner swaps.
