World.title: Prague to Add 51 New Trams Next Year as Network Expands
World.content:
Prague is set to receive 51 new trams next year as the city expands its tram network and begins replacing some of its oldest vehicles.

The Prague Public Transport Company (DPP) has ordered another 25 Škoda 52T trams under an existing framework agreement with Škoda Transportation.

Each tram costs CZK 82.5 million, including CZK 40 million in European subsidies. Prague has now committed to buying 71 of the new vehicles in three separate orders.



The first 20 Škoda 52T trams entered regular service in Prague last year. Another batch is being delivered this year, while the latest orders will continue into 2027.

The newest order for 25 additional trams is due to be completed by December 3 next year.

The new vehicles are needed not only because Prague is building new tram lines but also because the existing fleet needs to be renewed. Some of the oldest trams still in operation are the T3M models, while a large part of the fleet consists of reconstructed T3R.P and T3R.PV vehicles and their derivatives.

Replacing older models with a smaller number of standardised tram types should also reduce maintenance and servicing costs, according to the deputy mayor. The new trams are expected to remain in service for around 20 to 30 years, compared with approximately 15 years for buses.

The Škoda 52T is 32 metres long and 2.5 metres wide and can carry up to 243 passengers. Of these, 173 can travel standing. The tram therefore offers almost 16 percent more capacity than Prague’s Škoda 15T trams.

The maximum operating speed is 70 kilometres per hour.

The 52T was designed specifically for Prague’s tram network, including sections with narrow and sharply curved tracks. This allows the vehicles to operate on existing routes without requiring major changes to the infrastructure.

World.title: Prague Castle to Celebrate Václav Havel With Four-Month Festival
World.content:
Prague Castle will host a four-month festival celebrating the legacy of Václav Havel, with theatre, film, music, design and public debates taking place from October through January.

The Havel ALIVE festival will mark what would have been Havel’s 90th birthday and explore the continued relevance of his ideas. Most events will be free.

One of the main highlights will be the Czech premiere of The Warning, an unfinished Havel play that remained hidden for almost 40 years. The manuscript was discovered by David Dušek among the papers of writer Zdeněk Urbánek.



The production has been prepared by Jiří Havelka, artistic director of Dejvické Theatre, and will feature actors Martin Myšička and Ivan Trojan. The theatre will also present We’ll Start It Tomorrow, or Who’s the Gentleman Here at Prague Castle’s Riding Hall.

The festival will also focus on Havel’s influence on Czech design. In cooperation with Designblok, Prague Castle will present Design for Václav Havel, featuring objects connected with his presidency, including Bořek Šípek’s Olga chair, original glass pieces and Castle Guard uniforms designed by Theodor Pištěk.

For the first time, the exhibition will also show the entire presidential office, including Havel’s library. It will open during Designblok on October 7 and remain at the Riding Hall from October 21 to January 17.

Music and dance will feature prominently as well. On November 18, students and teachers from the Academy of Performing Arts in Prague will present a gala evening directed by Magdalena Švecová. Other performances will draw on Havel’s writings, his Anticodes poetry collection, his relationship with the underground music scene and the events of November 1989.

The programme will also include screenings of Citizen Havel and Leaving, a musical evening led by Pavel Klusák, and discussions about art, architecture, freedom and democracy.

Selected festival events

October 4 — Guided tours of Lány Chateau and Prague Castle focused on Havel’s presidency. Free.

October 7 — Opening of Design for Václav Havel at the Prague Castle Riding Hall.

October 8 — Pavel Klusák’s All the President’s Rockers: Václav Havel & Music. Free.

October 14 — Citizen Havel screening followed by a discussion. Free.

October 22 — Thinking Havel Live: Democracy and the Future of Europe. Free.

November 4 — Dejvické Theatre presents We’ll Start It Tomorrow, or Who’s the Gentleman Here. Tickets CZK 390–490.

November 5–6 — Czech premieres of Havel’s The Warning. Tickets CZK 390–490.

November 12 — Thinking Havel: Between the Individual and the System. Free.

November 18 — Havel: Inspiration for a New Generation, a gala evening at the Prague Castle Riding Hall from 7 p.m. Tickets CZK 250.

November 26 — Lecture on Havel’s designer and architect Bořek Šípek at the Supreme Burgrave’s Office from 5 p.m. Free.

December 3 — Thinking Havel: Politics and Spiritual Values, a debate with Alice Koubová, Milena Bartlová and Petr Kratochvíl at the Riding Hall from 6 p.m. Free.

December 8 — Literature at the Castle: Writing Havel, a lecture at the Supreme Burgrave’s Office from 5 p.m. Free.

December 15 — Screening of Leaving, followed by a discussion with Dagmar Havlová and other guests at the Supreme Burgrave’s Office from 6 p.m. Free.

January 14 — Ceremonial presentation of the Jindřich Chalupecký Award 2027 at Prague Castle.

World.title: Prague Airport to Expand Border Control at Terminal 1
World.content:
Prague Airport is expanding and modernising the border control area for arriving passengers at Terminal 1 to increase capacity and reduce waiting times.

The project will add five new passport control desks and four EasyGoGate (EGG) self-service gates for eligible European passport holders.

The work is scheduled to begin in September 2026 and is expected to be completed by the end of April 2027.



The expansion comes as Prague Airport faces increased pressure at border control, particularly during peak hours. The introduction of the European Entry/Exit System (EES) in October 2025 has added to the workload at the airport.

The project will also enlarge the waiting area before passport control and upgrade the ventilation system throughout the border control area.

The total investment is estimated at CZK 290 million, including construction, design and engineering work, technical supervision and safety coordination. The new passport control equipment will be supplied and installed by the Police of the Czech Republic.

Police representatives said the changes are also intended to strengthen security at the Schengen Area’s external border while ensuring the new facilities meet current security and legal requirements.

Some queues and restrictions are expected

The renovation will take place in stages to limit disruption to airport operations. However, passengers may encounter temporary restrictions at passport control and longer queues during some phases of the work.

At one stage, three passport control desks will be temporarily closed. This phase will be scheduled during a period of lower passenger traffic.

EU citizens will continue to be able to use the passport control desks and EGG self-service gates designated for European passport holders. They are not required to register through the EES.

During the other stages of construction, restrictions will mainly affect the area immediately before passport control. Passenger routes will be adjusted around the construction zones, while the overall flow through border control will remain unchanged.

World.title: Prague Bids to Host 2029 European Figure Skating Championships
World.content:
Prague is preparing a bid to host the 2029 European Figure Skating Championships, with the O2 Arena expected to serve as the main venue if the Czech capital wins the right to stage the competition.

Prague City Council approved the candidacy on Monday following an approach from the Czech Figure Skating Union.

The proposal comes several months after Prague hosted the 2026 World Figure Skating Championships in March.



City councilor for education and sports Antonín Klecanda (STAN) said the success of that event helped encourage the city to pursue another major international competition.

“The response was very positive, and other countries asked whether another event of this kind could be held in Prague,” Klecanda said on Monday. “We reached an agreement, and today we approved our candidacy to host the European Figure Skating Championship in 2029.”

The 2026 World Championships attracted a record number of spectators for a figure skating world championship, according to Klecanda. He also said international visitors had responded positively to Prague’s role as host city.

The city has not yet determined when the 2029 championship would take place. The date will be discussed at a later stage, while Prague currently expects the competitions to be staged at the O2 Arena.

The financial impact of hosting the championships has not yet been calculated. The city would have to cover not only the direct costs of organizing the competition but also additional expenses linked to public services, including increased public transport capacity, emergency services and police deployment.

Klecanda said these costs could reach tens of millions of Czech crowns. He argued, however, that part of the expenditure could be offset by additional tax revenue generated by the event, while the championship would also strengthen Prague’s international profile.

The final decision on the host city for the 2029 European Figure Skating Championships has yet to be made.

World.title: Pickles Prague Festival: A Celebration of Pickled and Fermented Vegetables
World.content:
The Pickles Prague Festival will take place on September 19-20 at the Prague Exhibition Grounds, bringing together producers, food enthusiasts and visitors interested in pickled and fermented vegetables.

The festival will run from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. and will focus on the wide variety of vegetables preserved through pickling and fermentation.

More info here.

Visitors can expect everything from traditional pickled cucumbers, peppers and beets to less familiar varieties from the Czech Republic and abroad.

Alongside tastings and opportunities to buy pickled products, the programme will include workshops and educational talks covering pickling techniques, fermentation, the nutritional aspects of fermented vegetables and the role of preserved foods in different culinary traditions.



The event will also feature live music throughout the day, while a dedicated children’s area will offer activities for younger visitors, making the festival suitable for families as well.

Admission to the Pickles Prague Festival is free.

World.title: Czech Politicians Divided Over AfD Victory in Saxony-Anhalt
World.content:
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) has secured a major victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, prompting different reactions from Czech politicians.

While some have congratulated the party and called for dialogue with its leaders, others have warned that the result reflects the growing strength of political extremism.

The result has also renewed debate in the Czech Republic over migration, security and how mainstream parties should respond to the AfD.



Martin Kupka, chairman of the Civic Democratic Party (ODS), described the result as a warning for Europe. He said democratic parties could not counter extremist movements simply by labeling them or ignoring issues that concern voters.

“Democratic parties must offer clear solutions: a tough migration policy, security, less regulation and no populist waste of public money,” Kupka said.

He added that the Czech Republic should avoid following the same political path.

Vít Rakušan, leader of the Mayors and Independents (STAN), similarly said the election should serve as a lesson for Czech politicians.

According to Rakušan, mainstream democratic parties risk losing voters when they leave issues such as migration and social problems to populist movements.

Rather than focusing solely on the AfD’s success, he said, democratic parties should develop practical and sustainable responses to issues that voters consider important.

Former Prime Minister Petr Fiala offered one of the strongest warnings. In a post on social media, the ODS politician called the result a “political earthquake” and said the AfD’s success could not be explained solely by the failure of mainstream democratic parties to address voters’ concerns.

Fiala argued that the reasons were more complex than economic dissatisfaction alone. “The causes are deeper and far from just economic,” he wrote.

The response from the Czech government’s current Foreign Minister Petr Macinka was more cautious. Macinka said the next steps by the AfD and Germany’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) would be particularly significant.

He said it would be important to see how the winning party uses its strong mandate and how the CDU responds to the result.

Tomio Okamura, chairman of the Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) party and speaker of the Czech Chamber of Deputies, took a more positive view of the AfD’s performance.

He congratulated the party and said the election showed that voters were dissatisfied with the policies of Germany’s established parties, particularly the CDU.

“The people of the former East Germany have made it clear that they no longer want this policy to continue,” Okamura said in an interview with Czech Television.

Okamura also rejected criticism based on the AfD’s classification as a far-right party. He questioned the credibility of reports concerning extremism and pointed to similar accusations involving his own SPD.

Radek Vondráček of the ANO movement also called for a different approach to the AfD. Speaking to Czech Television, the chairman of the Chamber of Deputies’ foreign affairs committee said the election had given the party a clear mandate and expressed hope that it would be able to form a stable government.

“I hope that the time for dialogue is coming, when citizens will receive some appropriate result for what they have chosen,” Vondráček said.

World.title: A surprise exception for Hungary: US gives Hungarians visa priority
World.content:
The United States has resumed processing immigrant visa applications from Hungary and Poland, while applicants from dozens of other countries remain affected by a temporary pause. The unusual move reportedly came directly from the White House.

Hungary and Poland given priority

In an unexpected development, the United States has restarted processing immigrant visa applications submitted in Hungary and Poland, even as a wider pause on immigrant visa appointments remains in place elsewhere.

Four people familiar with the matter told Reuters that processing resumed last week. Two of the sources said the White House had specifically instructed US diplomatic missions in Hungary and Poland to prioritise immigrant visa applications from the two countries.

It remains unclear why Washington singled out Hungary and Poland for special treatment. Reuters noted, however, that US President Donald Trump and his senior advisers have cultivated close relationships with right-wing political allies in both countries.

Trump has been a vocal supporter of Viktor Orbán, Hungary’s former prime minister, who lost April’s election. In Poland, meanwhile, Trump has publicly backed nationalist President Karol Nawrocki, whose political relationship with centrist Prime Minister Donald Tusk has been increasingly tense.

Neither the Hungarian nor Polish governments immediately commented on the reported decision.

Photo: Anadolu/Kyle Mazza

A major change amid Trump’s immigration crackdown

The development comes against the backdrop of an extensive US crackdown on both illegal and legal migration under Trump’s second administration. While Trump has long made stopping illegal immigration a central political priority, his administration has also introduced measures aimed at reducing legal migration.

Washington has imposed travel restrictions on citizens of dozens of countries, introduced costly new fees for certain work visas and ordered enhanced checks of visa applicants’ social media histories.

In January, the US State Department announced that it was temporarily suspending the processing of immigrant visas in 75 countries, arguing that applicants from those countries were at greater risk of becoming reliant on public assistance.

The measure affected countries across several regions, including Brazil, Colombia and Uruguay in Latin America, Bosnia and Albania in the Balkans, and Pakistan and Bangladesh in South Asia.

Hungary and Poland are now notable exceptions to the broader disruption.

Why did Hungary receive special treatment?

The White House has not publicly explained why immigrant visa processing was restored specifically in Hungary and Poland.

One potentially relevant episode dates back to May, when US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau reportedly instructed senior State Department officials to facilitate a US visa for a fugitive former Polish cabinet minister who had fled to Hungary amid corruption allegations.

The politician was former Polish Justice Minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who, together with former deputy justice minister Marcin Romanowski, had received political protection from the Hungarian government under Orbán.

Following the change of government in Hungary, however, Prime Minister Péter Magyar signalled that the two men should not expect to remain in the country indefinitely. Polish media subsequently reported that Ziobro had left for the United States with his wife. Ziobro later told a television channel that he intended to remain in America and “enjoy American freedom”.

The episode has added an intriguing backdrop to Washington’s decision to prioritise visa processing in Hungary and Poland, although there is no official confirmation that the cases are connected.

Visa pause follows court ruling

The current disruption to immigrant visa processing has itself followed a legal challenge. A US federal judge, Jeannette A. Vargas, struck down the Trump administration’s January policy on 21 August, calling it “patently unlawful”.

In the aftermath, the State Department instructed US missions around the world to cancel immigrant visa appointments as officials introduced new training on how to assess whether applicants could support themselves financially in the United States without relying on public benefits.

The department said on 25 August that the global pause would remain in place until staff had completed the new training.

Although the government initially said interviews would be rescheduled through 31 August, the disruption could reportedly last for months. The training programme requires US missions to work through materials provided by Washington, followed by visits from consular officers who certify that the training has been completed.

Applicants in several countries have reported cancelled appointments extending into September.

Hundreds of thousands of visas affected

The scale of the policy is significant. US embassies and consulates traditionally conduct hundreds of thousands of immigrant visa interviews every year, many involving relatives of American citizens or permanent residents.

In 2024, the final year of Joe Biden’s presidency, the United States issued approximately 600,000 immigrant visas.

World.title: EU Parliament set to drop Article 7 against Hungary as Magyar government wins Brussels backing
World.content:
The European Parliament is reportedly preparing to end its long-running Article 7 procedure against Hungary, potentially marking a dramatic shift in relations between Budapest and Brussels following Viktor Orbán’s election defeat.

Hungary’s Article 7 procedure could be coming to an end

The European Parliament is on course to withdraw the EU’s so-called “nuclear option” against Hungary, according to Euronews, as lawmakers increasingly recognise reforms introduced under Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s new government.

The Article 7 procedure was launched by MEPs in 2018 over concerns about the rule of law and alleged breaches of EU values under Viktor Orbán’s government. Among the issues raised were judicial independence, corruption, media freedom, fundamental rights and the treatment of minorities and migrants.

But Orbán’s defeat in April’s election and the arrival of Magyar’s Tisza government have dramatically changed the political environment.

Several MEPs and European Parliament officials reportedly believe that many of the concerns underpinning the procedure have now been addressed, with a senior member of the European People’s Party (EPP) saying that it would be “reasonable” for the procedure to end soon.

The EPP, the Parliament’s largest political group, is reportedly prepared to support the move. Magyar’s Tisza Party is a member of the European political family.

If you missed it: PM Magyar signals Tisza’s next EU move after meeting with Manfred Weber

Decision could come after October mission

The potential withdrawal is not expected to happen immediately. A European Parliament fact-finding mission is scheduled to visit Hungary in late October. MEPs are expected to meet government representatives, public institutions, civil society organisations, stakeholders and NGOs as they assess the country’s current rule-of-law situation.

The delegation will then prepare a report on its findings. Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, who is leading the Article 7 file, expects the report to be completed in early 2027. Some Parliament officials, however, believe a recommendation to end the procedure could come as early as December.

Strik has stressed that the assessment will follow a set of specific criteria rather than simply reflecting Hungary’s change of government. One important issue will be the fate of Hungary’s controversial 2021 child protection law, which restricts minors’ access to certain books, films and other content depicting or promoting homosexuality or gender transition.

Hungary’s government has so far neither repealed the legislation nor announced plans to do so. The Court of Justice of the European Union ruled in April 2026 that the law breached EU law and the bloc’s fundamental values, according to Brussels Signal.

A two-thirds majority is needed

Ending the Article 7 procedure will not be automatic. At least two-thirds of the European Parliament’s 719 members – meaning a minimum of 480 MEPs – must support the withdrawal.

The EPP’s 184 lawmakers are expected to back the move, while conservative and right-wing groups are also likely to support it. The European Conservatives and Reformists, Patriots for Europe and Europe of Sovereign Nations together have almost 200 MEPs.

However, the centre-left Socialists and Democrats (S&D) and liberal Renew Europe groups could hold the decisive votes. Both groups have acknowledged that Hungary has made progress, but have warned that any decision must be based on a comprehensive assessment of the country’s legislation and actual reforms.

Renew Europe MEP Sandro Gozi told Euronews that ending the procedure must be based on “real changes”, warning that otherwise it could appear to be merely a political decision.

From Orbán-era confrontation to a new relationship?

The possible end of Article 7 would represent a major change in Hungary’s relationship with Brussels. The procedure has only been triggered twice in the EU’s history. The European Commission launched one against Poland in 2017, while the European Parliament initiated the Hungarian procedure a year later.

Neither case reached the final sanctions stage, which would require unanimous backing from EU member states to suspend a country’s voting rights. The Polish procedure was closed in 2024 after Donald Tusk’s coalition replaced the Law and Justice government and began implementing reforms demanded by the European Commission.

Hungary could now be heading down a similar path under Magyar. The new government has already agreed to a reform package with the European Commission, while Brussels unblocked around EUR 16.4 billion in frozen EU funding in May.

If the European Parliament ultimately votes to end Article 7, it could provide Magyar with a significant political victory – and signal that the EU considers Hungary’s post-Orbán government to be moving substantially closer to European rule-of-law standards. But the October fact-finding mission, the fate of the child protection law and the crucial two-thirds parliamentary majority mean that the final outcome is far from guaranteed.

World.title: The zártkert trap: when a rural Hungarian property is not what it seems
World.content:
There is one word that almost everyone in Hungary’s rural property market knows, yet many only understand its real significance after the purchase: zártkert. An attractive holiday home on a vineyard hillside, a manor house in wine country or a village house with a garden may all conceal this classification – and a buyer who looked only at the listing photographs rather than the land registry title sheet may be in for an unpleasant surprise. A thorough legal due-diligence review before purchase can usually be completed within a few days; failing to carry it out can create a legal dead end lasting for years.

Guest article for Daily News Hungary readers – by Emese Széll, Private Real Estate Advisor for Premium Clients in Hungary

What is a zártkert, and why is it not the same as a residential property?

Zártkert is a historical category, but its present legal status cannot be reduced to a simple formula of ‘outlying area + agricultural cultivation category’. Under the current Land Registry Act, zártkert is a special unit within an outlying area. The registered cultivation category – such as vineyard, garden, arable land, grassland or ‘land withdrawn from cultivation’ – is a separate issue, and the zoning classification under the local building regulations (HÉSZ) is separate again. These three layers together determine the legal framework for acquisition, use and development. Since 2025, where authorised by a municipal decree, it is possible to apply for a property recorded as zártkert in the land register to have its cultivation category registered as ‘land withdrawn from cultivation’; however, this does not automatically make the property an inner-area property or make it developable.

This may also interest you: Water-law permit in Hungary: 3 hidden traps only insiders discover

What you see and what the law sees: what the listing does not show

In practice, this means the following. An attractive, perhaps partly renovated holiday home, hillside house or winery building may be advertised as a ‘family home’ or ‘vineyard estate’. From the photographs, the buyer imagines a residential or holiday property. The land registry title sheet, however, may record the land as ‘vineyard’ or ‘garden’, with zártkert or outlying-area status. Physical reality alone does not override the land-registry and building-law status of the property. The possibility of registering a permanent address, the lawful use classification of the building and its suitability for habitual residence must be examined separately: zártkert status in itself means neither that the building has residential use nor that address registration is automatically prohibited. It may also be the case that the existing building is not properly shown on the cadastral map or that its legality under building law has not been regularised.

The three most common traps

The first, and most common, trap is an unresolved building status. On zártkert land it is common for the building actually standing on the plot, the cadastral map and the building-authority records not to match. Depending on when and how the building was constructed, the relevant document may be a building permit, a simple notification, an occupancy document, a retention permit or another official instrument. If the building’s legality cannot be demonstrated, administrative proceedings may be initiated and, depending on the circumstances, compliance measures, alterations or even demolition may be required.

The second trap is the illusion of reclassification. The legal status of a zártkert property consists of several distinct layers. Changing the zoning classification under HÉSZ is a municipal planning procedure: the municipal council decides by decree, and the procedure is governed by the current planning and consultation rules. The cultivation category is a separate matter. If the property is registered in an agricultural cultivation category, withdrawal from cultivation is generally a matter of agricultural land-protection law; however, since 26 June 2025, Section 72/E of the Land Registry Act has provided a separate route under which, where authorised by a municipal decree, the cultivation category of a zártkert property may be registered as ‘land withdrawn from cultivation’. This registration does not automatically rezone the land, bring it into the inner area, or confer development rights. Before purchase, the registered location status, cultivation category and HÉSZ zoning classification must therefore be checked separately.

The third trap is the restriction imposed by agricultural land-transfer rules. If a zártkert plot is recorded on the land registry title sheet as vineyard, garden, arable land, grassland or another agricultural or forestry cultivation category within the meaning of the Land Transaction Act and therefore qualifies as ‘land’ under that Act, the statutory land-acquisition rules apply. As a general rule, a foreign natural person who is not a ‘Member State national’ within the meaning of the Act may not acquire ownership of such land; a Member State national who is not registered as a farmer may generally acquire it only if the combined area of land already owned and the land to be acquired does not exceed one hectare, subject to the statutory exceptions. The classification depends on the land-registry data, not on whether there is actually a house on the plot or when cultivation ceased. If the local municipality has opened the route under Section 72/E of the Land Registry Act, registration as ‘land withdrawn from cultivation’ may be applied for in a separate procedure; until that registration is completed, the agricultural land-transfer status must be assessed on the basis of the existing land-register entry.

Five checks to carry out before buying a zártkert property

Due diligence is not complicated, but failing to do it can have serious consequences. There are five checks every buyer should have carried out before purchasing a zártkert property.

First: obtain the complete certified land registry title sheet – not merely an uncertified extract attached to a property listing. Part I contains identifying and descriptive data on the property, including, among other things, its registered location, area, cultivation category or ‘withdrawn from cultivation’ designation, and may include the building’s principal use classification; Part II contains ownership data; Part III records rights and facts affecting or encumbering the property. Importantly, the zoning classification under HÉSZ is not an item recorded in Part I of the title sheet; it must be checked separately in the local building regulations and the municipal plan.

Second: review the local building regulations (HÉSZ) and the municipal plan, including the regulatory plan where applicable. These documents establish the permitted development intensity, the uses that may be placed on the plot, other local building conditions and whether there is any realistic prospect of a later change to the planning classification.

Third: verify the building’s land-registry and building-law status. If a building stands on the plot, check whether it is correctly shown in the state land-registry cadastral database and, depending on when and how it was built, which permit, simple notification, occupancy, retention or other official document establishes its legality. The documents required vary from case to case; mere physical existence or the description used in an  does not prove that the building is lawful.

Fourth: check the cultivation category recorded in the land register and whether the Land Transaction Act applies. The buyer’s status as a Member State national, any registered farmer status, the area of land already owned and any statutory exceptions must be considered to determine whether the acquisition is possible at all and which pre-emption, authority-approval or other procedural rules apply.

Fifth: investigate the municipality under Act XLVIII of 2025. The Act authorises a municipality to introduce local protective measures by decree – for example, a right of pre-emption, a prohibition on or conditions for establishing residence, or a ‘settlement contribution’ requirement (betelepülési hozzájárulás). These measures do not automatically apply in every municipality, and statutory exemptions also exist, so the municipality’s current decree and the buyer’s personal circumstances should be checked before any deposit is paid. For zártkert land, the agricultural land-transfer rules and local identity-protection rules may need to be examined together.

What can be resolved – and what cannot

Not every zártkert property is a dead end. A viable solution may exist, for example, where the building’s legality and cadastral representation are in order; the use permitted by HÉSZ matches the buyer’s intended use; the municipality has enabled registration as ‘land withdrawn from cultivation’ under Section 72/E of the Land Registry Act and the applicable conditions can be met; or the buyer intends to use the property for agricultural purposes and meets the acquisition requirements under the Land Transaction Act. The simplified ‘withdrawn from cultivation’ registration, however, does not by itself cure building-law defects, change the HÉSZ zoning classification or bring the property into the inner area. Where neither lawful building status, intended use nor a legally available route to acquiring agricultural land can be regularised, a spectacular view and an old wine cellar cannot make up for the missing legal foundations.

The lesson every buyer should know

Hungary’s premium rural property market is genuinely attractive. But so is the risk assumed by a buyer who postpones due diligence until after paying a deposit. When purchasing a zártkert property, the land registry title sheet, HÉSZ zoning classification, state cadastral map and the building’s legal status under building law must all be consistent with the intended use. Compared with a simpler urban apartment purchase, the key difference is that agricultural land-transfer, agricultural land-protection, municipal planning and, in some cases, local identity-protection rules must all be considered together. An attractive zártkert holiday home is worth exactly what the legal foundations behind it allow – no more.

Legislation referred to

This article is intended as general market and legal information and does not constitute individual legal advice. The legislative references were checked against the law in force on 20 August 2026. Before any specific transaction, the current legal position of the property, the buyer and the applicable local regulations should be reviewed by a Hungarian lawyer.

World.title: From Torgyán’s ‘pest control’ to Toroczkai’s ‘worm’: The dehumanising language of Hungarian politics
World.content:
Many may not remember it, but Hungarian politicians were already fond of calling their opponents “worms” some 30 years before László Toroczkai’s latest infamous remark.

In Hungarian political discourse, it sometimes feels as though the same pattern keeps repeating itself. An opponent is no longer simply wrong, dishonest or misguided. Instead, they become a parasite, a rat, a bedbug, a stray dog — or, in the latest case, a worm.

In the most recent controversy, Toroczkai told Péter Magyar in Parliament not to “run away like a disgusting, cowardly worm”. But anyone who thinks Hungary has never seen anything like this before would be seriously mistaken.

Torgyán and the ‘pest control’

If there is one classic example in the history of Hungarian political insults, it is József Torgyán’s speech of 14 March 1996. The then leader of the Independent Smallholders’ Party was speaking at a rally held on the eve of the 15 March national holiday, attacking the government of Prime Minister Gyula Horn. Torgyán spoke of “pseudo-liberal, disgusting worms” and “vultures” that, in his view, had overrun the country.

The speech became so closely associated with Torgyán that it was later simply referred to as his “pest-control speech”. Even at the time, the reaction was divided. Some thought he had finally said out loud what others were afraid to say. For many others, however, the language was simply too much.

Either way, the recipe was already there three decades ago: turn a political opponent into a biological pest, and a political argument can quickly become a question of getting rid of the pest rather than defeating an opponent in debate.

Stray dogs, rats and bedbugs

The language of political name-calling did not disappear with the 1990s. During the 2006 election campaign, then Prime Minister Ferenc Gyurcsány also caused controversy with an animal comparison. In a speech in Veszprém, he said that stray dogs had to be caught and taken to a shelter. The opposition interpreted the remark as a comparison between stray animals and those who stood against his government.

Then, in 2019, came the infamous “rat” comment. During an interview on ATV, Socialist MP Ildikó Bangóné Borbély was asked why support for Fidesz was growing. Her answer was blunt: “There are many rats in Hungary.” The remark caused a nationwide political storm. Fidesz called for her resignation, and the comment quickly became one of the most notorious examples of animal-based political rhetoric in recent Hungarian politics.

Six years later, the rhetoric took another turn. On 15 March 2025, Viktor Orbán spoke of “bedbugs having survived the winter” and promised a “spring clean-up”. Many interpreted the reference to “bedbugs” as an attack on Péter Magyar, who had by then emerged as the government’s most prominent political challenger and had secretly recorded conversations involving his former wife. The words had changed, but the pattern had not.

And now there is the worm — again

In 2026, László Toroczkai added another chapter to the story. During a heated exchange in Parliament between Toroczkai and Péter Magyar, the Prime Minister accused the opposition leader of intervening at ministries on behalf of family-owned companies.

Toroczkai demanded evidence or an apology from Magyar, telling him not to run away “like a cowardly, disgusting worm”. And so the list continues.

With Torgyán, there was “pest control”. With Gyurcsány, there were stray dogs and a shelter. With Bangóné, there were rats. With Orbán, bedbugs had survived the winter and were waiting for a spring clean-up. And now, once again, there is the worm.

When political opponents become pests

Of course, political language has always been colourful. Politicians insult one another. Election campaigns are built around attacks. Sarcasm, mockery and deliberately provocative language are hardly new. The problem begins when political opponents are no longer treated as people with whom one disagrees, but as pests that need to be removed.

There is an important distinction here. Calling someone incompetent, dishonest or hypocritical may be unpleasant, but it still treats them as a political actor. Describing an opponent as a rat, bedbug or worm changes the nature of the argument. The suggestion is no longer simply that the other person is wrong or even harmful. It is that they themselves are something undesirable that needs to be eliminated.

That is a dangerous direction for political discourse. Hungary is hardly unique in this respect. Politicians and political movements around the world have used animal imagery to portray their opponents as dirty, dangerous or somehow less than human. Such language is powerful precisely because it reduces complicated political conflicts to something instinctive: get rid of the pest.

A long list of insults

The examples above are only the most memorable ones. Hungarian political discourse has produced countless other insults over the decades — some aimed at a person’s intelligence, others at their appearance, masculinity, femininity, morality or character.

Not all of these expressions are equally serious, of course. Politics without sharp disagreement would hardly be politics at all. But there is a difference between attacking an idea and attacking the person expressing it. And there is an even greater difference between insulting a political opponent and describing them as something that needs to be exterminated.

That distinction seems to be getting increasingly blurred. Perhaps that is the real lesson of the latest controversy. Political opponents will continue to disagree. Governments will continue to face criticism. Parliamentary debates will inevitably become heated, particularly in a country where political divisions have become so deep.

But there should still be a line. Because once political opponents become rats, bedbugs, stray dogs or worms, the argument is no longer simply about who is right. And perhaps that is precisely where the line should be drawn.

Interested in reading more about Hungarian politics? In this article, we look at the possibility of a potential merger between Fidesz and Mi Hazánk.

World.title: “Debt slavery is coming”: Viktor Orbán sounds alarms and attacks Tisza government
World.content:
Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán has returned to the political spotlight after several weeks away on holiday, launching a sharp attack on the Tisza government over fuel prices, the budget deficit and rising public debt.

“This was not a day for the Hungarians…”

Orbán summarised his criticism in a short Facebook post, warning that “debt slavery” could once again be on the horizon.

“Fuel prices are sky-high! The budget deficit has run wild! Debt slavery is on the horizon again! This was not a day for the Hungarians…”

As Index writes, the former prime minister had spent several weeks on holiday, first in Serbia and later in Croatia.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Fidesz attacks government’s economic record

Orbán’s remarks came alongside criticism from the Fidesz parliamentary group, which accused the Tisza government of delivering a poor economic performance since taking office. According to Fidesz, Hungarian families are currently facing the highest fuel prices seen so far this year, placing additional pressure on household budgets.

The parliamentary group also pointed to what it described as a rapidly worsening budget deficit and growing public debt, arguing that the combination of higher fuel costs and deteriorating fiscal indicators represents a serious burden for the population.

Stay up-to-date: Russian senator claims Hungary was forced to “prove its loyalty” to Brussels

Warning over public debt

Fidesz claimed that the government’s economic management had been characterised by a series of negative records, with both household costs and key macroeconomic indicators moving in an unfavourable direction. The opposition party argued that rising public debt and a larger state budget deficit could threaten Hungary’s economic stability over the longer term.

Orbán’s brief intervention echoed those concerns, framing the economic situation as a return to the threat of “debt slavery” — a phrase frequently used in Hungarian political discourse to describe excessive public indebtedness and dependence on external financing.

The former prime minister did not provide further details or figures in his post, instead delivering a concise political message focused on the three issues he presented as the main economic problems facing Hungarians: fuel prices, the budget deficit and public debt.

World.title: Russian Embassy says Hungary’s pledge of dialogue ‘worth nothing’ after expulsion of 10 diplomats
World.content:
Russia has sharply condemned Hungary’s decision to expel 10 employees of the Russian Embassy in Budapest, describing the move as an unprecedented and unjustified escalation and warning that it would trigger a response.

Moscow accuses Hungary of anti-Russian rhetoric

The criticism came after Foreign Minister Anita Orbán announced on Tuesday that Hungary had ordered 10 members of the Russian diplomatic mission to leave the country because, according to the Hungarian authorities, they had engaged in activities incompatible with diplomatic status under the Vienna Convention.

Russian Ambassador to Hungary Evgeny Stanislavov said in a statement published by the embassy in Budapest that the expulsions showed the new Hungarian government had fallen “captive to ideologically motivated, anti-Russian rhetoric”. He also dismissed Budapest’s assurances that it wanted to preserve dialogue and continue pragmatic cooperation with Moscow.

According to the ambassador, statements by the Hungarian side about maintaining channels of communication with the Kremlin and continuing practical cooperation were now “worth nothing” in light of the decision. Moscow views the move as an “extremely unfriendly step” and an “unprecedented and unjustified escalation”, Stanislavov said, adding that it would receive an appropriate response.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Hungary insists diplomatic relations will continue

Anita Orbán stressed when announcing the expulsions that the measure does not mean Hungary is breaking off diplomatic relations with Moscow. Budapest still intends to maintain the necessary dialogue with them, she said, based on mutual respect and compliance with international rules. The Hungarian government has said the decision was taken to protect the country’s security and sovereignty, while Russian MP’s claim it was only to pledge loyalty to Brussels.

András Rácz, deputy director-general of the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, said that, according to the conventions of diplomatic language, the foreign minister’s statement strongly suggested that the 10 expelled Russian representatives had been working under diplomatic cover while allegedly carrying out intelligence activities.

The Kremlin has already signalled that retaliatory measures could follow. A spokesperson for the Russian Foreign Ministry reportedly promised a “tough and painful” response. Aleksey Chepa, deputy chairman of the State Duma’s International Affairs Committee, told Russian state news agency TASS that Moscow would first respond in kind. He also warned that Hungary’s decision could lead to a reduction in joint economic projects with Moscow.

Stay up-to-date: POLITICO claims Paks II could be delayed until 2035 as Rosatom schedule reveals setback

Opposition parties attack the government’s decision

Hungary’s opposition parties Fidesz and KDNP have also criticised the expulsions, although for different reasons. Fidesz described the move as “nothing more than a distraction”, arguing that the government should instead address issues including the budget deficit, public debt and fuel prices.

The KDNP warned that the decision and the Russian response it may provoke could have “unforeseeable consequences”. The party argued that Russia remained difficult to replace as a source of natural gas and crude oil imports, warning that a hasty diplomatic step could ultimately affect Hungarian households through higher energy bills.

While stressing that every government has a duty to protect national security and sovereignty, the KDNP said the move marked the abandonment of Hungary’s previous “peace policy” and the beginning of a dismantling of the country’s pragmatic relationships outside Europe.

The diplomatic dispute now appears set to deepen, with Moscow promising retaliation while Budapest maintains that it wants to keep communication channels open despite the unprecedented expulsion of 10 Russian embassy employees.

World.title: Danube falls to historic low water levels in Budapest: just 1 centimetre
World.content:
The Danube has fallen to a historic low in Budapest, with water-level gauges showing just 1 centimetre on Tuesday, according to Időkép.

The Danube’s water level is at its lowest ever in Budapest

The reading is significantly lower than the levels recorded during the severe drought conditions earlier in the summer. In July, the Danube had already broken the previous negative record set in 2018, when the water authority measured a level of 27 centimetres at the end of the month, reports Időkép.

The river continued to recede throughout August, falling by almost another 20 centimetres. By Tuesday, the water level had dropped to just 1 centimetre. The exceptionally low level is creating serious difficulties for river navigation and can also pose a direct safety risk to vessels, as obstacles normally hidden beneath the surface become exposed or much easier to encounter.

Some of the consequences of the unusually low water level have already become visible elsewhere along the Danube. Near Baja, a shipwreck emerged from the riverbed to such an extent that it could reportedly be walked around. In Budapest, the remains of the former Ferenc József Bridge, which sank near what is now the Liberty Bridge, also became clearly visible.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

There might be light at the end of the tunnel

Water management experts attribute the extreme conditions to prolonged rainfall shortages and exceptionally dry conditions across the Danube’s catchment area. There could, however, be some relief in sight. A weather front is expected to bring rain to the Danube basin on Wednesday and reach Hungary by the evening. The rainfall could lead to a rise in the river’s water level.

The record low water levels show how Hungary, and all of Europe has become the victim of the all-summer-long dry conditions, with consequences extending beyond the river itself to navigation and water safety.

World.title: Remarkable: Remains of Ice Age animal found in Hungary’s River Tisza
World.content:
An extraordinary prehistoric discovery has been made in River Tisza, in Hungary, where water management workers found what is believed to be the skull of a cave bear that lived during the Ice Age.

Workers first thought they found an old anchor

Staff from the Middle Tisza District Water Directorate (Kötivizig) spotted the object while kayaking between Szolnok and Kisköre. Initially, they thought the object protruding from the riverbed might be an old anchor.

A closer inspection, however, revealed the remains of a large animal. Around three-quarters of the find was buried in the gravel bed, from which the workers were able to recover it thanks to the Tisza’s low water level.

The remains were taken to the Damjanich János Museum in Szolnok, where experts conducted an initial examination. Their preliminary assessment is that the find is probably the skull of an Ice Age cave bear.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

What to know about cave bears?

Cave bears (Ursus spelaeus) lived across much of Europe during the Pleistocene and became extinct thousands of years ago. Their remains are often associated with caves, where the animals sought shelter and hibernated.

The exact age of the newly discovered skull has yet to be established. Museum specialists will carry out further examinations to determine when the animal lived. The discovery demonstrates how falling water levels can expose objects and remains that have been hidden beneath river sediments for centuries or even millennia.

This is how cave bears used to looked like. Illustration. Photo: Sergiodlarosa/Wikimedia Commons

World.title: Serbia, Bosnian Serbs Slate Sarajevo’s Expulsion of Diplomats over Mladic
World.content:
The Serbian embassy in Sarajevo. Photo: Serbian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Serbia’s Foreign Ministry on Tuesday condemned the expulsion of two of its diplomats from Bosnia and Herzegovina as “yet another unconstructive move” that serves neither good-neighbourly relations, regional stability, nor the easing of political tensions.

It said Bosnia’s Foreign Minister, Elmedin Konakovic, “continues to resort to escalation and uses extremely difficult and painful issues from our shared past as an instrument of day-to-day politics and an election campaign”, adding that “such issues require responsibility and serious dialogue, rather than political instrumentalisation and unilateral moves that further deepen divisions.”

The ministry said Serbia will “examine all legal and political aspects of the announced decisions, including the issue of jurisdiction and the procedures for adopting them,” as well as their consequences for diplomatic relations.

On Tuesday, Konakovic announced the expulsion of two members of the Serbian embassy in Sarajevo after Serbia hosted the funeral with military honours of the convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic in Belgrade.

Konakovic said Serbian military attache Milan Dulanovic and Danko Maksimovic, an adviser to Serbia’s BIA intelligence service, were personae non grata and had 48 hours to leave Bosnia.

Officials in Bosnia’s mainly Serb Republika Srpska entity, also condemned the move and challenged its legality.

Republika Srpska Justice Minister Goran Selak insisted such foreign policy decisions fall under the authority of Bosnia’s tripartite state presidency, while the Foreign Ministry merely carries out adopted policy – which he said Konakovic “would have to know” before making moves that are “unconstitutional and illegal.”

He said the expulsion order “can hardly even be called a decision,” since such a decision must have grounding in the constitution and law. “This looks more like a pre-election pamphlet than a serious act of an institution,” Selak said, referring to upcoming national elections next month.

Selak said Konakovic has the right to his opinions, “including personal antipathy toward Serbia”, but not to present them as the country’s position or speak for Republika Srpska, adding that “Serbia is Republika Srpska’s most important partner”.

The Serb member of Bosnia’s three-member state presidency, Zeljka Cvijanovic, said Konakovic “cannot determine what Bosnia and Herzegovina is, or dictate to Serbia”. She claimed one of the two embassy staff had already left Bosnia after his mandate expired.

Konakovic based the decision on a 2004 rulebook of the state presidency, Under it, only the presidency can expel heads of diplomatic missions but the foreign minister can expel other embassy staff for cases including interference in internal affairs, espionage, or insulting statements.

World.title: Ex-Yugoslavia’s Queer Literary Heroes Tell Tales to Inspire
World.content:
After the Belgrade Pride march last weekend, Pride season in the former Yugoslavia – stretching from June to September – has drawn to a close. Whistles, rainbow flags and glitter (the queer community has a microplastics problem that we really need to discuss) are being stored away for the next time.

The intensified vitriol directed at those who believe their non-normative genders and sexualities are worth celebrating begins to wane. Familiar polemics within the LGBTQ+ community, however, continue: we keep asking ourselves, and those marching alongside us, whether Pride parades – organised by professional NGOs in coordination with the state and the police – are still worth showing up for.

As the season ends, and that question remains open, let’s keep Pride going through a Yugo Queer reading list.

World.title: ‘Disposable’ IP Firms in Serbia, Montenegro Obscure Origins of Russian Cyber Meddling
World.content:
Between late 2022 and February 2024, Azarov’s eServer said it was managing two IP ranges that subsequently came under the control of Stark Industries Solutions.

Following the EU sanctions, Stark Industries Solutions rebranded as PQ Hosting and transferred its IP resources under the umbrella of Dutch WorkTitans.

In May this year, Dutch police arrested the owners of WorkTitans and MIRhosting on suspicion of aiding Stark Industries Solution in circumventing sanctions.

Archived routing data show that at the end of 2024, Azarov was an upstream provider for PQ Hosting, i.e. the rebranded Stark Industries Solutions.

BIRN identified at least eight IP ranges that WorkTitans listed as being located in or used from Serbia and Belgrade, with Serbian Open Exchange, an internet traffic exchange point, serving as the internet gateway for all the ranges. These include two previously advertised by eServer.

Azarov said his company “had no direct business relations with Stark Industries”.

“Subnets roam between some providers and if we get request from any of our clients to announce network we just do so – that’s our part of hosting business,” he said in a response to BIRN, written in English.

“And you say it later came under control of Stark – then maybe they acquired it somehow.”

BIRN also identified three other IP ranges that have, over the past several years, moved between eServer, Stark Industries Solutions and Aeza Group.

An analysis of the RIPE NCC database shows that numerous IP ranges previously controlled by Azarov have since passed to two providers previously linked to the Russian bulletproof ecosystem and infrastructure used in cyberattacks: Cypriot-registered IT-Hostline and Russia-based Fortis.

IT-Hostline was previously a partner of Stark Industries Solutions and now provides infrastructure to Aeza Group, according to France-based cybersecurity firm Intrinsec, while Fortis’s infrastructure was used by FIN7 hacking group, responsible for mass financial theft and corporate extortion, Insikt Group reported last year.

Former eServer ranges are also now advertised by Global Connectivity Solutions and Global Internet Solutions, both linked to Aeza Group, Insikt Group said, and identified a number of ransomware groups that it said had used their infrastructure.

According to RIPE NCC data, among the current users of IP ranges previously held by eServer are: Russian provider Rost, whose infrastructure was also reportedly used in the Doppelganger campaign; Russian Timeweb, where researchers this year found more than 300 active C2 servers – systems used to send instructions to malware-infected devices and steal data; and US-based Baxet Group, whose infrastructure has been linked to cyberattacks by Russia’s military intelligence service, GRU, as reported by Arctic Wolf Networks, an American cybersecurity company, in November 2025.

Today, Azarov advertises an IP range belonging to Neterra Ltd, a Bulgarian provider previously used by the hacking-for-hire and corporate espionage group DeathStalker and whose infrastructure was also partly used to distribute Pegasus spyware, according to Amnesty International.

Azarov, however, insisted his eServer “has a strict anti cybercrime policy on all of our locations”.

“By targeting on B2B and B2C markets we always monitor our networks and try to keep environment safe and trustworthy,” he wrote to BIRN.

“You can see that our networks are not in SBL and other lists and if some IPs get into it we act immediately. So as I told you we did not work directly with Stark Industries but even if their networks were announced by some of our clients, they were applied the same strict rules and filters so I don’t think there was any malicious activity.”

Typically in cybercrime, when one network is shut down or sanctioned, attackers simply transfer IP addresses and other internet resources to linked providers and continue their operations. This is how sanctioned companies Aeza and Stark Industries have continued to operate.

“Today, it is no longer a single server, but an entire dynamic infrastructure that is constantly changing,” Radunovic told BIRN. “That makes it difficult to track because it operates across multiple jurisdictions and legal procedures, so investigators, alongside technical traces, also follow money flows, cryptocurrencies and other connections.”

World.title: Ratko Mladic’s Lavish Funeral was an Indictment of Serbia’s Govt: Experts
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Criticism has echoed across Europe over the high-profile funeral of Ratko Mladic on Monday in Belgrade, raising questions about the potential repercussions for Serbia of giving a convicted war criminal a hero’s farewell.

His funeral with military honours was attended by senior officials of Serbia and Bosnia’s mainly Serb entity, Republika Srpska.

Ministers from the Serbian government included Defence Minister Bratislav Gasic, Justice Minister Nenad Vujic and Culture Minister Nikola Selakovic.

World.title: Montenegro Prosecutors Open Case Against Bishop for Praising Mladic
World.content:
Montenegro’s Higher State Prosecutor’s Office in Podgorica has opened a case against a Serbian Orthodox Bishop after he praised the late convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic during a religious service, the Vijesti newspaper reported on Tuesday.

The prosecutor’s office told the newspaper that the bishop was suspected of inciting national, racial and religious hatred. It did not provide further details about the investigation or say whether Bishop Metodije of Budimlje-Niksic Diocese had been questioned.

The bishop praised Mladic during a service at the Piva Monastery in northern Montenegro on August 28, the day after he died, saying people had recognised in Mladic “all those wonderful and holy qualities of Serbian warriors and knights.

“May the most holy Mother of God … raise his soul among all the holy Serbian knights, the famous general Ratko,” Metodije said, according to a recording and transcript published by local media.

The diocese later published a statement on its website saying that, after the liturgy, a memorial service had been held for “the newly departed servant of God, General Ratko Mladic”.

At the same time, Montenegro’s Higher State Prosecutor’s Office in Bijelo Polje has dismissed criminal complaints against Metodije over speeches praising a notorious World War II-era Nazi-alligned commander, Pavle Djurisic, held responsible for mass killings during the war, Vijesti reported on Tuesday.

Mladic, who died on August 27, while serving a life sentence at the UN detention facility in the Hague, commanded Bosnian Serb forces during the 1992-95 war in Bosnia. He was convicted of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes by a United Nations tribunal and sentenced to life imprisonment.

The tribunal found him responsible for various crimes including the 1995 massacre of more than 8,000 Bosniaks in Srebrenica – Europe’s worst atrocity since World War II, and the prolonged siege of Sarajevo.

Mladic remains a hero to many Serbs, while victims’ families and survivors regard him as responsible for some of the 1992-95 Bosnian war’s gravest crimes.

Montenegro, a NATO member and candidate for European Union membership, has laws criminalising the incitement of ethnic, racial and religious hatred.

World.title: Turkey’s Ruling Party Seizes Back Control of Important Mayoralty
World.content:
Dundar Ziya Gultekin, candidate of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party, AKP, was elected as acting Mayor of Uskudar on Tuesday, defeating Sibel Tan Cetinkaya, the joint candidate of the opposition Republican People’s Party, CHP, and the New Party.

The vote in Uskudar followed the arrest and removal from office of the elected CHP mayor, Sinem Dedetas, in July on alleged corruption charges. Gultekin will serve as acting mayor, as he was elected by the municipal council rather than by popular vote.

The result came after a dramatic shift in the council’s balance. Four councillors elected for the main opposition CHP defected to the AKP days before the vote, while two CHP councillors were detained and so unable to vote.

This left the rival blocs with 21 councillors each. Yet, Gultekin received 23 votes in the secret ballot, indicating that two councillors from the CHP-New Party bloc also backed the AKP candidate. Their identities remain unknown.

“They told people elected from our lists: ‘Either join the AKP or go to prison, either wear the party badge or wear handcuffs,’” Ozgur Celik, Istanbul Provincial Chair of the New Party said after the vote, alleging that some councillors defected because they feared arrest.

The New Party, which cooperated with the CHP in the Uskudar vote, was established earlier this year by Ozgur Ozel and other politicians who broke away from the CHP after a controversial court ruling annulled the 2023 party congress over alleged irregularities, removing Ozel as leader and reinstating his predecessor, Kemal Kilicdaroglu.

Uskudar is a traditional conservative stronghold and was ruled by the AKP and other conservative and Islamist parties for decades. However, the AKP lost the district and major cities and towns in the 2024 local elections.

Uskudar is located on the Asian side of Istanbul and is home to more than half a million people.

Cetinkaya initially won a mayoral election in August, but a court ordered a rerun following an AKP challenge.

Over the last year, dozens of CHP mayors and hundreds of party members have been arrested on corruption and terror charges. Those include the arrest of Istanbul’s Mayor and opposition presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu on March 19, 2025. The prosecutor’s office is demanding a 2,352-year prison sentence for him. Imamoglu denies all the accusations.

Opposition politicians, rights groups and international organisations have said that the government is using the judiciary to crush political rivals in what they describe as an unprecedented crackdown.

World.title: Kosovo Parliament to Reconvene, ‘Chaos’ Looms over Election of President
World.content:
Kosovo’s new parliament reconvenes for its inaugural session on Wednesday, despite continued uncertainty over whether lawmakers will agree on the election of a head-of-state.

The session started on August 6, following elections in June, but was paused after the victorious Vetevendosje party asked for “more time” for negotiations with other parties on the candidate for Kosovo’s next president.

At the end of the month, Vetevendosje leader Albin Kurti and his counterpart from the opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, Lumir Abdixhiku announced that their parties would both back Judge Bekim Sejdiu as president, only for a third of the LDK’s MPs to cry foul.

Such is the depth of animosity between Vetevendosje and its rivals, constituting parliament and electing a president has become a major challenge, complicated by a rift within the LDK over Abdixhiku’s leadership.

World.title: Croatia: Glorifying Ratko Mladić is Contrary to EU Values – Suspend Serbia Talks
World.content:
September the 9th, 2026 – Through various political figures, Croatia has sent out the clear message that glorifying Ratko Mladić is contrary to EU values and that all talks with Serbia must be suspended.

Croatian politician Tonino Picula has warned that glorifying Ratko Mladić or relativising his crimes is “contrary to the values on which the European Union is founded.” “The burial of Ratko Mladić cannot be viewed solely as a private event because the participation of representatives of state institutions, members of the army and members of the authorities sends a clear political message.

Index reports that the disgraced war criminal Ratko Mladić was finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, crimes against humanity and war crimes. “Any glorification of him or relativisation of his crimes is directly contrary to the values on which the European Union is founded,” Picula stated.

serbia must confront its past

“Serbia’s desired EU path is not only a matter of opening negotiating chapters and fulfilling technical criteria, but above all a question of political choice and acceptance of European values. Serbia cannot at the same time claim that membership in the European Union is its strategic goal while tolerating or institutionally accompanying the glorification of people convicted of the most serious war crimes.

The European Union must not relativise such an event. The authorities in Belgrade must be required to make a clear break with the policy of historical revisionism and an unambiguous attitude towards the judgments of international courts. The European perspective also implies the ability of society and the state to confront the past, rather than glorify its darkest protagonists. Serbia chooses its own path, but the credibility of its European path will also depend on whether it is prepared to accept the truth about the crimes committed and stop glorifying their perpetrators,” Picula added.

a convicted war criminal for the world is apparently a man deserving of the highest honours in serbia

The former commander of the Bosnian Serb army, Ratko Mladić, who was finally sentenced to life imprisonment for the genocide in Srebrenica in July 1995, for the persecution and forced displacement of Bosniaks and Croats throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, sniper activity, shelling and terrorising of civilians during the siege of Sarajevo, and for taking members of UN peacekeeping forces hostage in retaliation for NATO bombings in 1995, died on 27 August in the prison hospital of the Hague Tribunal.

He was buried yesterday in the family tomb at Topčider Cemetery with church rites and military honours. Among the thousands of people in the procession and funeral cortège were individual ministers of the Serbian government and officials of Republika Srpska, while the service in the church was led by Patriarch Porfirije with bishops of the Serbian Orthodox Church.

World.title: Croatia Imports 870,000 Tonnes of Waste Each Year, But Why?
World.content:
September the 9th, 2026 – The hazardous waste scandal that has taken Lika and Croatia by storm shows no sign of dying down, but few realise Croatia actually imports 870,000 tonnes of waste each year. The question is: Why?

If Croatia has truly become Europe’s dumping ground, the 2024 statistics don’t really show it: about 90,000 more tonnes of waste actually left the country than entered it. However, that isn’t enough proof that there are no problems to speak of. The same system in which a Croatian factory legally imports scrap iron, paper or waste wood as raw material can be abused so that hazardous waste ends up buried in Lika.

Slobodan Mufic reports for Index that according to data from the Ministry of Environmental Protection and Green Transition, after Croatia’s entry into the European Union back in July 2013, an increase in waste imports was recorded, but exports also continuously grew. Since 2015, waste imports have only twice exceeded exports on an annual basis, and then by roughly five percent. As such, back in 2024, the last year for which official data exists, Croatia imported 871,255 tonnes of waste, of which about 7,100 tonnes of hazardous waste with prior approval. Five Croatian companies carried out the import of hazardous waste in 2024: C.I.A.K., Holcim, NEXE, Premifab and Spectra-Media. The largest part of the imported non-hazardous waste, more than half, consists of metal, paper, cardboard and wood that domestic companies process and use as secondary raw material in production.

During the same year, 961,442 tonnes of waste were exported from Croatia, of which hazardous waste accounted for 26,851 tonnes, or 2.8 percent of the total quantity. All exported hazardous waste ended up in other European Union member states, mostly in Austria, Germany, Poland and Hungary.

it isn’t possible for croatia to entirely ban waste imports

It should be emphasised that Croatia cannot simply ban the import of all types of waste from other EU member states, nor would that be good for Croatian industry. Cross-border waste shipments within the EU are regulated by European rules. Waste is considered goods and no EU Member State can prevent (by way of a general ban) what European Union regulations currently allow. As of the 21st of May 2026, the new EU Regulation 2024/1157 on waste shipments applies, which introduces different cross-border regimes depending on the type of waste and whether the waste is destined for disposal or recovery (reuse of waste as raw material or energy source). For waste intended for disposal, shipments are in principle prohibited, unless the competent authorities give consent. For waste going for recovery there is a prior consent procedure, depending on the degree of toxicity.

Recovery means that the waste is directed to some useful purpose such as recycling, composting or incineration and thereby replaces material or energy that would otherwise have to be obtained from other sources. Disposal means finally removing the waste at a landfill, storage facility or incinerator without energy recovery. Croatia, however, does not have to accept every waste that someone wants to send it. The law already prohibits some categories, for example the delivery of hazardous waste and mixed municipal waste for disposal, and gives the minister the possibility to additionally restrict certain flows if they endanger the domestic waste management system or public health.

why does croatia even need imported waste?

A ban on waste imports would also be harmful to Croatian industry. Existing energy recovery facilities alone have permitted capacities of almost 400,000 tonnes per year, and the largest consumers are cement plants. Našice’s NEXE energy-recovered 58,000 tonnes of waste in 2023 alone, Holcim in Koromačno today consumes tens of thousands of tonnes and plans to reach around 60,000 tonnes per year, while CEMEX in Kaštel Sućurac and Solin already obtains more than a third of the energy for cement from alternative fuels.

Cement plants do not need just any rubbish, but fuel from waste of precisely defined properties. Every shipment must meet quality and composition criteria, including calorific value and content of moisture, chlorine, sulphur and heavy metals, and facilities that incinerate waste are subject to special rules on combustion temperature, process monitoring and emission limit values.

In addition, low-quality or hazardous waste could damage the kilns. The estimate is that from the total municipal waste, of which Croatia collects around 1.9 million tonnes annually, only about 20 percent could become sufficiently high-quality fuel for existing facilities. This also explains the apparent paradox: Croatia can simultaneously have too much of its own waste and import the waste that industry needs. It does not matter to a factory where the scrap iron obtained waste status. What matters is how much it costs, what quality it is, whether it suits its process and whether it can obtain it in sufficient quantity.

the difference between legal trade and illegal disposal

That’s why the entire question of waste imports doesn’t really have a straightforward answer. The import of clean metal waste into a Croatian foundry and the illegal burial of hazardous waste are two completely different things. The first can reduce the consumption of primary raw materials and energy and represents a desirable part of the circular economy. The second is the opposite of the economy and constitutes a criminal offence. The grey area begins precisely between the word “recovery” on the document and what actually happened to the waste. A shipment can neatly and legally cross the border, arrive at a registered entity and still end up completely differently from what the documentation suggests. Exactly such an appearance of legality occurred in Gospić.

Regardless of the State Inspectorate’s data that from 2020 to 2025 the environmental protection inspection examined a total of 2,610 shipments and discovered as many as 1,611 illegal waste shipments, or almost 62 percent, the system was not entirely without supervision.

The problem was that supervision, permits and existing documentation did not ensure reliable tracking of the movement of waste to final treatment and did not prevent enormous quantities of waste from ending up where they should not have. Likewise, this does not mean that 62 percent of the total waste entering Croatia is illegal. Inspection controls are targeted, cover imports, exports and transit, and are also carried out subsequently at companies. An illegal shipment can refer to various offences, including incorrect classification or documentation. Not every such case is criminally similar to the current one in Gospić.

Europe and specifically Croatia are currently trying to close the space in which legitimate waste trade can turn into a cover for illegal disposal. New European rules strengthen digital tracking of cross-border shipments, and an important change is also coming in Croatia from tomorrow.

who took it first isn’t important, but who resolved it last is…

The Ordinance on amendments and supplements to the Ordinance on waste management was published on 31 August and enters into force tomorrow – 8 September. The waste recipient will have to provide the consignor with data on final treatment: the name and PIN of the final processor, their authorisation for treatment of the shipment, the date of completion of treatment and the final treatment procedure.

This goes straight to the heart of the problem exposed by the scandal in Gospić: it should no longer be enough to prove to whom the waste was handed over at the first step, but what happened to it at the last. But even the best electronic form will not help if the data are not checked, if capacities exist only on paper or if the inspection reacts only when tens of thousands of tonnes of hazardous waste are already underground. Tracking the movement of waste is not filing papers in a binder, but the state’s ability to determine for every disputed tonne where it ended up.
