World.title: Run or hide? Benguet school tests active-attack response without fake gunfire
World.content:
DRILL. Learners move out of a classroom under the supervision of a teacher during the “run” portion of the drill, used when a safe route away from the reported threat is available.

The drill was designed to test decisions, communication, police coordination, and recovery without using imitation weapons, simulated gunfire, or other hyper-realistic elements that could unnecessarily frighten learners

LA TRINIDAD, Benguet — No fake gunshots rang through the campus and no one played an armed attacker. Yet classrooms locked down, some learners moved to safety, others hid, and police teams swept through Benguet National High School on Wednesday, September 9.

The exercise was part of a nationwide school safety drill for active-attack incidents, with Benguet National High School serving as the Cordillera ceremonial venue. It was designed to test decisions, communication, police coordination, and recovery without using imitation weapons, simulated gunfire, or other hyper-realistic elements that could unnecessarily frighten learners.

Forty senior high school learners took part in the exercise. Schools Division Superintendent Carmel Meris said parents were informed beforehand and signed waivers allowing their children to participate. Learners were also oriented before the drill, while participating agencies conducted a series of preparations ahead of the exercise.

“Today, we are gathering not because we expect an emergency to happen, but because we believe in being prepared before it happens,” assistant school head Eugene Espiritu told participants.

The drill was originally scheduled for September 3, to coincide with the nationwide active shooting drill of the Department of Education (DepEd), but was moved because of weather-related class suspensions.

Different threat, different response

The first scenario involved a suspected armed threat outside the school perimeter.

Security personnel were expected to recognize the threat, secure gates and access points, alert school authorities and law enforcement, and place the campus under a lockout.

Under the drill plan, learners and personnel were to remain inside secured buildings while outdoor activities and unnecessary movement were stopped. Teachers were tasked to keep learners calm and together, monitor official communications, and wait for verified instructions.

Police responders then simulated containing the threat before an all-clear was issued.

A separate scenario began with the threat already inside the school. This time, the exercise demonstrated that there was no single response for everyone.

One classroom, located away from the reported direction of the threat, practiced a controlled run response using a pre-identified safe route. Another classroom, positioned closer to the danger, practiced hiding and remaining inside a secured room.

The drill plan stressed that running and hiding were not sequential steps. Different groups could take different protective actions at the same time depending on the location of the threat, available information, and whether a safe escape route existed.

Once a full lockdown was declared, teachers were expected to account for learners while police took over the law-enforcement response.

Personnel from the La Trinidad Municipal Police Station acted as first responders, with additional support from the Benguet 2nd Provincial Mobile Force Company. Tactical operations remained under police authority, with the school instructed not to direct or interfere with the police response.

The drill did not end at “all clear.”

The exercise also tested what should happen after the immediate threat had been contained.

Police had to confirm that the designated area was secure before the school could begin a controlled transition out of lockdown.

Teachers then rechecked attendance and reported whether all learners were accounted for. Movement from classrooms was controlled, with learners brought to a reunification area rather than simply dismissed.

SCHOOL DRILL. A teacher guides senior high school learners through the drill as they practice staying low, calm, and away from exposed areas during a simulated threat inside the school. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno

The drill plan also required verification before a learner could be released to a parent, guardian, or authorized representative.

Psychosocial first aid was built into the recovery phase for learners who might experience fear, anxiety, confusion, or emotional distress during the exercise. Participation in such support was voluntary, and learners were not required to recount or relive the simulated incident to receive assistance.

The school safety evaluation tool likewise required organizers to check whether the exercise was age-appropriate and trauma-informed and whether it avoided prohibited fear-inducing elements such as aggressor role-playing, imitation weapons, simulated casualties, and simulated gunfire.

Police spot gaps beyond the exercise

Police officials said preparedness should go beyond completing a drill and include identifying ordinary security weaknesses that could matter in a real emergency.

La Trinidad police chief Lieutenant Colonel Zacarias Dausen said schools should continue strengthening control of entry and exit points, improve inspection procedures, and review CCTV coverage for possible blind spots.

He also stressed the importance of coordination among schools, police, disaster response teams, and medical personnel.

That accountability aspect was built into the evaluation tool, which covered not only learner behavior but also the school’s contingency plan, safe areas, evacuation routes, emergency communications, coordination with police, accountability procedures, medical services, and post-incident recovery.

Meris said district and school officials who observed the exercise were expected to bring the lessons back to their own areas and replicate the preparedness measures.

The point of the exercise, officials said, was not to make schools feel like places under siege.

It was to make sure that in the unlikely event of a serious armed threat, learners, teachers, and responders would not be encountering the procedures for the first time. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: No Turkish police deployed to secure BARMM polls
World.content:
Election watchdog groups pointed out that Turkey was invited to send election observers, not police officers

Claim: Turkish police will guard the first parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) and arrest violators of election laws.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The Facebook page “Bagong Kapantay Moro” claimed in a September 6 post that Turkish police officers will be deployed to secure the upcoming BARMM parliamentary elections on September 14.

The post reads: “Turkiyé polis (sic) magbabantay sa kauna-unahang parliament election sa BARMM? Upang panatilihin na walang dayaan sa eleksyon. Huhuliin nila ang lalabag at mandaraya.”

(Turkish police will guard the first parliamentary elections in BARMM to prevent cheating. They will arrest violators and cheaters.)

The post also alleged that Turkey was intervening because most media organizations were supposedly “fake.” As of writing, the post has garnered around 2,000 reactions, 434 comments, and 853 shares.

Some commenters appeared to believe the claim. One thanked foreign countries for supposedly helping the United Bangsamoro Justice Party and the Bangsamoro.

The facts: Election watchdog groups Independent Election Monitoring Center – BARMM and the Institute for Autonomy and Governance debunked the claim in a September 8 Facebook post, and urged the public to verify claims about supposed foreign involvement in the elections.

“This is false. No foreign police force, including Türkiye’s, can be deployed to enforce, patrol, or police another country’s elections. Election security in BARMM remains the responsibility of [Commission on Election]-BARMM, the Armed Forces of the Philippines, and the Philippine National Police,” the post read.

The watchdog groups pointed out that the viral claim likely misrepresents a real appeal from Moro Islamic Liberation Front chairman Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim. Inquirer.net reported that Ebrahim, in an August 30 letter ahead of the September 14 polls, called on foreign governments and international organizations to send election observers.

The same report mentioned that Turkey was among the diplomatic missions invited to participate, but the invitation was for observers, not police officers. The invitation made no mention of granting foreign personnel the authority to make arrests or conduct security operations.

The Commission on Elections (Comelec) opened the BARMM election to local and international observers under Resolution No. 11247. Accredited observers may monitor different stages of the election, subject to Comelec’s rules. Observers must also remain impartial and free from political, economic, or other conflicts of interest.

As of writing, there are no public statements issued by the Turkish Embassy in Manila or Turkey’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs regarding the invitation.

Unrelated photo: A reverse image search using Google Images traces the photograph to o the Daily Sabah’s April 10 report on the Turkish Police Organization’s 181st anniversary, which says the photo is credited to Anadolu Ajansi (AA). Other AA photos of the same event can be found on Anadolu Images and Reuters.

The original caption places the police parade in Kayseri, Turkey, on April 10, 2026. The image does not show Turkish police officers preparing for deployment to secure the BARMM polls.

Securing the elections: The first-ever BARMM parliamentary elections will be held on September 14, marking a historic milestone in the region’s transition from the 2014 peace agreement between the Philippine government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) to a functioning parliamentary system. (LIVE UPDATES: First BARMM parliamentary elections)

The election also comes amid real security and turnout concerns. Monitoring groups have flagged a rise in gun-related incidents and voter uncertainty over the new parliamentary system, warning that these could affect turnout and public confidence in the polls.

To address security concerns, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. approved the deputation of Philippine law enforcement agencies through Memorandum Order No. 48. The government’s security plan for the elections includes nearly 9,000 Philippine National Police officers, five joint task forces deployed by the Armed Forces of the Philippines, and Philippine Coast Guard support.

Debunked: Rappler has previously debunked other false claims involving BARMM officials, as well as other disinformation about Philippine elections:

– James Bones/Rappler.com

James Bones is a Research and Data volunteer at Rappler. He is a fourth-year Bachelor of Science in Industrial Engineering student at the Polytechnic University of the Philippines – Manila.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: 2026 NDC: Philippines promises to reduce more carbon emissions on its own
World.content:
FLOOD. Residents of Barangay San Pedro Cutod, Pampanga, continue their daily lives while enduring floodwaters for nearly three weeks, caused by recent rains from the southwest monsoon, on September 7, 2026.

In its latest submission to the United Nations, the Philippines underscores its high vulnerability to climate impacts despite minimal contribution to the crisis

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines has recommitted to a 75% reduction in carbon emissions, 7% of which the country would undertake and fund on its own, while the remaining 68% target is conditional upon international support.

These are emissions from sectors such as energy, transport, and agriculture covering the period of 2025 to 2035.

“With all identified policies and measures, the Philippines is projected, based on current analysis, to be a net sink over the 2025-2035 period,” the Philippines’ submission to the United Nations read. A net sink absorbs more emissions than it releases — like forests and oceans.

In its latest submission to the United Nations, the Philippines underscored its high vulnerability to climate impacts despite minimal contribution to the crisis. With this in mind, the Philippines set adaptation to severe impacts, such as massive flooding and heat, as a “central and continuous priority.”

Previously, the Philippines had committed to the same 75% target — the difference being that the targets that hinged on international support were bigger at 72.29%. The Climate Change Commission under the Office of the President leads the updating and submission of climate targets.

Whys and hows

Setting these climate targets, or the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), is part of countries’ commitment to the Paris Agreement.

Reducing emissions is highly technical work that cuts across industries and sectors. But the objective is supposed to serve communities: decent work, social protection, and clean and sustainable livelihoods.

Under the Paris Agreement, countries voluntarily set their reduction targets based on capacity. It espouses a bottom-up approach, a revision from the previous international treaty that prescribed set targets for countries.

Parties to the agreement are required to update their NDCs every five years. The latest round of updates was due February 2025, but the Philippines wasn’t able to submit it by then. (READ: Philippines’ new climate targets won’t make it in time for COP30)

To finance its emissions reduction and green transition, the Philippines intends to “access and maximize broad sources of public and private finance.”

The financial support that relies on wealthier and industrialized countries “must be highly concessional, non-debt creating.”

Leaders and civil society representatives from developing nations continuously advocate for climate finance to be given as grants instead of loans. – Rappler.com

World.title: How Martin Romualdez avoided jail by going to hospital
World.content:
CONFINED. The Philippine National Police-CIDG released a photo of former speaker Martin Romualdez when he was served an arrest warrant in his hospital room on Monday, September 7. The cops took his fingerprint and placed a detainee uniform on top of him as part of the booking process, but his mugshot was not taken yet given his condition. Courtesy of PNP CIDG

'In this case, actually, dito lang kay [former] speaker Martin nangyari 'yan... Si [former] speaker lang ang dumiretso talaga sa hospital,' DILG chief Remulla says

Former speaker Martin Romualdez, the cousin of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., is facing a non-bailable plunder case courtesy of the Office of the Ombudsman.

The Ombudsman charged the Leyte representative on Monday, September 7, after months of investigation. It alleged that he got P7.44 billion in kickbacks from the national budget courtesy of flood control and other government projects.

Since plunder is non-bailable, the expectation was that Romualdez would immediately be arrested (he has a pending precautionary hold departure order) and brought to jail.

But this did not happen.

As of September 9, Romualdez remains confined in a hospital in San Juan City.

Hospitalization before arrest

So here’s what happened.

Before Monday, there was buzz going around that there could be a major movement related to the flood control case. A quick thought was that the Office of the Ombudsman would finally charge the former speaker since it had been months since it launched its probe.

In fact, from months ago, the Sandiganbayan already issued a travel ban (precautionary hold departure order) against him, and the Court of Appeals had frozen some of the assets linked to him.

By past lunchtime on Monday, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla announced the filing of plunder against Romualdez whom they alleged to have gotten P7.44 billion in kickbacks from the national budget.

At around 1:30 pm, the case was raffled to the 3rd Division, the same chamber that handles the flood control case of former senator Bong Revilla and the plunder case of Senator Rodante Marcoleta.

In the recent high-profile flood control cases, the warrant was issued either a day or days after the filing of the case with the Sandiganbayan. But at around 5:20 pm, multiple sources had already confirmed to Rappler that the 3rd Division found probable cause to issue a warrant against Romualdez.

Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) chief Juanito Victor “Jonvic” Remulla told Rappler earlier that day that they were ready to arrest the former speaker.

So if the warrant was there and the DILG was willing to arrest, why is Romualdez not in jail?

It’s simple. The former speaker went to the hospital even before the police could get to him. The warrant was out by 5 pm, but Romualdez had already been confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center by 4 pm that day, said Remulla.

“Ayun ang mahirap dito eh. Wala kaming karapatan na i-intercept sila bago lumabas ‘yung warrant of arrest. So, telegraphed lagi kasi na-file na, alam nilang na-raffle na, so inunahan nila,” said the DILG chief. (That’s the hard part here. We don’t have the right to intercept them before the issuance of a warrant. So the movements are telegraphed because they know the case has been filed, has been raffled, so they plan ahead.)

At 6:30 pm, the Romualdez camp filed a manifestation of hospital confinement and urgent motion ad cautelam (as a precautionary measure) for continued hospital confinement under custody. In the said motion, Romualdez claimed to have the following diseases:

Hypertensive Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease

Unstable Angina

Coronary Artery Disease

Post percutaneous coronary intervention

Cerebrovascular Ischemic Disease

Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus

Hypertension

Dyslipidemia

Primary Hypothyroidism

Before 8 pm, Remulla announced outside the hospital that Romualdez had been arrested. The Philippine National Police (PNP) implemented the warrant, read his rights, and took his mugshot while he was in bed.

After the arrest and booking procedures, an accused is usually transferred to the court for the return of warrant and the commitment order, the document that states where the accused will be detained.

“Will wait for the hospital clearance,” Remulla told Rappler when asked if they would wait for a clearance from the hospital before moving the former speaker.

“The aforementioned doctors further informed [the Sandiganbayan officials] that the movement or transport of accused may pose a risk to him, considering his medical condition,” said the 3rd Division’s September 8 order.

In other words, in the window between the filing of the case and the issuance of the warrant, Romualdez was already in the hospital. And this delayed his commitment to the detention center he was supposed to be in.

“Well, I don’t believe in coincidences. So, take it at that,” DILG chief Remulla said in a September 8 press conference, when asked if Romualdez deliberately went to the hospital before his arrest.

Play Video

Unusual

In charging Romualdez, the Ombudsman called him the alleged “central figure” in the flood control scandal, saying that he used his “institutional influence” as the then-House speaker.

Asked if Romualdez is considered the “big fish” in the alleged corruption, Ombudsman Revilla replied, “Sa ngayon, sa ngayon (For now).”

But what makes Romualdez’s case a bizarre one is not only his alleged role in the scheme, but also how he handled his arrest.

The high-ranking politicians recently arrested for corruption cases either surrendered or immediately faced the Sandiganbayan. But the former speaker took his time. He stalled the process by staying at the hospital.

Former senator Bong Revilla surrendered to Camp Crame in January, after the Sandiganbayan issued a warrant for his flood control case. He is facing graft and malversation cases over a P92.8-million flood control project in Bulacan.

By January 21 or two days after his surrender, Revilla was detained at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas.

Senator Jinggoy Estrada, who’s facing plunder and graft cases due to flood control projects, also immediately headed to authorities. He went to the Sandiganbayan to surrender and post bail for his graft case on May 29, the same day the court issued a warrant against him.

The following Monday, on June 1, Estrada was arrested in the Senate over his plunder case and was detained in Payatas the same day.

Even officials who cited medical conditions while facing cases — like Senator Rodante Marcoleta and former Department of Public Works and Highways secretary Manuel Bonoan — surrendered to authorities after the issuance of their warrant.

Play Video

“In this case, actually dito lang kay [former] speaker Martin nangyari ‘yan. Kay former secretary Bonoan, dito (Camp Crame) nakita ang kanyang kondisyon. Hindi siya dumiretso sa hospital. Kay Senator Marcoleta, ganoon rin. Dito nakita ang kondisyon niya, hindi sa hospital. Si [former] speaker lang ang dumiretso talaga sa hospital,” said DILG chief Remulla.

(This only happened in former speaker Martin’s case. Former secretary Bonoan’s condition was discovered in Camp Crame. He did not go directly to the hospital. That’s the same case for Senator Marcoleta. We discovered his condition here, not in the hospital. It’s only the former speaker who went directly to the hospital.)

Hospital request in limbo

For now, Romualdez will remain in Cardinal Santos Medical Center until the court resolves his motion for hospital confinement.

In an order dated September 8, the 3rd Division set a hearing for Thursday, September 10, to tackle Romualdez’s request. If ever, this is also the first time that the former speaker will have his day in court for his flood control case.

“Accused Romualdez is directed to appear before the court should his condition permit,” said the order signed by the 3rd Division justices.

The chamber also subpoenaed Romualdez’s doctors for the hearing. The Ombudsman was given two days to comment on the former speaker’s motion.

Meanwhile, DILG chief Remulla said they do not approve of Romualdez’s confinement in a private hospital and seeks to move him to the PNP General Hospital. This was what happened in the case of Bonoan. The latter was put under hospital arrest, but inside Crame.

The Ombudsman believes that Romualdez should be held in jail if his medical condition does not really require hospitalization.

“The prosecutors will strongly oppose the motion. In fact, the prosecutors will ask that not just one doctor, but a team of government doctors assess whether or not the illnesses declared need confinement or can be managed outside of the hospital,” Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano told reporters on Wednesday, September 10.

“If his illnesses can be managed from outside of the hospital, the prosecutors will move that he be immediately transferred to the regular detention facility as all other accused in non-bailable cases,” he added. – Rappler.com

World.title: [OPINION] Next decade of Philippine climate action set in new but incomplete NDC
World.content:
It is true that we need to secure finance, technologies, and means for capacity-building from developed countries. Yet the impacts of the climate crisis would not stop affecting our economy and society if we just wait for developed countries to fulfill their obligations.

If our nation got P1,000 every time someone in government mentioned that the Philippines is one of the most climate-vulnerable countries, maybe this country would not be in so much debt.

But the risk we face due to the climate crisis is real and of serious concern. If the past few weeks of flooding or extreme heat — depending on where you live — have not made that apparent, then look at what has happened to our country in the past year or two alone. Or look at Nepal or Indonesia or Antarctica — or almost anywhere else in this world.

This should make us wonder: what is the vision for our response to the climate crisis, especially as we also continue to pursue sustainable development?

On September 8, we got our answer to that question with the publication of the Philippines’ updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), our pledge for climate action as part of the Paris Agreement.

The positives

Compared to a “business-as-usual” scenario, the new NDC sets our target for reducing climate pollution by 75% between 2025 and 2035. Of this figure, 7% is unconditional — meaning no foreign assistance is needed to implement climate solutions — from energy efficiency and conservation and some nature-based solutions (NbS) like reforestation.

It is true that we need to secure finance, technologies, and means for capacity-building from developed countries. This is not just because we do need these resources, given the enormity of the problem; it is because those countries are the ones who polluted the world the most on their way to achieving high-income economy status, causing the climate crisis. Polluters must pay.

Yet the impacts of the climate crisis would not stop affecting our economy and society if we just wait for developed countries to fulfill their obligations. We still need to pursue national sustainable development — which necessitates a higher unconditional target.

Is the proposed 2027 national budget actually prioritizing these unconditional climate solutions? If the Marcos Jr. administration truly prioritizes the climate agenda — which the President claimed at the start of his term — then this must be reflected in every national budget until 2035.

Look at our NbS, for example. Using all government-led actions under the third thematic area of our National Climate Change Action Plan as the basis for the scale of its funding, the 2026 funding for NbS is 28 times lower than for climate-tagged new roads, bridges, and other gray infrastructure. It is also five times lower than the ASEAN benchmark for the NbS-to-public expenditures ratio.

A big part of the higher target is due to the full integration of the forestry and other land use sector in the updated NDC, unlike the first version. How much more signs does the government need to invest public funds in ecosystem protection, conservation, and restoration?

The negatives

You might ask yourself — why does the Philippines need to decrease its climate pollution?

Yes, we do not emit as much pollution as the rich countries. But to paraphrase what a lawmaker said once, the cost of inaction is greater than the cost of action now.

The Philippines has been playing catch-up to the rest of its ASEAN neighbors and the rest of the world on many aspects of development — from public transport to renewable energy. Every climate extreme that hits our country — and there is still a Super El Niño headed our way — forces us to spend more on response and rehabilitation instead of investing in these areas that lead to climate-resilient development that also creates green jobs and ensures food, water, energy, and human security.

This is why implementing the NDC matters. This is why we need to decarbonize as a country.

Yet there are many challenges to which the government has not properly responded, despite calls from civil society groups in recent years.

Among these is the lack of a strong commitment to transitioning away from fossil fuels (TAFF). The national government has refused to join a global coalition of the willing to initiate an approach that everyone will have to do anyway. It has even eased restrictions on the coal moratorium under the guise of advancing projects it considers nationally significant.

The impacts of the war in the Middle East — higher oil prices, inflation in other goods and services, disruptions in work and schooling, among others — should have already taught us the lesson of making the TAFF choice. Instead, the country remains on the path to an energy sector dominated by fossil fuels — which has given us high electricity bills and alerts of different colors on our energy supply.

Sooner or later, the Philippine government will make the TAFF choice. It should have been sooner.

The benchmark

There are still many questions left unanswered in this process of updating our climate pledge. How much of the first NDC submitted in 2021 has been fully implemented? How much would it cost to implement it?

Failing to provide these critical pieces of information is, at the minimum, arguably considered neglect of the national government’s responsibilities in addressing the climate crisis. This is established under the 2025 International Court of Justice Advisory Opinion on climate change, which is politically reaffirmed through a United Nations General Assembly resolution passed this year — one that the Philippines itself voted for.

These global decisions reinforce the 1.5°C warming limit as the benchmark with which we assess whether our government is doing enough to address the climate crisis. Yes, that threshold will be exceeded in at least the next few years, largely because developed countries failed to do what is right.

Yet this should make our country more determined to enact a just transition toward a low-emissions, climate-resilient nation, where no one is left behind. That can start with properly implementing our NDC.

After all, no matter how ambitious a promise is, climate action speaks louder than words. – Rappler.com

John Leo Algo is the national coordinator of Aksyon Klima Pilipinas.

World.title: ‘Plug and play’ Oftana completes Gilas’ Asian Games roster
World.content:
VETERAN. Calvin Oftana in action for Gilas Pilipinas in the 2025 FIBA Asia Cup.

Taking over the spot initially reserved for Justin Brownlee, Calvin Oftana joins Gilas Pilipinas just a couple of days before it opens its title defense in the Asian Games

MANILA, Philippines – Calvin Oftana returns to national team duty as he completes Gilas Pilipinas’ 12-man roster in the Asian Games.

Taking over the spot initially reserved for Justin Brownlee, Oftana flew to Japan on Wednesday, September 9, just two days before the Philippines opens its title defense against Bahrain at the Aichi International Arena in Nagoya on Friday, September 11.

“Calvin Oftana is stepping in as our 12th man. He is arriving this afternoon, we hope in time to make our practice schedule today,” Cone said through a Viber exchange.

Oftana, who stars for TNT in the PBA, last suited up for Gilas Pilipinas in March in the second window of the FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers before injuries kept him out of national team action.

Cone previously said the Asian Games team is ready to compete with just 11 players if Brownlee, who has been dealing with injuries that sidelined him for the last three Asian Qualifiers games, is unable to play.

But with Oftana becoming available, Cone and his staff decided to bring him in.

“Calvin was always on the list to play, but we were uncertain of his health status. He has since returned to TNT’s practice and is good to go,” said Cone.

Despite Oftana coming in at the last minute, Cone sees him fitting seamlessly into the squad, with the 30-year-old forward boasting extensive national team experience.

In fact, Oftana is the only remnant of the 2023 crew that won the Philippines its first men’s basketball gold medal in the Asian Games since 1962.

“Because of the system we are running and his previous experience in the window teams, he’s a plug and play player and will fit right in,” said Cone.

After Bahrain, the Philippines will battle Kazakhstan and China on September 12 and 14, respectively. – Rappler.com

World.title: Who can use the Lido name? SC cancels ‘Lido Cocina Tsina’ trademark
World.content:
(1st UPDATE) Years after the falling out between old partners, the Supreme Court says the trademark still belongs to the partnership they left behind

MANILA, Philippines – Just as Lido, a household name in Chinese dining, marks its 90th year, the Supreme Court settled a decades-long dispute over who owns the restaurant’s name.

The SC canceled two Lido trademark registrations held by Panciteria Lido Chinese Cuisine Co., including one for “Lido Cocina Tsina,” after finding that the company registered the marks in bad faith.

“Through Alipio, respondent knew that the right to register the Lido mark belonged to Eng Son Co., yet it caused the registration of the subject marks in its own name,” read part of the SC ruling.

But the SC did not award the Lido name to the King family, whose heirs brought the case. It instead upheld the earlier finding that “the right to register the trademark ‘Panciteria Lido’ is vested to the partnership” Eng Son Co., with no proof that the partnership had been wound up or that the marks had been transferred elsewhere.

When one Lido became two

Lido traces its roots to 1936. King and Alipio later formed Eng Son Co. in 1997 to operate Lido Restaurant.

The two were once close business partners, but their relationship eventually soured. The falling out also divided the restaurant business, with some franchisees going with Alipio and others with the King family. The Alipio side eventually became Lido Cocina Tsina, while the King side operated as Salido.

The trademark fight soon followed.

Alipio applied in 2008 to register Panciteria Lido in her own name. King opposed the application, and the Intellectual Property Office ruled in 2010 that the right to the mark belonged to Eng Son Co.

King died that same year. His death dissolved the partnership, but under the Civil Code, dissolution did not terminate it. The partnership continued to exist until its affairs were wound up.

Alipio later formed PLCCC with other partners, and the new partnership obtained two Lido trademark registrations in 2012. King’s sons Albert and Arthur eventually challenged them.

Who owns the name now?

The SC sided with the King heirs and ordered the registrations canceled, but it made clear that winning the case did not make them owners of Lido.

“While such hereditary interest did not automatically vest in petitioners ownership over specific partnership assets prior to liquidation, it nevertheless gave them a sufficient legal interest” to challenge the registrations, the High Tribunal said.

The SC found no evidence that Eng Son Co. had ever been liquidated, that its affairs had been wound up, or that ownership of the Lido marks had been lawfully transferred elsewhere.

That leaves the Lido trademark in the unusual position of remaining a partnership property even though the business relationship behind that partnership fell apart years ago.

The ruling does not order either Lido Cocina Tsina or Salido to close. It also does not resolve who may ultimately use, license, or assign the Lido name once the old partnership’s affairs are finally settled. – Rappler.com

Disclosure: The author previously had an ownership interest in a Panciteria Lido and Salido franchise.

World.title: [In this Economy] PISA 2025: Much better scores, but the learning crisis remains
World.content:
The improvements are real, but that’s what you get from intense preparation. As with any student determined to ace an exam, preparation is key.

After a long wait, on September 8, we now have the results of the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) which measures the skills of 15-year-old students.

There’s good news all around. Philippine scores have improved in all three subjects tested: our reading score rose from 347 in 2022 to 367, math from 355 to 371, and science from 356 to 373.

All three increases were statistically significant, meaning the analysis finds evidence of improvement beyond sampling and measurement uncertainty. PISA noted that we were among eight participating education systems that exhibited significant gains in all three subjects. Great!

In addition, the share of Filipino students below baseline proficiency in science, or PISA’s minimum expected skill level, also fell by a significant 8.9-percentage points between 2022 and 2025.

All of this is welcome news, and our teachers and students deserve recognition.

What accounts for the improvement? On the one hand, such a result should be hardly surprising, given the intense preparations of the Department of Education (DepEd).

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. himself directed DepEd, as early as 2024, to improve its PISA ranking. In response, DepEd formed a “Task Force PISA” whose job was to help teachers and especially students prepare for the computerized tests. They provided computers to the hundreds of schools which would potentially be sampled at random by the PISA test administrators, and took pains to allow students to practice on “PISA-type reviewers”—so that they’re less anxious to take the PISA test in case they are chosen to take it. These were so-called “familiarization sessions.” During test day itself, DepEd also made sure to put in place a “festive” mood in the schools, to make the exam less scary for students.

In 2024, DepEd also rolled out a “special science program” which involved teachers training their students in PISA-type questions. (This raised concerns that selected students were being trained for the sake of PISA 2025, a phenomenon called “teaching to the test.”)

Meanwhile, within the DepEd hierarchy, certain regional offices proferred incentives (e.g. awarding of plaques in special events) for “PISA Participating SDOs and Schools” after the exam was administered. The idea was to “recognize the efforts and commitment of PISA-participating schools” and, prospectively, “incentivize continued improvement in learning outcomes to drive future enhancements in educational performance.”

The singular focus of the public education system on PISA 2025 seems to have paid off. The improvements are real, but that’s what you get from intense preparation. As with any student determined to ace an exam, preparation is key.

The Philippines’ improvement is especially amazing given the broader trend in rich countries showing a significant deterioration especially in reading and math scores. According to the official press release, “Average reading scores fell by 28 points across OECD countries between 2015 and 2025, equivalent to about one and a half years of learning. Mathematics scores fell by 22 points, equivalent to just over one year of learning. Among non-OECD PISA participants, reading scores fell by 16 points and mathematics scores by eight points over the same period.”

Whether this unsettling result is because of worsening digital distractions or greater use of AI, we don’t quite know yet. At least for us, we seem to be bucking this global trend—for now.

Beyond the headline gains

Of course, there’s much more to say about the Philippines’ PISA results beyond the headline-grabbing gains.

First, our 2025 reading score of 367 is still quite low compared to the OECD average of 461. In math, the comparison is 371 versus 463, and in science, 373 versus 482.

Our ranking in ASEAN also still leaves much to be desired (Figure 1). While we managed to overtake Indonesia in reading and math, the differences are not statistically significant. Cambodia managed to overtake us in science, so that in the region we’re now last in science. Vietnam, which became an upper-middle income country this year (like us) is also way ahead of us in terms of math and science.

Figure 1.

While the DepEd was gleeful to list the countries that now rank below us, we cannot treat every country below us as a country we overtook. Some countries and economies below us in 2025 were absent in 2022.

More troubling, the vast majority of Filipino students are still below the baseline proficiency level called Level 2 (Figure 2). As much as 70% are below-proficiency in reading, 79% in math, and 68% in science. Meanwhile, 64.3% of Filipino students, or nearly two in three, were below baseline proficiency (Level 2) in all three subjects simultaneously.

Figure 2.

The gains were also unequal. Between 2022 and 2025, science scores rose by 36 points among the most socioeconomically advantaged quarter of Filipino students, versus 10 points among the most disadvantaged quarter. The latter increase was not statistically significant, while the gap widened by a significant 26 points.

What worked, what didn’t?

Naturally, DepEd was in a self-congratulatory mood when the PISA 2025 results were announced. But higher scores do not, by themselves, establish which specific DepEd program worked, how much it contributed, or which specific official deserves credit.

Better instruction could have contributed, alongside greater familiarity with the computer platform and question formats. Preparation can include actual teaching, too, which means learning and test preparation are not always separable. The score increase alone cannot tell us how much came from each.

DepEd’s preparation materials warrant scrutiny. Since we joined PISA 2022, resources already included computer-based familiarization and practice materials, so these may have helped in the most recent round.

Some people allege that DepEd handpicked good students and schools. But PISA follows a prescribed sampling process, and the OECD says Philippine data met its quality standards. The 2025 sample included 8,072 students in 208 schools.

Nonetheless, since DepEd knew weeks in advance which specific schools would participate, it’s worth asking: did PISA-participating schools receive substantial extra support that comparable schools elsewhere did not?

Till now, we don’t exactly know what happens after random selection, and how much additional resources were poured to sampled schools. Maybe DepEd should publish the coverage, timing, and intensity of its preparations so that researchers can study their contribution. Establishing which measures helped would also inform whether they should reach more schools.

PISA’s coverage has limits, too. The Philippine sample represented about 82% of the country’s 15-year-old population, leaving young people outside its coverage whose learning also deserves attention.

More research needs to be done. A 2023 study published in the Economics of Education Review studied Vietnam’s exceptional PISA performance despite being an emerging economy. They found that Vietnam’s advantage persists even after adjustments for better-off students being overrepresented, adolescents outside school being excluded, and possible differences in test preparation and effort. Measured household and school characteristics explain only part of Vietnam’s exceptional performance, and much remains unexplained.

For the Philippines, that study suggests that poverty alone need not determine educational outcomes. Researchers must find out: how much of our learning gap persists after accounting for family circumstances and who gets tested? And what could explain the remainder?

Lingering learning crisis

Finally, by no means do the new results tell us that we have eradicated our long-standing learning crisis.

Apart from the 90% learning poverty rate that previously shocked the country, the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) also reported that proficiency rates plummet from 30% in Grade 3 (abysmal as it already is) to as low as 0.47% by Grade 12.

EDCOM 2’s executive director, Karol Mark Yee, also lamented recently on social media that the national government’s budget documents for 2027 are replete with the phrase “at least nearly proficient”—meaning that DepEd’s performance indicators are considered met if students are “at least nearly proficient” (not quite “proficient”). Karol argues that this is too low a bar, and may serve to mask systemic underperformance.

On top of this, Education Secretary Sonny Angara also divulged that for 2027 the budget proposed by the executive for the ARAL Program amounted to zero. ARAL involves remedial interventions for students lagging in reading. As things stand, there’s also no budget yet to hire teachers next year.

Worse, the Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism (PCIJ) recently reported that politicians have made schools their milking cows as well. They said, “Data from the DPWH Transparency Portal reveals that contractors tied to the flood control scandal were the same ones awarded a large share of school infrastructure contracts.” Moreover, “Construction tycoons Curlee and Sarah Discaya bagged some P13.4 billion worth of school building and facility contracts from 2016 to 2026–the largest haul among all contractors.”

In sum, let’s celebrate the recent PISA gains. But that should not lull us into thinking that the education crisis is now gone. DepEd still needs to establish what caused the improvement and whether the measures behind it can help students across the country, especially those who remain below baseline proficiency.

Most importantly, the DepEd must ensure that these gains are persistent and not just one-off. – Rappler.com

Jan Carlo “JC” Punongbayan, PhD is an associate professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics (UPSE). His professional experience includes the Securities and Exchange Commission, the World Bank Office in Manila, the Far Eastern University Public Policy Center, and the National Economic and Development Authority. JC writes a weekly economics column for Rappler.com. He is also co-founder of UsapangEcon.com and co-host of Usapang Econ Podcast.

His first book, False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, was published by Ateneo de Manila University Press in February 2023. His second book, Twin Plagues: How Duterte and Covid-19 Wrecked the Philippine Economy, was published by Penguin Random House SEA in June 2026. Follow him on Instagram (@jcpunongbayan).

World.title: Valencia City secures P2.74-B LandBank loan for major projects
World.content:
The current city hall of Valencia, Bukidnon, located at the heart of the city, is set to be replaced by a modern structure, funded by a P2.74 billion loan agreement with the Land Bank of the Philippines. (INQUIRER Mindanao / Mel N. Velez)

VALENCIA CITY, Bukidnon — The city government here officially finalized a P2.74 billion loan from the Land Bank of the Philippines (LANDBANK) on Wednesday, marking a significant milestone in accelerating the city’s development.

The loan is strategically earmarked for major capital expenditures, including the construction of a new Valencia City Hall, the upgrade and expansion of the Valencia City Good Samaritan General Hospital, the improvement of evacuation centers and community facilities, and the procurement of heavy and medical equipment.

Mayor Amie Galario said these projects support the city’s growth and its aspirations to accommodate a rising population and economy.

Article continues after this 

LandBank’s financing program for the local government units is anchored on countryside development, providing long-term repayment structures, competitive interest rates, and support for high-urbanization goals.

Repayments for the loan are typically sourced from regular LGU revenues, such as the National Tax Allocation (NTA) and local tax collections, secured through standard credit enhancers and strict loan-purpose clauses to ensure transparency and proper financial compliance. /gsg

World.title: Endangered seabird spotted in Aurora, released into wild
World.content:
An endangered seabird rescued after it was found struggling to fly along the coast of Barangay Masagana in Dilasag, Aurora, was assessed by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources before being released into its natural habitat in Barangay Dicabasan. (Photo courtesy of DENR Region 3)

OLONGAPO CITY — A brown booby, an endangered seabird, was rescued and released back into the wild after it was spotted along the coastline of Barangay Masagana in Dilasag, Aurora, marking the first documented sighting of the seabird in the province.

In a statement on Sept. 9, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) said its community environment and natural resources office in Casiguran worked with the municipal government of Dilasag to rescue and assess the bird.

City Environment and Natural Resources Office officer Ariel Mendoza said a resident found the bird struggling to stay aloft and immediately sought help from local authorities.

Article continues after this 

The bird was turned over to the DENR for assessment, where wildlife enforcement officers found it in good physical condition, with no visible injuries or signs of distress.

“With the help of the municipal authorities of Dilasag, we immediately released it into its natural habitat in Barangay Dicabasan, in accordance with established wildlife rescue, handling, and release protocols,” Mendoza said.

READ: Mindoro’s rarest bird captured on camera after nearly two decades

Ralph Pablo, DENR regional executive director, urged the public to immediately report wildlife sightings to the DENR or local authorities to ensure proper handling and prevent unnecessary disturbance of wild animal habitats.

The brown booby (Sula leucogaster) is listed as an endangered wildlife species under DENR Administrative Order No. 2019-09 and is protected under Republic Act No. 9147, or the Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act. /mcm

World.title: Man found dead near river in Bulacan
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

CALUMPIT, Bulacan — The body of a man who had been missing for two days after leaping into a river near his house was located on Tuesday, Sept. 8.

Rey Lequin, a resident of Sto. Niño village in Calumpit town, had reportedly jumped into a river near their house at around 4:30 p.m. on Sept. 6, according to Enriquito Del Rosario, Calumpit municipal disaster risk reduction management officer.

Lequin was having a heated argument with his wife. Before the argument, he may have also been intoxicated after a round of drinks with friends, Del Rosario told Inquirer.

Article continues after this 

READ: Bulacan businessman found dead along Pampanga dike

As soon as Lequin plunged into the river, his brother-in-law attempted a rescue but was pulled back by neighbors due to the strong river current.

A family member tried to get Lequin to grab hold of a long wooden pole and pull himself toward the riverbank, but the victim was carried away by the river.

At around 6 a.m. on Tuesday, residents of Barangay Sta. Elena in the adjacent town of Hagonoy found Lequin’s remains floating on that side of the riverbank.

Calumpit rescuers retrieved his body. /mcm

World.title: Palace assures efforts being done to curb rising unemployment
World.content:
Palace press officer Claire Castro. Screengrab from Presidential Communications Office/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang has assured the public that the government is continuously working to improve the employment situation in the country after the latest unemployment rate surged to a four-year high of 6 percent in July, up from 4.9 percent in June.

Palace press officer and Undersecretary Claire Castro, in reference to a statement from Department of Economy, Planning, and Development Secretary Arsenio Balisacan, said the unemployment rate can be addressed by improving the ease of doing business.

Castro explained that when investors can obtain the necessary requirements more quickly, it becomes easier for them to enter the country and hire Filipinos for their businesses.

Article continues after this 

READ: Jobless rate rises to 4-year high of 6% in July

“At patuloy pa rin po ang pagreporma sa National Education and Workforce Development Plan for 2026 to 2035, ito po ay ayon na rin sa ASEAN [Association of Southeast Asian Nations] Mutual Recognition Arrangements for Qualification and Skills Certification,” Castro said.(And the government continues to reform the National Education and Workforce Development Plan for 2026 to 2035, in line with the ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) Mutual Recognition Arrangements for Qualifications and Skills Certification.)

According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), the 6.0 percent is the highest unemployment rate recorded since June 2022, when it stood at 6.03 percent.

Citing the conflict in the Middle East, the Palace official said many overseas Filipino workers who lost their jobs and were repatriated have also contributed to the rise in unemployment.

Despite this, Castro said the Department of Labor and Employment continues to hold nationwide monthly Trabaho Agad job fairs and strengthen placement networks such as Public Employment Service Offices.

Article continues after this 

What the data says

The latest figure amounted to 3.14 million jobless Filipinos, up from 2.59 million the previous month.

Meanwhile, the employment rate eased to 94 percent from 95 percent, with the number of employed Filipinos falling to 49.21 million from 50.55 million.

Article continues after this 

In addition, the labor force participation rate also fell to 63.6 percent from 65.1 percent, bringing the labor force to 52.36 million from 53.25 million.

For the number of underemployed Filipinos, the PSA said it rose to 12.9 percent from 12.1 percent as they sought additional work or longer hours to increase their income.

World.title: Senate OKs on 2nd reading bill setting barangay, SK term to 5 years
World.content:
Residents of Quezon City troop to the SM North EDSA (North Towers) on January 31, 2023 on the last day of Commission on Elections voters registration for the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections. (File photo from NIÑO JESUS ORBETA / INQUIRER.net)

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate on Wednesday approved on second reading a bill fixing the term of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) officials to five years.

The measure was passed despite the opposition of five senators.

Sen. Francis “Chiz” Escudero sponsored Senate Bill No. 2397, which fixes the term of BSK officials to five years.

Article continues after this 

In effect, this reschedules the upcoming BSKE from November 2026 to November 2028.

Voting against the measure are Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III, Sens. Joel Villanueva, Risa Hontiveros, Bam Aquino and Kiko Pangilinan.

Sotto previously expressed reluctance to support the bill, stating that postponing the upcoming BSKE would “deny voters to choose their local leaders,” after the same polls have already been moved from 2025 to 2026.

The last of these elections were held in 2023.

During the period of amendments in the Senate, Sotto reiterated his sentiment, urging his colleagues to review the measure before voting on its approval.

Article continues after this 

“Considering that this is the eighth time that we have postponed barangay elections, it might give the impression to the public of how little regard we are giving to the unit of government closest to the people,” the senator said.

He told his fellow senator: “My dear esteemed colleagues, the Comelec (Commission on Elections) is ready and equipped to conduct the November 2026 BSK elections. Thus, I am hopeful that it will proceed.”

Article continues after this 

“I urge my colleagues to review and study closely this unconstitutional extension before casting their approval,” he pleaded.

READ: Sotto opposes postponement of BSKE, cites violation of right to vote

After his speech against the measure, Sotto proposed an amendment, disqualifying from a term extension or holdover the barangay officials who are facing charges.

“There are 149 cities, 1,493 municipalities, 42,011 barangays and there is no single city or municipality without a barangay official being charged with something…,” he claimed.

“There is no single city or municipality where all the barangays are clean. There are no cases against any councilor or any barangay official,” he further told his colleagues.

“This is a safety measure. If you have a case, you cannot be on holdover. Will we give you an extension? Are you still on holdover until 2028? You have a case! You have a graft case. You have an administrative case,” Sotto remarked.

Escudero, though acknowledging the concern, responded to Sotto’s proposal, saying there are risks to Sotto’s proposed provision.

“With this measure, what will happen is that the mayor will only do what he has to do,” Escudero pointed out.

“He will be sued or his enemies in the barangay will sue him. The effect is that he will not be able to perform his duty, according to the amendment,” the lawmaker further said.

“So it seems that just by filing a case, effectively, we are suspending and removing the barangay official,” Escudero told Sotto.

Escudero said this is the same reason why a final conviction is required for disqualifications.

READ: House OKs bill setting barangay, SK execs’ term to five years

Nevertheless, he included an amendment to the bill, which states that “incumbent officials with [administrative, civil or criminal] cases may be prevented from sitting in a holdover capacity, in accordance with law, as may be ordered by the courts or competent authority.”

The new provision also prevents the measure from exempting or excusing incumbent officials from investigations on administrative, civil or criminal cases or liabilities. /apl

World.title: Solons say ‘good’ that Carpio complaint close to being junked
World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte (left) and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio. — File photos

MANILA, Philippines — It is only right that the complaint from Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, should move closer to dismissal since there is no basis to charge lawmakers over alleged breach of bank secrecy and data privacy laws, lawmakers said on Wednesday.

In a press briefing on Wednesday, Manila Rep. Joel Chua — one of the respondents in the case filed by Carpio before the Quezon City prosecutor’s office — said that they were expecting that the complaint will be dismissed as it was merely a means to harass lawmakers who pushed for the inclusion of Carpio and Duterte’s bank and tax records as evidence for the impeachment case.

According to Chua, it is only now that he has heard about a case being filed against lawmakers who merely agreed with a motion.

Article continues after this 

“Well, we expect this decision because it was clear that this will be dismissed because first, this is a clear case of harassment towards us, as we were just fulfilling our duties. Second, the complaint really has no basis,” Chua, a member of the prosecution team for Duterte’s impeachment trial, said.

READ: Prosec junks Carpio’s rap vs AMLC on disclosure of his, Duterte’s bank files

“In fact, his complaint against me was, if I am not mistaken, because I agreed with a motion. When did such a thing became a crime? That’s why we welcome this decision, and this will not be a reason for us to lose focus from our work at the impeachment trial,” he added.

Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon said the development only shows that the world of the Duterte-Carpio couple is shrinking.

“It is only right that the prosecutor junked the malicious and baseless case from Mans Carpio against us House prosecutors and other lawmakers,” Ridon said. “The world of the Duterte-Carpio couple is truly shrinking, and we are nearing the exciting part.”

Article continues after this 

Akbayan party-list Rep. Chel Diokno, meanwhile, welcomes the decision of the prosecutor to recommend the dismissal of Carpio’s complaints.

Diokno, like Chua and Ridon, are members of the public prosecution panel.

Article continues after this 

“We welcome the decision of the prosecutor’s office to dismiss the case. We trust our justice system and at the end, the truth and justice prevails against a baseless accusation,” Diokno said in a separate statement.

Earlier, Carpio’s counsel Peter Paul Danao confirmed that the Quezon City prosecutor’s office has recommended the dismissal of their complaint regarding the disclosure of Carpio and Duterte’s financial records at the hearing of the House of Representatives’ committee on justice.

The said panel was then discussing the two impeachment complaints against Duterte, specifically allegations that the vice president had unexplained wealth, or assets not included in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth.

“We acknowledge the Sept. 7, 2026 Resolution of the Quezon City prosecutor’s office recommending the dismissal of our client’s complaint against the respondents,” the lawyer said in a statement.

“Once received, our client reserves the right to exhaust all available legal remedies to challenge the Resolution, consistent with his right to seek appropriate relief under the law and existing rules,” he said.

Aside from lawmakers, Carpio also sued resource persons invited by the committee on justice, like officials of the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC).

Chua said this development will allow potential witnesses — like those who showed up at the committee on justice and were eventually charged also — to testify without fear before the impeachment court.

“This has an impact because, at least, we can now see that there will no longer be anything that would prevent them from testifying in this impeachment trial, especially since what will be discussed now concerns unexplained wealth, which is what their complaint is about,” he said.

“And I believe that the witnesses here will no longer be afraid because of the pending case that has been filed,” he added.

The prosecution has finished presenting evidence and witnesses for Article IV or the allegation that Duterte betrayed public trust when she threatened President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his relatives.

On Tuesday, counsel for the prosecution Lorna Kapunan said that they will forego the remaining 15 witnesses for Article I or the alleged misuse of confidential funds under Duterte’s office, while reserving their right to call the vice president to the witness stand, so she herself can address issues hurled at her.

Due to this development, the Senate Impeachment Court did not hold trial on Wednesday and instead devoted the day the marking of additional evidence.
