With the prosecution wrapping up Article I, the panel is expected to proceed to Article II or Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth by Monday, Sept. 14. /das

World.title: NLEx travel back to normal after floods and gridlock
World.content:
Motorists taking the North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) can expect smooth travel now that all three lanes in Tulaoc and near the San Simon Interchange have been flood-free since Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026, according to the tollway’s operators. INQUIRER.net file photo / JONATHAN VICENTE

PULILAN, Bulacan—Motorists taking the North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) can expect smooth travel now that all three lanes in Tulaoc and near the San Simon Interchange have been flood-free since Tuesday, according to the tollway’s operators.

This stretch of the freeway along Pampanga was nearly crippled by floods brought by weeks of monsoon rains and other weather disturbances, which caused an 8-hour gridlock on August 29. Floods, which were aggravated by clogged waterways that brought downcascading waters from Nueva Ecija, had to be siphoned off the expressway.

READ: NLEx traffic eases, nears normal after 8-hour gridlock

Article continues after this 

Travel has returned to a normal pace of 80-100 kph for nearly 351,000 NLEx motorists traversing Balintawak to Pampanga.

The normalization of NLEx travel paved the way for the lifting of toll rebates that NLEx Corporation has been providing motorists who endured disrupted traffic flow along the San Fernando–Pulilan stretch.

As of 12:01 p.m. on Wednesday, the rebate was terminated. It started on Sept. 2 upon the directives of the Department of Transportation, while flood conditions persisted. However, the temporary toll exemption for provincial buses will remain in effect.

NLEx continues to undertake flood mitigation measures, including dredging the Tulaoc River and clearing and improvement works along the NLEX embankment, to ease water flow and help control flooding in the area./coa

World.title: 630 kilos of imported meat seized in Agusan del Sur town
World.content:
MEAT SAFETY OPERATION. Personnel unload and dispose of some 630 kilograms of imported meat confiscated during a joint operation by NMIS Caraga and the San Francisco municipal government in Agusan del Sur for noncompliance with meat safety requirements. Photo courtesy of NMIS Caraga

SAN FRANCISCO, Agusan del Sur— Authorities confiscated and disposed of 630 kilograms of imported meat allegedly found noncompliant with meat safety requirements during a joint enforcement operation on Wednesday in this town.

The National Meat Inspection Service (NMIS) in Caraga and the San Francisco municipal government conducted the operation in support of meat safety and consumer protection.

Mayor Grace Carmel Paredes-Bravo said the confiscated products were disposed of in accordance with established procedures.

Article continues after this 

READ: Pork prices fall as farmers rush to sell amid ASF fears

“This collaborative effort demonstrates the continuing commitment of NMIS Caraga and the LGU of San Francisco to ensuring that only safe, wholesome, and properly handled meat and meat products reach consumers,” Bravo said.

The proliferation of imported meat in Mindanao was also the subject of earlier complaints from vendors and hog raisers in Kidapawan City, North Cotabato./coa

World.title: Golden Horde History Challenges Europe-Centered View of Medieval Eurasia, French Historian Says
World.content:
ALMATY – For centuries, the history of the Golden Horde has often been told from the perspective of the societies it encountered. French historian Marie Favereau is trying to turn that perspective around. Her book, now available in Kazakh, examines the Ulus of Jochi not as a peripheral chapter in European or Mongol history, but as a powerful Eurasian state with its own political institutions, commercial networks and multicultural society.

Favereau presented the Kazakh-language edition of her book “The Horde: How the Mongols Changed the World” at the Kazakh National Academy of Sciences in Almaty on Sept. 8. The event was organised by the Academy together with Steppe & World Publishing and the Embassy of France in Kazakhstan.

The publication comes at a time when Kazakhstan is placing renewed emphasis on the study of the Ulus of Jochi and the history of the Golden Horde. But Favereau’s work offers something more than another account of a familiar historical period: it asks readers to reconsider how the history of the steppe has traditionally been interpreted.

Looking at the steppe from within

Favereau’s interest in the Golden Horde began nearly 25 years ago, when she was a student at the Sorbonne in Paris. She recalled that when she proposed studying the Ulus of Jochi, her supervisor warned her that the subject would be difficult because France had few sources on the period. Rather than discouraging her, the response sent her in the opposite direction.

“I thought, I’m going to travel all around the world and I will gather all the archives, all the material, all the objects I can to document, to explain the history of Ulus Jochi,” Favereau said at the presentation.

Her research subsequently took her to archives and collections in Vienna, Venice, Genova, Istanbul, and Crimea, while academic cooperation brought her into contact with historians and researchers in Kazakhstan and Tatarstan.

That experience shaped the central approach of her work: understanding the Golden Horde on its own terms. Favereau said Western academic discussions of empire have traditionally focused on examples such as the Roman, Greek and Ottoman empires, while nomadic political systems have received far less attention.

“I had to write a book, a book that I would have needed as a student about Ulus Jochi, but from inside, from the nomadic perspective,” she said.

For Favereau, this distinction matters because the political and social structures of a steppe empire cannot simply be measured against those of Rome, Paris or Vienna. The Golden Horde was born as part of the Mongol Empire in the 13th century before developing into an independent political power under the descendants of Jochi, the eldest son of Genghis Khan. Its political organisation, Favereau argues, was more complex than the image of a state ruled solely by a khan suggests.

The begs, nomadic elites, assemblies and negotiations all played important roles in political decision-making. Favereau also draws attention to the role of elite women in the highest levels of government.

“I really wanted to show in my book the importance of collective power, of assembly, of negotiations, of the place of elite women as the highest leader of the states,” she said.

An empire connected to a wider world

The book also challenges the perception of the Golden Horde as an isolated nomadic power. Its geographical position placed the Ulus of Jochi at the intersection of Central Asia, the northern Russian principalities and European trade routes. Its connections extended to the Black Sea and Mediterranean, while diplomatic correspondence reached Poland, Lithuania, France and England.

“It’s about diplomacy, letters exchanged with Poland and Lithuania, letters exchanged with Europe, letters exchanged with France and England,” Favereau said.

Trade was central to those connections. Italian merchants, the Byzantine world and the Mamluk Sultanate were among the partners involved in networks that moved goods, people, knowledge and cultural practices across Eurasia. Favereau highlights that the Jochids expanded the scale of existing Eurasian trade networks, including those associated with the Silk Road.

“The Jochis made the system bigger, because the scale is not the same,” she said, pointing to the vast territory controlled by the Golden Horde.

That perspective places the Golden Horde within global history rather than treating it exclusively as a regional phenomenon. Its importance, in Favereau’s interpretation, lies partly in the connections it created across political and cultural boundaries.

A multicultural society in the medieval steppe

The same approach applies to religion. Favereau challenges the idea that Islamisation in the Golden Horde was merely superficial. She points to the conversion of Berke Khan and his relations with the Mamluk Sultanate, which developed into a broader exchange involving scholars, religion, literature, science and crafts.

At the same time, the Ulus of Jochi retained a tradition of religious diversity, with Christian, Buddhist and Jewish communities living within its territories. For a medieval empire extending across much of Eurasia, such diversity complicates the image of the Golden Horde as simply a military power built through conquest. It also highlights one of the broader arguments of Favereau’s research: nomadic societies should not be understood through stereotypes of political or cultural simplicity.

Why translation matters

The Kazakh edition gives that research a new audience. For Favereau, translation is not simply about making a text accessible. It is part of the scholarly exchange itself.

“Without translation, we are limited to our own circle,” she said.

She described translating historical concepts as a process of interpretation, requiring scholars and translators to consider how ideas developed in one linguistic and cultural environment can be understood in another.

“The translation in Kazakh language goes deeply to my heart,” Favereau said, highlighting that the translation also reflects a broader effort to bring international scholarship into Kazakhstan’s academic and educational space while strengthening dialogue between researchers working on the history of Eurasia.

Building bridges through history

French Consul General Maxime Gehringer said such exchanges have significance beyond the publication of a single book.

“Countries are not built through political dialogue, economic exchange alone. We depend on a better knowledge of one another,” he said.

He described cultural, scientific and academic exchanges as an integral part of the growing strategic partnership between France and Kazakhstan. Gehringer also highlighted Favereau’s long engagement with Central Asia, including her work as director of the French Institute for Central Asian Studies in Bishkek. He said her research contributes to continuing discussions in Kazakhstan and elsewhere in the region by bringing together different sources and perspectives on the history of nomadic societies.

“The authors present nomadic societies in all their complexity,” Gehringer said. “Political organizations, histories, trade and diplomacy are brought together within a vast space connecting Asia and Europe.”

A history beyond modern borders

Favereau’s book ultimately asks readers to reconsider where the history of the Golden Horde belongs. It is certainly part of the history of the Eurasian steppe and of the territories that include present-day Kazakhstan. But its networks extended far beyond modern national borders, linking Central Asia with the Middle East, Russia and Europe.

That makes the history of the Ulus of Jochi relevant not only to understanding Kazakhstan’s past, but also to understanding how political power, commerce, religion and cultural exchange operated across Eurasia centuries before the emergence of today’s states.

For Kazakhstan, having that scholarship available in Kazakh adds another dimension. It allows international interpretations of the Golden Horde to enter the country’s own academic and public discussion in the national language. For Favereau, that dialogue is part of what historical research is meant to achieve.

“Research and science is a trans-generation thing,” she said, reflecting on the scholars who influenced her work and the students who will continue it.

World.title: Can Kazakhstan Take its Capital Markets to Next Level?
World.content:
The sense of progress and economic momentum in Kazakhstan is tangible and impossible to ignore. Speaking to Kazakhstan’s financial leaders, policymakers, and leaders in the leadup to the Astana Finance Days conference, I understand why. The government’s clear growth agenda, combined with bold steps to reform the nation’s capital market, is having a real, positive impact.

Throughout my time in Astana so far, the question has increasingly shifted from whether Kazakhstan can attract international capital, but what the country should do next to become a true global center.

The foundations are already in place. Kazakhstan is the largest economy in Central Asia and has a growing role as the bridge between major European and Asian markets. The country has spent recent years developing the financial infrastructure needed to open its market and connect domestic companies, investors, and global capital. The Astana International Financial Centre, with its English common law framework, and the Astana International Exchange have complemented the domestic market by providing an international platform for investment and cross-border issuance – drawing in over $21 billion in investment since 2018.

Technology is already part of Kazakhstan’s vision for what comes next. Speaking at a Bloomberg event in 2025, NBK Governor Timur Suleimenov highlighted the importance of financial technology as a major force for financial growth and the role of modern infrastructure in supporting the next stage of market development. Opening the market, however, is only the beginning. The next challenge is making it easier to participate in.

Looking around the world, Poland offers a useful lesson in what sustained market development can achieve. Its emergence as Central and Eastern Europe’s leading financial center was not the result of any single reform. Debt market digitization, regulation, international accessibility, trading and settlement infrastructure, liquidity and investor participation reinforced one another over time. In 2018, that cumulative development helped Poland become the first country from Central and Eastern Europe to be upgraded from emerging to developed-market status by FTSE Russell.

No two markets are the same. Kazakhstan is at a different stage in its economic journey and will follow its own path. But there are undoubtedly parallels to be drawn with Poland a decade ago: a market with growing international ambitions, strategically located, but still considerable scope to deepen participation and strengthen the infrastructure supporting its financial market.

Kazakhstan is already moving in this direction. The recent digitization of government services across the country and the presidential decree on digital assets show a clear direction in one asset class. Last week, authorities announced plans for a new capital-market development program aimed at creating a deeper, more liquid and diversified market and improving businesses’ access to long-term financing. Among the measures under consideration is a centralized securities-lending mechanism designed to improve liquidity in the secondary stock market.

The same focus on liquidity is relevant to Kazakhstan’s sovereign debt market. Authorities are seeking to broaden the investor base and increase appetite for Kazakh debt. Recent reforms to the primary dealer system are intended to bolster liquidity and pave the way for government securities to enter global indices, ultimately helping to reduce government borrowing costs.

Further development of the secondary market can reinforce that progress. A market works better when investors are not simply able to buy but assets but can trade them efficiently once they own them. More active secondary markets support effective price discovery and give investors greater confidence that they can enter and exit positions efficiently. Over time, stronger public markets can become more effective mechanisms for allocating capital across the economy.

As Kazakhstan itself has recognized, technology can help deliver this next stage of development. Electronic trading, integrated data and analytics, pricing systems and modern market infrastructure can reduce friction and make it easier for market participants to transact with confidence. Efforts to digitalize securities issuance, modernize settlement processes and connect its markets more closely with global infrastructure are already moving this agenda forward. As markets become more sophisticated and internationally connected, the infrastructure supporting them needs to evolve as well.

We have seen first-hand the impact that this infrastructure development can have in other emerging markets. In Georgia, Bloomberg worked with the National Bank to introduce electronic trading for the country’s repo market. By integrating trading systems with Bloomberg’s data, analytics and market-surveillance capabilities, interbank transactions became more automated and ultimately more efficient. Similar partnerships with central banks and financial institutions around the world show how modern financial infrastructure and technology can complement wider capital-market reforms and support greater participation.

Kazakhstan has already built much of the foundation and opened its doors further to international investors. The strength and international connectivity of the markets will determine how fully Kazakhstan can capitalize on the opportunity. Get that next stage right, and it will be better placed not only to attract global capital, but to put it to work across its economy.

The author is Sallianne Taylor, the Head of Government Relations for Europe and Central Asia at Bloomberg LP.

World.title: The Semipalatinsk Treaty at 20: Enduring Logic of Nuclear-Free Central Asia
World.content:
Twenty years ago today, representatives of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan gathered in Semipalatinsk, now Semey, to sign a treaty that would make Central Asia the first nuclear-weapon-free zone in the Northern Hemisphere. It was also the first such zone established in a region where nuclear weapons had actually been tested and deployed.

I remember that day well. I was there as a representative of the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies. Kazakhstan was represented by its then Foreign Minister, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who signed the Treaty on behalf of the country. The ceremony itself, held at the Abai State Kazakh Musical Drama Theater, was relatively modest. Its significance was anything but.

The idea of a nuclear-weapon-free Central Asia was hardly inevitable. It was first proposed by Uzbekistan at the UN General Assembly in 1993 and developed over the following years, as the newly independent states were dealing with borders, economic dislocation and an uncertain security environment. The region also carried an extraordinary nuclear legacy: the Semipalatinsk test site, uranium mining, radioactive waste and communities affected by decades of Soviet nuclear activities.

Yet the five Central Asian states made a strategic choice. They decided that their common security would not be built around nuclear weapons. But translating the idea into a legally binding regional commitment was not an easy process as it required persistence and, above all, agreement among all the parties.

The Treaty prohibits the development, production, acquisition, possession, stockpiling or use of nuclear weapons and other nuclear explosive devices. At the same time, it preserves the right to peaceful uses of nuclear energy. Its parties also accepted important obligations relating to IAEA safeguards and the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty.

There is more to the Semipalatinsk Treaty than the absence of nuclear weapons. It was also an early demonstration that the five Central Asian states could develop a common approach to a question of fundamental importance to their security and future. That is perhaps the Treaty’s most interesting legacy today.

Central Asia has changed considerably since 2006. The region is more economically connected, more strategically important and more closely engaged with the major powers than it was two decades ago. At the same time, the international arms control architecture has come under unprecedented pressure. Nuclear rhetoric has returned to the center of global security debates, while confidence in many traditional arms-control arrangements has weakened.

Against this backdrop, it is tempting to regard the Semipalatinsk Treaty as a relic of a more optimistic era. I would argue the opposite.

Its importance lies precisely in the fact that it was created under difficult circumstances and has survived major changes in the regional and global environment. The Treaty entered into force in 2009 after all five states completed ratification. In 2014, all five nuclear-weapon states recognized under the Non-Proliferation Treaty signed its Protocol, committing themselves, among other things, not to use or threaten to use nuclear weapons against the Central Asian parties. Four have since ratified it; U.S. ratification remains outstanding.

There is also a lesson here about Central Asia itself. The Semipalatinsk Treaty was the first regional security agreement to bring all five Central Asian states together, including neutral Turkmenistan. That achievement should not be underestimated.

But anniversaries should not be occasions only for looking backward. The next twenty years will be more important than the last twenty.

The Treaty provides a framework, but a framework is only as effective as the cooperation built around it. Encouragingly, the five states have expressed interest in the institutional development of the CANWFZ and in closer cooperation with other nuclear-weapon-free zones. This points toward a more practical agenda: strengthening cooperation on nuclear security, peaceful uses of nuclear energy, radioactive waste and environmental remediation, emergency preparedness, and the prevention of illicit trafficking of nuclear and radioactive materials. Its value could also grow as the region’s nuclear energy ambitions develop.

This would give the Semipalatinsk Treaty a renewed practical dimension without changing its basic character.

The Treaty also helped establish something larger than a legal prohibition. It became part of Central Asia’s emerging security architecture – one based not on military blocs or strategic rivalry, but on the idea that regional stability could be strengthened through common rules and restraint.

The significance of the Semipalatinsk Treaty, therefore, is not that it solved every security problem facing Central Asia. It did something more durable: it established a common regional commitment at a moment when the future of the region was still uncertain.

Twenty years later, that commitment has become part of Central Asia’s security identity. The challenge now is to ensure that the Treaty remains a living instrument rather than simply a historic achievement. In a world where the value of restraint, dialogue and nonproliferation is once again being tested, Central Asia has a stake – and perhaps a responsibility – in showing that regional cooperation on nuclear security can endure even when the global environment becomes more difficult.

The author is Dauren Aben, the deputy director at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies under the President of Kazakhstan.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Almaty and Astana Maintain Economic Lead as Central Asia’s Cities Race to Catch Up
World.content:
ALMATY – Almaty and Astana are likely to retain their position as Central Asia’s leading economic centers, even as Tashkent and Bishkek record rapid growth and invest heavily in their future expansion. Kazakhstan’s two largest cities benefit from an economic scale, financial infrastructure and established business ecosystems that have been built up over decades, reported the Times of Central Asia.

Almaty has long combined Kazakhstan’s commercial and political functions and established itself as Central Asia’s leading business center. After Astana became the country’s capital, the two cities gradually developed more complementary roles. Almaty remained the region’s main business and financial hub, while Astana accumulated political, institutional and corporate weight.

Updated figures show Astana’s economy grew by about 10% in 2025, while Almaty recorded growth of about 5%. Together, the two cities generated nearly $107 billion in economic output last year.

Their position is supported by Kazakhstan’s broader economic weight. The country accounts for more than half of Central Asia’s GDP and nearly two-thirds of the region’s inward FDI stock, according to The Times of Central Asia’s Central Asia Balance Sheet. That larger economic base provides greater fiscal capacity for infrastructure and urban development, which in turn supports business activity.

Kazakhstan also has the region’s most developed capital markets. The Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE) in Almaty and the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) and Astana International Exchange (AIX) in Astana provide companies with access to equity and debt financing, institutional investors and financial infrastructure on a scale not currently available elsewhere in Central Asia.

Kazakhstan is also the only Central Asian country with an investment-grade sovereign rating. That status can reduce the country-risk premium and financing costs for companies and projects compared with lower-rated regional markets.

Tashkent and Bishkek are also growing rapidly

Tashkent is the most significant challenger to Kazakhstan’s two leading cities. Uzbekistan’s political and commercial capital had an economy of about $29 billion in 2025, nearly 40% the size of Almaty’s and about three-quarters that of Astana.

Its growth rate, however, has been considerably higher. Tashkent’s real GRP increased by 11.3% in 2025, according to preliminary national figures. Tashkent also benefits from Uzbekistan’s demographic scale. The country’s population is almost twice that of Kazakhstan, giving its capital access to a considerably larger domestic market and labor pool.

That advantage comes with its own demands. A larger and growing population requires continuous investment in employment, housing, transport and other infrastructure. If productivity and investment do not keep pace with demographic growth, population size can become a constraint rather than an economic advantage.

The difference in economic output per resident remains substantial. In 2025, GRP per capita stood at approximately $29,900 in Almaty and $23,700 in Astana, compared with about $9,300 in Tashkent. These figures measure economic output per resident rather than labor productivity, household income or living standards, but they nevertheless illustrate the difference in the economic scale of the cities.

Bishkek is growing from a considerably smaller base. Its economy was only about 30% the size of Tashkent’s in the reporting years used here, although the Kyrgyz capital recorded real GRP growth of 15.8% in 2024.

Its economic advantages are different from those of Tashkent. The Kyrgyz Republic’s 10% standard corporate profit-tax rate is below the standard rates in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. The country’s predominantly hydropower-based electricity generation also provides a relatively low-carbon energy base, with further development potential.

At the same time, seasonal electricity shortages remain a constraint. Bishkek’s much smaller population and economy also mean a narrower domestic market and a smaller economic base from which to finance major infrastructure projects.

Can Tashkent catch up?

Tashkent’s ability to narrow the gap with Kazakhstan’s leading cities will depend on more than maintaining high growth rates. The city’s ambitious expansion will require enormous amounts of capital from public funds, domestic and foreign private investment and international borrowing.

Uzbekistan’s economy was about $147 billion in 2025, less than half the size of Kazakhstan’s $306 billion economy. Its sovereign credit remains below investment grade, while its capital markets are still less developed. Remittances also remained significant, accounting for 14.3% of GDP in 2025. Kazakhstan, by comparison, combines a larger economy with investment-grade sovereign credit and substantially greater financial and resource buffers.

These differences do not prevent Tashkent from growing rapidly. They do, however, mean that sustaining large-scale investment over several decades will require continued development of capital markets, labor-market reforms and stronger institutions capable of reducing investment risk and mobilizing capital. Tashkent is therefore narrowing the gap with Astana, but the current data do not indicate that it is on the verge of overtaking it.

The difference in recent growth rates is also smaller than it might initially appear. Tashkent recorded 11.3% real GRP growth in 2025, compared with 10.2% in Astana, giving it an advantage of only 1.1%.

Both cities are also expanding their physical and economic capacity. Construction of New Tashkent began in 2023. Its first phase is designed for 600,000 residents, while the eventual city is planned to accommodate up to 2 million people. By 2034, plans call for 200,000 apartments, together with business, education and transport infrastructure. Residential complexes, business facilities and university campuses are already under construction.

Astana is simultaneously adding substantial capacity of its own. Around 2.2 million square meters of housing were completed in January–July 2026, while new transport and utility infrastructure continues to be developed. The city’s master plan envisages a population of 2.275 million by 2035.

Almaty is a much higher hurdle

The challenge is substantially greater when Tashkent is compared with Almaty. Almaty’s economy is currently more than twice the size of Tashkent’s. Tashkent recorded 11.3% real GRP growth in 2025, compared with 4.9% in Almaty, giving Uzbekistan’s capital a considerably wider growth advantage over Almaty than over Astana. But again, the size of the existing gap matters.

Based on the 2025 economic sizes, Tashkent would need to maintain an average annual real-GRP growth advantage of about 1.75% over Almaty for 50 years simply to reach parity, assuming both economies continued to grow. There is little reason to assume that such a differential could be maintained indefinitely. Growth rates generally slow as economies become larger, while long-term OECD projections also point to slower growth in emerging markets as they converge toward higher-income economies.

Tashkent could therefore continue to grow faster than Almaty while still requiring several decades to close the existing gap.

Almaty, meanwhile, is not standing still. The city’s development programme and 2040 master plan envisage five key economic and urban centers intended to distribute business activity and development more broadly across the city. Revised proposals anticipate population growth to as much as 3.6 million by 2040, alongside additional housing and infrastructure.

Nearby Alatau City, although separately administered, is also being developed as part of the wider Almaty agglomeration. It could add employment, investment and economic activity to the metropolitan area, although its contribution is not included in the Almaty city GRP used in this comparison.

Can Bishkek overtake Tashkent?

Bishkek’s growth is impressive, but its much smaller economic base makes a near-term challenge to Tashkent unlikely. The Kyrgyz capital recorded real GRP growth of 15.8% in 2024. Yet its economy was only around 30% the size of Tashkent’s on the reporting years used here.

Even if Bishkek maintained relatively high growth for an extended period, it would need to sustain a significant advantage for many years before reaching a comparable economic scale. The city is nevertheless expanding. A 2024 administrative-territorial reform more than tripled Bishkek’s territory, from 12,900 to approximately 41,000 hectares, incorporating 24 surrounding settlements.

The city has since approved a development plan through 2030, with water networks and social infrastructure being developed in the newly incorporated areas. Its approved 2050 master plan prepares for a population approaching 2 million. Bishkek’s lower operating costs and hydropower base could help it attract investment in selected sectors. Its smaller domestic market and limited economic base, however, remain significant constraints on its ability to compete with the region’s larger centers.

Central Asia’s economic map is changing

The most likely outcome is not necessarily one city replacing another, but a more competitive and interconnected regional economy. Still, Almaty and Astana enter this competition with substantial accumulated advantages. Their combined economic output, financial infrastructure, corporate networks and access to Kazakhstan’s broader resource and investment base provide a strong foundation for continued regional leadership.

Tashkent can narrow the gap, particularly if it succeeds in sustaining productivity growth and mobilizing the capital required for its ambitious expansion. But current city-level data do not indicate that either Almaty or Astana is close to losing its position.

Central Asia’s economic geography is changing, but the region’s established leaders are expanding alongside the challengers. The competition is therefore less about one city simply overtaking another and more about whether the region’s major urban centers can convert growing economic scale into higher productivity, stronger connectivity and greater international competitiveness.

The article was originally published in the Times of Central Asia.

World.title: Kazakhstan Announces Teams for 2026 FIDE Chess Olympiad in Samarkand
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has announced its national teams for the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad, which will take place in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, on Sept. 16-27.

The women’s team will be led by Grandmaster Bibisara Assaubayeva, currently ranked fifth in the FIDE women’s world rankings. She will be joined by Alua Nurman, Meruert Kamalidenova, Elnaz Kaliakhmet and Zarina Nurgaliyeva. Pavel Kotsur will serve as the team’s captain, reported the Kazakhstan Chess Federation.

Three members of the squad – Assaubayeva, Nurman and Kamalidenova – were part of the Kazakhstan team that won the silver medal at the 45th FIDE Chess Olympiad in Budapest in 2024. It was Kazakhstan’s best-ever result in the women’s competition.

The men’s team will consist of Daniyal Sapenov, Denis Makhnev, Zhandos Agmanov, Sauat Nurgaliyev and Aldiyar Ansat. Sapenov will make his debut at the Chess Olympiad, while the remaining players have previous international experience.

The 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad is one of the world’s largest team chess competitions. Players will compete in Open and Women’s sections over 11 rounds under the Swiss system. The event brings together national teams featuring many of the world’s leading players.

Kazakhstan enters the competition following a series of notable performances by its leading chess players.

Assaubayeva has been among the country’s most successful players in recent years. In June, she won the Norway Chess Women 2026 title in Oslo, defeating several leading players, including reigning Women’s World Chess Champion Ju Wenjun.

In July, Assaubayeva reached a career-high fifth place in the FIDE women’s world rankings with a rating of 2,538, entering the global top five for the first time.

Her rise adds to an already strong record. In December 2025, Assaubayeva won her third Women’s World Blitz Championship title and became Kazakhstan’s second female Grandmaster.

Other Kazakh players have also achieved success on the international stage. Kazybek Nogerbek became the 2024 FIDE World Junior Chess Champion, winning the title in Gandhinagar, India.

In August, four Kazakh chess players, all under 18, took a step toward earning higher titles. Seventeen-year-old Alikhan Daulet finished fourth at the Rudar GM Round Robin tournament in Serbia, earning an International Master norm.

Fifteen-year-old Elnaz Kaliakhmet won the second women’s prize at the 2026 Kanizsa Open and Hungarian Championship in Hungary, also earning an International Master norm. Meanwhile, 15-year-old Sauat Nurgaliyev finished second at the 27th Sants Open–Ciutat de Barcelona in Spain, securing his second Grandmaster norm.

At the same tournament in Barcelona, 16-year-old Malika Japparbekova won the second women’s prize and earned a Woman International Master norm.

The women’s team will also seek to build on its recent international experience, with several players having represented the country at major team competitions.

The upcoming Olympiad comes as chess continues to gain prominence in Kazakhstan, both through international results and the development of young players. Kazakhstan has increasingly hosted major international chess competitions, while its players regularly compete for medals at world and continental events. In August, Almaty hosted the inaugural FIDE World University Team Chess Championship bringing tems from the world’s leading universities, including Harvard, Oxford and Cambridge.

The Samarkand Olympiad will provide another opportunity for Kazakhstan’s teams to test themselves against the strongest chess nations and build on the women’s historic silver-medal finish in Budapest.

World.title: EBRD Supports Alatau Zharyk’s Grid Modernization Program
World.content:
ASTANA – The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) will provide a long-term loan of up to 102 billion tenge (US$224.2 million) to Alatau Zharyk Company (AZhC) to modernize its electricity distribution infrastructure and expand digitalization.

The financing will help AZhC, a regional electricity distribution company supplying around 4 million people and around 50,000 commercial consumers in Almaty and the region, procure automated metering and telemechanic equipment and upgrade its low- and medium-voltage electricity transmission and distribution infrastructure, the bank’s press service reported on Sept. 7.

The project is part of Kazakhstan’s National Project for the Modernization of Energy and Utility Sectors (MEKS), a government-led program to modernize heat, electricity, water supply and sewerage networks and facilities.

The EBRD-supported investment will further digitize AZhC by installing smart meters at substations and piloting smart grid technologies. It will also strengthen the company’s cybersecurity and support related efforts at Samruk-Energy, AZhC’s parent company.

The modernization is expected to generate annual electricity savings of approximately 22 gigawatt-hours (GWh) and reduce annual CO2 emissions by around 12,000 tons. It is also expected to support renewable energy growth in the Almaty Region.

As part of the five-year enhanced partnership framework between Kazakhstan and the EBRD, the project will also support Alatau city’s development by reconstructing the Zhetygen electricity substation and an associated 110-kilovolt (kV) transmission line.

The EBRD has invested almost $13.6 billion in Kazakhstan through 358 projects, making the country the largest and longest-running recipient of EBRD investment in Central Asia.

World.title: Experts: Kazakhstan’s AI Balancing Could Challenge Old Logic of Geopolitical Rivalry
World.content:
ASTANA – For decades, Kazakhstan has built its foreign policy around a principle central to its place in the world: maintaining productive relations with competing powers without becoming dependent on any one of them. This has allowed Astana to work with Russia, China, the United States (US), the European Union and others, even as those powers have competed for influence in Eurasia. AI may be about to test that model in an entirely new way.

But the question may not be whether Kazakhstan will eventually be forced to choose between Washington and Beijing. A more consequential question is whether AI could encourage a different way of organizing international relations in the first place, one in which cooperation, interoperability, transparency and trust become as strategically important as alignment.

Kazakhstan is already at the center of that debate. It is participating in both the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative and China’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), two frameworks that reflect different approaches to the emerging AI landscape.

The overlap has already attracted attention in Washington. Reuters reported in August that the U.S. State Department was preparing to tell countries participating in both Pax Silica and China’s competing AI framework that they would have to choose one side. According to a draft letter reviewed by Reuters, countries seeking to participate in Pax Silica would be expected to commit exclusively to the U.S.-led initiative, although Washington had not decided whether or when to send the letter. Kazakhstan was among the countries identified as participating in both.

That possibility reflects a familiar logic of great-power competition: as a strategic technology becomes more important, major powers seek trusted partners and become less comfortable with those partners maintaining deep ties to their rivals. AI, however, may ultimately make that logic harder to sustain.

Two visions of the AI era

Pax Silica is broader than an AI organization. Launched by the US in late 2025, it is built around securing supply chains that underpin the AI economy, extending from critical minerals and energy to semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, computing infrastructure and logistics. It emphasizes resilience, trusted partners and the protection of sensitive technologies.

WAICO, established in Shanghai on July 16 by 29 founding countries including Kazakhstan, presents itself differently. Beijing describes it as an international intergovernmental organization focused on AI cooperation and global governance.

At a July 17 press briefing, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said China would work with other countries on the basis of “extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit” and seek greater coordination on AI development strategies, governance rules and technical standards. He said China was ready to work with all parties to respond to AI’s opportunities and challenges.

The wording is significant. Pax Silica emphasizes building a trusted technology ecosystem. WAICO is being presented as a platform for broader international participation and coordination. Neither approach is free of geopolitics. Both clearly serve national interests. But they suggest two different ways of thinking about the future of AI: one centered on technological security and trusted supply chains, the other on international cooperation and governance. The question for countries such as Kazakhstan is whether these approaches must ultimately become mutually exclusive.

AI is not simply another strategic industry. There is a temptation to compare AI with oil, gas or telecommunications, all of which have at different times become arenas of strategic competition. The comparison is useful, but incomplete. Oil was a strategic resource. Telecommunications infrastructure created long-term dependencies. AI increasingly encompasses both, while adding another layer: computing, data, software, research and models that can affect almost every sector of the economy.

The AI “stack” begins with critical minerals and energy and extends through chips, computing capacity, data, models and applications. That means competition over AI is simultaneously competition over infrastructure, supply chains, standards, investment and technological capabilities.

But the same characteristics also make AI unusually dependent on cross-border cooperation. No country is likely to control the entire AI ecosystem alone. Research, capital, talent, energy, data and hardware move across borders, while AI applications are increasingly integrated into global industries. That creates a paradox. AI’s strategic importance gives governments a reason to build separate, trusted ecosystems. Its inherently interconnected nature gives them a reason to preserve interoperability between those systems. Kazakhstan is now sitting directly in the middle of that tension.

Kazakhstan’s position

For Astana, participation in both Pax Silica and WAICO fits a foreign policy built on preserving options rather than narrowing them. Kazakhstan needs access to advanced technologies, computing infrastructure, investment, expertise and markets. It also possesses resources and geographic advantages that make it relevant to the emerging AI supply chain.

Alexander Dergay, founder and managing partner of Orbis Nova, has described WAICO as part of China’s broader effort to expand AI cooperation and capacity building across the Global South. He says that the organization is designed around openness and inclusivity while also helping Beijing deepen technological ties with participating countries.

That combination is important. China does not necessarily need countries to make dramatic declarations of political allegiance if its companies, infrastructure, technologies and standards are already becoming embedded in their economies. Temur Umarov, a fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center who focuses on Central Asian countries’ domestic and foreign policies and China’s relations with Russia and Central Asia, says Kazakhstan is unlikely to make a clean choice even if Washington puts pressure on Astana.

“If the US puts Astana in front of an ultimatum in the spirit of the Cold War, it will be a step backwards for American foreign policy in Central Asia,” he wrote on his Telegram channel.

For Umarov, this would run against the region’s basic logic, where successful external partners have historically had to coexist with Russia and China rather than try to displace them.

“Instead of ultimatums in the face of a ban on cooperation with the United States or anyone else, Beijing usually uses the tools it already has,” he said.

Those tools, he says, include Chinese corporations, technology, investment and digital infrastructure, making a sharp technological break with China difficult and, from Kazakhstan’s perspective, unnecessary. His conclusion is deliberately unsentimental.

“Astana and its neighbors in the region will simply do what they are good at — quietly feeding each of the great powers the illusion of their exclusive loyalty while cooperating with everyone,” he said.

That may be precisely what Kazakhstan has done successfully for years. But AI could require something more sophisticated than strategic ambiguity.

The American dilemma

A senior fellow at the Hudson Institute Ken Moriyasu offers a different reason for why Washington may ultimately find it difficult to force Kazakhstan into a binary choice. He describes Kazakhstan as one of the most important “swing states” in the U.S.-China competition and argues that its flexibility is itself strategically valuable to the US.

“This very flexible stance of Kazakhstan is very beneficial for the US strategy,” he said to the Astana Times.

From that perspective, forcing Kazakhstan to choose could undermine one of the very characteristics that makes the country useful to Washington.

“And if the US tries to force Kazakhstan to choose sides, then that really goes against the multi-vector foreign policy, the balancing act, which keeps Kazakhstan very relevant,” he said.

Moriyasu notes that Kazakhstan’s ability to maintain influence with China can itself serve American interests in Eurasia.

“Keeping Kazakhstan a trusted ally and partner in this endeavor is more important than forcing it to choose sides in Pax Silica,” he said.

His argument raises an important question for Washington. Is the objective to build an exclusive American technological bloc, or to preserve a wider strategic balance in which countries such as Kazakhstan can engage China while maintaining close ties with the US? Those two goals may not always lead to the same policy.

The real issue may be bigger than Pax Silica or WAICO

The deeper issue is not formal membership but whether competing AI ecosystems can coexist. Can Chinese models run on U.S.-designed infrastructure? Can data move between systems without creating risks of leakage, surveillance or technology transfer? And who decides what qualifies as a trusted system?

Those questions may matter more than Kazakhstan’s continued membership in both frameworks. AI could therefore force governments to rethink strategic autonomy. Great-power rivalry will remain, but the technology also creates a need for rules that preserve interoperability between competing systems. China’s language around WAICO reflects that logic, emphasizing coordination on AI strategies, governance rules and technical standards. Beijing’s approach is clearly geopolitical, but it also shows how cooperation can become a tool of influence without requiring exclusive blocs.

A new geopolitics of AI

Kazakhstan could translate its balancing diplomacy into a new model of technological governance: neither treating every Chinese technology as a threat nor opening strategic systems indiscriminately, but setting transparent rules for foreign technology, data access, system isolation and security standards.

That would allow Astana to work with competing ecosystems on its own terms and give Washington and Beijing a different basis for competition: whose technologies are more secure, innovative, accessible and trusted. For Kazakhstan, the goal would no longer be to prove loyalty by choosing one side, but competence by managing relations with both.

However, the stakes extend beyond Kazakhstan. AI depends on a network of minerals, energy, chips, computing, data, models and applications. Dividing that network into exclusive spheres could reduce its value. That does not eliminate the need for restrictions around critical infrastructure, advanced chips, sensitive data and dual-use technologies. But it does challenge the assumption that major-power rivalry must force smaller countries into one camp.

Kazakhstan may be an early test of whether a middle power can connect competing technological systems while maintaining enough transparency, security and trust to keep them compatible. Its objective would not simply be to maintain good relations with everyone, but to create rules under which everyone can work with Kazakhstan without requiring exclusive allegiance.

For Washington, that means choosing between treating Kazakhstan as a prize in a contest for technological loyalty and recognizing its value as a connector. For Beijing, it means showing that openness and cooperation can produce trust rather than dependence. And for Astana, the opportunity is to demonstrate that strategic autonomy is not about staying outside the system. It may be about becoming the country in the middle that knows how to make different systems work together.

World.title: Kazakhstan Expands Air Links to Southeast Asia with New Singapore Route
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is continuing to broaden its aviation network across Asia, with SCAT Airlines set to launch flights from Shymkent to Singapore via China’s Sanya on Oct. 20. The new service comes amid a wider expansion of routes by Kazakh carriers to China and other Asian destinations.

Via Sanya

The Shymkent-Sanya flight will take around 6.5 hours, followed by an approximately two-hour transit in Sanya. Passengers will remain in the airport’s sterile transit zone and continue their journey without passing through Chinese passport control.

The Sanya-Singapore segment will take nearly three hours, the airline reported on Sept. 7.

The new route comes as Kazakhstan’s airlines continue to expand connectivity with China and other Asian destinations.

Growing Asian Connectivity

The Air Astana Group reported an 81% increase in capacity to China during the 2026 summer season, reaching 49 flights per week across seven destinations.

The group launched new services from Almaty to Shanghai and Xi’an, from Astana to Guangzhou and from Aktau to Urumqi. FlyArystan is also scheduled to launch twice-weekly flights between Almaty and Chongqing on Sept. 23.

Across the wider network, the group increased services to Central Asia, the Caucasus, Europe, Türkiye and Asia during the summer season.

Passenger Advisory

FlyArystan has advised passengers traveling to or from China to arrive at the airport at least three hours before departure following updated entry and exit procedures that will take effect on Sept. 15.

The airline said immigration checks may take longer and advised passengers to check passport validity and current entry requirements in advance.

The visa-free regime between Kazakhstan and China remains in effect, allowing Kazakh citizens to stay in China for up to 30 calendar days per trip.

World.title: Conflict analyst’s view on clash between Georgia’s former and current prime ministers
World.content:
According to conflict analyst Paata Zakareishvili, members of Georgia’s ruling team have more sympathy for former prime minister Irakli Garibashvili than for the current prime minister, Irakli Kobakhidze. Zakareishvili links the activity of the jailed Garibashvili and his recent letters to this sense of his own political strength.

Zakareishvili believes Garibashvili may have come to believe that Kobakhidze could lose the next election. Kobakhidze, meanwhile, may have realised that even a former prime minister in prison has more political influence than he does.

However, the conflict analyst believes Garibashvili should set out his position more clearly in his letters.

On 1 September, Irakli Garibashvili issued another letter from prison. He called on government officials to answer questions about the circumstances surrounding the death of former human rights defender Lazare Jorbenadze. On 3 September, law enforcement officers questioned Irakli Garibashvili in prison as part of the investigation into Jorbenadze’s death. The prosecutor’s office said Garibashvili’s public doubts about the circumstances of Jorbenadze’s death had no factual basis. It added that the former prime minister had failed to provide investigators with any significant new evidence.

Paata Zakareishvili: “Irakli Garibashvili’s letters should contain more facts, and everything should be made more specific, with names given. When he spoke about Lazare Jorbenadze, he clearly said that Jorbenadze had been murdered, not that he had taken his own life. This means Garibashvili knows something and wants to see the case through. But if he cannot prove it, this issue will be discredited.

However, his latest letters increasingly resemble toasts. It seems he has enjoyed the impact his letters have had. For example, Mamuka Mdinaradze left politics, the minister of regional development. It did not happen because of the letters, though. Mdinaradze simply failed to silence Garibashvili or rein him in.

I am deeply convinced that Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze decided to destroy the Garibashvili ‘clan’ before the 2028 parliamentary elections. Then it suddenly became clear that Garibashvili was not alone and that politically killing him would not be so easy. Garibashvili received a signal that he was more popular within the ruling Georgian Dream party than Kobakhidze. He sensed his strength and now wants to harness it. He realised that Kobakhidze could lose the upcoming election.

Garibashvili followed the decision of ruling party founder Bidzina Ivanishvili and went to prison. Yet it suddenly turned out that this was not enough for Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze. Garibashvili feels that Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze are afraid of him. We should also remember that Georgian Dream Secretary General Kakha Kaladze has remained in the shadows, watching everything, including developments in Ukraine. He is watching and sees that Irakli Kobakhidze is very weak, and that Garibashvili could take the entire team with him before the election.

Kobakhidze has discovered that even Garibashvili, sitting in prison, is stronger than him. Garibashvili has a great many supporters in the regions. As a political figure, he is weak, but he has built a very strong, old-school system of corruption based on the principle: ‘I eat, and I let you eat too.’

Irakli Kobakhidze has been ‘sidelined’ and has no allies. So what could happen today — his resignation — will happen later, probably by 2028. Unless Bidzina Ivanishvili calls an early election.”

Garibashvili and Kobakhidze

World.title: Progress or decline: what study found about the quality of school education in Georgia
World.content:
In 2025, Georgian 15-year-old school students performed better in mathematics, reading and science than they did in 2022. However, there has been no broad or sustained progress over the past decade. In fact, Georgian school students now struggle more with reading comprehension than they did in 2015.

These are the findings of PISA (Programme for International Student Assessment), the largest international study of the quality of school education, conducted by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

OECD (English: OECD) is an international economic organisation that brings together developed countries with high-income economies and established democracies. The organisation is often referred to as a “club of rich or developed countries”.

Despite the positive trend, Georgia remains significantly below the OECD average in all three core areas. Reading is particularly concerning, with 61% of students failing to reach even the basic level.

Georgia’s results

According to the 2025 PISA study, Georgia’s average scores were:

Science — 422 points;

Mathematics — 416 points;

Reading — 384 points;

Problem-solving using computational methods — 413 points.

In 2022, Georgia scored 384 points in science, 374 in reading and 390 in mathematics. The country therefore improved in all three areas in 2025.

The biggest change came in science, with an increase of 38 points. Reading rose by 10 points, while mathematics increased by 26 points.

However, 2022 was a low point for comparison. It was the first study conducted after the pandemic, when education systems were still dealing with its consequences.

The report’s authors also link the decline between 2018 and 2022 to a change in the testing format, alongside the pandemic. Georgia moved from paper-based tests to an electronic format.

Comparing the results with 2022 therefore mainly shows a partial recovery from the losses caused by the pandemic. It cannot, however, serve as a sufficient measure of the education system’s long-term success.

he 10-year results are less impressive

Compared with 2015, Georgia improved its science score by 10 points. Its mathematics score rose by 8 points. In both areas, the country achieved its best result of the past decade.

However, its reading score fell by 17 points. Georgia’s average score stood at 401 points in 2015, but fell to 384 points in 2025.

This means that Georgia’s result in one of the three core areas is worse than it was ten years ago. This is particularly significant because reading skills provide the foundation for learning other subjects.

The short-term improvement therefore does not amount to a systemic breakthrough. Georgia has recovered some of the ground it lost after the pandemic. But it has failed to achieve consistent progress across all three areas over the past decade.

The gap between Georgia and the OECD remains wide

In PISA 2025, the OECD average was 482 points in science. The average mathematics score was 463 points, while reading stood at 461 points.

Georgia trails the OECD average by:

60 points in science;

47 points in mathematics;

77 points in reading.

Georgia comes closest to the OECD average in mathematics. Even there, however, the gap remains significant.

With 422 points in science, Georgia ranks at the same level as Serbia, Romania and Mongolia. The same group also includes Costa Rica, Moldova, Bulgaria, Kazakhstan and Malaysia.

Georgia scored 384 points in reading. Thailand, Vietnam, Peru, Argentina and Kazakhstan recorded statistically similar results.

In mathematics, Georgia trails neighbouring Azerbaijan, which scored 422 points..

What the basic level means

A country’s average score tells only part of the story. A more important question is how many students have the minimum skills they need for everyday life.

In PISA, Level 2 is considered the basic level. At this level, students should be able to apply their knowledge in simple, practical situations.

In Georgia, 55% of students reach the basic level in science. The OECD average is 74%.

In mathematics, 47% of Georgian school students reach the basic level. The average across OECD countries is 65%.

Reading is the most problematic area. Only 39% of Georgian students can identify the main idea and find information in a moderately long text. The OECD average is 69%.

This means that 61% of Georgia’s 15-year-old students do not reach even the basic level in reading.

A shortage of high-performing students

Georgia’s rise in the average score was mainly driven by a decline in the share of low-performing students. The share of high-performing students, however, has not increased significantly.

In science, only 1% of Georgian school students reach the highest performance levels. The OECD average is 7%.

In mathematics, around 2% of students reach the highest levels. The average across OECD countries is 8%.

In reading, virtually no Georgian students reach the highest performance levels. The OECD average is 6%.

The system has therefore managed to help some of its weakest students catch up. However, it still does not create an environment where high-performing students can fully develop their potential.

First place in just one indicator

After the study was published, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said that the country had ranked first among 91 countries.

“In terms of improving performance in science, Georgia ranked first among the 91 countries around the world that took part in the study,” the prime minister said at a government meeting.

The statement refers not to Georgian school students’ overall level of knowledge, but to the change in their science score between 2022 and 2025. Georgia’s score rose by 38 points during this period, the largest increase among all participating countries.

But Georgia does not rank first in the overall results. Its average science score is 422, compared with the OECD average of 482.

The study also stresses that it is impossible to determine countries’ exact rankings. PISA relies on a sample of students, so average scores have a margin of statistical error.

The second achievement highlighted by the Georgian authorities concerns the decline in the number of low-performing students. Georgia did indeed rank among the top three countries on this indicator. Between 2022 and 2025, the share of such students fell by 19.6 percentage points. That is significant progress. However, the share of high-performing students increased by just 0.6 percentage points over the same period.

How the authorities interpret the study’s results

Representatives of the ruling Georgian Dream party and pro-government media have focused mainly on three indicators: the rise in scores compared with 2022, first place for the rate of improvement in science, and the decline in the share of low-performing students.

These figures do appear in the report. The problem lies in presenting them without context.

The authorities’ version barely mentions that Georgia started this improvement from a very low baseline. The large gap with the OECD averages and the decade-long decline in reading also receive little attention.

Kobakhidze noted that “the best results in mathematics and science have been achieved over the past decade”. He also said that “despite the global decline in performance, Georgia continues to show a steady trend of improvement”.

The first statement is correct, although incomplete. Georgia’s best results in science and mathematics remain significantly below the international average.

The second statement raises questions. Georgia’s results did not improve steadily from one PISA cycle to the next. Scores fell in all three areas between 2018 and 2022, while the 2025 reading score remains below the 2015 level.

The authorities presented the public with the most favourable part of the study. However, the full picture shows both some achievements and long-term problems within the education system.

The urban-rural gap has narrowed, but not disappeared

The prime minister also highlighted the narrowing gap between urban and rural schools.

The report confirms this trend. The narrower gap in science and mathematics resulted from improved performance among students in rural areas and settlements.

In reading, however, the gap narrowed for another reason as well: students in the capital performed worse.

This is an important distinction. A reduction in inequality does not always mean that performance has improved across all groups. Sometimes the gap narrows because the stronger group becomes weaker.

In 2025, students in Tbilisi scored an average of 441 points in science. Students in other cities scored 417, while those in villages and settlements scored 405.

In reading, Tbilisi’s score was 401 points. Other cities scored 384, while villages and settlements scored 363.

In mathematics, Tbilisi scored 434 points. The score for other cities was 410, while schools in villages and settlements scored 403.

Private, state and Azerbaijani-language schools

The report shows inequality between private and state schools just as clearly as the gap between urban and rural schools.

Private-school students scored 465 points in science, compared with 418 points for students in state schools. In reading, the corresponding scores were 419 and 381, while in mathematics they were 464 and 412.

The mathematics score for private schools is almost equal to the OECD average. State schools, however, remain significantly below it.

Azerbaijani-language schools perform particularly poorly:

Science — 338 points;

Reading — 307 points;

Mathematics — 341 points.

The corresponding scores for Georgian-language schools are 426, 387 and 420 points.

This gap points to deep inequality within the education system. However, the difference between the languages of instruction did not feature at all in the prime minister’s statement.

Girls outperform boys in reading and science

In Georgia, girls outperform boys in reading and science. The gap is particularly wide in reading.

In science, girls scored an average of 430 points, compared with 415 for boys. In reading, girls scored 399 points, while boys scored 364.

In mathematics, girls scored 417 points, compared with 416 for boys. This difference is not statistically significant.

According to the report, the gender gap in reading narrowed after 2015, but widened again in the latest cycle.

A new challenge in the digital world

PISA 2025 introduced a new area of assessment: “Learning in the Digital World”. One of its components was problem-solving using computational methods.

This component assesses computer modelling and programming skills. The assessment also covers conducting experiments and creating digital products.

Georgia scored 413 points in this area, compared with an OECD average of 500.

This is Georgia’s largest gap among the four areas assessed in the study. Statistically, the country is on a par with Jordan.

Poor reading performance and a lack of digital skills are interconnected problems. Both require students to understand and process information and solve problems independently.

What is PISA?

PISA assesses the knowledge and practical skills of 15-year-olds. The study does not simply test whether students remember the school curriculum. It measures how well they can apply their knowledge to real-life situations.

The 2025 assessment was the ninth cycle of PISA. The study was previously conducted every three years. From 2025 onwards, the interval between cycles has increased to four years.

Georgia first joined PISA in 2010 as part of the PISA 2009+ programme. Subsequent assessments took place in Georgia in 2015, 2018, 2022 and 2025.

A total of 6,855 students from 265 schools in Georgia took part in the latest assessment. Parents, school principals and 1,350 science teachers also completed questionnaires.

PISA 2025 study on Georgia

World.title: What Georgian, Russian and Tskhinvali sides discussed at 134th IPRM meeting
World.content:
The 134th meeting of the Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism (IPRM) was held in the village of Ergneti, in Georgia‘s Gori municipality.

The sides discussed developments along the occupation line in the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) since the previous meeting, as well as the current security situation.

The IPRM is a forum for addressing urgent security and humanitarian issues in the Georgian-Ossetian and Georgian-Abkhaz conflict zones. Its main objectives include securing the release of detainees, preventing incidents and addressing everyday problems faced by people living along the occupation line. Representatives of Georgia, Russia and the Tskhinvali region/Abkhazia take part in the meetings, facilitated by the OSCE and the EU Monitoring Mission.

According to Georgia’s State Security Service (SSG), the meeting included a detailed discussion of key incidents recorded in the occupied region and along the occupation line. Particular attention was paid to restrictions on freedom of movement at the so-called crossing points.

Irakli Antadze, deputy head of the SSG’s Analytical Department, said the Georgian side had demanded the release of all those it says are being illegally detained.

“We called for a humanitarian approach to ensure that all those illegally detained can return to their families. Our international partners also supported us on this. At this stage, I cannot say anything about specific results, as consultations are continuing,” Antadze said.

Irakli Antadze

According to Antadze, the sides also discussed new cases of so-called “borderisation” recorded in the Tskhinvali region since the previous meeting.

“Our positions were once again diametrically opposed, and we were unable to find common ground on this issue,” Antadze said.

At the meeting, Georgian officials again condemned what they described as illegal “borderisation” and highlighted what they said were continuing violations of fundamental human rights in the occupied Tskhinvali region.

The Georgian side also raised again the killing of Georgian citizen Tamaz Ginturi, demanding accountability and justice for the member or members of what it described as the Russian occupation forces responsible for his death.

The Georgian side also strongly demanded the immediate release of all those it says are being illegally detained.

The next IPRM meeting is scheduled for 22 October 2026.
