World.title: ‘It was a stitch-up’: Camberwell Golf Club dumps every woman from its board
World.content:
Exclusive SportGolfWorld golf ‘It was a stitch-up’: Camberwell Golf Club dumps every woman from its board Sam McClure September 9, 2026 — 7:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A local golf club that recently merged separate women’s and men’s clubs is embroiled in a gender dispute after every woman on its committee was dumped from their positions at a meeting on Tuesday night. The dispute has erupted only months after Camberwell’s historically separate men’s and women’s golf clubs came together, and centres on an increasingly acrimonious battle over how the new club should be governed and whether its female members have an equal voice. (Left to right) Michelle Trewin, who was vice captain of the Camberwell Ladies Golf Club, Sue Thek, who was its president, Julia Trafford, the secretary, and Lynne O’Brien and Jill Douglas. Four women walked out of the fiery committee meeting on Tuesday after the male president of the amalgamated Camberwell Golf Club, based at a council-owned course in Boroondara, informed them their appointments to the club’s general committee were invalid. Club president Craig Atkins confirmed the women had been removed but dismissed the events as a “storm in a teacup”, saying their appointments had been made incorrectly because of an error in the club’s constitution. There are 13 male members on the committee.



“They were appointed inappropriately through an error in the constitution and we had to correct the error,” Atkins told this masthead. But Julia Trafford, secretary of the Camberwell Ladies Golf Club and one of the women involved, was angered by the president’s actions. The Camberwell Golf Club is based at Freeway Golf Course. Joe Armao “It was a stitch-up and [we were] ambushed by the president,” Trafford said. “We left and some of the women were quite distressed.”



Minutes before the women were removed from the committee, David Greenhill – Golf Australia’s head of governance and risk – had completed an hour-long presentation to the club about modern governance, including the importance of gender equality. Soon after Greenhill finished speaking, the women were told they no longer held their committee positions. A sign at the Camberwell Golf Club, welcoming new members. Joe Armao Golf Australia has increasingly encouraged clubs to modernise their governance and improve female participation in leadership. Its general manager of “Places to Play”, Damien de Bohun, said boards should reflect the communities they serve.



“That is not negotiable,” he said. “You cannot build a welcoming, inclusive game if the people making decisions at club level don’t reflect the membership they serve. “At the invitation of women committee members, Golf Australia provided governance advice to Camberwell Golf Club as it reunified its men’s and women’s playing groups. Our advice was clear: review and modernise the constitution, adopt skills-based board composition, and ensure meaningful representation of women, consistent with the Australian Sports Commission’s governance principles and the Victorian government’s Balance the Board policy. “Removing women from a governance structure at the very moment a club is being asked to strengthen female representation is indefensible. “This is exactly why Golf Australia partnered with the Australian Institute of Company Directors to launch a national governance education program for the 11,000 volunteer directors who lead golf clubs across Australia.



“Golf will not advance while those in positions of leadership exert that influence to exclude the very people whose views and expertise the game’s continued growth depends upon.” Atkins insisted there was “nothing untoward” about the decision and conceded the process of modernising the club’s constitution had become “a little messy”. Four women walked out of Tuesday night’s committee meeting after being removed from their positions. Joe Armao He said the women had subsequently been offered a pathway back onto the committee “in a legal manner”, but claimed they had left the meeting before hearing the proposal. “They were disgruntled and stormed out of the meeting and didn’t even stay to hear the rest of the outcomes,” Atkins said.



Trafford strongly disputed Atkins’ version of events and said tensions had been building throughout the process of bringing the two clubs together. “We have felt all the way through this time that the president has been railroading us, trying to jam things through and acting as a gatekeeper,” she said. “It comes down to this line of thinking: ‘Yes, we will allow the ladies to do this, but only if we agree’. “We have never asked the men to do anything different. We are members of this club and we should have a voice on the committee.” Camberwell Golf Club and Camberwell Ladies Golf Club were previously separate, with 70 women and 230 men respectively. Both clubs played on Freeway Golf Course, which is run by GreenSpace (a golf course management company) on land owned by the City of Boroondara.



At the heart of the dispute is a disagreement over whether the union of the two clubs represented an amalgamation of equals or, as the women contend, their absorption into a club controlled by its male members. Trafford said the women believed the prevailing attitude at the golf club had been: “It’s really the men’s club and we are letting you join us, but you have to join us on our terms”. Atkins maintained the removal of the women was a constitutional correction rather than an attempt to exclude them from the administration of the club. But Trafford said the women intended to fight on, with an annual general meeting looming.



“We’re not disheartened. We do have an AGM coming up,” she said. “I think we need a changing of the guard, but it is difficult when the club is captured with an autocrat at the helm.” Boroondara CEO Daniel Freer was at the meeting. Boroondara Mayor Wes Gault said the council expected that community sport be “welcoming, inclusive and accessible to everyone. “That’s the standard we expect of all organisations operating on council-owned land,” he said.



“We strongly oppose any move that would deny women the opportunity to serve on a club board or hold membership on equal terms.” Boroondara Council has also been asked to investigate a separate recent local sporting incident involving a club from its area. The Boroondara Eagles Football Club claimed their under-12 girls match at Caloola Reserve – in a separate council area – was halted so an under-11 boys’ team could use the field instead. Football Victoria is also investigating. Sports news, results and expert commentary.

World.title: Disgraced businessman, fraudster and domestic abuser jailed over abuse of wife
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWDomestic violence Disgraced businessman, fraudster and domestic abuser jailed over abuse of wife Amber Schultz September 9, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The coercive control, abuse and gaslighting Narghiza Ergashova endured throughout her relationship with disgraced businessman and fraudster Enrico Pucci left her questioning reality. The 50-year-old logged into her Tesla app to track her, slow her car down to 40 kilometres per hour on main roads, manipulate climate controls and disconnect charging. He repeatedly contacted her employer until she was fired, forged an employment contract to trick her into believing she had a lucrative job and coerced her to hand over her life savings. Narghiza Ergashova said her sense of reality was slowly eroded under Enrico Pucci’s control. PENNY STEPHENS He strangled her, beat her, stalked her and convinced her he was serving a prison sentence to protect her from facing charges, causing her to become fearful and distrustful of the police. “I didn’t have a day’s worth of reality,” Ergashova said.



“Every ounce of my independence was taken away because the only way he could be with me is to make me completely and utterly dependent and subservient to him ... I felt like a slave.” Pucci has been convicted of 30 domestic violence-related offences, including eight counts of stalking, six counts of assault, two counts of choking, five counts of contravening an AVO, one count of coercive control, assault occasioning actual bodily harm, financial deception, revenge porn and theft. He pleaded guilty a week before his trial started and was sentenced last week to two years in prison. With time served, he will be released on parole in February. Narghiza Ergashova said Enrico Pucci’s abuse started slowly. He is one of the first tranche of people to serve jail time for coercive control, a criminal offence introduced in July 2024. He was also issued a five-year apprehended violence order.



Extreme violence and control Pucci and Ergashova met in 2018. “The first year and a half was bliss … [but he] is skilled in misrepresenting and lying,” she said. The couple’s relationship was built on a lie: Pucci was still married despite telling her he was divorced, and was engaged to both Ergashova and another woman simultaneously. Soon, the violence started. In 2020, Pucci dragged her out of a car in a park and drove off, before returning and accelerating toward her, braking just in front of her. Twice he strangled her, once until she lost consciousness. He threatened to send sexually explicit images to her employer. He broke her finger and texted her death threats. “Don’t tempt me, you know I can kill you with one hand,” he wrote. “I will destroy you.”



Each time Ergashova tried to leave, Pucci threatened her until she returned, convincing her it was safest to stay. They lived separately, with Pucci dropping into Ergashova’s home in Sydney’s north-west. They married in 2021. In July 2024, Pucci made repeated anonymous calls and emails to her employer until she was fired. In early 2025, he presented her with a fake employment contract offering a consulting role with a nearly quarter-million-dollar salary, and created false email addresses to which Ergashova wrote. She was never paid and turned down legitimate accountancy work. Shortly after, Pucci solicited $100,000 from her, promising to repay it within a week. She transferred her life savings.



“Unemployed at home [and] surveilled through my car, through my watch, from my computer … I was completely vulnerable,” she said. “He created such lies in my head that I lived my life thinking he saved my life, that he was my rescuer.” By late 2025, Ergashova thought she had left for good, but Pucci stole her smartwatch to track her and tampered with her Tesla app. He manipulated settings remotely and set up parental controls to lock her out, and showed up at her home and social outings. Pucci later sent photos of injuries Ergashova had inflicted in self-defence, claiming police were planning to charge her with grievous bodily harm.



Enrico Pucci has also been banned from managing corporations for five years after engaging in illegal phoenix activity. LinkedIn “I wouldn’t open the door to police… not knowing that they’re trying to get a statement from me against him,” she said. It was only when she provided evidence for coercive control charges that the full reality of the abuse dawned on her. “I’m reading [the evidence], thinking, ‘No, this can’t be my life’.” In sentencing, Judge Stuart Devine said Pucci had engaged in “sustained and deliberate” behaviour to control Ergashova. “[Through] repeated surveillance, economic manipulation, exploitation of victim’s vulnerabilities … [he] was coercive and controlling in nature, to entrench power and compliance,” Devine said.



A series of frauds Pucci also defrauded another woman out of $490,000, whom he was engaged to at the same time he was both married and in a relationship with Ergashova. Weeks after loaning him the money, he broke up with the woman, who goes by the online nom de plume Lady Whistleblow. When she requested the money back, he sent her a photo of him sitting next to piles of cash, according to court documents. Pucci then used some of the cash to pay back the money he owed to Ergashova. Lady Whistleblow launched legal proceedings alleging she was a victim of a “sophisticated scam” devised by Pucci, his family and Ergashova to lure her into handing over money. According to her case, the group convinced her Pucci was single. Her case claims the group targeted her with a “concerted campaign of harassment”, lodging more than 40 police complaints – none of which resulted in charges.



As the pair battled a civil case arising from the half-million-dollar fraud, Pucci convinced Ergashova they needed to win together for her to regain her accounting career. ‘Lady Whistleblow’ has never been paid back her $490,000 by Enrico Pucci despite a court order. A Current Affair The initial judgement found that while Ergashova intimidated Whistleblow, her role in the alleged conspiracy was unclear. Pucci’s assets were frozen and the case remains before the courts. Ergashova has filed a motion to dismiss herself from the case. The district court ordered Pucci to repay the funds in 2021. He declared bankruptcy. Pucci has also been banned from managing companies for five years after the Australian Securities and Investments Commission found he engaged in illegal phoenixing with three failed firms. This follows a 2017 Federal Court ruling that he and his brothers exploited vulnerable employees under a “shameless” scheme.



Related Article Careers GPS cleaning company treated vulnerable employees as 'slaves': court A path to healing Since leaving Pucci, Ergashova has moved interstate and rekindled her career. “I’ve embraced the fact that anyone can be a victim of domestic control,” she said. She is speaking out to help others recognise abuse and challenge victim stereotypes.



“I’m back in my power, but I’m also looking back and thinking, how did I let this happen to me? It’s years of my life I can never get back.” Their divorce will be finalised in November. Pucci will be released on parole in February. He is appealing his sentence. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: How three coaches living together conjured the NRL’s biggest turnaround
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 How three coaches living together conjured the NRL’s biggest turnaround Adrian Proszenko September 9, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It has all the ingredients for a hit reality television show. Three rugby league coaches, living together for more than two months, in a three-bedroom Airbnb on Newcastle’s Bar Beach last summer. It is here, in a share house in Merewether, that the Knights took the first steps in ridding themselves of the wooden spoon and commencing a storied run that has taken them into the finals. The first big call Newcastle coach Justin Holbrook made after succeeding Adam O’Brien was arranging accommodation and inviting assistant Brett White and Steve Hales to live with him. It resulted in a trio who had never worked together before spending every waking moment together from the start of pre-season last October until the Christmas break. In doing so, they formed a strong bond that helped them identify their coaching philosophy and the culture they wanted to instil into a side that became the NRL’s biggest improver in 2026.



“It was the best thing for us,” said Holbrook, whose team takes on South Sydney in an elimination final on Friday night. “I’d worked with both of them over the years separately, but they had never met each other. “With us starting straight away, none of our families had moved up. They put us all in together and it worked out as the best thing that could have happened. Newcastle Knights coach Justin Holbrook lived with his assistants, Brett White and Steve Hales, during the NRL pre-season. “We were together every day, would come home from work and go out and have dinner. We were always communicating and connecting. It was a really enjoyable time.” It quickly became evident that the housemates had very different personalities. Holbrook and White would be in bed by 8pm most nights, in order to train early the next day. Hales was a night owl who had little interest in exercise. Or cleaning.



“When Halesy worked out we had to do the dishes, he wanted to put a stop to that,” Holbrook chuckled. “He’s not very well domesticated. “When Whitey’s young bloke come down to stay, we thought he was a five-star Michelin chef, he made some great dinners for us. Knights assistants Steve Hales and Brett White. “We had the cheap eat nights at Newcastle, we’d rotate through the different pubs and steak nights. We did a lot of that, not a lot of cooking.” Despite their differences, they quickly formed strong bonds. They would swim at the beach every day after work, play wall tennis with the locals and take training sessions out into the community.



During a pre-season staff development day, as is custom at the club, the newbies are required to lead a singalong on the bus. When it was Hales’ turn, he chose What about me? He had barely got through the first verse when a colleague handed him a mobile phone. On the Facetime call was Shannon Noll. “Someone tells me you might need some help with this song,” Noll said, before accompanying Hales on the tune. “There was always something going on, it was always upbeat,” Holbrook said.



Such is the turnaround at Newcastle this season that Holbrook is one of the leading contenders for the Dally M coach of the year award. Regardless of whether he wins it, the former Titans mentor is thankful to again be working at the Knights, where he made his NRL playing debut as the understudy to Immortal halfback Andrew Johns. “I always hoped one day to coach Newcastle and the fact I’m doing it now, I’m grateful for that opportunity,” he said. “I love coaching, I’m excited coming to work every day and that always helps. I enjoy who I’m working with – that makes my job easier.” Asked if he believed the Knights could make the finals in those early days in the Merewether sharehouse, Holbrook said: “Yeah, we did. It began with us coaches coming in and putting some good plans and principles in place. “Once the players come back to pre-season training, they are the ones who gave me confidence through their work ethic.



Related Article NRL 2026 ‘Money’s not everything’: The contract conundrum facing Panthers “We had a lot of work to do as players and coaches, but we all gelled together and we’re enjoying what we’re doing. When you’re enjoying it you work harder, because you don’t see it as work. “The players delivered in that area. We were confident right from the start.” Sports news, results and expert commentary.

World.title: Superannuation shouldn’t be untouchable, says expert: ‘People get hysterical’
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalSuperannuation Superannuation shouldn’t be untouchable, says expert: ‘People get hysterical’ Paul Sakkal September 9, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A leading superannuation expert has called for an open debate on the use of retirement savings for housing and non-retirement purposes as the Coalition’s top brass splits on how to respond to One Nation’s plan to use super to top up wages. Days after Labor declared the next election a referendum on superannuation, Dr Emily Millane – who is about to publish Super, a history of Australia’s multitrillion-dollar private pension scheme – said the debate on super had become “hysterical”. Labor Treasurer Jim Chalmers and One Nation treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce on Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen One Nation announced a policy on Monday allowing people to cash out a quarter of their 12 per cent yearly superannuation contribution as an effective wage rise for three years to deal with high inflation. The Coalition was considering a similar plan during Sussan Ley’s leadership and is now mulling more radical options, including using super as collateral to buy a home or as a mortgage offset.



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Treasurer Jim Chalmers said Pauline Hanson’s plan would undermine the purpose of compulsory retirement savings and showed Hanson was anti-worker. While Millane did not offer specific support to Hanson’s idea, the former federal Labor adviser said, “super has also always had uses and roles beyond building retirement wealth”. Related Article Superannuation Joyce says he’s ‘not Jesus Christ’ when pushed on controversial superannuation policy “Super has always been deeply political. It was an idea that rose up through the union movement and was given legislative expression by the ALP,” she said, noting a key objective for the policy at its inception in the 1980s was to counter stagflation by substituting short-term wage rises with contributions for retirement. “Now that we have around $4.8 trillion sitting in the system, it is even more reasonable that we would have conversations about super’s role in the broader economy. The reasons we see people shut this conversation down are political, ideological and because of self-interest.



“There is something about super ... that makes people hysterical. Super needs to be locked away and preserved. But this shouldn’t preclude a reasonable discussion about the role of super in the economy, including proposals to boost housing affordability on both the demand and supply sides.” Millane is a senior fellow at Melbourne Law School and a former researcher at the Grattan Institute, an independent centre-left think-tank, and the ANU’s Tax and Transfer Policy Institute. On Tuesday, former Grattan chief John Daley said he agreed with the core of One Nation’s proposal, though warned it may be inflationary. “The core of [the One Nation] plan is right. The idea that people don’t need to save 12 per cent [of their wages for retirement] is true for the vast majority,” Daley told The Conversation. Daley said 9 per cent was the “break-even” point. One Nation’s super scheme caught Opposition Leader Angus Taylor off guard as his party trailed Hanson and worked through slow internal processes to develop policies on superannuation and housing.



Some senior Liberal MPs want to counter Hanson by shaking up the superannuation system in an even bigger way than One Nation and to link the policies to housing rather than topping up wages. Related Article Superannuation Why Australia’s pension payment bill is about to plummet Housing spokesman Andrew Bragg said this week that “mortgage offsets, collateral arrangements, cash-out measures” were all being looked at and included “pluses and minuses”. However, some of Bragg’s senior shadow cabinet colleagues have expressed reservations about taking on a big fight with the influential super movement and its union links. On Wednesday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers released forecasts from the upcoming intergenerational report showing the share of government spending on the age pension is expected to fall due to growth in superannuation assets. The report forecasts that the pension’s call on the budget will fall from 2.3 per cent of GDP now to 1.8 per cent by 2066.



Bill Kelty, an architect of the Hawke-Keating accords that led to superannuation, cautioned against Labor “jumping up and down saying [housing-for-super] is a terrible policy” because Keating himself took to the 1993 election a policy to use super savings to pay for deposits. Labor ultimately walked away from the policy because it could stoke house prices. Kelty said Australia’s pension system was the international gold standard, as demonstrated when Albanese used the huge pool of funds as leverage when he met Donald Trump in Washington last year and said super funds could invest in US businesses. The former ACTU head said Hanson and the Coalition might have good intentions in putting forward ideas for how to boost household incomes, but that Hanson’s plan is misguided. “It’s like Santa Claus stealing from the kids’ money box to buy them their Christmas presents,” he said. World.title: Albanese, Taylor hold talks on migration, as Labor eyes low-key policy reveal
World.content:
PoliticsFederalImmigration Albanese, Taylor hold talks on migration, as Labor eyes low-key policy reveal Paul Sakkal September 9, 2026 — 7:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor have held talks on migration as Labor seeks a pathway to get its fresh crackdown through the Senate, but the Coalition’s demands on how to crunch the overseas intake means a deal is not yet in sight. If the two major parties can resolve their differences, government sources said Labor’s highly anticipated migration plan could be put to parliament as early as next week. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor reacts as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaks during question time. Alex Ellinghausen A planned National Press Club speech to announce the policy from Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, which was spectacularly cancelled last month, is unlikely to be the method by which Labor announces measures to reduce the net overseas migration figure from 300,000 to 225,000. Barring any belated change, Labor is expected to reveal its plan in a more low-key manner rather than a set-piece speech, which may create an unwanted sense of theatre as Labor comes under pressure from One Nation and the Coalition after years of overshooting migration targets.



Labor is highly unlikely to secure the Greens’ support for any reduction in migration, so Albanese sought a meeting with Taylor in parliament on Wednesday to discuss potential points of agreement. But Coalition sources said the parties remained far apart. Opposition MPs are concerned about any perception that the Coalition would support Labor on migration, which could fuel Pauline Hanson’s talking point on the Labor-Coalition “uni-party”. Labor, under political pressure to act on migration without offending the left and migrant communities, is prepared to use regulation rather than legislation to make as many changes as possible if it cannot secure support in the Senate. It needs either the Greens or Coalition to pass bills as it does not hold a majority. Taylor wrote to Albanese on Wednesday saying Australians had “lost confidence in your government’s ability to protect our borders” and said the net overseas migration figure should be about 50,000 fewer than Labor’s target. He set 10 red lines for any legislation, including making it illegal to repatriate ISIS families; establishing a UK-style safe-country list to stop sham asylum applications; removing legal aid for people appealing visa decisions; restricting access to graduate courses to students seeking in-demand skills; deporting the 77,000 unlawful non-citizens; and turning the Australian Values Statement into a visa condition.



Related Article Immigration Five days later, Hanson still struggles to articulate migration policy This masthead has previously reported that Labor was considering a heavier focus on deportations, visa-hopping, bogus asylum claims, and aligning the international education system more closely with the need of the economy. But Taylor’s hard line on the saga surrounding ISIS brides presents as one potential sticking point that may preclude a deal. Taylor, who is well behind Hanson in the polls, could claim to be controlling the debate on migration if he helped Labor formulate a tough package. But he would open himself up to One Nation criticism that he had gone soft by working with the government in a critical area of policy to conservative voters.

World.title: Embattled football club used school clinic funds to pay rent on luxury Sydney apartment
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsNSWNSW State Parliament Embattled football club used school clinic funds to pay rent on luxury Sydney apartment Max Maddison September 9, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Macarthur Bulls A-League franchise spent thousands of taxpayers’ dollars earmarked for after-school football clinics on a luxury residential apartment complex. Facing a parliamentary inquiry established to examine the Football in Schools program, the embattled Bulls on Wednesday launched an aggressive counterattack, claiming a draft auditors’ report critical of the Department of Education administration of the program had been removed. The Macarthur Bulls’ use of taxpayer funds – including for entertainment – has come under the microscope of a parliamentary inquiry. SMH The most recent revelation compounds allegations the club misspent the $6 million in taxpayer funds. Weeks after the Herald discovered club staff had spent thousands of dollars on restaurants, cafes and alcohol, Macarthur offered to repay $3415.93 it claimed had been “incorrectly coded”. The club’s spending will undergo a forensic audit by McGrathNicol, an advisory firm. However, the club’s expenditure records reveal taxpayer funds may have been used for residential rental payments. Expenditure statements show a $3033.76 BPAY payment made to Lateral Residences – a collection of “resort-style” apartments located in Zetland, Liverpool and Wolli Creek – in early 2024 was attributed to the program, with Macarthur classifying it as “HO rental”.



Related Article Exclusive

Government grants A-League clubs slammed over taxpayer-funded $14.5m Football in Schools scheme Macarthur was approached for comment. A departmental spokesman noted the ongoing forensic audit, saying: “The department has the right to withhold, or recover, grants funding if compliance with the funding deed is not addressed.” The discovery compounds concerns that large sums of taxpayer funds supposed to pay for school and holiday clinics in south-western Sydney have instead been spent underwriting the club’s commercial operation and on expenses unrelated to the program. The club previously apportioned $148,941.54 of taxpayer funds to Titanium Waste Management – a company of which the Macarthur Bulls chairman Gino Marra and chief executive Sam Krslovic are shareholders – for head office rental in Oran Park.



As it acknowledged misspending taxpayer funds, Macarthur used Wednesday’s inquiry hearing to blame the program’s administrative mishaps on the department, urging the committee to recommend the Football in Schools program be “preserved, continued and expanded”. “The administrative problems that have attracted attention are, overwhelmingly, the consequence of how the Department of Education established, funded and administered this program,” the club said in a submission to the inquiry. Macarthur claimed they were told by bureaucrats the department never wanted to administer the program, and complained the club was unjustly barred from spending funds on items such as coaches uniforms. The department had deemed Macarthur’s $100,000 outlay on coaches’ uniforms and sneakers was non-eligible. Asked to provide evidence to substantiate claims, Peter McLaughlin, club’s government relations manager, who fronted the inquiry in the absence of Marra, said he was unable to reproduce evidence about the department’s unwillingness to run the program because the claims had only been conveyed verbally. Requests for copies of the original audit were also taken on notice. In later evidence, departmental secretary Murat Dizdar categorically rejected the claims. A departmental audit executive said the only edits made to Grant Thornton’s audit report were altering capital letters and wording, denying any material of substance was changed.

World.title: ‘It was a stitch-up’: Camberwell Golf Club dumps every woman from its board
World.content:
Exclusive SportGolfWorld golf ‘It was a stitch-up’: Camberwell Golf Club dumps every woman from its board Sam McClure September 9, 2026 — 7:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A local golf club that recently merged separate women’s and men’s clubs is embroiled in a gender dispute after every woman on its committee was dumped from their positions at a meeting on Tuesday night. The dispute has erupted only months after Camberwell’s historically separate men’s and women’s golf clubs came together, and centres on an increasingly acrimonious battle over how the new club should be governed and whether its female members have an equal voice. (Left to right) Michelle Trewin, who was vice captain of the Camberwell Ladies Golf Club, Sue Thek, who was its president, Julia Trafford, the secretary, and Lynne O’Brien and Jill Douglas. Four women walked out of the fiery committee meeting on Tuesday after the male president of the amalgamated Camberwell Golf Club, based at a council-owned course in Boroondara, informed them their appointments to the club’s general committee were invalid. Club president Craig Atkins confirmed the women had been removed but dismissed the events as a “storm in a teacup”, saying their appointments had been made incorrectly because of an error in the club’s constitution. There are 13 male members on the committee.



“They were appointed inappropriately through an error in the constitution and we had to correct the error,” Atkins told this masthead. But Julia Trafford, secretary of the Camberwell Ladies Golf Club and one of the women involved, was angered by the president’s actions. The Camberwell Golf Club is based at Freeway Golf Course. Joe Armao “It was a stitch-up and [we were] ambushed by the president,” Trafford said. “We left and some of the women were quite distressed.”



Minutes before the women were removed from the committee, David Greenhill – Golf Australia’s head of governance and risk – had completed an hour-long presentation to the club about modern governance, including the importance of gender equality. Soon after Greenhill finished speaking, the women were told they no longer held their committee positions. A sign at the Camberwell Golf Club, welcoming new members. Joe Armao Golf Australia has increasingly encouraged clubs to modernise their governance and improve female participation in leadership. Its general manager of “Places to Play”, Damien de Bohun, said boards should reflect the communities they serve.



“That is not negotiable,” he said. “You cannot build a welcoming, inclusive game if the people making decisions at club level don’t reflect the membership they serve. “At the invitation of women committee members, Golf Australia provided governance advice to Camberwell Golf Club as it reunified its men’s and women’s playing groups. Our advice was clear: review and modernise the constitution, adopt skills-based board composition, and ensure meaningful representation of women, consistent with the Australian Sports Commission’s governance principles and the Victorian government’s Balance the Board policy. “Removing women from a governance structure at the very moment a club is being asked to strengthen female representation is indefensible. “This is exactly why Golf Australia partnered with the Australian Institute of Company Directors to launch a national governance education program for the 11,000 volunteer directors who lead golf clubs across Australia.



“Golf will not advance while those in positions of leadership exert that influence to exclude the very people whose views and expertise the game’s continued growth depends upon.” Atkins insisted there was “nothing untoward” about the decision and conceded the process of modernising the club’s constitution had become “a little messy”. Four women walked out of Tuesday night’s committee meeting after being removed from their positions. Joe Armao He said the women had subsequently been offered a pathway back onto the committee “in a legal manner”, but claimed they had left the meeting before hearing the proposal. “They were disgruntled and stormed out of the meeting and didn’t even stay to hear the rest of the outcomes,” Atkins said.



Trafford strongly disputed Atkins’ version of events and said tensions had been building throughout the process of bringing the two clubs together. “We have felt all the way through this time that the president has been railroading us, trying to jam things through and acting as a gatekeeper,” she said. “It comes down to this line of thinking: ‘Yes, we will allow the ladies to do this, but only if we agree’. “We have never asked the men to do anything different. We are members of this club and we should have a voice on the committee.” Camberwell Golf Club and Camberwell Ladies Golf Club were previously separate, with 70 women and 230 men respectively. Both clubs played on Freeway Golf Course, which is run by GreenSpace (a golf course management company) on land owned by the City of Boroondara.



At the heart of the dispute is a disagreement over whether the union of the two clubs represented an amalgamation of equals or, as the women contend, their absorption into a club controlled by its male members. Trafford said the women believed the prevailing attitude at the golf club had been: “It’s really the men’s club and we are letting you join us, but you have to join us on our terms”. Atkins maintained the removal of the women was a constitutional correction rather than an attempt to exclude them from the administration of the club. But Trafford said the women intended to fight on, with an annual general meeting looming.



“We’re not disheartened. We do have an AGM coming up,” she said. “I think we need a changing of the guard, but it is difficult when the club is captured with an autocrat at the helm.” Boroondara CEO Daniel Freer was at the meeting. Boroondara Mayor Wes Gault said the council expected that community sport be “welcoming, inclusive and accessible to everyone. “That’s the standard we expect of all organisations operating on council-owned land,” he said.



“We strongly oppose any move that would deny women the opportunity to serve on a club board or hold membership on equal terms.” Boroondara Council has also been asked to investigate a separate recent local sporting incident involving a club from its area. The Boroondara Eagles Football Club claimed their under-12 girls match at Caloola Reserve – in a separate council area – was halted so an under-11 boys’ team could use the field instead. Football Victoria is also investigating. Sports news, results and expert commentary.

World.title: Disgraced businessman, fraudster and domestic abuser jailed over abuse of wife
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWDomestic violence Disgraced businessman, fraudster and domestic abuser jailed over abuse of wife Amber Schultz September 9, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The coercive control, abuse and gaslighting Narghiza Ergashova endured throughout her relationship with disgraced businessman and fraudster Enrico Pucci left her questioning reality. The 50-year-old logged into her Tesla app to track her, slow her car down to 40 kilometres per hour on main roads, manipulate climate controls and disconnect charging. He repeatedly contacted her employer until she was fired, forged an employment contract to trick her into believing she had a lucrative job and coerced her to hand over her life savings. Narghiza Ergashova said her sense of reality was slowly eroded under Enrico Pucci’s control. PENNY STEPHENS He strangled her, beat her, stalked her and convinced her he was serving a prison sentence to protect her from facing charges, causing her to become fearful and distrustful of the police. “I didn’t have a day’s worth of reality,” Ergashova said.



“Every ounce of my independence was taken away because the only way he could be with me is to make me completely and utterly dependent and subservient to him ... I felt like a slave.” Pucci has been convicted of 30 domestic violence-related offences, including eight counts of stalking, six counts of assault, two counts of choking, five counts of contravening an AVO, one count of coercive control, assault occasioning actual bodily harm, financial deception, revenge porn and theft. He pleaded guilty a week before his trial started and was sentenced last week to two years in prison. With time served, he will be released on parole in February. Narghiza Ergashova said Enrico Pucci’s abuse started slowly. He is one of the first tranche of people to serve jail time for coercive control, a criminal offence introduced in July 2024. He was also issued a five-year apprehended violence order.



Extreme violence and control Pucci and Ergashova met in 2018. “The first year and a half was bliss … [but he] is skilled in misrepresenting and lying,” she said. The couple’s relationship was built on a lie: Pucci was still married despite telling her he was divorced, and was engaged to both Ergashova and another woman simultaneously. Soon, the violence started. In 2020, Pucci dragged her out of a car in a park and drove off, before returning and accelerating toward her, braking just in front of her. Twice he strangled her, once until she lost consciousness. He threatened to send sexually explicit images to her employer. He broke her finger and texted her death threats. “Don’t tempt me, you know I can kill you with one hand,” he wrote. “I will destroy you.”



Each time Ergashova tried to leave, Pucci threatened her until she returned, convincing her it was safest to stay. They lived separately, with Pucci dropping into Ergashova’s home in Sydney’s north-west. They married in 2021. In July 2024, Pucci made repeated anonymous calls and emails to her employer until she was fired. In early 2025, he presented her with a fake employment contract offering a consulting role with a nearly quarter-million-dollar salary, and created false email addresses to which Ergashova wrote. She was never paid and turned down legitimate accountancy work. Shortly after, Pucci solicited $100,000 from her, promising to repay it within a week. She transferred her life savings.



“Unemployed at home [and] surveilled through my car, through my watch, from my computer … I was completely vulnerable,” she said. “He created such lies in my head that I lived my life thinking he saved my life, that he was my rescuer.” By late 2025, Ergashova thought she had left for good, but Pucci stole her smartwatch to track her and tampered with her Tesla app. He manipulated settings remotely and set up parental controls to lock her out, and showed up at her home and social outings. Pucci later sent photos of injuries Ergashova had inflicted in self-defence, claiming police were planning to charge her with grievous bodily harm.



Enrico Pucci has also been banned from managing corporations for five years after engaging in illegal phoenix activity. LinkedIn “I wouldn’t open the door to police… not knowing that they’re trying to get a statement from me against him,” she said. It was only when she provided evidence for coercive control charges that the full reality of the abuse dawned on her. “I’m reading [the evidence], thinking, ‘No, this can’t be my life’.” In sentencing, Judge Stuart Devine said Pucci had engaged in “sustained and deliberate” behaviour to control Ergashova. “[Through] repeated surveillance, economic manipulation, exploitation of victim’s vulnerabilities … [he] was coercive and controlling in nature, to entrench power and compliance,” Devine said.



A series of frauds Pucci also defrauded another woman out of $490,000, whom he was engaged to at the same time he was both married and in a relationship with Ergashova. Weeks after loaning him the money, he broke up with the woman, who goes by the online nom de plume Lady Whistleblow. When she requested the money back, he sent her a photo of him sitting next to piles of cash, according to court documents. Pucci then used some of the cash to pay back the money he owed to Ergashova. Lady Whistleblow launched legal proceedings alleging she was a victim of a “sophisticated scam” devised by Pucci, his family and Ergashova to lure her into handing over money. According to her case, the group convinced her Pucci was single. Her case claims the group targeted her with a “concerted campaign of harassment”, lodging more than 40 police complaints – none of which resulted in charges.



As the pair battled a civil case arising from the half-million-dollar fraud, Pucci convinced Ergashova they needed to win together for her to regain her accounting career. ‘Lady Whistleblow’ has never been paid back her $490,000 by Enrico Pucci despite a court order. A Current Affair The initial judgement found that while Ergashova intimidated Whistleblow, her role in the alleged conspiracy was unclear. Pucci’s assets were frozen and the case remains before the courts. Ergashova has filed a motion to dismiss herself from the case. The district court ordered Pucci to repay the funds in 2021. He declared bankruptcy. Pucci has also been banned from managing companies for five years after the Australian Securities and Investments Commission found he engaged in illegal phoenixing with three failed firms. This follows a 2017 Federal Court ruling that he and his brothers exploited vulnerable employees under a “shameless” scheme.



Related Article Careers GPS cleaning company treated vulnerable employees as 'slaves': court A path to healing Since leaving Pucci, Ergashova has moved interstate and rekindled her career. “I’ve embraced the fact that anyone can be a victim of domestic control,” she said. She is speaking out to help others recognise abuse and challenge victim stereotypes.



“I’m back in my power, but I’m also looking back and thinking, how did I let this happen to me? It’s years of my life I can never get back.” Their divorce will be finalised in November. Pucci will be released on parole in February. He is appealing his sentence. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: How three coaches living together conjured the NRL’s biggest turnaround
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 How three coaches living together conjured the NRL’s biggest turnaround Adrian Proszenko September 9, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It has all the ingredients for a hit reality television show. Three rugby league coaches, living together for more than two months, in a three-bedroom Airbnb on Newcastle’s Bar Beach last summer. It is here, in a share house in Merewether, that the Knights took the first steps in ridding themselves of the wooden spoon and commencing a storied run that has taken them into the finals. The first big call Newcastle coach Justin Holbrook made after succeeding Adam O’Brien was arranging accommodation and inviting assistant Brett White and Steve Hales to live with him. It resulted in a trio who had never worked together before spending every waking moment together from the start of pre-season last October until the Christmas break. In doing so, they formed a strong bond that helped them identify their coaching philosophy and the culture they wanted to instil into a side that became the NRL’s biggest improver in 2026.



“It was the best thing for us,” said Holbrook, whose team takes on South Sydney in an elimination final on Friday night. “I’d worked with both of them over the years separately, but they had never met each other. “With us starting straight away, none of our families had moved up. They put us all in together and it worked out as the best thing that could have happened. Newcastle Knights coach Justin Holbrook lived with his assistants, Brett White and Steve Hales, during the NRL pre-season. “We were together every day, would come home from work and go out and have dinner. We were always communicating and connecting. It was a really enjoyable time.” It quickly became evident that the housemates had very different personalities. Holbrook and White would be in bed by 8pm most nights, in order to train early the next day. Hales was a night owl who had little interest in exercise. Or cleaning.



“When Halesy worked out we had to do the dishes, he wanted to put a stop to that,” Holbrook chuckled. “He’s not very well domesticated. “When Whitey’s young bloke come down to stay, we thought he was a five-star Michelin chef, he made some great dinners for us. Knights assistants Steve Hales and Brett White. “We had the cheap eat nights at Newcastle, we’d rotate through the different pubs and steak nights. We did a lot of that, not a lot of cooking.” Despite their differences, they quickly formed strong bonds. They would swim at the beach every day after work, play wall tennis with the locals and take training sessions out into the community.



During a pre-season staff development day, as is custom at the club, the newbies are required to lead a singalong on the bus. When it was Hales’ turn, he chose What about me? He had barely got through the first verse when a colleague handed him a mobile phone. On the Facetime call was Shannon Noll. “Someone tells me you might need some help with this song,” Noll said, before accompanying Hales on the tune. “There was always something going on, it was always upbeat,” Holbrook said.



Such is the turnaround at Newcastle this season that Holbrook is one of the leading contenders for the Dally M coach of the year award. Regardless of whether he wins it, the former Titans mentor is thankful to again be working at the Knights, where he made his NRL playing debut as the understudy to Immortal halfback Andrew Johns. “I always hoped one day to coach Newcastle and the fact I’m doing it now, I’m grateful for that opportunity,” he said. “I love coaching, I’m excited coming to work every day and that always helps. I enjoy who I’m working with – that makes my job easier.” Asked if he believed the Knights could make the finals in those early days in the Merewether sharehouse, Holbrook said: “Yeah, we did. It began with us coaches coming in and putting some good plans and principles in place. “Once the players come back to pre-season training, they are the ones who gave me confidence through their work ethic.



Related Article NRL 2026 ‘Money’s not everything’: The contract conundrum facing Panthers “We had a lot of work to do as players and coaches, but we all gelled together and we’re enjoying what we’re doing. When you’re enjoying it you work harder, because you don’t see it as work. “The players delivered in that area. We were confident right from the start.” Sports news, results and expert commentary.

World.title: Superannuation shouldn’t be untouchable, says expert: ‘People get hysterical’
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalSuperannuation Superannuation shouldn’t be untouchable, says expert: ‘People get hysterical’ Paul Sakkal September 9, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A leading superannuation expert has called for an open debate on the use of retirement savings for housing and non-retirement purposes as the Coalition’s top brass splits on how to respond to One Nation’s plan to use super to top up wages. Days after Labor declared the next election a referendum on superannuation, Dr Emily Millane – who is about to publish Super, a history of Australia’s multitrillion-dollar private pension scheme – said the debate on super had become “hysterical”. Labor Treasurer Jim Chalmers and One Nation treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce on Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen One Nation announced a policy on Monday allowing people to cash out a quarter of their 12 per cent yearly superannuation contribution as an effective wage rise for three years to deal with high inflation. The Coalition was considering a similar plan during Sussan Ley’s leadership and is now mulling more radical options, including using super as collateral to buy a home or as a mortgage offset.



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Treasurer Jim Chalmers said Pauline Hanson’s plan would undermine the purpose of compulsory retirement savings and showed Hanson was anti-worker. While Millane did not offer specific support to Hanson’s idea, the former federal Labor adviser said, “super has also always had uses and roles beyond building retirement wealth”. Related Article Superannuation Joyce says he’s ‘not Jesus Christ’ when pushed on controversial superannuation policy “Super has always been deeply political. It was an idea that rose up through the union movement and was given legislative expression by the ALP,” she said, noting a key objective for the policy at its inception in the 1980s was to counter stagflation by substituting short-term wage rises with contributions for retirement. “Now that we have around $4.8 trillion sitting in the system, it is even more reasonable that we would have conversations about super’s role in the broader economy. The reasons we see people shut this conversation down are political, ideological and because of self-interest.



“There is something about super ... that makes people hysterical. Super needs to be locked away and preserved. But this shouldn’t preclude a reasonable discussion about the role of super in the economy, including proposals to boost housing affordability on both the demand and supply sides.” Millane is a senior fellow at Melbourne Law School and a former researcher at the Grattan Institute, an independent centre-left think-tank, and the ANU’s Tax and Transfer Policy Institute. On Tuesday, former Grattan chief John Daley said he agreed with the core of One Nation’s proposal, though warned it may be inflationary. “The core of [the One Nation] plan is right. The idea that people don’t need to save 12 per cent [of their wages for retirement] is true for the vast majority,” Daley told The Conversation. Daley said 9 per cent was the “break-even” point. One Nation’s super scheme caught Opposition Leader Angus Taylor off guard as his party trailed Hanson and worked through slow internal processes to develop policies on superannuation and housing.



Some senior Liberal MPs want to counter Hanson by shaking up the superannuation system in an even bigger way than One Nation and to link the policies to housing rather than topping up wages. Related Article Superannuation Why Australia’s pension payment bill is about to plummet Housing spokesman Andrew Bragg said this week that “mortgage offsets, collateral arrangements, cash-out measures” were all being looked at and included “pluses and minuses”. However, some of Bragg’s senior shadow cabinet colleagues have expressed reservations about taking on a big fight with the influential super movement and its union links. On Wednesday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers released forecasts from the upcoming intergenerational report showing the share of government spending on the age pension is expected to fall due to growth in superannuation assets. The report forecasts that the pension’s call on the budget will fall from 2.3 per cent of GDP now to 1.8 per cent by 2066.



Bill Kelty, an architect of the Hawke-Keating accords that led to superannuation, cautioned against Labor “jumping up and down saying [housing-for-super] is a terrible policy” because Keating himself took to the 1993 election a policy to use super savings to pay for deposits. Labor ultimately walked away from the policy because it could stoke house prices. Kelty said Australia’s pension system was the international gold standard, as demonstrated when Albanese used the huge pool of funds as leverage when he met Donald Trump in Washington last year and said super funds could invest in US businesses. The former ACTU head said Hanson and the Coalition might have good intentions in putting forward ideas for how to boost household incomes, but that Hanson’s plan is misguided. “It’s like Santa Claus stealing from the kids’ money box to buy them their Christmas presents,” he said. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Albanese, Taylor hold talks on migration, as Labor eyes low-key policy reveal
World.content:
PoliticsFederalImmigration Albanese, Taylor hold talks on migration, as Labor eyes low-key policy reveal Paul Sakkal September 9, 2026 — 7:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor have held talks on migration as Labor seeks a pathway to get its fresh crackdown through the Senate, but the Coalition’s demands on how to crunch the overseas intake means a deal is not yet in sight. If the two major parties can resolve their differences, government sources said Labor’s highly anticipated migration plan could be put to parliament as early as next week. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor reacts as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaks during question time. Alex Ellinghausen A planned National Press Club speech to announce the policy from Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, which was spectacularly cancelled last month, is unlikely to be the method by which Labor announces measures to reduce the net overseas migration figure from 300,000 to 225,000. Barring any belated change, Labor is expected to reveal its plan in a more low-key manner rather than a set-piece speech, which may create an unwanted sense of theatre as Labor comes under pressure from One Nation and the Coalition after years of overshooting migration targets.



Labor is highly unlikely to secure the Greens’ support for any reduction in migration, so Albanese sought a meeting with Taylor in parliament on Wednesday to discuss potential points of agreement. But Coalition sources said the parties remained far apart. Opposition MPs are concerned about any perception that the Coalition would support Labor on migration, which could fuel Pauline Hanson’s talking point on the Labor-Coalition “uni-party”. Labor, under political pressure to act on migration without offending the left and migrant communities, is prepared to use regulation rather than legislation to make as many changes as possible if it cannot secure support in the Senate. It needs either the Greens or Coalition to pass bills as it does not hold a majority. Taylor wrote to Albanese on Wednesday saying Australians had “lost confidence in your government’s ability to protect our borders” and said the net overseas migration figure should be about 50,000 fewer than Labor’s target. He set 10 red lines for any legislation, including making it illegal to repatriate ISIS families; establishing a UK-style safe-country list to stop sham asylum applications; removing legal aid for people appealing visa decisions; restricting access to graduate courses to students seeking in-demand skills; deporting the 77,000 unlawful non-citizens; and turning the Australian Values Statement into a visa condition.



Related Article Immigration Five days later, Hanson still struggles to articulate migration policy This masthead has previously reported that Labor was considering a heavier focus on deportations, visa-hopping, bogus asylum claims, and aligning the international education system more closely with the need of the economy. But Taylor’s hard line on the saga surrounding ISIS brides presents as one potential sticking point that may preclude a deal. Taylor, who is well behind Hanson in the polls, could claim to be controlling the debate on migration if he helped Labor formulate a tough package. But he would open himself up to One Nation criticism that he had gone soft by working with the government in a critical area of policy to conservative voters.
