World.title: 'There will be no turning back': Murder co-conspirator reveals details of Ellerslie killing
World.content:
The details of a vicious attack on Auckland couple Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok and his wife Mei Han Chong in their Ellerslie home have been revealed in court today.

Shu Man Poon, who earlier pleaded guilty to the murders of the couple in 2023, said an air pistol and tomahawk were used during the attack, and that the victims' heads were stomped on.

His former co-defendant Lok Fung Lorrence Li is on trial in the High Court at Auckland, accused of murdering Kwok and Chong in their Ellerslie home.

He had also pleaded not guilty to conspiring to murder his former landlord with Poon.

Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok and Mei Han Chong with their son. (File photo) Supplied / NZ police

Poon earlier pleaded guilty to his role in the Kwok killings as well as the murder plot, and on Wednesday gave evidence against the man he said had pressured him to kill.

He was asked by prosecutor Matthew Nathan why he would be involved in the murder of the Kwoks, two people he had never met before.

After a long pause, Poon spoke.

"Before all this happened, I was being threatened by Mr Li my co-offender that he will promise to destroy my family," he said.

"Also, I had a debt with him of $7000."

The Kwok killings

Warning this section contains descriptions of graphic violence.

Poon recalled Li earlier showing him an email containing the Kwok's address.

Jurors had earlier heard Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok and Li had been in a traffic accident that was taken to the Disputes Tribunal.

Kwok had asked the tribunal to keep his address confidential, a request that was denied due to a lack of safety concerns.

Poon had recalled Li saying he had been in a traffic accident with Kwok.

Li claimed Kwok was driving drunk, but was worried Kwok would turn around and say it was Li instead.

While outside his former landlord's rental, Li angrily changed the target of their plot, Poon said.

"On that morning, I remember in a tone of anger, Mr Li's said 'let's move all the plan for Mr Kwok then'," he said.

"That was the reason why the whole thing from that morning (...) went into murdering Mr Kwok and Mrs Kwok."

Poon said at that moment, he was afraid.

More CCTV footage was played of Li and Poon travelling to the Kwok's home in the early hours of the morning.

On the way, Poon had said he once again tried to convince Li not to go through with the plan.

"There will be no turning back," he told Li.

But Li was sure, Poon said.

When they got to the property, Poon went to knock on the door.

He had hoped if he knocked lightly, no one would answer, but Li urged him to knock again harder.

Li readied the air-pistol they had bought to the home and the door opened.

Poon said he was pushed through the door, and found himself bear-hugged by Kwok.

"I can hear so many sounds 'pop pop pop pop pop pop pop', quite close or next to my ear.

Poon said Li had shot Kowk in the head.

Li was holding Poon so tight he could move, and flailed his arm in an effort to make him let go, Poon said.

"He just keep shooting at him," he said.

Kwok called out three times for his wife, Poon said.

He knelt on a chair before collapsing on the ground.

Kwok's wife Mei Han Chong came downstairs, and Li opened fire at her, Poon said.

Poon said Chong was shot multiple times by Li.

Li ran at Chong, slapping her in the face continuously.

She fell to the ground, and Li began stomping on her, Poon said.

Nathan asked Poon about the force Li used.

"Just like kicking an enemy, just like they have been hated for so, so long," Poon said.

Li turned his attention back to Kwok, stomping him also in the head, Poon said.

Poon was asked what happened next, taking a long pause.

He shuddered, eyes clenched shut as he composed himself.

Poon said he had told Li there was a tomahawk he had sharpened in their backpack.

Li took it out, and brought it down on Kwok.

He shouted at Poon to "do something".

"I picked up the tomahawk without my will, at that time I have completely lost control of my body," Poon said.

Crown prosecutors then brought the tomahawk before the court, held in a clear box.

They placed it in the witness box before Li, who winced.

"Is that the tomahawk that was used to strike Mr Kwok on the 5th of November?" Matthew Nathan asked.

"Yes," Poon replied.

The murder plot shifts

Earlier that afternoon, Poon was asked about a visit he and Li made to the landlord's property, when they had hoped to enact their plot.

CCTV footage was played of Poon picking up Li and driving to his former landlord's house.

"Mr Li climbed over the fence, first he spray paints the back camera and the sensor, and then he walked into the side way further..." Poon said.

Poon entered the property as well and went around the back, before catching sight of another camera.

"That was the time I pulled him to walk out, to abort the mission, just quit, get out," Poon said.

The pair left, and came back the next day.

They were going to try again, caught on CCTV walking around in front of the property, but saw the cameras once again.

"I just said 'hey man, if she really done so much bad to some other tenants, maybe she will have her own karma or judgement'," Poon said.

Getting back in the car, the duo drove to Celtic Crescent where the Kwoks lived.

Poon said they did not leave the car but recalled Li saying he needed to be familiar with the route.

The following day, Li had planned with Poon to kidnap his landlord from the former rental, but she never appeared.

It was after that, the murder plan shifted.

The pair meet

Poon told the court he met Li through the Amazing Grace Christian Church in May 2023.

He had been was asked by a pastor to look after his new church mate.

Lok Fung Lorrence Li is on trial. Nick Monro

"I was trying to fulfil my promise to look after him," Poon said.

"I thought that we are Christians, so that looking after each other will be a blessed thing."

Poon said he took on the role of older brother to Li.

The pair would frequently spend time together, multiple days a week, and would talk.

Poon told the court Li would talk about people he believed had treated him poorly.

"He mentioned some of the people that he met, and then he said that they haven't treated him nicely," he said.

"One of them is his landlord..."

The scene of the deaths on Celtic Crescent in Ellerslie. (File photo) RNZ / Nick Monro

Li's hatred toward his landlord was fierce, Poon recalled.

"In my memory he said that, 'if there's no law I would probably punish him, punish them, like even murder them'."

Poon spoke about being used as a decoy, so Li could place a GPS tracker in his landlord's car.

"He actually wanted to rob her family, and after robbing her, murder her," Poon said.

Li had told Poon he believed the landlord was rich, Poon said.

The two had gone to Li's old rental, with Li telling his landlord he wanted to look for something he had left behind.

The plan was to later go to the landlord's property and 'make them suffer' in order to get the codes to their credit cards.

"Then (Li) will go to one of the ATM machines to collect the money," Poon said.

"He said if the code is not correct, he will tell me to make them suffer more to disclose the card number or the code."

Poon said he had originally thought Li was joking, chalking it up to an expression of his anger toward his landlord.

But soon, the two were buying night vision goggles, military boots, a baton, and a tomahawk.

Li had also told Poon he had stolen license plates.

Concerns raised over alleged murder plot

Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok and Mei Han Chong with family. Supplied / NZ police

Poon expressed his concerns to Li, telling him what they were doing was illegal.

"This is not right," he recalled telling Li.

Li told him no one would find out.

Jurors had earlier heard Poon confided the plan to his church leaders, who encouraged him to go to the police.

The report Poon made to authorities was later filed away and wouldn't be revisited until after the Kwoks were dead.

Poon said he had wanted to be honest with his church, and ask for help in clearing his debt to Li.

At the police station, Poon said he told the authorities everything.

"I explained that this friend Mr Li was trying to push me to do some illegal action, because of this debt, he tried to force me to do some criminal acts with him."

Poon told police about the plan to rob and murder, he said.

Shortly after, Poon said he had a serious headache as taken to a 24-hour urgent care clinic where he would stay overnight.

Poon read out a suicide note he wrote in September 2023 to the court.

In it, Poon said he had enough evidence to prove he was mentally 'unstable' at the time he was associated with Li.

He had only agreed to help in order to try divert Li's 'mistaken thoughts', Poon said.

Poon had hoped someone would find his body with the note.

He told jurors he had tried to convince Li to abandon the plot.

"I actually tried to change or convince him to stop, that's why I delayed so many times," Poon said.

Conspiracy over Text

The court went through translated messages between Li and Poon, including Li's frustration over an apparent change in Poon's attitude toward the plot against Li's landlord.

"You said we can't go back on what we did. Now you tell me that the people from the church treat you well? are you OK?," Li wrote.

"You need to know, this b.... deserved it."

Li was trying to encourage him back into the plot, as he continued to send messages intended to provoke Poon, he said.

The court had earlier heard Poon messaged Li that the police may have learned of their plot.

He told the court he had fabricated this to further delay the plan.

Crown prosecutor Matthew Nathan pointed to messages where Poon said he would take the blame for everything.

"At that time I still think I'm the big brother, I'm the older brother of him, I'm just trying to protect him at the time," Poon said.

"Because of this protection and promise, I'm trying to protect him from being arrested."

He had told Li he was gangster, but apologised in court, saying that was not the case.

It was just another effort to get Li to fall in line, and call off the plan, Poon said.

Poon believed Li knew he was lying.

World.title: SPCA to benefit from doghouse that evolved from April Fool's joke
World.content:
Building company in the dog house, but on to a winner Morning Report Download MP3 3m

The public response to an April Fool's Day ad featuring a luxurious doghouse was so positive, the building company behind it went ahead and built one for real and is auctioning it off for charity.

The house features a double-glazed window, carpet and long run metal roofing and will be sold to raise money for the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (SPCA).

Landmark Central Auckland owner Warwick Aldridge who helped build the house told Morning Report his team were caught off guard by the popularity of the concept that was never meant to materialise.

"It's a rather large doghouse with a little bedroom for the dog, it comes complete with a dog bed and a little area out the front just to hang out and enjoy the sun," Aldridge said.

Two dogs make themselves at home. Landmark Central Auckland

The response from the public to the company's April Fools joke was so positive, the team decided to create the house for real.

"I was involved with drawing up a plan for it and dusted the apron off to help build it with one of our other project managers."

The doghouse will be given away by way of a raffle at the Auckland Home Show. Tickets cost $5 each, with proceeds going to the SPCA.

Aldridge said the home show was taking place in a challenging time for the sector.

"It's still pretty tough in Auckland. Other regions around the country are showing signs of improvement, but Auckland's still a very tough market for residential new homes.

World.title: Water regulator tells Canterbury Regional Council long-term nitrate limits being considered
World.content:
New report on high nitrate levels in Canterbury Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Almost a year on from the previous Canterbury Regional Council declaring a nitrate emergency, a new report pointing to high nitrate levels across the region has been presented to councillors.

The council also heard from Greenpeace, Health New Zealand and the water regulator, Taumata Arowai, who proposed an additional limit on nitrate to protect people from possible long-term health effects.

The water regulator floated introducing a new maximum acceptable value (MAV) for nitrates.

Taumata Arowai science advisor Jim Graham told the council he thought calls to lower the legal limit of nitrate allowed in drinking water was based on a misunderstanding.

However, he said the agency was considering a new long-term value in response to increasing scientific evidence of long-term health effects at levels far lower than the current limit.

"We have a short-term MAV, we should keep that, but if people are concerned about the impact of consumption of nitrate over a long period of time at a much lower level, what they're asking for is the introduction of a long-term MAV," he said.

"I think that's the work that we'll do over the next 12, 18 months. Looking at all the evidence to see if that's what we should do, that's our function as setting MAV."

Earlier this year, RNZ revealed the Ministry of Health had quietly launched a review into the health effects of nitrate in drinking water.

The outcome was expected to be public by the end of the year.

Taumata Arowai was also reviewing drinking water standards.

The meeting also heard from council staff about long overdue nitrate maps released on Wednesday - seven months behind schedule.

The maps follow the council's controversial declaration of a nitrate emergency last September.

Te Whatu Ora's Dr Cheryl Brunton accepted there was a growing body of research linking health problems to nitrates in drinking water at levels lower than the current limit of 11.3 milligrams per litre.

She said the studies were inconclusive, but the limit didn't consider all possible risks.

"It may be set with blue baby syndrome in mind to avoid that, but it's really concerning to see what you will be seeing later this afternoon, which is the evidence of just how many water bores exceed already the current MAV, never mind if the MAV should be reduced," Brunton said.

She said there were many sources of nitrates in people's diets and drinking water only made up a small portion.

Greenpeace executive director Russel Norman commended the council for its "bravery" in declaring an emergency and urged them to keep speaking out.

"Obviously we don't know how long elected regional councils are going to survive because they've said they want to do them in, but for God's sakes please speak out about it," he said.

"You are the elected representatives, you have a right and a duty to speak up for the values of your constituents and most people in this country believe in clean water and you are their representative, so please keep speaking out."

The maps released by the council showed 15 percent of wells tested recorded a reading above the legal limit and another 23 percent recorded a reading above half the current limit.

Brunton told the council the best prevention was the reduction of nitrate, especially as alternative water sources were becoming harder to find.

"Increasingly it's becoming difficult to source low nitrate water for supplementing drinking water supplies and that includes within the wider districts of Canterbury," she said.

"The Selwyn District for example is one of the districts finding that a challenge."

World.title: Waikato University wants millions in ratepayer subsidies for new medical school
World.content:
Waikato University is asking for millions of dollars in ratepayer subsidies for its new medical school, but one Hamilton councillor says it is a central government issue and ratepayers should not foot the bill.

The university wants Hamilton Council to waive more than $5 million in development contributions, which help pay for infrastructure. It has also asked the council to pitch in $250,000 a year for five years.

In making his pitch, Waikato University vice chancellor Neil Quigley revealed the government's funding only covered about 28 percent of the project's cost.

From 2028, the Waikato medical school is expected to train an additional 120 doctors a year, with students doing clinical placements in regional areas.

But Hamilton councillor Sue Moroney told Checkpoint it was a matter for central government.

"There is already enough that central government is putting on local government to pay for that we have no say over, and the ratepayers end up paying those things. This medical school is one decision we do have control over as a council and from me it's a hard 'no'.

"We can't afford it because we are actually trying to do all the things that the fastest growing city in the country needs to do, with a ratepayer cap that is coming from central government as well. So we've already got enough on our plate, we've got a lot of expenditure that is our responsibility, let alone picking up responsibility that really does belong to central government."

Waikato Uni asking for ratepayers subsidies to fund medical school Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

She said the council had a good relationship with the university and was proud of it, but the entire country would benefit from the extra doctors.

"Yes, there will be benefits to Hamilton, but the decision and the responsibility is definitely with central government, it's not one that ratepayers or their representatives have any role in making a decision about."

Moroney said ratepayers had asked her why the council needed to give extra funds to the university when it was in a good financial position, at a time when the council was struggling to keep costs down.

The millions in development contributions the university was asking the council to waive were needed in the local community, she said.

"We have forecasted development contributions for the forecasted growth in our city and every bit of developer contribution that we do not get - including those ones being caused by fast track projects that are right on our boundaries - means that that's an extra burden for the existing ratepayers and existing ratepayers have had enough of funding those sorts of ventures."

The request from the university to provide financial assistance will now be considered as part of the council's 2027-2037 long-term plan.

World.title: ASA partly upholds complaint against 'misleading' National attack ad
World.content:
The Advertising Standards Authority has partly upheld a complaint against a National Party attack ad, and told the party not to use it again in its current form.

The complaint focused around National's criticisms of Labour's capital gains tax (CGT) policy.

A complainant told the ASA that in July they had received a flyer promoting Chris Bishop as the National Party candidate for Hutt South, as well as general National Party election campaign material.

A section called 'Keeping Taxes Low', the complainant said, had a statement about what was at risk.

"Labour's capital gains tax would hit the family bach, rentals, small businesses and KiwiSaver," the flyer said.

Labour has maintained KiwiSaver is exempt from its CGT proposal, which is designed to cover commercial property and residential investment property only.

The family home (including lifestyle blocks), farms, inheritances, shares, businesses, and other commercial items are also exempt.

Small businesses wanting to sell and move into a bigger property would not have to pay the tax, and the vast majority of small businesses lease their buildings so are not subject to the tax.

The complainant was concerned it was misleading for National to claim the CGT would hit small businesses and KiwiSaver.

National's response to the ASA was that the CGT would affect businesses that owned the premises they operated from (such as salons, dairies, service stations, or corporate offices).

National falls foul of advertising standards with flyer aimed at Labour Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

While small businesses selling their premises to buy a bigger one would not be taxed, small businesses selling commercial property for other reasons, and larger businesses selling commercial property for any reason, would be taxed.

Therefore, people whose KiwiSaver accounts invested in businesses which owned the commercial buildings would be impacted by the tax, National argued.

However, in a majority ruling, the ASA found the claim that KiwiSaver would be "hit" by the CGT to be in breach of the principle of truthful presentation, that s must be truthful, balanced and not misleading.

The majority of the board found that the "consumer takeout" for most would be that their KiwiSaver funds would be subject to the CGT.

While the family bach, rental properties, and small businesses (when property was sold) would be affected by the CGT, linking KiwiSaver in the same sentence indicated it would be "hit" in a similar way, which the ASA said could mislead or confuse consumers.

"The majority said it was misleading to refer to KiwiSaver in the  alongside the other assets, without a qualifier or clearer explanation of the impact," the ruling said.

A minority of the complaints board believed the statement was making a more "general claim" that KiwiSaver funds would be affected in some way, and that National's explanation was sufficient.

The claim about the impact on small businesses was not found to be in breach, as a majority of the complaints board believed it was unlikely to mislead or confuse most consumers.

"The Advertiser's example of a small business selling for reasons other than to buying larger premises was sufficient to support that some small businesses would be directly impacted by the capital gains tax," the ASA said.

The majority decision found the KiwiSaver claim to be in breach of the principle around truthful presentation, and the rules around truthful presentation and advocacy advertising.

The ASA told National not to use the advert again in its current form.

Academic encourages fair fight

Ekant Veer, a professor of marketing at the University of Canterbury, told Checkpoint the ASA's ruling was significant.

"To see our ASA saying no, you can't go out and confuse people receiving this advertising is a good step forward," he said.

Ekant Veer, a professor of marketing at the University of Canterbury. Nate McKinnon

Veer said the ASA did not just look at what might be factually correct, but also what might potentially confuse or provide ambiguity.

"We want to be able to trust what we're reading out in the advertising, we want to have a clean, fair fight between the major parties, and we want to be able to see whether we can trust what is being put out there," he said.

"What we also know is that people who maybe are not as involved with politics, people who don't go and do the research themselves, are more likely to be swayed by messages like this. So we want to try and stop that. We want people to make decisions based on full and factual information. And in this case, the ASA says that's not happened."

Complainant wants an apology

The complainant Catherine Bindon told RNZ she complained as she was getting "entirely fed up with the amount of misinformation and disinformation I've seen in this campaign so far," which felt different to previous campaigns.

"I think once a seed is sown, it's very hard to change that perception of what's actually happening," she said.

Bindon said National's claims around KiwiSaver were "a blatant lie" and she was happy with the ASA's ruling.

"I would actually like to see the party make an apology. I think they really need to own it. I think they need to be honest, and I think they need to be accountable for for what they said."

National sticks to its guns

But following the ruling, National's campaign chair Simeon Brown doubled-down, insisting many KiwiSaver funds invested in businesses that owned property, and so a CGT would have a flow-on effect.

"The Advertising Standards Authority has not said KiwiSaver wouldn't be affected by Labour's capital gains tax - it has only suggested that KiwiSaver may not be impacted to the same extent as rental properties, baches and businesses," he said.

"So, the fact remains that KiwiSaver will still be impacted and National will continue to make this point clear to New Zealanders."

Brown also said the ASA's ruling "confirmed that Labour's claim that small businesses are exempt from its capital gains tax is false," and said it was Labour that needed to update its advertising.

Labour's campaign chair Kieran McAnulty said National was relying on fear, misinformation, and misleading advertising, and had been caught out.

"From billboards to letterboxes, National is running a campaign of lies because it can't run on its own record," he said.

World.title: 'More than praise, we need a raise': Thousands of public service workers strike across the country
World.content:
Almost 10,000 public servants went on strike across the country on Wednesday afternoon, with some taking industrial action for the first time in decades.

The Public Service Association (PSA) organised 18 rallies across 16 locations as part of its campaign against the government's approach to public sector pay, staffing and plans to replace thousands of public sector jobs with AI by 2029.

PSA national delegate Vaughan Trounson, who works at the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), said salary bands for some people hadn't moved in half a decade.

Trounson, who works as a patent examiner, said members of his team were struggling.

"I've got a colleague who's said he hasn't had a pay rise in five years... I know for myself I moved into a house four years ago and rates were 5k a year, now they're 8k or 9k.

Hundreds gathered in the capital for Wednesday's strike. RNZ/Zachary Cornelisen

"We've seen these massive increase in costs, and all these bills, and the pay has just gone backwards."

Tara, who was also striking in Wellington today, said her colleagues deserved to feel valued for the work they do.

"The country needs public servants putting forward the evidence and helping the decisions that get made. We stand for evidence-based decision-making."

Tara said the pay offer her colleagues had received was insulting.

She said uncertainty in the public service affected the mood in Wellington, which underwent public sector job cuts last year.

"People are thinking about having to replace cars that have died, having to replace their homes' ... leaking bathrooms and leaking bedrooms and they don't have any security in order to make those decisions that families across the region and across New Zealand are having to make."

Paige Connell Culver, an MBIE worker, was one of 200 people striking at Te Komititanga Square in Auckland Central.

She said the pay offer they received would mean they were better off next year, but in the following years they were being asked to take an effective pay cut.

She said her colleagues were already making difficult sacrifices.

PSA national secretary Duane Leo said many of the workers represented by the union earned between $65,000 and $75,000 a year.

He said the largest group striking was immigration officers, most of whom earned about $70,000.

"People aren't asking for large sums of money or exorbitant amounts. We're simply saying to survive, to live out there at the moment, you need to meet us in terms of cost-of-living payments, and they're not doing that."

Leo said the union had repeatedly raised concerns about the cost of living during negotiations.

Numerous workers and union delegates told RNZ that the cost of living had taken a toll on workers. RNZ/Zachary Cornelisen

"We're very much getting to a tipping point here. And the reality is, these agencies, as well as a number of others we represent, have been bargaining for months."

In a statement, Public Service Minister Paul Goldsmith said while the PSA had a right to strike, he did not agree with its approach.

He said the union was running an active campaign to "change the government" and argued New Zealanders would be inconvenienced by what he described as a broader political campaign.

Goldsmith said public servants had received significant pay increases under the previous Labour government, while the current government had continued with more modest increases.

Government workers across the country walk off the job Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons said members were insulted at the government's attitude.

She said the union would prefer to be bargaining in good faith and was hoping today's strike will prompt the government to pick up the phone.

World.title: No hard feelings: Rakesh Naidoo refuses to hit back after police row
World.content:
Labour's top cop candidate Rakesh Naidoo has declined to fire back at police top brass over their criticism of his move into politics, despite maintaining he did nothing wrong.

Speaking to RNZ for the first time since being recruited by Labour, Naidoo said he would not do anything differently with hindsight, pointing to a police review which cleared him of any wrongdoing.

Quizzed on various law and order issues, he told RNZ he did not believe there was institutional racism in the police force.

Naidoo's candidacy, announced in June, prompted public criticism from Police Commissioner Richard Chambers and Minister Mark Mitchell, with both claiming the superintendent should have declared his intentions earlier.

An internal review later concluded that Naidoo had complied with police policy, though noted it would have been "prudent" for him to have given his superiors more advance warning.

Naidoo shrugs off criticism from police top brass

In a sitdown interview marking his entry into the election campaign, Naidoo remained diplomatic about the criticism levelled at him by his superiors.

"In my view, they were expressing themselves based on the information that they had," he said.

"I am grateful that once they looked into it, the review found that I'd follow the right process."

Naidoo said he was also thankful for the apology he received from Assistant Commissioner Tim Anderson, "a man of honesty and integrity".

Asked whether he wanted an apology from Chambers as well, Naidoo said only that he respected the process.

He would not say whether he had been hurt or angered by Chambers' public criticism, nor whether he felt his reputation had been smeared.

Naidoo also declined to repeat Labour leader Chris Hipkins' criticism of Chambers at the time. Then Hipkins said Chambers had been a bad employer for casting aspersions on an officer with "no evidential base behind it".

Naidoo said he was approached by a Labour member in February about the possibility of standing as a list candidate.

Asked why he did not immediately declare that to police at the time, Naidoo said the discussion was "very much a hypothetical".

"I hadn't made any decision. I hadn't formed an intent. It was something that was very hypothetical," he said.

"As soon as I had formed an intent and wanted to make a decision, police were the first to know."

Naidoo said he told his supervisor in May that he was giving the idea serious consideration, and then again in June when he decided to attend a formal Labour committee meeting.

He was offered a list spot that evening: "I gave that contemplation over the next day, and then informed police, and then informed the Labour Party."

Asked whether he would do anything differently with hindsight, Naidoo responded: "no".

Labour's new police recruit says no institutional racism in force

Naidoo said the commotion following his entry into politics had left him "more committed than ever" to the job.

Asked whether he had on ambitions on becoming Police Minister, the rookie candidate described himself as a "new recruit" and said he was not getting ahead of himself.

"I'm just really focused on the next few days," he said. "In fact, today I'm just trying to focus on getting through the media interviews."

Naidoo was largely unwilling to proffer his opinions on law and order policy, saying it would be "highly inappropriate" for him to share his thoughts on, say, the gang patch ban, given his recent involvement.

But asked about systemic racism, Naidoo said he had seen no evidence of it during his nearly 25 years in the police force.

"I've personally never witnessed any racism within police," he said. "I do not believe there is institutional racism."

Naidoo said officers themselves were subjected to racism while dealing with the public, pointing to a broader rise in hate and declining trust in institutions as issues that motivated him to enter politics.

Asked whether Labour had been "soft on crime" in government - as alleged by National - Naidoo again punted the question to Hipkins or police spokesperson Ginny Anderson.

Pressed again, Naidoo said his values aligned strongly with Labour.

"When people start making tough choices, when they can't get good healthcare... when you can't put food on the table... when you're unemployed and you're stressed... then that flows on into wider consequences... things such as crime and victimisation."

He said former police colleagues had given him "a fair bit of ribbing" about abandoning a secure career and taking a pay cut, but many had also backed his decision.

"My colleagues have been very excited because they see it as I see it: as a continuance of my service to our communities and to our country."

Naidoo, who was the ethnic, iwi and communities relationship manager for police, was announced as Labour's 13th ranked candidate on 8 June, virtually guaranteeing him a seat in Parliament.

Mitchell pounced on the announcement, questioning what sensitive information Naidoo had access to while quietly talking to Labour.

Chambers quickly followed, declaring Naidoo's position with the police to be "untenable" and launching an investigation.

Chambers said Naidoo should have declared his intentions earlier, saying he had been notified only days before the announcement.

But a police statement, issued on 13 August, later confirmed Naidoo had notified his supervisor in the week beginning 25 May.

World.title: SA government backed a risky horse in LIV Golf — lucky it hedged its bets
World.content:
Spending at least $45 million to upgrade a golf course so it can host a tour that's filed for bankruptcy is a hard sell.

But that's the position the Malinauskas government would have been lumped with had it not secured hosting rights to the Australian Open golf tournament from 2028.

The announcement in May that the prestigious, traditionalist golf event would be coming to the redeveloped North Adelaide Golf Course has taken some of the sting out of what would otherwise have been a nasty political headache surrounding LIV Golf's financial demise.

The acquisition of LIV Golf until 2031 was the impetus for a controversional redevelopment of the North Adelaide Golf Course., (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

The breakaway tour filed for bankruptcy in the US overnight, four months after Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund announced it would be pulling its billions in funding.

LIV Golf chief executive Scott O'Neil said the move was intended to keep the league in business while transitioning to a player-first ownership model. It hopes to exit bankruptcy in early 2027.

But the optimism of the press release doesn't quash the uncertainty about what LIV Golf will look like next year and whether it can hold onto the top talent — and party-like atmosphere — that made it such a success in Adelaide.

The tour owes huge sums to creditors, including its star players. Jon Rahm is owed more than $10 million, Bryson DeChambeau nearly $8 million, and Australian Cameron Smith about $6.5 million.

They could all walk away if not convinced by LIV's new model.

Premier Peter Malinauskas went all in on the LIV Golf vision back in February 2025, announcing a six-year contract extension until 2031 and that it would be moving to a new Greg Norman-designed championship course at North Adelaide in 2028.

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas announced the six-year LIV Golf contract extension in 2025. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The government has been consistent that there was more to the course upgrade than just LIV Golf, pointing out it will be used by the public outside of events.

But it's also hard to imagine a world where the $45 million upgrade gets green-lighted without LIV Golf in the picture; indeed, the premier indicated as much at the time, saying the 2031 extension "justifies the investment".

"We didn't want to invest heavily in North Adelaide and face the prospect of it [LIV Golf] being lost from South Australia," he said in February 2025.

" This gives us the security that it requires to be able to justify that investment. "

As the negative headlines about LIV Golf's finances piled up, so too did the questions about the justification for the course upgrade.

The development and its loss of 585 trees was always going to spark opposition from parklands advocates, the Greens and elements of Adelaide City Council.

Trees were cut down at the course in May. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

But the prospect of spending $45 million on an upgraded course without a major event connected to it risked a much broader backlash.

If you wanted a sense of the political importance of securing the Australian Open, you only have to look at how prominently it featured in the government's talking points about LIV Golf's bankruptcy today.

Can the SA government justify a $45m golf course upgrade without LIV Golf? The Malinauskas government took a calculated risk to redevelop the North Adelaide Golf Course in time for LIV Golf in 2028. It might not pay off.

"We've been focused on not just LIV Golf but other opportunities," Labor minister Clare Scriven said, "which is why we've been so keen to secure the Australian Open."

Cabinet colleague Nick Champion — who in April said the prospect of LIV Golf ceasing to exist was "just speculation" and "not a question we would ask ourselves" — said today that the state government was not "over-reliant" on one event.

"I appreciate that we're going to have endless media speculation about LIV Golf, but we're upgrading the golf course so that we can have a world class golf course next to a world class [Adelaide] Oval in a world class city," he said.

"And we've got the Australian men's and women's open."

The debate moves on

The fight over the North Adelaide course upgrade appears to have largely moved on.

That's partly due to the Australian Open announcement, but also because attention has shifted to the government's controversial MotoGP circuit in the eastern parklands, which will require the felling of at least 377 trees.

The government recently unveiled designs for the MotoGP redevelopment affecting another part of the parklands. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

Opposition leader Ashton Hurn was today asked whether LIV Golf filing for bankruptcy raised questions about the need for the North Adelaide Golf Course upgrade.

"It does, but I think that we're kind of past that point really when you look at how many trees have now been pulled out," she said.

" But certainly, when this massive project was announced it was done so really with the idea that LIV Golf would be the major project underpinning that. "

Liberal leader Ashton Hurn says LIV Golf was the primary reason for the North Adelaide redevelopment. (ABC News: Isabella Carbone)

Ms Hurn was more focused today on questioning whether South Australian taxpayers had any exposure in LIV Golf's demise — something the government denies.

"We are good at writing events contracts," Mr Champion said, "we don't provide support for events that aren't held."

Over to you, Kooyonga

If LIV Golf can get out of its current predicament, it is next due in Adelaide in March 2027 at the Kooyonga Golf Club.

The western suburbs club has been waiting on an advanced payment from LIV Golf to help prepare.

The status of that fee remains unclear.

Adelaide's next LIV event is scheduled for March. (ABC News: Will Hunter)

But Australian golf commentator Jimmy Emanuel believes LIV Golf will put on a tournament next year, even if it looks a little different.

"The cost of putting on a tournament in that scale to attract music acts like Fisher is a lot," he said.

"Just building grandstands, building hospitality, those are big commitments financially — the scale of the investment is not going to be the same as it was from Saudi Arabia.

" It might not be quite as grand, but I imagine it's going to be their biggest event still. "

What happens beyond next year is a matter of anyone's guess — but the government remains certain of one thing.

Even if LIV dies, the North Adelaide course upgrade is set to survive.

World.title: Lynagh makes timely return after Wallabies fly half Gordon breaks leg
World.content:
Tom Lynagh's timely return at number 10 for the Queensland Reds and Zac Lomax's move to the centres for the Western Force will have Wallabies ramifications in a pre-season Ballymore hit-out.

Super Rugby AUS starts on Saturday in Brisbane and there will be immense interest in how both fare ahead of next year's World Cup on home soil.

Lynagh, the starting fly half in all three British and Irish Lions Tests last year, managed just 18 minutes for the Reds because of a series of injuries last season.

Wallabies escape with draw against Pumas after late penalty try A penalty try close to full-time sees the Wallabies and Pumas finish in a 28-28 draw in Mendoza, giving the visitors a history-making series win on Argentine soil.

All going to script, he will get at least 40 minutes against the Force at Ballymore in new Reds coach Vern Cotter's first game in charge since his historic move from Auckland's Blues to replace Les Kiss.

Lynagh's return comes as Reds teammate and fly half Carter Gordon enters two months of rehabilitation after fracturing his fibula in last weekend's Test draw against Argentina in Mendoza.

Gordon had established himself as the Wallabies' first-choice fly half, leaving Kiss with some big calls ahead of a clash with South Africa and a two-Test Bledisloe Cup in the next six weeks.

"I'm really enjoying Tom in a playmaker role," Cotter said of the son of former Wallabies great Michael.

"He's got a great head on his shoulders, he sees the game well, he's calm and decisive.

"With the niggles he has had, we will probably be a bit careful with him, so it probably won't be 80 minutes, but certainly a good 40 minutes to start with.

"He's a great player in organised play but brilliant at unstructured (play).

"It's a good opportunity for Tom to get out there and boss the team around … pull a few strings and get some combinations."

Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, released by the Reds to join the Force this season, will oppose Lynagh and consider himself in the thick of Wallabies discussions after being part of their training camp earlier this year.

Kurtley Beale has been named on the bench for the Force, but new signing James O'Connor, another sure to be in Kiss's considerations, will not play.

Lomax, an Australian and NSW State of Origin rugby league winger, revealed this week he would be deployed in the number 13 jersey against the Reds.

A dominant showing there would add intrigue to Kiss's midfield selection headache after fellow code-hopper Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii's struggles to nail down the jersey in 24 Tests.

Japan-bound fullback Jock Campbell, replaced in the number 15 by Tom Wright after one Test in July despite a good showing against Ireland, will also get a chance to show something when he comes off the bench for the Reds.

Fellow Wallabies Matt Faessler, Zane Nonggorr and Josh Flook have been named, while Australian under-20s captain Tom Robinson will wear the number 6, and exciting fullback Will McCulloch will start.

NSW Waratahs lock Miles Amatosero, red-carded in his second Test appearance in Osaka, will mount his comeback against the ACT Brumbies on Sunday in Bungendore, east of Canberra.

Teddy Wilson and Max Burey, after earning an early release from the Force, will partner in the halves, while Sid Harvey will start at fullback.

Triston Reilly will wear the Brumbies' number 15 against his former club a week after piloting the First Nations and Pasifika XV to victory in Tonga, while Wallabies wing aspirant Corey Toole will add pace on the flank.

AAP

World.title: Major state fears cricket will be worse off with private investment
World.content:
The decision to introduce private investment into the Big Bash leagues risks leaving cricket in Australia "strategically and financially worse off", according to Cricket NSW.

On Tuesday, Cricket Australia announced it would seek private investment into Australia's franchise T20 leagues, beginning with the sale of the Melbourne Renegades.

The announcement came following months of speculation about whether private investment was the right move for CA, and the game in Australia more broadly.

Private investment in Big Bash Cricket Australia agrees to bring private investment into the Big Bash League, starting with the sale of the Melbourne Renegades.

Ahead of Tuesday's announcement, it was reported that state cricket bodies in NSW and Queensland were opposed to the plan which included exploring sell-offs of 49 per cent stakes in BBL franchises.

On Wednesday, Cricket NSW in a statement said it was disappointed Cricket Australia had pushed forward with the decision to seek private investment without having all stakeholders on board with the process.

"Cricket NSW is disappointed by Cricket Australia's decision to proceed with introducing private investment into the Big Bash leagues without alignment across Australian cricket," the statement read.

"This decision risks leaving cricket in NSW and Australia strategically and financially worse off, with direct consequences for our ability to invest in grassroots cricket.

"We see our role at Cricket NSW, alongside Cricket Australia and all states, as custodians of our game. Our purpose is to inspire everyone to play and love cricket. This starts with growing participation in our sport, ultimately producing great players for our W/BBL clubs, NSW and Australia.



"The profits from our successful and healthy Big Bash clubs – the Sydney Sixers and Sydney Thunder – are reinvested into growing participation in cricket."

Cricket NSW owns the Sydney Sixers and Sydney Thunder franchises.

It said it feared the private investment model would threaten its ability to invest in growing the sport, especially at the grassroots level.

Cricket Australia green lights BBL privatisation The Big Bash League is set to look like it never has before as Cricket Australia prepares to welcome private ownership to the competition.

"Yesterday’s announcement threatens this system. The redistribution of profits to external investors reduces our ability to invest in community cricket, creating long-term impacts at all levels," Cricket NSW said.



"The Cricket NSW board is also disappointed by the process leading to this decision.

"We have raised concerns directly with Cricket Australia, proposed an alternative pathway to strengthen the Big Bash, and highlighted significant risks within the proposal, informed by high-quality external advice."

On Tuesday, Cricket Australia chair Mike Baird said the introduction of private investment into the Big Bash would result in greater investment in the sport at all levels.

"By opening the door to private investment in the Big Bash leagues, Cricket Australia is taking a deliberate step to strengthen and secure the long-term future of the game, accelerate growth and ensuring we can keep investing in community cricket and grassroots participation, domestic and international pathways and the elite level," he said.

"This is a significant decision that has involved an enormous amount of analysis, discussion and collaboration over many months. I'd like to thank all involved as we move to what we believe is the best way to secure cricket's future in this country, strengthen the Big Bash and protect our standing on the global stage."

Cricket Australia is hopeful that the Melbourne Renegades franchise will play the 2027/28 season under new ownership.

World.title: The departing Panther who shapes as Penrith's finals wildcard
World.content:
Jack Cole's chance on the NRL's biggest stage has been a long time coming, but now the Penrith five-eighth could shape as the Panthers finals wildcard.

Sunday's semi-final against the Sydney Roosters will be just his fifth game of the year and 22nd of his career since his debut four years ago.

Cole has spent the time since in and out of first grade, and while the 23-year old was always part of the team he only sporadically strapped up on match day, especially as the season heated up.

For four straight Septembers, Cole ran opposed sessions and tried to do whatever else he could to get the top side ready for whatever finals battle was to come, waiting for his chance as he bore witness to the greatest dynasty of modern times.

Cole has started at five-eighth in Penrith's last two matches of the regular season. (Getty Images: Matt King)

It was not always easy to be patient, but now, at the very end of his Panthers tenure before he joins Perth Bears next season, Cole's time has come.

The Orange man signed with the Bears to try and be a first grader every week, now he is a first grader in one of the weeks that counts the most.

"The last few years, watching the boys kick on and win grand finals, you try and help where you can," Cole said.

"But it's a different perspective now — going on the camps, being in the meetings, it's a good opportunity and I'm really looking forward to it.

"It has been a little bit [hard to wait]. There's been a few soft tissue injuries over the past couple of years as well, that's been more frustrating. You get close, you have an injury, and you need to work your way back up.

"It's all been character building though. I haven't had it the easy way, I've gone up and come down and known what I've had to work on and tried to work my way back up."

Cole's combination with Cleary will prove crucial for Penrith in their finals tilt. (Getty Images: Ethan Miller)

Cole has spent some time under the bright lights. He got a start in the World Club Challenge against Wigan in 2024 and began last season as the team's starting five-eighth, including in the win over Cronulla in Las Vegas.

Chances have been harder to come by since, but Blaize Talagi's demotion to reserve grade and Jack Cogger's three-game suspension for a high tackle opened the door for Cole.

He has also combined well with Nathan Cleary as Penrith warmed up for the finals with back-to-back wins.

"He's [Cogger] had a few [suspensions] this year, so we thought he might get suspended and I didn't know if Ivan [Cleary] would go Blaize or me or someone else. But it was definitely something I started thinking about straight away," Cole said.

"[Cleary] just said to me to defend well and if I see something attack, just do it.

"He wants me to keep it simple, do my role and the rest will fall into place."

With the best player in the world on his inside and lethal centre-wing duo Casey McLean and Thomas Jenkins on his left, Cole's job is a simple one — take a little pressure off Cleary when he can, shuffle it out to the weapons early and often, always keep talking and tackle well.

But simple is not the same as easy. If it were, Penrith would not have made the change with Talagi in the first place.

After signing with Penrith as a 15-year old, Cole will head to Perth Bears at the end of the season. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Cogger is due to return from suspension for the Panthers next match, but it feels like there is every chance Cole sticks around in one spot or another.

Throughout Penrith's ascension and well into their dynasty, coach Cleary has a great tradition of shaking up his side on the eve of the finals to give it a little extra juice.

In 2021 he benched talismanic backrower Viliame Kikau for Liam Martin for the final six games of the season.

The following year Cleary did the same, only with hookers Api Koroisau and Mitch Kenny, in the club's three finals games.

In 2023 it was Cogger who seized a bench utility spot for the preliminary final and the decider, a move which paid off handsomely when he played a key role in Penrith's epic comeback against Brisbane.

How this unlikely hero set the stage for Nathan Cleary's grand final heroics Nathan Cleary is rightly earning all sorts of praise for his grand final performance but the Penrith halfback couldn't have spearheaded his side's remarkable comeback without the efforts of Jack Cogger.

Paul Alamoti has been the choice two years in a row. In 2024 he replaced Casey McLean at left centre for the final five games of the season and ended up scoring the final try of the grand final win over Melbourne.

Last year he came in for Tom Jenkins on the wing for the semis, scoring five tries in three games leading up to the preliminary final loss to Brisbane.

If all goes well on Sunday, Cole could be this year's version of the late-season adrenaline shot which has worked so well for the Panthers for so many years.

Cogger's proven ability to impact a game off the bench could keep Cole in the starting side, or Cole himself could act as the club's utility given he can also cover centre.

But we are getting ahead of ourselves, which Cole refuses to do. Big dreams about a grand final exit before he heads to Perth will have to wait.

Cole has been with the Panthers since he was 15 and is determined to put into practice everything he has learned since, first on Sunday and then with whatever comes next.

"When it was first happening [getting to the end] I was a bit sad cause I only had six or seven games left and I've been here for eight years," Cole said.

"But now there's a job to do and I can't dwell on that. It won't benefit me or the team.

"I want to use it as an opportunity to help me moving forward and hopefully end on a good note.

"This is the time of year you wait for. This is what it's all about."

World.title: Socceroo Cristian Volpato's fate uncertain after failed cocaine test
World.content:
Cristian Volpato's immediate availability for the Socceroos rests in the hands of Football Australia after NSW Police confirmed the World Cup star had tested positive for cocaine on a secondary test.

Volpato was pulled over by police on Sydney's Anzac Bridge on July 24 and returned a positive roadside reading for cocaine.

The 22-year-old then underwent independent testing at a private clinic, where it was claimed he returned a negative reading.

Police catch Socceroos star Police say they stopped the 22-year-old in a BMW Coupe about 1am today and allege he was travelling 109 kilometres per hour on the Anzac Bridge.

But Volpato was then sent for a secondary oral fluid test by police, which again confirmed a positive result for cocaine.

"On Tuesday 1 September 2026, a 22-year-old man was issued a Traffic Infringement Notice for drive motor vehicle with illicit drug present in oral fluid," NSW Police told AAP.

Volpato, who will face no further action, was handed a $722 fine as a result of the second positive test.

The Sassuolo forward had been pulled over by police after driving at 109 kilometres per hour in a 60km/h zone.

The Sydney-born youngster was a late inclusion for the Socceroos' World Cup campaign after switching his international allegiance from Italy to Australia on the eve of the tournament.

Volpato has maintained his innocence over the failed drugs test when he spoke to Football Australia (FA) staff, insisting that he never knowingly ingested the substance.

He also undertook a test when he returned to Italy which was negative, his club side, Sassuolo, said.

In a statement provided to AAP, Football Australia (FA) said: "Football Australia has been made aware of information concerning a reported secondary oral test result relating to one of our players. We are currently seeking independent verification.

"The matter is being managed in accordance with Football Australia's established protocols. To protect the integrity of this process and ensure procedural fairness, we will not comment further."

But the positive reading on Volpato's secondary police test could have major ramifications for his availability heading into January's Asian Cup.

Sources have told AAP that Volpato could be hauled before FA's disciplinary and ethics committee, where the sport's governing body has the power to suspend him from national team action.

The closest comparable case to Volpato's is that of A-League Women goalkeeper Teresa Morrissey, who tested positive for cannabis while driving.

Morrissey claimed the cannabis had been used for medicinal purposes, but was still slugged with a three-game ban by FA last year, which the goalkeeper's legal team had argued was disproportionate with her public profile.

Volpato's off-field indiscretion attracted headlines in Australia and in Italy, where he plays in Serie A.

Popovic knocked back extension Socceroos coach Tony Popovic has revealed he turned down a four-year contract offer from Football Australia (FA) to take the team through to the 2030 World Cup.

He has played three games for Sassuolo this season, but failed to finish their last game against Bologna because of a suspected hamstring injury.

Socceroos coach Tony Popovic would not be drawn on whether he would pick Volpato for this month's friendlies with Brazil when he spoke at a press conference in Sydney on Tuesday.

"I don't know exactly the details of what happened and it would be wrong to speculate on what happened," Popovic told reporters.

"These young men, things happen and you can get caught for something we have to look into.

"There is a process that's playing out at the moment and we need to follow that process.

"When that is played out as it should, [only] then I can really comment on that."

AAP

World.title: US Open thriller finishes after 3:30am as Shelton knocks out Alcaraz
World.content:
Ben Shelton has triumphed in a five-set thriller that set a new US Open record as the latest finish ever to a match at the New York grand slam.

The clock passed 3am local time midway through the final set, as Shelton advanced to the semifinals at Flushing Meadows with a 6-7 (5-7), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 (10/7) win.

Alcaraz won the first set in a tiebreaker, before the big-serving American eighth seed roared back into the match.

Shelton had the New York crowd in his corner as he took a 2-1 lead in sets, as Alcaraz looked tired and sluggish.

Carlos Alcaraz looked down and out after three sets, but roared back into the match. (AP: Heather Khalifa)

But the Spaniard, a two-time winner at Flushing Meadows (2022 and 2025) dominated the fourth set to set up the thrilling finish.

Neither player dropped their serve in the final set, but both had a break-point opportunity during the decider.

But a 10-point tiebreaker was needed to separate the two.

The tiebreaker was on serve at 3-3 when the players swapped ends, each having won a point off the other's serve.

Alcaraz had a chance to make it 7-5 with a mini-break, but his backhand went long as the players swapped ends again at 6-6.

Shelton then got a mini-break and made it stick, giving himself a chance to serve for the match at 9-7, which he converted with an ace.

The 4 hour and 28 minute battle finished at 3:34am in New York.

Alcaraz was also part of the previous latest finish at the US Open, when his quarterfinal win over Jannik Sinner in 2022 finished at 2:50am.

Shelton will face American Frances Tiafoe, who came from two sets down to win his own five-set quarterfinal.

Tears flow as tennis star lets two-set lead slip in first major quarterfinal

Frances Tiafoe has cut short his celebration to console friendly rival Alex Michelsen after coming back from two sets down to reach the US Open semifinals for the third time.

Frances Tiafoe assured a distraught Alex Michelsen that he would be back. (Getty Images: Sarah Stier)

The 11th seed recovered time and time again to beat Michelsen 5-7, ​3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6(10/6) and end the 22-year-old's first trip past the second round at his home slam.

Unseeded world number 46 Michelsen, whose previous best at a grand slam was a fourth-round berth at the 2025 Australian Open, was up a break in the third set and served for the match at 5-4 but Tiafoe won seven straight games to stay alive and take a commanding lead in the fourth frame.

Michelsen refused to go away though, taking a 3-0 in the decider, only for Tiafoe to once again storm back and take the set in a 10-point tiebreak.

After drilling a forehand passing shot down the line to secure the win after four hours and 38 minutes, Tiafoe began to celebrate his great escape before cutting his elation short to embrace his compatriot, who cried into his shoulder.

"As soon as I hugged him I saw he was crying already," Tiafoe told ESPN.

"I was like 'Man I know. I've been there twice, lost in five.' … He's young and he hasn't been there.

"We're super tight. We've always had a great relationship. We laugh and joke all the time. He's one of my good buddies on tour.

"I know how much that hurts. I know how much he wanted that today. It's something that you dream about.

"I just told him, 'You're going to be here so many more times, man. And I'm going to be in a rocking chair when you do.'"

Tiafoe appeared to have lost all the magic of his early campaign before ​wresting the momentum in ‌the third set and clinching it with a forehand winner to the deafening cheers of the fans at Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Michelsen had flown under the radar in his deepest major run but ‌he earned respect on the biggest stage of American tennis with 21 aces and 55 winners against Tiafoe, although he counted the cost of 61 unforced errors in the marathon match.

"I slowly, slowly started ​getting my rhythm there," ‌said Tiafoe, who will next play either eighth seed Ben Shelton or defending champion Carlos Alcaraz.

"He's a hell of a player. I mean, he easily could have won today."

Michelsen said after his fourth-round victory that he had improved and would try to change things, but was glad to have shared the court with a friend.

"I was trying to keep it together and I didn't do a good job of that," Michelsen said.

"He's also an unbelievable guy and a very good friend of mine," he added.

Michelsen left the court with a towel on his head, raising his arm to acknowledge the cheers from the crowd.

World.title: How Ned overcame a decade of pain to return to running
World.content:
The doubts that occasionally flit across Ned Buckell's mind are likely to be familiar to runners whatever standard they're at.

Buckell's story is different to most, though.

A life-threatening infection as a teenager.

A year-and-a-half on crutches.

Another serious infection just when it felt like things were on track, resulting in a hip replacement before he was 21.

And a race number from the 2016 Melbourne Marathon Festival pinned to his wall, reminding him that there is still a destination to reach despite the darkness.

"There's definitely been times when you think to yourself, what am I doing this for?" Buckell tells ABC Sport.

"Why am I still trying to get back running at a reasonably high level?

"I think the biggest thing is because I knew I would do it.

"Those thoughts always creep into my mind like, 'Why am I still going? You're not going to get the most out of it,' but I can get the most out of what I can, and I've always told myself I can.

"That's probably why I haven't given up.

"Even though there've been countless times when you want to, when you keep getting struck down, there are signs, and the universe is telling you to stop.

"You have to just sort of not ignore them, but just push them aside and prove that it's not."

'If it had gone any further, then that would have been the end of me'

Running was Ned Buckell's life. After his injury and illness, it still is. (Supplied: 2045)

Buckell was always going to be a runner.

His dad, John, was a runner and both Ned and his twin brother, Matt, would tag along to cross-country races around Bendigo and run from the age of five.

Theirs was an early introduction to the lung-busting freedom that a pair of trainers and the open trails of the countryside can afford.

"Me, my twin brother and my two older brothers were all always very competitive," Buckell says.

"That turned us into sporty individuals that always want to be better than each other.

"I've always been a runner, but it wasn't until maybe 14 or maybe 13 where I quit footy and was trying to focus on it a bit more.

"I knew me and my brother had some sort of talent, that we could take it to the next level.

"My twin brother has done that, but I haven't. I've just been struck down with this, really."

Sometimes you have to really love running to get up in the freezing cold of winter. (Supplied: 2045)

Buckell's issues all stem back to an infection he got when he was 14 years old, just after he turned to running seriously.

"The night it all happened, I was playing basketball with my mates at his house," Buckell recalls.

"It was a warm September night, the boys were in shorts and T-shirts, and I was in trackies and a hoodie, I was getting these fevers.

"We were all thinking that something's not right, so I rode home with Matt and then the fevers got really bad."

Buckell's parents were away, so it was up to his Nan and Pop to take him to the local GP, who initially diagnosed a twisting hernia, with Buckell struggling to stand due to the pain.

The GP sent Ned to a specialist, who instantly transferred him to the emergency department, where the scale of Buckell's issue became terrifyingly clear.

A staph infection had entered Ned's hip, driving up his temperature to dangerous levels.

"I ended up getting four hip washouts; three in Bendigo, which had no effect, basically, and then they sent me to the Royal Children's Hospital for another one," Buckell says.

The then-14-year-old spent the next three-and-a-half weeks in hospital, fortunate to be alive.

"I was on the cardiac ward because the infection had spread to my heart," Buckell explains.

"If it had gone any further, then that would have been the end of me.

"I never realised how severe it was, probably until now that I've finished my degree."

'Sometimes it's impossible to see that light'

Ned Buckell says the support of his family was essential. (Supplied: 2045)

Ned was discharged from hospital just in time to celebrate his 15th birthday.

It was a bittersweet moment.

The teenager spent the next 18 months on crutches, "torture" for a kid who described himself as "one of the most active that you'd meet".

"There were times that I, you know, I'm very lucky that I've had a supportive family," Ned says, understandably struggling to find the words to recall what had been a horrendous time.

"If I hadn't had that support around me, I definitely wouldn't be here today.

"There were times when you just wanted a way out.

"I knew that I couldn't do that, but watching all my brothers start work, play their sports … I was never jealous, but I was so sad all the time about missing out.

"It was extremely tough. You wouldn't wish that upon anyone, really."

Buckell says he gets goosebumps talking about this period of his life, underlining what a tough topic it is to address even 10 years on.

But despite all the darkness, Ned says that he always kept an optimistic mindset, something which he knows helped him a lot.

"It has been pretty important just to try to find the good in things," Buckell says.

"It's a hard topic for me to talk about, but it's something that I've acknowledged, and I'm just grateful to be where I'm at right now, to be honest.

"I know everyone battles their own shit, and I think the way I've looked at it all is there's always a light at the end of the tunnel.

"And sometimes it's impossible to see that light. And sometimes it's not there.

"But you just have to keep going forward and pushing through.

"It's hard, but I think talking about it does help me try to word things a little bit better."

Running is 'just something I do'

Ned Buckell has had to deal with serious illness and a traumatic injury, but has found peace in running. (Supplied: 2045)

The positivity was tested in 2022 when, having fought his way back to a high level, running 14:42 at the Bendigo 5km Frenzy to break a local under-20 record, his hip started playing up again.

He was diagnosed with avascular necrosis, the death of bone tissue due to a lack of blood flow.

Surgery couldn't fix it, leading to a hip replacement and yet more time watching the rest of the world run away from him.

"I think it comes from within," Buckell says of his perseverance.

"It's something inside of me that hasn't allowed me to give up at all, me knowing that I'm capable of more."

Buckell can sometimes forget that he has a new hip as he runs, finding the same freedom that he had as a child chasing his two older brothers and his twin.

He describes the hip replacement as being "life-changing".

The reminders that things are different come afterwards, when the muscles that had to be so violently contorted to insert the new joint begin to ache.

But that's not enough to stop him.

"I feel like I don't reflect enough on it afterwards," Buckell says of his relationship with running now.

"I did a race the other week, and I won it, and people like my Nan and Pop cried to me on the phone and told me how proud they are, and I forget to realise everything that I've been through.

"I really do have to reflect deeply on how much I've actually endured and overcome. But for me, it's just like something that you do without thinking about it."

Perhaps running is just a part of him?

"It is, yeah," Buckell says.

"And I don't need to over complicate it more than that. It's just something I do, really.

"But I do have to look back and think of how lucky I actually am, to be more offline and running at the level I am because I was told that it was going to be impossible."

Ned Buckell's race number from a decade before has helped spur him on. (Supplied: 2045)

In October, he will prove that impossible is just a word, lining up at the Melbourne Marathon once more, this time in the 5km race.

The race number that he wore the last time he ran the Melbourne streets as a teenager, just before the universe hit pause on his ambitions, is still stuck to the wall of his childhood bedroom.

"I probably won't actually ever realise how big it has impacted me," Buckell says.

"It was kept there as a reminder that I've got work to do to get back to where I want to be.

"And for a while it sort of just stayed there, and it didn't leave. And I was like, yeah, this is my constant reminder that things don't go your way, but I can get back to what I want to do.

"I feel like I've been working so hard for so long, and you just keep getting shit thrown at you, but honestly, I'm confident enough to say that this is sort of the end of it and I can actually test myself now."

World.title: LIV Golf players used to 'turbulence' as league files for bankruptcy
World.content:
LIV Golf has filed for bankruptcy in New Jersey, saying it intends to restructure its business with a $US49.6 million ($68.7 million) bankruptcy loan provided by the Public Investment Fund (PIF) of Saudi Arabia.

The company has between $US500 million and $US1 billion in liabilities and between $US100 million and $US500 ‌million in assets, according to its Chapter 11 petition.

LIV Golf said the bankruptcy will allow it to move forward with the support of a new backer, BC Partners Advisors ‌LP, and transition to a player-first ownership model.

BC Partners and other ⁠potential minority investors are expected to provide exit financing and ‌sponsor the company's debt restructuring, LIV Golf said.

LIV has been ‌preparing for its next iteration ever since the PIF said in April that further investment in the rebel circuit no longer aligned with its strategy and that it would cut funding at the close of the 2026 season.

PIF owns 100 per cent of LIV Golf's equity, according to its bankruptcy petition.

McIlroy fires shot at returning LIV Golf stars Masters champion Rory McIlroy says LIV Golf players who want to return to the PGA Tour face a tough road ahead.

The PIF has invested more than $US5 billion in LIV Golf since its ⁠launch in 2022 and the breakaway circuit ‌used massive signing bonuses to ‌poach big-name players from the PGA Tour like Australian Cameron Smith, Bryson DeChambeau, Jon Rahm and Dustin ‌Johnson.

Rahm, DeChambeau and Johnson are the company's top three unsecured creditors, according to the petition. Each is owed more than $US5 million.

Speaking in the build-up to the Irish Open, before news of the Chapter 11 petition broke, Rahm was asked if he knew what the future held.

"Yes and no, it hasn't really changed from my last interview in Indianapolis a few weeks ago," the two-time major winner said.

"And there's just a lot of things in place, right? There's a lot of things that could happen, and it's one of those things where time's gonna tell.

"To be fair for us, people that joined LIV, I'm pretty good at dealing with turbulence.''

LIV ‌Golf said bankruptcy is ⁠meant to keep the league in business while transitioning to an innovative player-first ownership model. The company hopes to exit from bankruptcy by early 2027.

"We believe deeply in LIV Golf's future, the opportunity in front of ⁠us, and the people who will help us realise it," LIV Golf chief executive Scott O'Neil said in ‌a statement.

The ‌professional men's golf league laid off most of its workforce in August, while it worked to secure new funding.
